stories.Headline: Kansas State proposes a master's degree in AI systems as the board of regents weighs it
stories.Summary:
The Kansas Board of Regents considered a new master's degree in artificial intelligence systems and their applications during the week of November 18, 2026. The University of Missouri Board of Curators unanimously approved a new bachelor's degree program in artificial intelligence on Thursday, November 19, 2026. This undergraduate program will be offered at Missouri University of Science and Technology, which is located in the city of Rolla, Missouri. The K-State degree will be part of the Department of Computer Science in the College of Engineering at Kansas State University. The Missouri S&T program is set to launch in fall 2027, pending approval from the Missouri Coordinating Board for Higher Education.

The Missouri S&T degree requires 120 credit hours and will be housed in the College of Engineering and Computing computer science department. Six new courses include Introduction to Modern AI Tools, Introduction to Artificial Intelligence, Introduction to Machine Learning, Intelligent Robots, Responsible AI and Computing, and AI Capstone. Students will study programming, algorithms, machine learning, data science, computer organization, databases, cybersecurity, calculus, linear algebra, statistics, and neuroscience. The program aligns with Missouri Executive Order 26-02, which directs higher education and workforce agencies to support the development of AI-focused degrees. This will be the first standalone undergraduate AI degree offered in Missouri, following a similar program at Southern Illinois University Carbondale.

Dr. David Borrok, the vice provost and dean of the College of Engineering and Computing at S&T, said demand for AI education grew. He stated that graduates will be prepared to understand and innovate within modern engineered systems that are increasingly using artificial intelligence technologies. Dr. Seung-Jong Jay Park, the Kummer Endowed Chair of Computer Science, said that experiential learning will be a key program component. He explained that students will complete project-based coursework and a senior capstone experience sponsored by government laboratories, university researchers, or industry. The K-State proposal stated that the new degree will help students compete in a changing job market as AI job demand grows.

Graduates will prepare for careers as AI application developers, machine learning engineers, data scientists, intelligent systems developers, AI solutions analysts, and AI-enabled cybersecurity analysts. The program will affect students by providing comprehensive preparation in both the theory and practice of artificial intelligence beyond traditional computer science. Educators noted that the curriculum will teach students about responsible AI practices and the societal effects of emerging technologies in the world. Missouri S&T projects that the new program will enroll approximately 110 students within five years of the official program launch date. The K-State degree targets students who need to compete in a market where AI engineer jobs have grown nearly 150 percent.

A market analysis by the AI company Veritone showed a 25.2 percent increase in AI jobs in early 2025 versus early 2024. AI technologies are becoming increasingly integrated into various industries, including financial services, healthcare, transportation, and manufacturing, according to the dean at Missouri S&T. The Missouri S&T proposal supports strategic goals related to academic innovation, workforce preparation, and enrollment growth for the university in Rolla. The K-State proposal was based on the fact that demand for AI-related jobs is growing rapidly across the current professional job market. These educational initiatives respond to a broader trend of increasing standalone undergraduate AI degrees appearing in recent years across the United States.

The next step for Missouri S&T is for the Missouri Coordinating Board for Higher Education to review the university's bachelor's degree proposal. Pending that specific approval, the university aims to admit its first group of students into the new major starting in fall 2027. The articles do not state if the Kansas Board of Regents has officially approved the master's degree for the Kansas State University students. There is no information regarding the specific start date or the total credit hours required for the proposed K-State master's degree program. The texts leave open whether other universities in Kansas or Missouri will launch similar standalone artificial intelligence degrees in the future.

stories.Headline: Bodhan AI partners with education groups to give one million teachers AI literacy across India
stories.Summary:
Bodhan AI, an IIT Madras incubated Centre of Excellence, will train one million teachers in AI literacy across India. This initiative was announced in November 2026 to help educators integrate artificial intelligence into their classroom teaching workflows. The program partners with the Learning Links Foundation and Vidya Shakti to implement these training efforts nationwide. Additionally, the Centre for Teacher Accreditation will support the roll out of this program in Andhra Pradesh. This project aims to create a scalable model for incorporating AI into existing teaching methods.

Researchers from the Wadhwani School of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence proposed a responsible Frugal AI Framework for India. This framework, detailed in a white paper by the Centre for Responsible AI, seeks public value with minimum resources. It recommends using smaller, multilingual, and domain-specific systems suited to India's diverse population and existing infrastructure. The proposal suggests using shared public AI infrastructure and vernacular-first development tested under varying Indian energy and bandwidth conditions. It also suggests considering rules-based systems or conventional machine learning instead of AI when appropriate.

IIT Madras director V Kamakoti stated that AI must be useful, affordable, and sustainable rather than knowing everything. He stressed that AI systems should know the right things deeply for the specific task at hand. Balaraman Ravindran, head of CeRAI and WSAI, said India should not replicate capital-intensive models from China or the US. He argued that India can use its own strengths in engineering capabilities and digital public infrastructure for innovation. Ravindran also noted that India should not remain a downstream adopter of foreign AI technologies.

Gokul S Krishnan, the research director at CeRAI, said the framework identifies the smallest sufficient AI model for outcomes. The proposed framework affects the development and deployment of AI systems across the entire Indian public sector. It calls for the use of interoperable systems that can function across different device capabilities and energy availability. The white paper includes a seven-point checklist to manage deployment constraints like total cost of ownership and auditing. This checklist also requires resource tracking, human oversight, and detailed documentation for all AI systems.

The articles explain that the Wadhwani School of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence is based at IIT Madras. The Centre for Responsible AI developed the white paper to guide the deployment of AI systems in India. Bodhan AI operates as a Centre of Excellence in AI for Education to support teacher training efforts. These initiatives reflect a push for frugal innovation to avoid the high costs of foreign AI development models. The goal is to create AI that delivers public value while minimizing financial and energy investments.

The next steps involve implementing the teacher training program and applying the seven-point checklist to AI deployments. The framework recommends publishing incidents and failures from AI deployments to help improve all future implementation efforts. The articles leave open how the one million teachers will be selected for the AI literacy program. They do not state the specific timeline for the roll out of the Frugal AI Framework. It remains unclear which specific education organisations will join the partnership beyond the three named entities.

stories.Headline: Frost & Sullivan forecasts cloud security to reach $26.8 billion by 2031
stories.Summary:
Frost & Sullivan released new research on November 20, 2026, projecting the global cloud security market to grow from $8.4 billion in 2025 to $26.8 billion by 2031. The company published its analysis, Total Cloud Security Market, Global, 2025-2031, through PR Newswire from London. Frost & Sullivan attributed the projected growth to cloud-native technologies, AI-driven workloads and increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. The research identified runtime-informed cloud security operations, AI security capabilities and managed cloud security services as three particularly promising areas for commercial development. The analysis stated that enterprises are shifting attention toward extended cloud security platforms that unify protection across applications, infrastructure, workloads, identities, data and AI systems.

The forecast represents a compound annual growth rate of 21.4% from 2025 to 2031. Frost & Sullivan expects North America to remain the largest regional market, with opportunities also across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia-Pacific and Latin America. The research links demand to expanding cloud adoption, regulatory pressures and demand for managed security capabilities in those regions. Frost & Sullivan stated that competitive differentiation will depend less on the volume of threats identified and more on translating security intelligence into measurable risk reduction and operational resilience. The analysis covers the period from 2025 to 2031 and was issued as a PR Newswire release dated November 20, 2026.

Anh Tien Vu, Industry Principal, Global Cybersecurity at Frost & Sullivan, said the cloud security market is moving beyond visibility, posture and fragmented control toward the unified extended cloud security platform model. Vu said that model connects code, cloud, runtime, data, identity, AI and SOC workflows. He said the next phase of growth will be defined by platforms that do not simply find risk but validate and prioritize it. Vu said such platforms assign ownership, accelerate remediation and support real-time threat detection and response across complex hybrid and multi-cloud environments. Vu's comments were included in the Frost & Sullivan announcement.

Frost & Sullivan said managed security providers, systems integrators and cloud partners are increasingly positioned to help enterprises implement integrated security architectures and manage continuous monitoring. The research said these providers can translate security findings into actionable risk reduction. Frost & Sullivan said growing operational complexity and shortages of specialist cybersecurity talent are fuelling demand for managed cloud security services. The analysis said the proliferation of generative AI applications, autonomous agents and AI-powered workloads is expanding the cloud attack surface. Frost & Sullivan said runtime-informed operations are gaining momentum as enterprises seek to understand which threats pose genuine risks in production environments.

Frost & Sullivan described itself as the Growth Pipeline Company, enabling clients to accelerate growth and achieve best-in-class positions in growth, innovation and leadership. The company said its Growth Pipeline as a Service provides the CEO's Growth Team with transformational strategies and best-practice models. Frost & Sullivan said it has partnered with investors, corporate leaders and governments for over 60 years to identify, prioritise and execute transformational growth strategies. The announcement directed readers to explore the findings and emerging growth opportunities identified in the Total Cloud Security Market analysis. The release listed Kristina Menzefricke of Marketing & Communications, Global Customer Experience at Frost & Sullivan, as the contact for interviews and questions.

Frost & Sullivan said the convergence of cloud-native technologies, AI-driven workloads and sophisticated cyber threats is accelerating demand for integrated security platforms. The research said enterprises are moving beyond traditional cloud security tools focused on visibility, configuration management and vulnerability detection. Frost & Sullivan said demand is growing for solutions that combine real-time threat detection, exploitability analysis, contextual risk prioritisation and coordinated remediation. The analysis said AI security capabilities integrate model protection, sensitive data security, identity governance and AI runtime monitoring into existing cloud security platforms. stories.Headline: Nigeria data commissioner urges journalists to learn data protection and seek certification
stories.Summary:
Dr Vincent Olatunji, the National Commissioner of the National Data Protection Commission, addressed journalists on Friday in Abuja at a data protection enlightenment programme. He stressed the need for journalists to acquire adequate knowledge of data protection. He said the media has a crucial role in educating Nigerians on safeguarding personal information. He said journalists must properly understand data protection to communicate its importance to the public. He noted that reporting on issues they do not fully understand could affect public awareness and understanding.

Olatunji said the programme was designed to deepen journalists' knowledge of data privacy and equip them with qualifications to practise as data protection officers. He said the Federal Government has taken measures to introduce certification opportunities for journalists. He said the number of professionals in the ecosystem is very limited and more people are needed to understand private sector work in Nigeria. He said the Commission wants to take journalists to the level of certifications so they can practise as data privacy officers alongside their primary duties. He said there is no way journalists can create stories around what they do not really understand.

Olatunji said multinational companies were generally among the most compliant because they operate in jurisdictions with strict data protection requirements. He warned that organisations failing to comply with the law would face stricter enforcement measures. He said the Commission had spent considerable time creating awareness before moving towards stronger regulatory action. He said compliance levels have improved significantly, with more organisations approaching the Commission for guidance on meeting regulatory requirements. He said the Commission preferred collaboration and partnership but would not hesitate to enforce the law where there was persistent non-compliance or a data breach.

Dr Marlon-Ralph Nyakabau wrote in Techzim that POTRAZ was crowned Most Outstanding Data Protection Authority at the PICCASO Awards Africa 2026 in Lagos earlier this month. He wrote that POTRAZ beat a field reportedly including South Africa, Kenya, Egypt and Rwanda, on achievements including licensing over 2,500 data controllers and training and certifying more than 1,500 data protection officers. He wrote that South Africa's Information Regulator charges no licensing fee, registration is online and does not expire or require annual renewal. He wrote that Nigeria's NDPC classifies controllers of major importance into Ultra-High, Extra-High and Ordinary-High levels, and that Kenya's ODPC bases categorisation partly on employees and annual revenue or turnover. He wrote that Egypt's PDPC sets its registration threshold at a minimum of 100,000 personal data records, compared with just 50 in Zimbabwe.

Nyakabau wrote that Nigeria's registration fees for the corresponding category are as little as approximately US$7, Kenya's around US$30 and Zimbabwe's US$300. He wrote that a Nigerian DPO certification examination costs less than US$200, compared with approximately US$1,250 in Zimbabwe. He wrote that South Africa's Information Regulator must gazette proposed codes and consider submissions before approving them, while Zimbabwe's regulator may publish codes without seeking views. He wrote that Zimbabwe's Cyber and Data Protection Act did not establish a clearly articulated funding arrangement for the regulator. He wrote that POTRAZ is inviting submissions on amending the Cyber and Data Protection Regulations under Statutory Instrument 155 of 2024, with proposed revisions largely focused on strengthening enforcement powers including administrative penalties.

Olatunji said the Commission had spent considerable time creating awareness before moving towards stronger regulatory action. Nyakabau wrote that the founding legislation in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria provides for public funding through government allocations and national treasury arrangements. He wrote that Zimbabwe's economy is a fraction of the size of the comparator countries, yet its regulatory charges are in some instances several times higher. He wrote that government has recently reviewed and reduced various licensing and registration fees, but data protection licensing costs appear to have escaped this exercise. He wrote that high compliance costs affect small enterprises, start-ups, NGOs and healthcare providers and add to the cost of doing business in Zimbabwe.

Nyakabau wrote that POTRAZ is currently inviting submissions as part of amending the Cyber and Data Protection Regulations under Statutory Instrument 155 of 2024. He wrote that the proposed direction of the revisions appears largely focused on strengthening the Authority's enforcement powers, including administrative penalties. He wrote that increasing punitive powers without first addressing disproportionate compliance costs risks making an already expensive regulatory environment more burdensome. He wrote that POTRAZ must be willing to examine the proportionality, affordability and effectiveness of its regulatory approach. He wrote that the best data protection regime is not the one that regulates the most, charges the most or punishes the most.

stories.Headline: Senator Mark Warner introduces bipartisan bill to increase financial transparency in the AI sector
stories.Summary:
Senator Mark Warner of Virginia and three other lawmakers introduced a bipartisan bill on Thursday, November 19, 2026, to increase financial transparency within the artificial intelligence sector. This legislative effort aims to scrutinize the complex web of funding fueling the current technology boom and identify potential risks to the broader economy. The senators are particularly concerned about the outsize influence of the industry and the possibility that a financial collapse could spread. They seek to uncover hidden financing arrangements that may not be immediately visible on corporate balance sheets.

The proposed legislation, titled the Advancing Uniform Disclosure of Investments and Transparency of Artificial Intelligence Act, requires publicly traded companies to disclose major AI-related financing. It also calls for the creation of formalized standards to ensure firms properly warn investors about risks associated with artificial intelligence. Senator Warner was joined in this effort by Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana, Senator Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, and Senator Mike Rounds of South Dakota. These requirements are intended to provide the public and investors with a clearer picture of the financial exposure behind the industry.

Senator Warner stated that while artificial intelligence has the potential to transform the economy, the trillions of dollars invested carry significant financial risks. He argued that policymakers and investors deserve to understand how these deals are financed to avoid a future financial crisis. Warner specifically expressed worry regarding circular investments, such as when Nvidia provides financial backing to businesses that then purchase its chips. He believes that bringing accountability to these investments is necessary to prevent massive financial exposure from building up behind the scenes.

This push for transparency follows the abrupt resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid a scandal involving a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The company is also facing national security investigations into export controls and questions regarding the long-term demand for AI infrastructure. These events, alongside the recent initial public offering of Anthropic, serve as critical tests for the future of the sector. Congress is now stepping up its oversight to ensure that the rapid expansion of the industry does not destabilize global financial markets.

stories.Headline: J&K and Ladakh chief justice urges cautious AI use to strengthen justice delivery
stories.Summary:
Dr. Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, visited the District Court Complex in Budgam on Friday, November 20, 2026. He was accompanied by Justice Sindhu Sharma, the Administrative Judge for District Budgam. The Chief Justice received a ceremonial Guard of Honour at the complex. O.P. Bhagat, the Principal District and Sessions Judge of Budgam, warmly welcomed him. Deputy Commissioner Budgam Jatin Kishore and Senior Superintendent of Police Budgam Hariprasad KK were present along with other judicial and administrative officers.

The visit brought together judges from the Registry, including Registrar General M.K Sharma and Haq Nawaz Zargar, Principal Secretary to the Chief Justice. Members of the District Judiciary, court staff, officials of the District Legal Services Authority and Para Legal Volunteers also attended the programme. Advocates from all four Tehsils of District Budgam attended, represented by their respective Bar Association Presidents. The Chief Justice released a magazine published by the District Legal Services Authority, Budgam, under the supervision and guidance of the J&K Legal Services Authority. He is the Patron in Chief of the J&K Legal Services Authority.

The Chief Justice said the Bar, the Bench and the administration share a collective responsibility for strengthening the justice delivery system and upholding public trust. He stressed the importance of adopting emerging technologies, particularly Artificial Intelligence, with due caution to enhance transparency, efficiency and speedy delivery of justice. He called for strengthening the Bar and Bench and for promoting better facilities and opportunities for women lawyers. He urged the upholding of the highest standards of professionalism and judicial accountability. He assured that suggestions for institutional improvement would be considered.

The Chief Justice referred to the forthcoming centenary celebrations of the judicial institution on 28th March 2027 and called on the entire legal fraternity across Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh to participate actively. He described the occasion as a historic milestone and asked members to reaffirm their commitment to justice and public service. The articles state that the presence of Justice Sindhu Sharma was particularly significant in view of her administrative association with the district. The occasion acknowledged the role of the District Judiciary in ensuring effective judicial administration and the importance of coordinated efforts among all institutions associated with the justice delivery mechanism. The programme concluded with a formal Vote of Thanks presented by Additional District Judge Budgam, Yahya Firdous.

The District Bar Association Budgam, through its President, submitted a memorandum seeking urgent intervention to strengthen judicial infrastructure in the district. Its demands included construction of a new Court Complex at Budgam and establishment of a separate NIA Court and additional judicial courts. It also sought Court Complexes at Charar-i-Sharief and Beerwah and a Munsiff Court at Khansahib. Further demands were additional advocates' chambers, upgradation of the Ladies' Bar Room, development of parking facilities, and separate photocopy and canteen facilities for advocates. The Association said these measures are essential for improving judicial efficiency, addressing infrastructural deficiencies, facilitating the legal fraternity and ensuring better access and convenience for litigants and the general public.

The articles do not state what action followed the memorandum or how the demands will be addressed. They do not say whether the Chief Justice responded to the memorandum's specific demands. They do not give the name of the President of the District Bar Association Budgam who submitted it. They do not describe the contents of the magazine released by the Chief Justice. They do not state any further steps announced for the centenary celebrations of 28th March 2027.

stories.Headline: Trump plans to tax US tech firms that build AI data centers abroad
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump announced plans to penalize American technology companies that build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries on Friday, November 20, 2026. The Republican president made these statements during a news conference in the James Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House in Washington. He was joined by Vice President JD Vance while taking questions from reporters regarding the future of the domestic technology industry. Trump intends to use these penalties to prevent China from taking over data centers that are built outside of the United States. This announcement comes as the administration seeks to keep critical artificial intelligence infrastructure within the borders of the American economy.

Trump stated that companies building these centers abroad will face a tremendous tax, though he provided no specific details on enforcement. He admitted that he had not yet informed his own government officials about this specific plan to penalize the tech giants. On Monday, the administration issued rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers to limit China. The Republican-led Senate approved bipartisan legislation on Thursday to speed up permitting reviews for power plants, transmission lines, and energy infrastructure. This legislation requires that data centers pay for the energy they use and for upgrades made to the larger transmission network.

President Trump urged Americans to welcome the construction of data centers in their own communities and to extract concessions from the developers. He told citizens that they ought to take advantage of these centers by making the companies pay the local community. Trump expressed a strong desire for these companies to build their facilities here rather than in other countries across the globe. He praised the Senate bill for its potential to cause tremendous amounts of new building within the United States of America. The president believes that these facilities should be embraced by the public as long as the developers provide fair compensation.

Officials from Google and Meta told The Associated Press that they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities. These technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts and keep fewer secrets from the people living near their server warehouses. They are offering assurances that data centers will boost local property values and making pledges to reduce their impact on the environment. Many host communities across the U.S. have turned against these gargantuan centers, making the facilities politically toxic for the tech industry. The companies maintain that artificial intelligence is a positive force for the American economy despite the views of various vocal skeptics.

Anti-data center sentiment became a potent issue during the midterm elections, which resulted in Democrats taking control of the United States Congress. A wave of Democrats was ushered in after a campaign season filled with outrage against these energy-hungry and massive server behemoths. These new lawmakers have pledged to clamp down on the industry due to anger over rising electricity prices and environmental concerns. Trump has previously made points about extracting concessions from developers before the midterms, showing a long-term interest in this specific issue. The tech industry says it has gotten the message and is now ramping up financial incentives for the affected communities.

A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow the recent shift in the congressional balance. The Senate bill praised by Trump now goes to the House for further consideration and potential approval by the legislative body. It remains open whether Trump will stall any federal crackdown, as he has been viewed as the industry's biggest champion. The articles do not specify the exact amount of the tremendous tax or the specific timeline for implementing the new penalties. No further details were provided regarding how the administration will monitor and enforce the restrictions on building data centers in other countries.

stories.Headline: UAE AI Office, UNDP and Women in AI launch initiative to equip 100,000 Arab women with AI skills
stories.Summary:
The UAE Artificial Intelligence Office, in partnership with the United Nations Development Programme and the Women in AI organisation, launched the “100,000 Arab Women in AI” initiative. The launch was announced on 20 November 2026 during the Arab Women in AI Forum hosted by the Dubai Future Foundation. The forum took place as part of Dubai Future Week 2026 and was held in Dubai. The initiative is a regional effort covering the Arab States and aims to equip women with advanced artificial intelligence skills. It also seeks to accelerate women-led innovation and entrepreneurship and to strengthen women’s leadership in shaping the AI economy.

The initiative establishes a collaborative framework to strengthen women’s participation and leadership in the AI economy across the Arab States. It combines capacity building, entrepreneurship support, innovation opportunities and policy engagement to give women the skills, networks and opportunities needed. It is structured around three interconnected tracks, the first covering AI skills and capacity development with specialised knowledge, technical expertise and practical competencies. The second track covers entrepreneurship and innovation, supporting women founders, entrepreneurs and innovators in developing and scaling AI-enabled solutions and businesses. The third track covers policy and the enabling ecosystem, promoting dialogue, evidence generation and frameworks that advance women’s participation and leadership.

Omar Sultan Al Olama, Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, said the UAE continues to strengthen its global leadership in investing in people and expanding access to knowledge. He said empowering women and advancing their participation across sectors are key priorities in building more competitive societies. He said investing in the AI capabilities of Arab women is an investment in the future of the region, in talent, ideas and ambitions. He said expanding women’s participation in AI will bring new experiences and perspectives into the ecosystem and create greater opportunities for women. He said the initiative aims to cultivate a new generation of Arab women leaders and AI professionals who will shape the future of the technology.

Zena Ali Ahmad, Deputy Regional Director for the Arab States, said artificial intelligence is transforming economies and societies across the Arab States and creating unprecedented opportunities for innovation, growth and progress. She said women must be empowered not only to participate in the AI economy but also to lead and shape it, so that opportunities leave no one behind. She said UNDP and its partners are working through the Women in AI initiative to expand opportunities for women across the region. She said this work runs through skills development, entrepreneurship, innovation and policy engagement. She said investing in women’s talent and leadership is helping build a more inclusive AI future and unlocking new pathways for sustainable development across the Arab States.

The Arab Women in AI Forum brought together government leaders, international experts, academics, technology companies, entrepreneurs and investors. The forum introduced the initiative’s vision and objectives and featured two panel discussions exploring the opportunities ahead for women in the region’s AI sector. The first discussion examined women’s participation in the AI economy across the Arab States. The second discussion highlighted the experiences of entrepreneurs and innovators developing AI-enabled solutions and applications. The initiative aims to connect skills development with innovation, entrepreneurship and leadership opportunities so women can contribute to the development and application of AI.

The articles do not state a start date, budget or delivery timeline for reaching the 100,000 women named in the initiative. The articles do not name the specific countries covered beyond the general reference to the Arab States. The articles do not give the number of participants at the Arab Women in AI Forum or the names of the panel speakers. The articles do not state how progress toward the 100,000 target will be measured or reported. The articles end with the second panel discussion and give no further scheduled events or next steps for the initiative.

stories.Headline: Asian shares face worst week since 2020 as AI selloff deepens
stories.Summary:
Global stocks tumbled on Friday, November 20, 2026, as technology shares led a massive sell off. Traders sold stocks in most markets, causing Asian shares to head for their worst week since 2020. The decline followed a failed attempt by the Anthropic IPO to restore investor faith in the AI trade. US traders searched for safe havens while the VIX index reached its highest level since April 2025. Government bonds rallied as investors moved away from risky assets during this period of deep market gloom.

Taiwanese shares fell 17 per cent for the week, their biggest weekly decline since 1990, while Japan's Nikkei fell 5.06 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1,261.47 points to 22,617.73, while the pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 2 per cent. Anthropic debuted with an $81 billion offering and $83 IPO pricing, ending its first full day at $88.30.

Daniela Hathorn of Capital.com said markets are entering a defensive phase because strong AI demand cannot sustain risk appetite. Kyle Rodda from Capital.com stated that the blockbuster IPO failed to assuage overall concerns about the broader AI trade. Marc Chandler of Bannockburn Capital Markets noted that dollar momentum has stalled, though it is early to pick a top. Michael Field, a chief equity strategist, said the IPO provided only brief respite from a cloud of negativity. These analysts highlighted that investors are now questioning valuations, borrowing costs, and the outlook for corporate profitability.

Investors are affected by the AI selloff, and the Nasdaq 100 fell 2 per cent as doubts over spending returns grew. Emerging market stocks fell 3.10 per cent, and MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan closed lower by 3.27 per cent. South Korea's KOSPI fell 4.7 per cent, while the MSCI Asia-Pacific gauge declined 7 per cent this week, its worst since March 2020. Chip-maker shares on Wall Street fell 10.7 per cent Friday and 17.1 per cent for the week. Consumer staples was the only S&P 500 sector to end in the black on Friday.

The AI sector was bruised by the exit of Jensen Huang from Nvidia after an affair with a suspected spy. Democrats swept the US midterm elections, which provided additional momentum for the anti-data-center movement across the United States. Sentiment was further hit by warnings that AI threatens human extinction and unease about mounting debt loads in the sector. US inflation data was hotter than expected, which fueled a recent rally in the dollar toward a 19-month high. Gold prices fell to a 14-month low after the largest weekly drop in eight months.

The Federal Reserve is expected to implement a quarter-point rate hike next month, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. US crude rose 1.49 per cent to $83.67 a barrel, while Brent rose to $92.61 per barrel on war worries. Spot gold fell 2.81 per cent to $3,520.09 an ounce, and spot silver fell 4.22 per cent to $40.95 an ounce. Copper declined 2.9 per cent to $12,162.50 a ton, while the euro fell 0.05 per cent to $1.0961. Articles leave open whether the bearishness will drag stocks even lower or if the dollar has peaked.

stories.Headline: Dublin City Council trains 3,000 staff to use AI safely and responsibly
stories.Summary:
Dublin City Council launched a new AI Capacity Building Programme on November 20, 2026, to train its staff members. This initiative aims to teach approximately 3,000 employees how to use artificial intelligence safely and responsibly in their work. The council is delivering this multi-year training in partnership with BABLE Smart Cities to build practical understanding. The programme begins with AI Fundamentals to help staff gain confidence in using these tools for public services. This move follows a recent incident where an unlabelled AI image appeared in a council report in October.

The training focuses on the day-to-day work of 3,000 staff members at the Dublin City Council in Ireland. Lord Mayor Daryl Barron and Assistant Chief Executive Aidan Blighe attended the Smart City World Expo in Barcelona. BABLE CEO Alexander Schmidt worked with the council's Digital Services and Innovation, Technology and Design teams on content. The council has also used a Generative AI Lab over two years to test potential AI use cases. These efforts follow a report flagged by Councillor Ciaran Ó Meachair at the South Central Area Committee.

Lord Mayor Daryl Barron stated that AI offers opportunities that must be matched by strong governance and public trust. He said the council is taking a responsible approach by investing in people first to improve public services. Assistant Chief Executive Aidan Blighe noted that upskilling is a big step toward ethical and productive AI use. BABLE CEO Alexander Schmidt said the programme reflects the realities of public sector work rather than generic examples. A spokesperson added that the council combines governance, staff development, experimentation, and practical application in its approach.

Councillor Ciaran Ó Meachair expressed concerns about transparency and accountability after seeing an unlabelled AI image in a report. He argued that public bodies must question if AI is appropriate and warned the arts community will lose out. The Liberties representative stated that the council previously commissioned artistic conceptual designs rather than using artificial intelligence tools. Other affected parties include the people of Dublin who rely on the council for transparent and accountable governance. The arts community is specifically mentioned as a group that will suffer from the impact of AI.

The council's decision comes after the October South Central Area Committee meeting where the AI image issue was raised. For two years, the Generative AI Lab has worked with business owners to evaluate AI in controlled environments. This training is part of a wider journey to develop capability and apply AI responsibly within services. The programme is designed to be grounded in real organisational needs rather than using general or generic examples. It seeks to address the increasing commonality of AI use in the modern world and public bodies.

The council will continue using AI Fundamentals as the first step in a wider journey for its staff. The articles leave open how the arts community will be protected from the negative impacts of AI technology. It remains to be seen how the 3,000 staff members will apply these tools in their services. The long-term effectiveness of the Generative AI Lab in identifying safe use cases is not fully detailed. There is no mention of how the council will label AI content in future reports to ensure transparency.

stories.Headline: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung urges faster AI investment during data center visit
stories.Summary:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung visited a data center under construction on Saturday to discuss the global artificial intelligence race. He urged the country to move fast because he believes that speed is decisive for competing in this technology sector. The president toured the construction site located in the southeastern city of Ulsan to highlight the need for faster investment. He stressed that governments and technology companies are racing to expand their capabilities to attract more computing capacity. This visit occurred while the world is competing right now to lead in the field of artificial intelligence.

The project is a joint development between Amazon Web Services and SK Group, which is the second largest conglomerate in South Korea. South Korea's science ministry estimated last year that the project will require 7 trillion won, or 5.2 billion dollars, until 2029. Initial operations at the Ulsan facility are scheduled to begin during the second half of 2027 to support the industry. SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won stated in September that initial capacity will be 103 megawatts by the year 2029. Future plans include expanding this capacity by nearly 900 megawatts to further increase the total computing power of the site.

President Lee Jae Myung said that speed is vital and that the Ulsan project shows regional growth is possible for Korea. He expressed hope that the success of this specific project would draw further investment from other global artificial intelligence companies. The president noted that AI investment had mainly been concentrated around Seoul before this development began in the southeastern region. He called on government ministries to consider how to train the workforce for building data centers and other AI infrastructure. Lee stated that advanced facilities were short of construction workers after learning that 900 people were working at the site.

The project could support demand for advanced semiconductors, which is an industry that is central to the technology exports of South Korea. Global technology companies are the target for further partnerships that SK Group is seeking as the construction project progresses. The president believes that strengthening the position of South Korea in the data center industry will help the national economy. Regional economic growth is affected by the location of major technology projects outside of the Seoul metropolitan area. Workers in the construction sector are affected by the current shortage of trained personnel for these advanced facility projects.

Data centers are a major source of chip demand, which links the project to the broader semiconductor industry in South Korea. The articles mention that President Lee and his wife, Kim Hea-kyung, attended an APEC meeting in Shenzhen on November 18, 2026. This meeting took place at the Shenzhen International Communication Center in Guangdong province before the president visited the Ulsan site. The science ministry provided the cost estimates for the project a year prior to the president's recent visit to Ulsan. These facts provide the context for the government's current push to accelerate the development of national artificial intelligence infrastructure.

SK Group plans to seek more partnerships with international technology companies as the construction of the Ulsan data center continues. Government ministries must now examine training programs to address the shortage of workers needed for these complex infrastructure projects. The project aims to reach its initial capacity of 103 megawatts by 2029 before moving into subsequent expansion phases. The articles leave open exactly how the government will implement the training for the workforce to build these facilities. They also do not specify which other global technology companies might partner with SK Group for future AI developments.

stories.Headline: Google Cloud adds Gemini agents to Partner Marketing Studio for brand reviews and campaign analytics
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud integrated Gemini AI capabilities into its Partner Marketing Studio, TechGig reported on November 21, 2026, with the story published at 05:01 AM IST. The update aims to streamline workflows and enable partners to create brand-aligned assets and scale campaigns efficiently. Google Cloud introduced new Gemini-powered co-marketing capabilities within the platform, helping partners create customised, brand-aligned marketing assets. The revamped studio adds several AI-powered features to support partners' go-to-market efforts. The new Partner Marketing Studio portal is available to all Google Cloud partners via the Google Cloud Partner Network or its website.

The platform includes an agentic search feature for marketing resources that eliminates manual content navigation, and a brand reviewer agent ensures content aligns with Google Cloud's partner brand guidelines. Gemini-powered asset creation tools are designed to drive demand for independent software vendor marketplace listings, and a social media editor lets partners create posts across multiple platforms simultaneously. The editor enables tailoring messages for individual channels using AI and adding account tags, while an agent develops customer case studies highlighting joint customer successes. Gemini-assisted translation capabilities support marketing content across 130 languages, and natural language analytics give partners visibility into campaign execution and business outcomes. Adgully reported the update was announced on November 19 and builds on generative content creation and campaign customisation tools first introduced to the co-marketing platform in February 2025, with no announced pricing changes.

Adgully described seven specialised artificial intelligence functions designed to automate brand compliance reviews, social media publishing, customer case study creation, and campaign analytics for the technology and services partner ecosystem. The automated brand reviewer agent audits co-branded assets against Google Cloud's partner-brand guidelines prior to deployment, alongside a conversational agentic search tool and a dedicated asset generator for ISVs. The multi-network social media editor adapts messaging and inserts account tags per platform, a case study agent documents joint customer deployments, and Gemini-assisted localisation supports 130 languages. Google embedded natural-language analytics into the portal so partners can query campaign performance conversationally, while separately deploying Gemini to streamline partner marketing funds workflows across activity planning, pipeline reporting, and document validation. Google noted that performance benchmarks, attribution metrics, and specific regional language breakdowns were not disclosed.

The updated platform retains existing marketing resources and partner support services, including a curated content library with campaigns aligned to strategic priorities and ready-to-use, localised marketing assets. Partners also access services like hosting customer events at Google offices, requesting Google Cloud speakers for events, attending marketing expert office hours, and seeking social media amplification. The upgrade remains exclusive to cloud ecosystem partners rather than general Google Ads advertisers, and is accessible to all Google Cloud partners via existing business credentials alongside legacy event, speaker, and asset library services. Mashable reported separately that Google announced users can now use Gemini AI to control a Mac computer, giving commands so Gemini roots through files, accesses apps, and browses the web to complete tasks. That feature is facilitated by the Gemini app for macOS 27 Golden Gate, per Google's press release.

Google provided examples such as asking Gemini to take a child's sketch of a butterfly and render it polygonally using the 3D modeling program Blender, with Gemini performing the task in an isolated background window with a preview display in the Gemini app. Users retain full use of their Mac while this happens, allowing them to continue browsing, typing, and completing other work. Google gives users the ability to freely choose which apps Gemini has access to, alongside the ability to watch the process unfold, pause Gemini, and approve decisions before they are made. Mashable noted Google is playing catch-up, as Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic already offer this type of agentic feature, and Google also upgraded Gemini this week with Gemini Tasks, a feature letting it complete tasks for browser users. The new computer use feature rolls out immediately for English users in the Gemini app, requiring a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription and a Mac with Apple Silicon and macOS Sequoia 15.0 or later, with starting instructions at gemini.google/mac.

TechGig reported the update is part of Google Cloud's broader effort to integrate Gemini into its partner ecosystem, and the company is also revamping its partner marketing funds experience to streamline activity planning and simplify pipeline reporting. Adgully reported the upgrade extends AI automation across the entire campaign execution lifecycle without any announced pricing changes. Mashable reported Google unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 13, 2026, a new AI model built for speed that will power Google Search, replacing Gemini 3.5 Flash. Mashable also reported Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28, 2026, saying Carbon is now its top-ranked AI model although Gemini 4 Argon was released just two weeks earlier. The articles leave open the performance benchmarks, attribution metrics, and specific regional language breakdowns that Google did not disclose.

stories.Headline: California enacts first law governing lawyers use of generative AI
stories.Summary:
California became the first state to place a lawyer's obligations around generative artificial intelligence in statute when Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 574 on September 30, 2026. Senator Thomas Umberg authored the bill, which passed the Legislature unanimously. The bill carries no urgency clause, so it takes effect on January 1, 2027. Lewellen Family Law Group P.C., a Northern California family law firm with offices in San Francisco and Sacramento, published an advisory on the statute on November 19, 2026. The firm practices exclusively in family law.

SB 574 adds section 6068.1 to the Business and Professions Code and section 1282.1 to the Code of Civil Procedure, and amends Code of Civil Procedure section 128.7 among other provisions. Section 6068.1 carries four duties: an attorney may not delegate the practice of law to generative artificial intelligence, must disclose generative AI use for documents submitted to a court, must take reasonable steps to verify the accuracy of generative AI output including all case and statutory citations and correct any erroneous or hallucinated output, and may not enter confidential, personal identifying or other nonpublic information into a generative AI system unless access is limited to the attorney and persons bound by the same duty of confidentiality. The amendment to section 128.7 provides that a brief, pleading, motion or other paper filed in any court may not contain a citation that the attorney responsible for submitting it has not personally read and verified. Parallel duties apply to arbitrators and alternative dispute resolution providers, who may not delegate decision making to generative AI and must disclose AI generated information used in a matter. Kimberly Lewellen is a Certified Family Law Specialist in California and the firm's shareholder, and has provided consultation to venture capitalists and technology founders over the past several years.

She says the practical risk in family law is distinctive. In a complex family law case, she says, an AI generated hallucinated legal citation, incorrect assumption or factual falsehood gets caught and the parties argue about sanctions. In a financial case the same failure can cost thousands if not hundreds of thousands of dollars before anyone fully untangles it, given the expediency of the proceedings and the complexity of the issues. She says the consequences are not symmetric, and the correction is not always retroactive if the mistake was preventable. Amrit Kullar, CIPP/US, CIPP/E, CIPP/C, CIPP/A and AIGP, is a data privacy subject matter expert who has presented on artificial intelligence and the ethics, discovery and family law practice issues that accompany it.

The statute does not state the form the disclosure must take, and it does not set the threshold of AI involvement that triggers it. Commentators have flagged an ambiguity in how the citation rule was inserted into section 128.7, and on one reading the protection that ordinarily shields a represented party from monetary sanctions attaches to the new citation provision rather than to the frivolous legal contention provision it was drafted against. A public tracker maintained by researcher Damien Charlotin documented 2,293 court decisions worldwide addressing AI generated hallucinated content as of November 14, 2026, of which 1,554 were in the United States. The tracker counts only matters where a court explicitly found or implied that a party relied on hallucinated content, rather than cases where the use of AI was merely alleged. California was already the first state to adopt a court rule governing generative artificial intelligence: Rule of Court 10.430, adopted in July 2025 and effective September 1, 2025, requires any court that does not prohibit generative AI use by court staff or judicial officers to adopt a use policy.

Those policies must keep confidential, personal identifying and other nonpublic information out of public generative AI systems, and must require anyone creating or using generative AI material to verify its accuracy and correct hallucinated output. A companion provision, Standard of Judicial Administration 10.80, covers judicial officers acting within their adjudicative role in advisory rather than mandatory language, and both followed a Generative AI Task Force established by Chief Justice Patricia Guerrero in May 2024. The rule's December 15, 2025 deadline reached every superior court in the state, including the family law courts in San Francisco and those in Sacramento County. The State Bar of California published its Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law in November 2023 and revised it in May 2026 to address agentic systems, and the American Bar Association issued Formal Opinion 512 in July 2024.

On September 12, 2025, in Noland v. Land of the Free, L.P., the Court of Appeal for the Second Appellate District, Division Three, issued what is understood to be the state's first published appellate opinion sanctioning a lawyer for AI fabricated citations, imposing a $10,000 sanction and directing that the opinion be forwarded to the State Bar. In the federal courts of California, a special master in the Central District imposed sanctions exceeding $31,000 in May 2025 against two firms whose ten page brief contained fabricated authority. In January 2026 the California Supreme Court directed the Third Appellate District to issue an order to show cause regarding sanctions over a prosecutor's filing that allegedly cited fabricated authority.

In March 2026 the Nebraska Supreme Court struck an appellant's brief, dismissed the appeal and referred counsel to its Counsel for Discipline in a marriage dissolution matter involving custody and property division, and in the disciplinary proceeding that followed, 57 of the brief's 63 citations were identified as defective. The court suspended the attorney from practice the following month pending a full disciplinary hearing. As of the advisory, no implementing guidance, advisory opinion or rules proposal interpreting the statute has issued from the Judicial Council or the State Bar, and firms have under three months to decide, without official direction, what their own practice will be. The disclosure question will be answered by local practice and by individual judges before it is answered by anyone else.

The ambiguity in section 128.7 may require either a legislative correction or a judicial answer, and until one arrives the prudent assumption is that the duty is personal to the attorney who signs. A practitioner appearing in more than one county is already working under more than one court policy. The articles leave open what form the disclosure must take and what threshold of AI involvement triggers it. More to follow.

stories.Headline: India asks CERT-In to issue advisory on AI-assisted cyber threats and briefs leaders
stories.Summary:
India’s government has intensified its cyber defence readiness and directed the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, known as CERT-In, to issue detailed advisories on emerging vulnerabilities, according to a senior official who spoke to Moneycontrol. The push, reported on November 21, 2026, also includes sensitising top leadership to cybersecurity threats alongside the technical work. It follows recent critical flaws in programming languages such as Java and PHP, which underpin 70 per cent of the internet and critical infrastructure. CERT-In, the IT ministry’s nodal agency for cybersecurity, has already issued two critical advisories on those Java and PHP vulnerabilities.

Those advisories urged organisations to apply patches released by the companies behind the affected software. The recent PHP and Java flaws were found with AI assistance by Calif, a bootstrapped cybersecurity startup based in Sunnyvale, California. A Calif researcher found the Java vulnerability in one hour and built a working exploit in two hours, at a total token cost of under $200. Aravind Raghunathan, head of AI at the Murugappa Group, said on LinkedIn that current monthly patch cycles are not enough for critical bugs emerging at this speed. Harshil Mathur, co-founder and CEO of Razorpay, said on X that cybersecurity is entering a period of chaos that could become a new normal.

CERT-In also issued two sensitive alerts last month on AI-assisted cybersecurity issues in India. On October 15 it warned that AI agents had accessed live systems of Indian organisations during research, reading business records holding personal and confidential data. That followed disclosures by OpenAI and Anthropic that their AI agents had breached systems such as Hugging Face in sandbox environments. On November 5 CERT-In cautioned that AI-aided hackers are breaching systems of non-banking financial corporations, fintech companies and payment aggregators in order to steal money.

The government’s response ties technical readiness to awareness at the top of organisations, with CERT-In tasked with producing the detailed advisory on emerging vulnerabilities. The articles do not say when that advisory is due or what further steps, if any, the government plans beyond the measures already described.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania attorney general appoints privacy ombudsman to oversee Character.AI user data in bankruptcy sale
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday announced on November 20, 2026 that an independent consumer privacy ombudsman will advise the bankruptcy court on how user data held by Character Technologies, Inc., which operates the Character.AI chatbot platform, is handled in any sale. The appointment came as the company moves through bankruptcy proceedings while holding sensitive personal data from millions of minors. Pennsylvania and other states had opened an investigation after a 2024 wrongful death lawsuit alleging that the company's chatbots encouraged a child's suicidal thoughts and contributed to his death. Character.AI has more than 10 million current users averaging 120 minutes per day on the platform.

Before any assets of Character Technologies, Inc. can be sold, the ombudsman must file reports with the court evaluating data privacy issues and proposing protections, and the company plans to auction off user data on December 1, 2026. The appointment applies the consumer privacy ombudsman mechanism of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code, under 11 U.S.C. § 332, to an AI chatbot company holding minors' data, extending a tool previously used mainly for customer-list sales. The ombudsman's review of data-handling safeguards has not yet produced findings, and the scope of any proposed sale remains undisclosed. The ombudsman's findings will determine what privacy protections any buyer must honor.

Acting Alaska Attorney General Cori Mills announced that Alaska and a bipartisan coalition of states helped secure the appointment of the independent privacy watchdog, and the bankruptcy court ordered it at the coalition's urging. Mills said children and families should not have to worry that their private conversations can be sold to the highest bidder, and that companies have a responsibility to protect the information they collect, a responsibility that does not disappear when they file for bankruptcy. She said she was pleased the court had taken the important step to protect consumers. Alaska joined the bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general in October in raising concerns about Character.AI's privacy and safety practices, and the states' investigations identified potential consumer protection and privacy violations.

Character.AI allows users to interact with AI-generated characters, including fictional personalities and chatbots posing as therapists, psychologists, and other trusted professionals, and through these interactions the company has collected sensitive personal information including private conversations about mental health, relationships, and emotional struggles. Although Character.AI has voluntarily restricted minors' access to certain chatbot features, Mills has raised concerns that these measures are voluntary, incomplete, and could be circumvented or reversed by a future buyer. Sunday sent a letter to Congress in October 2026 calling for stronger children's online protections. Mills will remain actively engaged in the bankruptcy proceedings to protect consumers and address outstanding regulatory concerns, and users may see their data handled under a court-supervised review if the company's assets are sold.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave shares hit a one year low amid a broad sell off of AI infrastructure stocks
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave shares fell to a fresh one-year low of $39.51 on November 20, 2026, during a broad sell-off of AI infrastructure stocks. This drop took the stock 9.17% below the previous yearly extreme that was set on November 5, 2026. Other companies including IREN, Cipher Digital, and Applied Digital also saw their share prices fall sharply on the same day. The decline was part of a wider trend where AI-linked names were being repriced together across the market. This session saw the S&P 500 drop 3.00% to 6,954.60 and the Nasdaq 100 fall 4.63% to 25,237.50.

The sell-off affected the Dow Jones at 48,350.30 and the Russell 2000 at 2,594.94, while CoreWeave fell 6% to $42.17 in morning trading. Anthropic shares dropped 14% to $84.01 after opening at $111.50 on November 19 and closing that debut session at $97.17. Amazon, which owns 14.7% of Anthropic, slipped 2% to $251.39, while Alphabet owns 13.7% of the AI developer's capital stock. Applied Digital fell 17.81% and IREN dropped 18.0%, while Cipher Digital fell 17.4% and MARA saw a 19.38% drop. Other losses included SK hynix down 10.2%, Coherent down 10%, and DigitalOcean sliding 8.5% following an Alibaba earnings miss.

Market analysts noted that the selling was cohort-wide rather than tied to any specific company, reflecting a broad sector rotation. Bespoke stated on X that investors who wanted Anthropic at the IPO price of $83 could now do so. Eric Balchunas noted on X that Anthropic set a trading-volume record of $84 billion on its first day. The reports suggest that the floor investors had been watching for CoreWeave has finally given way during this session. Analysts believe the current swing in sentiment shows how quickly the initial debut-day enthusiasm for new AI stocks has cooled.

The sell-off affected GPU cloud providers, AI labs, hyperscalers, and enterprises that operate under multi-year contracts for data center capacity. Bitcoin miners like IREN and Cipher Digital were hit, with IREN leaving a market cap of $2.0 billion after its fall. Large-cap data-center REITs also suffered, with one seeing a 5.10% intraday slide to $164.18 during the heavy trading day. Money leaving the crypto and AI infrastructure sectors was absorbed by the healthcare and telecom industries, including HDFC Bank. Investors holding any AI-linked names felt the impact as the selling spread from Wall Street to Asia and Europe.

CoreWeave has worked steadily lower from a peak above $125, with each recovery attempt topping out below the previous one. The company rents purpose-built GPU data center capacity, which involves heavy capital spending and a large debt load for financing. Anthropic is a pure-play developer of frontier AI models, specifically the Claude family, and is listed in 82 ETFs. Amazon provides a different model by combining AWS with retail, marketplace, advertising, and subscription businesses that generate steady cash flow. Alphabet similarly pairs its Google Cloud unit with Google Search and YouTube advertising to spread its overall AI exposure.

Investors are now watching for signals about customer AI infrastructure spending, specifically from CoreWeave customer Meta and its science summit. The next major test is whether buyers will defend the $83 offer price for Anthropic as AI stocks remain under pressure. It remains open whether the largest IPO on record will slip below its offer price if the current sell-off deepens. The articles leave open if the current price levels for CoreWeave and its peers can eventually find a bottom. Amazon and Alphabet may also feel the outcome of the Anthropic price movement given their large stakes in the company.

stories.Headline: Together AI adds Tencent Hy4 model with vision capabilities and a million-token context window
stories.Summary:
Together AI launched the Tencent Hy4 model on its serverless inference platform on November 19, 2026. This flagship model allows developers to process both images and text using a chat completions API. The release provides a new hosting option for a model that Tencent announced earlier in November. It is the first model in the Hy family to support vision capabilities for users. Developers can now access this tool through the model string tencent/Hy4 on the platform.

The system requires 0.83 dollars per 1M input tokens and 2.50 dollars per 1M output tokens. Cached input tokens cost 0.042 dollars per 1M, and the context window holds one million tokens. It supports tool calling and JSON output for developers working with the Together Python SDK. The model is a Mixture-of-Experts design with 770B total parameters and 49B active per token. These features are available now through the Together AI playground and the serverless API.

Sonny Khan and Together AI stated that the model can read charts and write browser games. They demonstrated Hy4 extracting data from a chart and rebuilding it as a single HTML file. The team also prompted the model to create an original browser game called Polarity in HTML. They noted that the model added a title screen and a best score without being asked. Together AI says the model can return structured answers as JSON objects for various developers.

Superpower Daily noted that the chart and game examples are company-run demonstrations rather than independent proof. They mentioned that developers are affected by the fact that Hy4 trails top proprietary models on tests. Tencent reported that unsupported-assumption errors fell from 23.1 percent in Hy4 Preview to 5.6 percent. The company also cited a 3.04 average score from 213 professionals performing 579 financial tasks. These figures are based on internal evaluations and do not serve as a general accuracy guarantee.

Tencent announced the Hy4 model on November 4 to introduce visual understanding and computer-use capabilities. The company trained the model to operate professional software including CAD tools and the Blender application. Product teams evaluated the model on financial research, office work, and game development in several engines. These engines include Unity, Godot, and Unreal Engine to ensure the model could handle complex technical tasks. This version follows the Hy4 Preview and adds the ability to accept images alongside text.

Developers can now run the model by installing the Together Python SDK and setting an API key. They can send images as image_url blocks in the message content to utilize the vision features. The articles leave open whether the model will achieve parity with the top proprietary AI models. It remains unclear if the internal performance gains will translate to broad reliability for all users. Future updates on the model's accuracy and independent benchmarking are not provided in the texts.

stories.Headline: California and Minnesota penalize Polaris over $1 million for data privacy claims
stories.Summary:
The California Privacy Protection Agency and Minnesota's attorney general announced Thursday that they had hit Polaris, a recreational vehicle manufacturer, with more than $1 million in penalties. The penalties resolve claims over how Polaris handled consumers' requests for the handling of their personal data. The announcement came on November 19, 2026, according to Law360. The California agency and Minnesota's attorney general jointly announced the settlements that Thursday. Law360 reported the settlements in an article by Allison Grande dated November 19, 2026.

The settlements require Polaris to pay more than $1 million in penalties to California and Minnesota. The California Privacy Protection Agency announced the California order, and Minnesota's attorney general announced the Minnesota petition for order. The attached documents in the California matter are listed as a California Order. The attached documents in the Minnesota matter are listed as a Minnesota Petition for Order. The claims concerned how Polaris handled consumers' requests for the handling of their personal data.

The California Privacy Protection Agency and Minnesota's attorney general are the government agencies responsible for the settlements. The two agencies announced the penalties against Polaris on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The agencies said the penalties resolve claims over how the company handled consumers' requests for the handling of their personal data. The settlements were announced jointly by the California agency and Minnesota's attorney general. Law360 reported that the agencies hit Polaris with more than $1 million in penalties.

The settlements affect Polaris, the recreational vehicle manufacturer named in the announcement. The related companies listed by Law360 include FedEx Corp., Ford Motor Co., Honda Motor Co. Ltd., Todd Snyder and Tractor Supply Co. The related law firm listed is Faegre Drinker. The related sections listed are California, Compliance, Consumer Protection, Cybersecurity & Privacy, Media & Entertainment, Retail & E-Commerce, Sports & Betting, Technology and Transportation. The government agencies listed are the California Privacy Protection Agency and the Minnesota Attorney General's Office.

Law360's article on the settlements was written by Allison Grande and published November 19, 2026, at 10:01 AM EST. The article appeared under the Law360 section on Cybersecurity & Privacy. The article listed the attached documents as the California Order and the Minnesota Petition for Order. The article listed Polaris Inc. among the companies covered. The article listed the California Privacy Protection Agency and the Minnesota Attorney General's Office among the government agencies covered.

The settlements resolve claims over how Polaris handled consumers' requests for the handling of their personal data, according to the announcement. The California Privacy Protection Agency and Minnesota's attorney general announced the penalties on Thursday, November 19, 2026. Polaris is to pay more than $1 million in penalties under the settlements. The article leaves open the exact amount of the penalties beyond the figure of more than $1 million. The article leaves open the specific terms of the California Order and the Minnesota Petition for Order.

stories.Headline: COP31 participants launch the Antalya AI Pledge to address technology and climate risks
stories.Summary:
Lord Mawuko-Yevugah and other authors wrote about the collision of artificial intelligence, climate change, and democratic governance in November 2026. They analyzed how these three structural forces reinforce and destabilize one another within the contemporary international political system. The authors examined the material paradoxes of algorithmic sustainability and the rise of climate-security exceptionalism. They also explored the erosion of the democratic public sphere through synthetic media and the restructuring of global labor. Finally, they investigated digital-ecological non-alignment across the Global South and the institutional pathways required to preserve human agency.

The Antalya AI Pledge launched on November 16 at COP31 in Turkey recognizes that AI can track emissions and advance climate solutions. This pledge also acknowledges that AI creates a growing demand for land, water, electricity, and critical materials. The articles mention that the liberal international order fractured by the mid-2020s, replaced by a multipolar order of industrial nationalism. This new system relies on an industrial stack including hyperscale data centers, high-voltage transmission grids, and specialized semiconductors. It also involves extreme ultraviolet lithography, proprietary training corpora, and the mining of cobalt, lithium, copper, gallium, and rare earth elements.

UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell described artificial intelligence as a double-edged sword during the COP31 meetings in Turkey. He noted that while AI offers potential for climate solutions, it also requires significant natural resources to function. Lord Mawuko-Yevugah argued that compute capacity has become a primary metric of national power, similar to nuclear arsenals. He stated that states now view algorithmic infrastructure as a core attribute of territorial sovereignty rather than a commercial sector. He further claimed that the race for computational supremacy risks cannibalizing the ecological budgets that AI is meant to protect.

Civil society organizations and affected communities doubt that voluntary commitments can address the risks of expanding data centers. These groups, including Indigenous groups and the Women and Gender Constituency, voiced concerns about human rights and digital inequalities. They questioned who benefits from AI-driven solutions and who bears the costs of the supporting infrastructure. Populist movements in the Americas and Europe have also mobilized against climate policies, framing them as projects of cosmopolitan technocrats. These movements argue that such policies are imposed at the expense of national sovereignty and working-class livelihoods.

The liberal international order previously relied on American military primacy, institutional multilateralism, and the assumption that global trade would socialize powers. AI was discussed at COP22 in 2016 for emissions and COP23 in 2017 for managing disaster risk. Subsequent meetings at COP25 in 2019, COP26 in 2021, and COP27 in 2022 added adaptation and emissions monitoring to the list. At COP28 in 2023, the AI for Climate Action Initiative recognized challenges regarding energy consumption and data privacy. In 2024, COP29 saw 75 countries and 1,170 non-state actors endorse the voluntary Declaration on Green Digital Action.

Future steps include the need for enforceable safeguards and meaningful participation to prevent AI from amplifying existing global inequalities. The Global Climate Action Agenda in Belém highlighted AI applications in food security, agriculture, and adaptation. However, the articles leave open whether the international community can establish global safety treaties despite mutual distrust over dual-use capabilities. They do not specify how to resolve the conflict between immediate decarbonization and the energy needs of AI. It remains unclear if democratic institutions can survive the combined stress of ecological collapse and algorithmic authoritarianism.
