stories.Headline: TensorWave signs six-year deal to supply OpenAI with 457 MW of AMD-powered AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
TensorWave signed a multi-year partnership with OpenAI to provide 457 megawatts of AI infrastructure powered by AMD hardware, the company announced on November 17, 2026. TensorWave is the infrastructure provider supplying the capacity, OpenAI is the recipient, and AMD is the silicon supplier whose hardware powers the deployment. The announcement appeared under TensorWave's dedicated TensorWave & OpenAI partnership coverage and was reported by Ashish Joshi. The 457-megawatt figure is the total scale of the deployment covered by the partnership rather than a partial tranche. The multi-year structure indicates sustained provision of infrastructure over the life of the agreement rather than a one-time transaction.

Futurum reported on November 19, 2026 that the agreement is a six-year, 457 MW infrastructure deal to deliver dedicated AMD Instinct MI455X GPU capacity across multiple U.S. data center sites. The deployment will use AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs in infrastructure purpose-built for AMD Helios rack-scale systems, with dedicated single-tenant capacity connected through high-performance Ethernet networking. TensorWave expects to bring the first capacity online in the first half of 2027 and complete the full deployment by early 2028. The deal makes TensorWave the first publicly announced neocloud provider supporting the OpenAI-AMD strategic collaboration, which targets 6 gigawatts of AMD Instinct GPU deployments beginning with 1 gigawatt in 2026. The agreement is TensorWave's largest to date.

AMD SVP of AI Vamsi Boppana stated that the three-way combination is building the foundation to deliver AI compute at extraordinary scale and advance the broader AI ecosystem. TensorWave President Piotr Tomasik said the ability to deliver hundreds of megawatts of advanced compute reliably and at speed will separate the companies that can support frontier AI from those that cannot. TensorWave was the first public cloud to deploy AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs and has continued expanding across successive generations including MI325X and MI355X. That track record as an AMD Helios launch partner gave OpenAI confidence in TensorWave's ability to operate purpose-built Helios rack-scale systems at extreme scale. TensorWave has more than 2 gigawatts of long-term data center capacity already secured.

In January 2026, Cerebras secured a strategic multi-year $10 billion compute agreement with OpenAI, validating its hardware for the most demanding frontier AI applications. In late February 2026, Meta announced a multi-year agreement to deploy up to 6 gigawatts of AMD-based infrastructure, including the co-design of custom Instinct MI450-based GPUs. OpenAI is deliberately distributing compute commitments across multiple vendors and infrastructure models, which reduces single-source dependency and ensures redundancy for large and complex AI model training and inference workloads. Hyperscalers bring their own software, operations teams, and increasingly their own silicon, whereas neoclouds, enterprises, telcos, and sovereign AI factories need the GPU vendor to supply much of the operating stack. For AMD-centric workloads, that distinction makes a dedicated neocloud like TensorWave a more natural fit than a hyperscaler optimized around its own silicon.

The agreement illustrates how frontier AI compute demand has grown to a scale where purpose-built, long-term neocloud capacity contracts are becoming the preferred procurement model for leading AI labs. At 457 MW committed over six years, this single neocloud deal illustrates how large individual infrastructure tranches within the 6 GW program will be. Multi-year, multi-hundred-megawatt, single-tenant capacity contracts with specialized neocloud providers are displacing the on-demand hyperscaler model for the most demanding workloads. The procurement logic is built around guaranteed capacity, hardware specificity, and operational control rather than flexibility and shared tenancy. As frontier model complexity continues to grow, this template is likely to become the norm rather than the exception for labs operating at OpenAI's scale.

What to watch includes whether TensorWave brings initial AMD Helios systems online on schedule in 1H 2027 and which additional neocloud providers announce roles within the 6 GW OpenAI-AMD program in Q1-Q2 2027. Also to watch is how NVIDIA-aligned neocloud providers respond with comparable long-term capacity offerings to retain frontier AI customers. Further items are whether Meta's up to 6 GW AMD infrastructure commitment advances to named neocloud or operator announcements in early 2027 and whether additional multi-year, dedicated-capacity agreements with new vendors are announced as the broader 6 GW AMD program scales through 2027. The articles leave open which additional neocloud providers will join the program and how NVIDIA-aligned providers will respond.

stories.Headline: Anthropic stock crashes after IPO as AI shares lose over 50 percent in five months
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched its initial public offering on the Nasdaq on November 19, 2026, but its stock crashed shortly after the debut. Gary Marcus reported on November 20, 2026, that AI stocks have lost over 50 percent of their value in five months. The company saw its share price drop steadily after opening, and it was set to fall nearly 10 percent more. This market decline is described as a crash that is happening faster than the original dot com debacle of the past. The overall technology sector on Wall Street fell across the board due to growing concerns over the weakening profitability of AI.

The IPO was priced at 83 dollars per share, which was above the earlier target range of 70 to 78 dollars. Anthropic raised 107.3 billion dollars, surpassing the 86.2 billion dollars raised by SpaceX in June, and was valued at 1.5 trillion dollars. Trading began at 111.50 dollars, reached a high of 114.99 dollars, and closed at 97.17 dollars on November 19 in New York. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,101.11 points to 49,097.06, while the S&P 500 ended at 7,175.83 and the Nasdaq at 23,879.20. SpaceX is set to open below its IPO price of 135 dollars, and SoftBank fell 14.5 percent overnight.

Chief Executive Dario Amodei stated that the company would pace the training and deployment of AI systems to ensure the technology remains safe. He added that an obsession with the public interest and safety has been embedded in the DNA of Anthropic from the start. Gary Marcus claimed that the IPO is on pace to be one of the most embarrassing in history for retail investors. He noted that his inbox was filled with media think pieces glorifying the IPO that were filed too soon by various writers. Marcus warned that a death spiral for the market has begun, which he has long predicted in his newsletter.

Other affected companies include Apple, which fell 0.92 percent, Microsoft at 1.78 percent, Nvidia at 3.30 percent, and Amazon at 3.87 percent. Alphabet dropped 3.46 percent, Meta fell 3.27 percent, Tesla decreased 2.43 percent, and the semiconductor firm TSMC saw a decline of 2.90 percent. Broadcom fell 2.09 percent, Eli Lilly dropped 2.25 percent, Walmart fell 1.04 percent, SK hynix fell 2.67 percent, and Micron fell 2.10 percent. Asian markets collapsed, with the Nikkei plunging over 4 percent and Taiwan's stock index falling 16 percent during its worst week since COVID. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index also closed sharply lower, ending the session with a total decrease of 2.42 percent.

The background includes a period where AI stocks were highly valued, with some companies reaching valuations as high as one trillion dollars. The S&P 500 had already extended its losing streak to six sessions before the events of November 19 and November 20 occurred. In other news, President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping met in Shenzhen, China, to discuss oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. West Texas Intermediate crude settled at 83.21 dollars a barrel, while Brent crude traded at 91.98 dollars on the ICE Futures exchange. These events occurred amidst rising military tensions in the Middle East and expectations of a global oil supply glut.

In the coming months or days, Gary Marcus predicts that Nvidia and the Neoclouds will be hit hard by the market crash. He suggests that OpenAI cannot possibly IPO at a valuation of 1 trillion dollars in this environment and may run out of cash. The articles leave open whether the AI sector can recover from this selloff or if the death spiral will continue. It remains unclear how the safety pacing mentioned by Dario Amodei will affect the long term financial viability of the company. The reports do not state if other AI firms will delay their public offerings to avoid the current market volatility.

stories.Headline: Singapore launches three AI missions to combat financial crime and improve business lending
stories.Summary:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Future of Finance Institute launched three national AI missions on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. These initiatives focus on preventing financial crime, improving business financing, and enabling the safe use of AI agents in financial transactions. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong announced these plans during the Singapore FinTech Festival held at the Singapore Expo. The programs aim to bring together researchers, public agencies, technology companies, and financial institutions to develop shared capabilities. These missions are part of a wider national AI program that was first announced in the 2026 Budget.

The first initiative targets financial crime by improving the detection of suspicious transfers across banks to stop scams from moving quickly. The Monetary Authority of Singapore will begin a design study in early 2027 for an industry-wide Scam Detection Utility for domestic accounts. The second initiative uses synthetic data to help small and medium-sized enterprises and start-ups access credit without needing extensive collateral. The third initiative involves an Agentic Money Sandbox where AI agents can conduct transactions using digital money within defined limits. The Future of Finance Institute will also work with the Agency for Science, Technology and Research on speech-to-text AI applications.

Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, who chairs the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said the missions build capabilities beyond individual institutions. He stated that scam proceeds move through several institutions in minutes, making it difficult for any single lender to intervene effectively. Gan explained that AI could help lenders assess a wider set of indicators to speed up decisions and lower borrowing costs. He stressed that greater autonomy for AI agents would not remove responsibility from the organisations that authorise those specific agents. He also noted that the government is engaging American officials regarding the implications of new United States export controls.

Five banks are already participating in a trial that securely combines transaction data to train and assess various AI models. Small and medium-sized enterprises and start-ups are affected because traditional credit assessments often overlook businesses with limited financial records. Technology companies are invited to develop lending tools using realistic synthetic data rather than relying on actual customer records initially. Participating businesses will be consulted to see if the proposed AI tools actually address their specific financing difficulties. Residents and visitors are affected by the second-phase report on PayNow, which includes an SGQR+ switching arrangement for payments.

The Future of Finance Institute began operations this month to coordinate work between financial institutions, technology developers, and various researchers. Its remit includes developing common standards and resources for managing AI risks that can be adopted beyond individual pilot projects. The AI Innovation Arena initiative provides developers with synthetic data to test AI solutions, focusing initially on preventing financial crime. The government wants to explore if AI can help lenders identify businesses approaching a financing need and offer options proactively. These initiatives follow the 2026 Budget, which established the broader national AI programme to strengthen the country's financial sector.

Authorities will assess promising applications against international practices before considering broader deployment rather than assuming demonstrations translate to commercial systems. The Monetary Authority of Singapore will examine the technical blueprint, governance arrangements, and operating model for the Scam Detection Utility. Officials want to establish how AI agents can use purpose-bound money without exceeding authority or compromising confidence in transactions. The articles leave open whether the Scam Detection Utility will eventually expand to include cross-border cooperation after the domestic phase. It remains unclear how the new United States export controls on advanced computing equipment will specifically impact Singapore's AI development.

stories.Headline: AI chip demand creates structural high bandwidth memory shortage for top suppliers
stories.Summary:
A high-bandwidth memory shortage emerged by November 21, 2026, as AI demand surged. Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron are the three main suppliers facing this structural crisis. These companies are shifting their wafer production to meet the needs of AI accelerators. This reallocation of resources has created a squeeze across the entire memory market. The shortage is driven by the massive silicon requirements of HBM stacks.

TrendForce reports HBM will take 23% of DRAM wafers in 2026 and nearly 30% by 2027. HBM requires three to four times the wafer capacity of general-purpose DRAM. HBM4 prices are at least $2.05 per gigabit in 2026 and $3.00 to $5.50 in 2027. Samsung is building an Onyang hub for HBM4E, costing between KRW 46 trillion and 56 trillion. Operations at Onyang moved up to June 2028 to increase packaging capacity.

SK hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung said demand will exceed supply capacity even beyond 2030. Sales chief Kim Ki-tae stated that customers request more than twice the volume they can supply. Samsung leadership was reshuffled on November 20 to treat HBM as a core business. Micron announced high-volume production of HBM4 for the Nvidia Vera Rubin platform. Micron also reported its 2026 supply is sold out, meeting only half to two-thirds of demand.

Conventional DRAM contract prices are expected to rise 10% to 15% in the fourth quarter. This price hike affects users of phones, handhelds, and PCs due to fewer available wafers. Nvidia, AMD, and Google are the primary buyers of these high-capacity AI memory pools. Nvidia's RTX Spark line offers 128 GB of unified memory for compact desktop computers. Logic makers and foundries are also competing for limited packaging tools and engineers.

HBM stacks several DRAM dies using through-silicon vias and mounts them on a shared interposer. TSMC currently holds a near-80% monopoly on the 2.5D packaging market used for AI chips. Samsung's HBM4 revenue tripled in the third quarter, making up 60% of its HBM revenue. SK hynix held 50% of HBM revenue in the second quarter of 2026. China has raised its share of domestically supplied semiconductor equipment to 20-30%.

New capacity from China's CXMT may change the market outlook starting around 2028. Major new memory fabs are not expected to add meaningful output before that same year. Experts say South Korean firms must build foundry and packaging capabilities to sustain their dominance. Paul Triolo suggested that securing High Bandwidth Flash is the next necessary technological task. The articles leave the final cost of Samsung's Onyang investment and HBM4E pricing open.

stories.Headline: Microsoft unveils Windows Server 2028 with hardened security and local AI inference
stories.Summary:
Microsoft announced Windows Server 2028, its next major server operating system release, at the Ignite 2026 conference on Tuesday, according to TechGig. Network World reported the announcement on November 18, 2026, calling it Microsoft's largest platform update since Windows Server 2025. TechGig published its report on November 19, 2026, at 05:34 AM IST. A second TechGig article on November 20, 2026, at 04:50 AM IST covered the public preview. The release is now in public preview, Network World said.

The release ships with a hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline, TechGig reported. The default security aligns with hardened DoD benchmarks including DISA STIG, according to the second TechGig article. Security settings include Kerberos over NTLM, LSASS protection, strong passwords, SMB signing and encryption, a firewall active in every profile, and legacy name resolution turned off. Cryptography is limited to modern TLS cipher suites with hybrid post-quantum ML-KEM key exchange, and the paging file is encrypted. Trusted Launch extends boot integrity protection to virtual machines, and Confidential VM support begins a journey toward integrity-protected runtimes on compatible CVM hardware.

Neil Hinnant, Director of Windows Server & I/O Fabrics PM, said the baseline lets administrators relax specific settings, reducing the effort to establish a secure environment from day one. Hinnant said the release "begins our long term investments extending Microsoft Foundry to bring AI inference to fleets of local token factories." He said this offers customers more choices to place intelligence with the right cost structure. In a blog post he wrote that different workloads have different needs shaped by cost, latency, IP protection, data residency, and regulatory requirements. Microsoft said the secure configuration is the starting state, not a project run after setup, which closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed.

John Annand, associate VP at Infotech, noted that because this is the public preview phase, a lot remains a promise on the roadmap. Annand said customers wanting local AI on existing hardware would need to add Nvidia or AMD accelerators and lots of ever more expensive RAM. He said 10GbE network cards will likely be a bottleneck until customers upgrade to 50 or 100GbE+. He called Server 2028 a viable midpoint upgrade for existing hardware and said later adopters may be the winners. Enterprises are affected, along with administrators who can register for the Windows Insider Program for Windows Server or apply to the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program for earlier access.

Windows Server 2025 will remain under extended support until 2034, Network World reported. Windows Server 2022 is covered until Oct 14, 2031, Windows Server 2019 until Jan. 9, 2029, and Windows Server 2016 sunsets on January 12, 2027, all through the Windows Long-Term Servicing Channel. AMD's Instinct MI350P card is to be in preview in the first half of 2027 for supported Windows Server systems including Server 2028. The hybrid intelligence capabilities are available to a limited number of customers through an early-access program that includes hardware requirements. NVMe and Intune management for servers are available for testing now.

Microsoft said Windows Server 2028 is a prerelease product, and some elements may be substantially modified before its official release. Microsoft advised enterprises to test apps and operational tooling against the locked-down security and memory defaults before deployment and to relax settings only when required. Microsoft said older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts may not work on Windows Server 2028 without configuration changes. The articles leave open when general availability will come and which features will change before release. The articles also leave open how many customers the early-access program includes.

stories.Headline: Worried About Nvidia? 3 Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stocks That May Be Safer Buys Right Now
stories.Summary:
Cerebras Systems went public in May 2026, and its stock spiked 68% on the first day of trading following its initial public offering. The stock has slid significantly since then, and it fell to a market cap of $17.79 billion as of 12:40 PM ET on 11/20/26. Cerebras released third-quarter results on Nov. 12, reporting a 70% year-over-year increase in core revenue to $231 million. That figure was well ahead of the $214.7 million consensus estimate, and its adjusted loss of $0.12 per share was lower than the Wall Street estimate of $0.14 per share. Nvidia stock is down 20% this year, while Broadcom has clocked gains of just 2%.

Cerebras designs and builds wafer-scale AI chips, which are dinner-plate-sized silicon wafers used as a stand-alone processor. The company claimed in September last year that its CS-3 wafer-scale AI supercomputer is 21 times faster than Nvidia's DGX B200 Blackwell supercomputing system. Cerebras pointed out that the CS-3 costs 33% less and has equally lower power consumption. Cerebras has contracts with major hyperscalers including Oracle, Microsoft, Amazon, and OpenAI, and it added three new hyperscalers to its clientele in the past six months. Cerebras management says it is on track to exit 2026 with 10x the manufacturing capacity it had at the beginning of the year, and the company will bring 700 megawatts of data center capacity online by late 2027.

Cerebras expects its revenue to grow 3x in 2027, and it expects $950 million in revenue this year. Cerebras has a 12-month median price target of $207, implying a 120% jump from current levels, according to CNN. Thirteen of the 14 analysts covering Cerebras rate it as a buy. Nvidia and Broadcom are expected to deliver gains of 66% and 48%, respectively, based on their 12-month median price targets. Harsh Chauhan wrote that now is a good time for investors to buy Cerebras following its recent slide.

Broadcom in April 2026 disclosed a long-term agreement to develop and supply future generations of Google TPUs, along with networking and other components for Google's next-generation AI racks through up to 2031. Marvell's August 2026 Google agreement covers custom silicon programs associated with the TPU ecosystem, including inference accelerators, storage controllers, network interface controllers, memory interface controllers and near-memory computing. The Marvell agreement contains a purchase-linked warrant arrangement, with most shares vesting in tranches tied to cumulative custom-product revenue, with one tranche for each $500 million. Nvidia faces a leadership transition following Jensen Huang's November 12 departure and the appointment of Colette Kress as interim CEO. The Information Network's illustrative 2025 model assigns 7.2 million merchant GPU units eight HBM stacks apiece and 1.5 million custom ASIC units three stacks apiece.

Hyperscalers began developing proprietary processors years earlier because of the economics of computing at enormous scale. Training emphasizes throughput and the coordination of many accelerators, while inference often emphasizes cost per token, response latency, energy consumption and the ability to serve many simultaneous users. Processing an incoming prompt, known as prefill, can make effective use of parallel computation, while generating an answer token by token, known as decoding, may be constrained by the speed at which model parameters are read from memory. GPUs offer programmability and flexibility across training and inference, and custom ASICs can be tuned to particular workloads and deliver favorable economics when deployed at scale. CPUs handle smaller models and supporting tasks, FPGAs can serve specialized low-latency applications, and NPUs support edge and client-device inference.

Broadcom's risks include customer concentration, expensive design programs, and pressure on pricing as cloud customers grow more technically sophisticated. Marvell's dependence on large customers and program execution warrants particular attention, and its contractual framework does not guarantee that all contemplated revenue will materialize. Nvidia continues to supply the flexible GPUs and integrated computing platforms that dominate many large-model deployments, and its software ecosystem and ability to support evolving models are meaningful competitive advantages. Advanced Micro Devices also supplies GPUs for AI acceleration and offers FPGA technology for specialized, reconfigurable inference. The articles leave open whether Cerebras' revenue will indeed reach $3 billion in 2027 and whether its stock will trade at 20 times sales then.

stories.Headline: House lawmakers urge Trump administration to create US open-weight AI initiative to counter China
stories.Summary:
House lawmakers recommended on Friday that the Trump administration establish a new initiative for American-made open-weight AI models. This proposal aims to entice various organizations to turn away from using open-weight models created in China. The House Select Committee on China published a report to support this recommendation on November 20, 2026. This report followed an investigation that began in April into why certain American companies used Chinese models. The committee wanted to understand the specific reasons why these firms adopted foreign technology for their operations.

The report highlights the widespread use of Chinese open-weight models known as DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, and GLM. It specifically mentions that American companies Airbnb, Anysphere, Cursor, and DoorDash turned to these foreign AI models. Lawmakers propose a national initiative pairing public compute, shared evaluation infrastructure, and lawful access to American frontier models. They suggest the White House prohibit federal agencies from using Chinese models and subject them to consistent evaluation. Finally, they recommended sanctioning any companies that illicitly distill models made in the United States for their own.

The House Select Committee on China is responsible for the report and the recommendations provided to the administration. Lawmakers stated that risks are increasing because Chinese models produce less secure code and autonomously build cyber exploits. They argued that the government must encourage the creation of U.S. open-weight models to counter these threats. The committee noted that Chinese models are widely used in the economy, though much of that use is hard to track. They believe that American-made alternatives are necessary to ensure national security and the integrity of software code.

Organizations using Chinese models cite their low cost, easy customization, and high performance as the key drivers. Experts told ISMG that open-weight models from Chinese labs are steadily closing in on the most advanced frontier models. Some proponents of proprietary models believe that open-weight versions are less secure and not as capable as closed ones. Cursor, which SpaceX recently bought, plans to stop using Chinese models according to a report from CNBC. This company previously built its coding model Composer 2 using Kimi K2.5 from the Chinese lab Moonshot AI.

The report explains that proprietary models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google do not require sharing weights or training data. Open-weight models provide weights for customization and often cost a fraction of the price of closed proprietary models. Meta provides open-weight models called Llama and Muse, while Nvidia distributes an open-weight model known as Nemotron. OpenAI and Google also offer open-weight options called oss and Gemma, respectively, to compete in the current market. Some Chinese labs use distillation, prompting teacher models like Claude Fable to create training data for their models.

The U.S. government says many Chinese labs illicitly distill American models without permission, citing information from Anthropic and OpenAI. The House committee warned that many current safety evaluations may not detect certain behaviors from these Chinese models. Future steps include the potential for federal procurement to create anchor demand for new American open-weight AI models. The articles leave open whether the Trump administration will actually adopt the specific measures proposed by the House committee. It remains unclear if sanctions will be applied to companies that use distillation to copy American AI technology.

stories.Headline: Oracle says it secures full funding for OpenAI infrastructure contract
stories.Summary:
Oracle said on X on November 20, 2026, that it had secured all the funding needed to fulfill its infrastructure contract with OpenAI. Oracle posted the statement at 9:01 PM that day, and the post drew 655,000 views. Oracle said its final capital raise earlier that month made it the first hyperscaler fully funded for this investment cycle. Oracle said the financing it outlined at Oracle Investor Day, including vendor financing, is in place. Oracle said any further private discussions with vendors are just additional options.

Oracle said its ability to deliver on the OpenAI contract does not depend on those vendor discussions. Oracle said any media reports that will come out and say the contrary are incorrect and wrong. Oracle said it and OpenAI are making rapid progress on their infrastructure partnership. Oracle said its Abilene campus, where Astra-6 was trained, is nearly complete. Oracle said Shackelford, its next gigawatt-scale campus, is fully permitted.

Oracle said the handover of NVIDIA Vera Rubin racks in its data halls is on track for the coming weeks. Oracle said it continues to expect positive free cash flow in the second half of FY2028. Oracle said it is targeting more than $30 billion in free cash flow in FY2029. Oracle said it expects to self-fund future growth beginning that year. Oracle attached a forward-looking statements disclaimer saying statements about its future plans, expectations, beliefs and intentions are subject to material risks and uncertainties.

Ed Zitron replied to the post, thanking Oracle for what he called a very reassuring message delivered one minute after market close. Techmeme carried Oracle's statement on November 20, 2026, at 8:20 PM. Techmeme's snapshot page also listed a Scientific American story by Joseph Howlett saying Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he used Claude to prove the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis. The Techmeme page also listed X posts on the Riemann claim, including one from Emily Riehl relaying Ravi Vakil's account of a proposed proof of GRH by Alessandro Masullo. That post said Brian Conrad had been looking closely at it for months and gave extensive feedback that is being incorporated, and that it is so far looking good and all human, with no AI. A post from Deedy said Alpöge claimed Claude resolved the General Riemann Hypothesis and that the proof is 250,000+ pages long. A post from Alex Kontorovich said it is only 17M lines of Lean. A post from Nuño Sempere said the Lean proof size is comparable to all human-written formal math or to about 2-3 months of arxiv math papers.

stories.Headline: US Senate passes bill to speed energy permits and require AI data centers to pay more grid costs
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Senate late on the evening of the 19th passed a bipartisan comprehensive bill to speed permitting for power plants, transmission lines and data centers by a vote of 62 to 33. The bill is titled the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, also called the bipartisan American Cost of Living Relief and Employment Act. It was led by four lawmakers, two Democrats and two Republicans, and took four years to craft. Most Republican senators were joined by 14 Democrats and one independent in supporting the measure. The bill now goes to the Republican-majority House of Representatives, and President Donald Trump has indicated he intends to sign it into law.

The bill sets stricter deadlines for federal environmental reviews and limits the scope and duration of reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. It restricts the period during which lawsuits can be filed and the circumstances under which permits can be revoked, and makes it harder to withdraw permits once granted. It requires large-scale AI data centers to bear a higher share of the costs of reinforcing transmission grids necessitated by their own power demand. It also expands federal authority over the siting and permitting of interstate transmission projects and accelerates planning and construction of transmission lines.

Co-sponsor Republican Senator Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia said the Senate finally passed permitting reform legislation, taking a major step forward in addressing Americans' concerns about the cost of living. Democratic Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, incoming chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and an author of the bill, said no big bipartisan bill is perfect for everyone but there is a real opportunity to make electricity more affordable for families. Heinrich said working people cannot afford to wait another few years, and that Americans sent a clear message that they want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable. Heinrich brokered the agreement with Senator Mike Lee, Republican of Utah, along with Senators Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island, and Capito, the top Democrat and Republican on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.

Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley of Oregon said on the Senate floor before the vote that consultations with tribes had not been adequately conducted, and that the bill touches states' authority, tribal rights and multiple matters of critical importance to energy. Merkley expressed the view that it should be carefully considered in 2027. Republican Senators Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota also voted against. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York, and more than a dozen Democrats voted to pass it over the objections of climate groups and tribes. Senator Ruben Gallego, Democrat of Arizona, said it would be legislation that makes the biggest difference for the next 100 years, especially bringing down carbon emissions once this president is gone.

Several tribal organizations maintained their opposition even after amendments were made to address concerns about historic preservation consultation procedures. Many environmental groups warned that safety safeguards under NEPA and other laws would be dangerously undermined, and the Natural Resources Defense Council said the House should not pass a bill that gives President Trump a blank check to reward oil and gas companies and data center developers. A broad range of energy and business groups lobbied for passage, and the AFL-CIO labor federation and numerous individual unions came out in support. The American Clean Power Association said it was a clean energy bill that will modernize America's energy systems and lower consumer prices, and the American Petroleum Institute called it a major breakthrough on historic permitting reforms. Senator Ron Wyden, Democrat of Oregon, pushed an amendment that would have blocked data centers from being built on public lands, saying he would not sit around and let these data centers scar our treasures.

Congress has long tried and failed to lighten permitting laws that industry complains are too burdensome, and both parties have long pointed out that construction of large infrastructure projects takes too long and procedural delays drive up costs. The vote split Democrats just weeks after they flipped enough seats from Republicans in the midterm elections to give them majorities in both chambers in January. Rhodium Group estimates the bill would allow an additional 17 to 249 gigawatts of clean energy to be built by 2040, raise natural gas exports 8% to 15% beyond a 76% to 145% rise already accounted for under current policy, and reduce greenhouse gases by 5 to 148 million metric tons annually in 2040. Rob Gramlich, founder and president of Grid Strategies, said expanding grid capacity would integrate a lot of clean energy and that you cannot get to 60 to 80% of the grid from renewable energy without a significant expansion of grid capacity. The bill aims to address the surge in electricity demand accompanying the spread of AI, with concerns mounting about power prices and grid expansion keeping pace with new data centers.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, Republican of Louisiana, was reported last week to have expressed confidence he can secure the votes needed for passage, and Republican leadership is expected to attempt to pass it. If differences arise between the two chambers, they must be reconciled within the year, leaving uncertainty over the schedule. Some Democratic lawmakers are calling for careful deliberation, with some arguing a separate bill should be assembled after taking control of Congress next year, while multiple supporters within the Democratic coalition believe there is no political room to amend the bill into a form Trump would sign. Representative Scott Peters, Democrat of California, said BAAJA lowers bills, cuts pollution and protects ratepayers and should pass before the end of this Congress. House Natural Resources ranking member and likely incoming Chair Jared Huffman, Democrat of California, urged Democrats to say no, saying they can produce a better deal.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang steps down as Nvidia becomes AI financing hub
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA’s longtime chief executive Jensen Huang has stepped down, and the company he led is now described by industry insiders as the “central bank” of the AI circular financing economy, a role that has drawn close attention from Wall Street and Silicon Valley. Under Huang, NVIDIA built the GPU chips that serve as the underlying foundation of the global AI wave and assembled what the article calls a huge capital ammunition depot. Regulatory filings show that as of September 30 the market value of NVIDIA’s shares in eight publicly listed companies exceeded 48 billion US dollars, with holdings concentrated in partners that buy its GPUs. Interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday’s earnings call that NVIDIA is proud of the role it has played in supporting the industry and will keep evaluating future transactions with a rigorous attitude, adding that the company still has a lot of work to do to judge whether these are the right investments to make.

The article reports that NVIDIA’s total investment portfolio exceeds 1000 billion US dollars, covering equity stakes in cutting-edge labs and bets on power producers and cloud computing companies, and that its shareholding in cloud computing unicorn CoreWeave has reached 10 percent. Its capital has also extended to cloud platform Nebius Group, semiconductor firm Intel and xAI before it was merged into SpaceX, and during Huang’s tenure it placed large bets on Anthropic and OpenAI, which lack investment-grade ratings. As part of Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday, NVIDIA committed to buying 10 billion US dollars of Anthropic shares, and Anthropic has reportedly signed a 350 billion US dollar agreement with Lambda, another NVIDIA-backed company, to lease data center computing power run on NVIDIA chips. According to PitchBook, as of November 13 NVIDIA had taken part in 129 venture capital and startup accelerator transactions this year, with the total venture capital it joined other investors in reaching 2200 billion US dollars, or 27 percent of the global total of that kind, and at least 293 investment and acquisition deals since the AI boom heated up in 2023.

NVIDIA reported on Tuesday that its commitments in areas such as long-term supply agreements and data center leases total 5180 billion US dollars, up sharply from about 850 billion a year ago. One guarantee is that NVIDIA will provide up to 1050 billion US dollars in backing for SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary, for its planned Ohio data center to help it issue bonds for construction costs, along with a 1.5 billion US dollar equity investment, and OpenAI has agreed to lease the computing capacity once the center is complete, with NVIDIA holding exclusive chip supply rights for the first half of the project. In August, Huang led efforts to obtain commitments from Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to raise 5000 billion US dollars, with NVIDIA providing fallback arrangements and guarantees, to help startup customers finance chip purchases, but people familiar with the matter say no funds have actually been invested so far. The article notes real doubt about whether many of these commitments and guarantees can be fulfilled, and says that since NVIDIA’s stock hit an all-time peak on October 6, the combined market value of the eight listed companies it holds has fallen by 820 billion US dollars, with SpaceX and Intel accounting for most of the decline, while rising borrowing costs are straining many AI enterprises.

stories.Headline: Cornell joins $12 million DOE project where Eun-Ah Kim leads machine-learning compiler work for quantum computing
stories.Summary:
Cornell University will participate in a multi-institution collaboration that has received $12 million from the U.S. Department of Energy to advance quantum computing through the use of Artificial Intelligence, the Cornell Chronicle reported on November 21, 2026. The project is called Application-Aware Error Correction Codesign for Scientific Quantum Computing, or ASQC, and Cornell is one of several institutions taking part in the work. The award is one of 12 Phase II awards announced on October 9 under the Genesis Mission, according to the articles. The Genesis Mission aims to integrate the world's best supercomputers, experimental facilities and AI systems to advance American research and innovation. Mirage News also reported on November 20, 2026, that Cornell joins the Genesis Mission to advance AI-powered quantum computing.

The project's principal investigator is Harvard Professor Mikhail Lukin, who is co-director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative, the articles state. Eun-Ah Kim, Hans A. Bethe Professor in the College of Arts and Sciences, is a co-investigator on the project, according to the reports. Other collaborators include researchers from MIT and the national laboratories at Los Alamos, Lawrence Berkeley, and Sandia, the articles say. The collaboration also includes QuEra Computing, NVIDIA, and Anthropic as partners on the project, according to the reports. The project is administered by the Advanced Scientific Computing Research division of the Department of Energy, the articles state.

Kim's group will lead machine-learning work at two points in the pipeline that connects a scientific question to the hardware, according to the articles. The first point is compilation, where the group will develop a reinforcement-learning compiler, the reports state. That compiler translates a quantum algorithm into the sequence of atom movements and gate operations that a reconfigurable neutral-atom quantum computer carries out, according to the articles. The articles describe the compiler work as one of the two points where Kim's group will lead machine-learning efforts. stories.Headline: Mikhail Lukin leads a $12 million Harvard project to link quantum computing with AI
stories.Summary:
A $12 million federal grant will fund a Harvard-led collaboration aiming to link quantum computing with artificial intelligence. The project is called Application-Aware Error Correction Codesign for Scientific Quantum Computing, or ASQC. It is part of the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission. Mikhail Lukin, Harvard's Joshua and Beth Friedman University Professor and co-founder of QuEra Computing, will lead the effort. The collaboration unites researchers from MIT, Cornell University and three national labs alongside tech partners NVIDIA and Anthropic.

The project is one of 12 Phase II awards announced Oct. 9 under the Genesis Mission. The grant is administered by the Advanced Scientific Computing Research division of the Department of Energy. Lukin is the project's principal investigator and co-director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative. He will work with Harvard physicists Markus Greiner and Susanne Yelin and researchers at MIT, Cornell University, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, QuEra Computing, NVIDIA and Anthropic. The team will train AI models to learn which errors matter for problems in quantum simulation, materials science, chemistry and nuclear science, use AI to design codes and decoders tailored to them, and test the results on hardware at Harvard, MIT and QuEra.

University President Alan M. Garber said Mikhail is a visionary leader who will do an excellent job driving progress and strengthening partnerships to ensure America's competitiveness in this area of vital importance. Lukin said this kind of collaborative approach is really needed in this case, and that the team wants to make something no one else has been able to make. He said the team will take all help. He said this is really an attempt to establish scientific foundations for useful fault-tolerant quantum computers and to really accelerate this progress using AI. He said that as we build larger and better quantum computers, we will really start making more and more scientific discoveries.

Garber said some of the most thrilling questions in science have long seemed out of reach, but the barriers to discovery are falling rapidly as quantum computing and artificial intelligence expand the realm of the possible. Lukin said you can really explore corners of the universe where you have never been, like a new kind of telescope. The team stated that we can really see these dreams the community has had for the last 40 years, for the first time, in the direct line of sight. Co-investigators on the program include Vladan Vuletić, Soonwon Choi and Hengyun "Harry" Zhou of MIT, Eun-Ah Kim of Cornell, Andrew Sornborger, Lukasz Cincio and Michael McKerns of Los Alamos, Wibe de Jong and Costin Iancu of Lawrence Berkeley, Andrew Landahl, Riley Chien and Kevin Thompson of Sandia, Nathan Gemelke and Michael Gullans of QuEra, Krysta Svore of NVIDIA and Alek Kemeny of Anthropic. The project will build on research Lukin and his collaborators published last year, which addressed a key challenge in quantum computing related to environmental noise and the inherently unstable quantum bits, or qubits, that make up quantum computers.

Through quantum error correction, the group suppressed errors to the point that adding qubits would reduce errors rather than add them, paving the way for larger, more complex calculations. Recent advances in quantum error correction have enabled the suppression of errors to the point where adding qubits now reduces, rather than increases, computational errors, a critical step toward building larger, more complex quantum computers. In an April preprint, Lukin, Yelin and colleagues described a neural-network decoder, software that identifies errors during computation, that cut error rates up to 17 times below existing versions and ran thousands of times faster. In another recent work, in collaboration with QuEra and Anthropic, the team used large language models to discover state-of-the-art quantum circuits for tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation and number theory. The Department of Energy grant specifically encourages partnerships between universities and national laboratories, an approach Lukin explained is unusual in quantum computing research, where institutions often operate more independently, and is essential to achieving goals previously considered unattainable.

The ASQC project will develop an AI-driven, fault-tolerant QEC system that can adapt to scientific problems relevant to the Energy Department. The Genesis Mission aims to integrate the world's best supercomputers, experimental facilities and AI systems to advance American research and innovation. Lukin and Greiner are co-founders of QuEra Computing, where Lukin is a chief scientist. Lukin views the resulting quantum computer not merely as a faster calculator, but as a novel scientific instrument capable of exploring previously inaccessible realms of knowledge. The articles do not say when the hardware tests will begin or how the $12 million will be divided among the partners.

stories.Headline: Harvard Berkman Klein Center seeks a director to lead its AI and youth safety research
stories.Summary:
Harvard University’s Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society posted a hiring notice on Nov 20, 2026 for a Director of Research, also called Project Director, AI and Youth Safety. The center is an interfaculty research center at Harvard. The posting says the center seeks someone to lead its AI and Youth Safety initiative. The role involves defining unanswered questions about young people’s relationships with AI and developing a research agenda. The director will also convene leading thinkers across disciplines and translate research into evidence for public understanding and policy.

The basic qualifications are a bachelor’s degree and 8 years of progressive experience, or a related advanced degree with 5 years experience. The appointment is a term position currently expected to extend to June 30, 2027, with potential for renewal subject to departmental funding and need. Harvard says it is unable to provide visa sponsorship for the position. The position is salary grade level 059, and all offers are made by HLS Human Resources. The work format allows some duties at a non-Harvard location, and hybrid employees must work in a Harvard registered state when not at a Harvard or Harvard-designated location.

The posting says the director will lead day-to-day direction of the initiative, shape research design, conduct original research and writing, and ensure outputs meet standards for quality, rigor, ethics, and real-world relevance. The director will provide technical and methodological leadership, review research plans, instruments, analyses, and drafts, and select and justify quantitative, qualitative, or mixed methods. The role includes managing and mentoring research teams, hiring and supervising staff such as research coordinators, research associates, employee fellows, research assistants, and interns. The director will help shape the emerging field by identifying high-impact and underexplored questions and adapting the research agenda as new evidence and technologies emerge. The director will build an interdisciplinary community across Harvard and beyond, including researchers, youth-serving organizations, policymakers, technologists, educators, civil society organizations, and industry partners.

The posting says the director will design convenings, workshops, and ongoing collaborations, and support grant development and funder engagement, including proposal narratives, methods and measurement sections, project plans, and reporting deliverables. The director will oversee research program operations and communications with Center teams, manage timelines and outputs such as publications, tools, events, and reporting, and support public-facing outputs consistent with the Center’s Open Access Policy. The director will represent the Center’s AI and youth safety work at convenings and events such as working groups, symposia, and briefings. Qualifications include deep familiarity with AI and online safety issues such as generative AI and AI companions, youth online safety and development, platform governance, privacy and data protection, content moderation, age-appropriate design, human-computer interaction, evaluation and measurement, and the policy landscape shaping AI systems. The posting also lists a demonstrated record of AI or machine learning research, such as publications at peer-reviewed venues, open-source contributions, or equivalent technical work, and strong writing, presentation, and collaboration skills.

The posting says the center is committed to making sense of the digital environment and ensuring it promotes human agency, dignity, and genuine connection. It describes the opportunity as rare and unusual and the community as flourishing and intellectually robust, with faculty, staff, students, fellows, and affiliates from multiple disciplines and backgrounds. It says a successful candidate will be open to learning from experiments, taking good ideas from wherever they come, and changing course quickly. It says Harvard offers a comprehensive benefits package including paid time off, parental leave, medical, dental, and vision coverage starting on day one, retirement plans with university contributions, wellbeing and mental health resources, family and caregiver support, professional development including tuition assistance and reimbursement, and commuter benefits, discounts, and campus perks. It says Harvard is committed to equal opportunity and non-discrimination and seeks talent from all parts of society and the world.

The posting says the work schedule and location will be set by the department at its discretion based on operational needs, and certain visa types and funding sources may limit work location. It says individuals must meet work location sponsorship requirements prior to employment. It says additional details will be discussed during the interview process. It says the site and its contents are licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Unported license unless otherwise noted. It says the page was last updated Nov 20, 2026.

stories.Headline: Trump and Xi agree humans must oversee military AI decisions
stories.Summary:
US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed that humans must stay involved in military decisions using artificial intelligence technologies. This agreement occurred during a meeting in Shenzhen, China, on November 19, as part of a larger trip to Asia. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the deal on November 20, stating that no major military operation should be launched without humans. The two leaders also spoke about the need for regulations, according to a report from Fox News published on Thursday. This deal was presented as one of the major achievements of the trip where Trump also met Vladimir Putin.

The agreement requires that super intelligence, the preferred term of the Trump administration, should not be allowed to be autonomous for actions. It does not change the competition for AI supremacy, but the US wants to maintain a lead against dangerous Chinese models. On November 16, the Commerce Department restricted China's access to advanced AI chips, including those used by overseas data centres. The interim rule, written by the National Security Council and Treasury Department, also curtailed remote access to AI chips and servers. China can only purchase the H200, which is the second tier AI chip from Nvidia, using specific government licences.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the lead official on China relations, said the agreement on human involvement would not be affected by competition. He stated that US AI labs must keep their technological lead to defend against Chinese models used in cyberattacks. Bessent previously met with Vice Premier He Lifeng to create a dialogue where both countries can notify each other of threats. When asked about cabinet disagreements, Bessent said that all officials are committed to following the instructions given by President Trump. He also noted that there has been a paucity of orders from China for the H200 AI chip.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was ousted after confirming a relationship with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese agent and business executive. Alice Huang is under investigation by the US government for potentially smuggling chips, but this topic was not raised with Xi. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced scrutiny for his role in preventing the export of advanced AI chips to China. Bessent had previously criticized the Commerce Department for not adding Megaspeed International, a company tied to Alice Huang, to a blacklist. These events involving Nvidia and the suspected agent occurred before the bilateral meeting between the two presidents in Shenzhen.

The US government believes that China is probably many years behind the United States in building out its own chip stack. The Trump administration has taken a very firm line on chip restrictions to ensure that proper controls are now in place. The US is concerned about the use of artificial intelligence in cyberattacks and the smuggling of advanced processors to China. The Treasury Department and National Security Council worked together to write the rules restricting remote access to servers and chips. These restrictions aim to limit the ability of Chinese entities to rent computing power from data centres located overseas.

The US will continue to tighten limits on remote access and advanced AI chips to maintain a necessary technological lead. The Trump administration expects that the current policy regarding the export of Nvidia chips will not undergo any immediate changes. The dialogue created between Bessent and He Lifeng will allow the two nations to notify each other about technology threats. The articles do not state if the US will add Megaspeed International to the trade blacklist following the recent criticisms. It remains open whether the two countries will reach further agreements on AI regulations beyond the scope of military actions.

stories.Headline: New Zealand cyber centre says hackers use AI tool Artex to automate attacks
stories.Summary:
New Zealand's National Cyber Security Centre warned on 21 November 2026 that hackers are using artificial intelligence to carry out cyber attacks, and it said organisations across the country must act. Its cyber defence operations director, Dr Emma Bickerstaffe, said there had been a rise over the past week in attackers using an open source AI tool called Artex to target organisations worldwide. Artex was developed by researchers to check for system vulnerabilities that hackers could exploit, and although it had been taken down from the internet, it had been replicated and was now being used to automate attacks on different organisations at the same time. Bickerstaffe said the key change was that phases of an attack could now be automated, which let threat actors act faster.

She said an attack that might previously have taken weeks could now go from initial reconnaissance and scanning of an organisation to exploitation in a matter of hours. Bickerstaffe said access to open source AI tools meant attackers could act opportunistically and were looking for any target they could gain access to. She said that if attackers got in using AI, they could move across a system, reach what she called an organisation's crown jewels, and access or change data. She said there had been instances in New Zealand where attackers used the tool to try to get into an organisation and failed, and other incidents where they successfully gained access and viewed data.

She advised organisations to limit the devices and systems they connect to the internet and to implement multi-factor authentication, which she said could stop an attack if a system was compromised. Her comments came after Forest & Bird and the New Zealand Defence Force both reported cyber security incidents on Friday, though the tools used by those hackers are not yet known. Forest & Bird confirmed supporters' details had been exposed, and chief executive Sam Rowland told RNZ it had taken immediate steps to secure its systems, including a forensic search of its website that uncovered malicious files. Rowland said the organisation was working with technology and cyber security experts to establish the full extent of the incident, was contacting people it knew were affected to explain what information had been accessed, and had notified NZ Police, the National Cyber Security Centre and the Office of the Privacy Commissioner.

Those affected were warned the stolen data could be used to create scam emails, phone calls or convincing text messages, and were told to be cautious about unexpected messages even if they contained personalised information. The New Zealand Defence Force took some of its websites down following a breach, after its website provider informed it of unauthorised access to its website systems. An NZDF spokesperson told RNZ that preliminary inquiries indicated a database associated with the Force4Families Defence Discounts scheme had been accessed, and that the database included names and email addresses of registered users. The NZDF said those who may have been affected had been contacted, and it advised individuals registered through the website to remain alert to phishing emails, scams and unsolicited requests for personal information.

stories.Headline: Schools and universities update curricula and policies to prepare students for an AI-driven workforce
stories.Summary:
The Standard Chartered Group announced plans in May to cut over 15 per cent of back-office roles by 2030. This decision affects about 7,800 employees globally as the bank replaces lower-value human capital with investment capital. On November 15, community members gathered at Woodstock Day School in Saugerties for an AI Reality Check event. This discussion was organized by trustee Eve Fox after her son Will expressed worries about his future career. These events highlight how artificial intelligence is currently reshaping the global workforce and the education system.

The bank's strategy involves replacing human roles with financial capital, though some employees may retrain and reposition. In Hong Kong, eight publicly funded universities will launch about 30 new programmes during the 2025-28 triennium. These courses cover AI, cybersecurity, and creative industries, while the Education Bureau's 2026-27 list includes intelligent information systems. Saugerties adopted an AI policy on January 14, 2025, and Onteora adopted its own policy on August 18. Hunter-Tannersville aims to complete its formal AI policy by the end of the 2026-27 school year.

Chief executive Bill Winters stated the bank's strategy focuses on replacing lower-value human capital with investment capital. Head of School Ashley Hughes said the school wants to hear from students about how they use AI. She expressed hope that schools can handle AI better than they did with the rise of social media. Rick Knutsen called the process of developing school policies an iterative process during a November 17 board meeting. He also wrote a resolution adopted on October 15 by the New York State School Boards Association.

Former Singaporean president Halimah Yacob described the bank's phrasing regarding human capital as disturbing and cold. Students like Will Fox and Luca Kaufman worry that their degrees might become arbitrary or useless in the future. College Board reported that 84 per cent of surveyed high school students used generative AI for schoolwork in May 2025. This figure rose from 79 per cent in January, showing that many students are already using these tools. Fresh graduates are worried because entry-level positions are the first to bear the brunt of AI automation.

The World Economic Forum's 2025 report says AI and robotics are simultaneously creating and eliminating jobs globally. By 2030, about 40 per cent of employers expect to reduce headcount in areas that AI can automate. New York Governor Kathy Hochul recently broke ground on Empire AI's permanent home at the University at Buffalo. An October 13 analysis found that over half of New York's 678 school districts lacked formal AI policies. Traditional business curricula are now integrating Python, data-driven strategies, and AI-related elective streams to maintain employability.

Universities are adjusting by emphasizing oral presentations, staged assignments, and real-world tasks to assess students without AI. Daniela Amodei believes companies will emphasize human communication, empathy, and collaboration, which increases the importance of the humanities. The New York State School Boards Association is lobbying for legislation requiring AI companies to meet safety standards. Schools are still deciding how to define the nature of work and what it means to be human. It remains open who will be marginalized and which specific human skills will be most amplified.

stories.Headline: IBM Philippines' Lope Doromal urges businesses to pair AI governance with orchestration for autonomous agents
stories.Summary:
Philippine businesses need to build real-time controls into their artificial intelligence systems as they move from individual AI applications to autonomous agents operating across enterprise workflows, an IBM Philippines executive said in an exclusive online interview with The Manila Times. Lope Doromal, technical community leader at IBM Philippines, said governance policies alone cannot ensure that AI systems operate within approved boundaries. Organizations must combine governance with orchestration to monitor AI agents, manage their access to data and applications, and intervene when their actions deviate from established rules. Doromal said that without orchestration, control remains separate from execution, leaving organizations to rely on teams to interpret and implement policies correctly. He said an enterprise can be fully compliant and still fully fragmented, adding that when AI systems cannot be coordinated under pressure, scale stops being an advantage and becomes a risk.

An IBM Institute for Business Value study cited by Doromal found that only 18 percent of surveyed organizations maintain a complete and current inventory of their AI assets. Just 27 percent know where AI is being used within their organizations. Doromal recommended establishing an agent registry, a continuously updated record identifying every AI agent deployed across an organization, including its purpose, owner, data access permissions, model version and operational status. He cited IBM Concert Observe, powered by IBM Instana Observability, as an example of technology that can discover AI components and map their interactions across applications. An IBV study on AI governance and business value found that 71 percent of organizations with high AI governance maturity had developed specific guidelines identifying acceptable and unacceptable uses of AI.

Doromal said every agent should also have a formal identity and access management framework defining its owner, authorized activities and access to enterprise systems. He said that access should be set to the minimum level needed to do the job, with the ability to revoke it instantly if behavior falls outside expected boundaries. He said a single misconfiguration can become an organization-wide liability when agents operate across multiple systems and no responsible team has been designated to handle incidents. He said the governance architecture must be built before anything goes wrong, not after. He said accountability in AI governance is distributed across leadership rather than concentrated in a single function.

The same IBV study found that 63 percent of surveyed organizations reported CEO involvement in ensuring effective AI governance, while approximately one in three had a CEO directly accountable for it. An IBV study cited by Doromal found that only 9 percent of surveyed global executives fully understood their dependencies across AI vendors, models and infrastructure. Organizations reported an average of six AI-related disruptions over the preceding two years, with vendor services identified as the leading cause. The study also found that 81 percent of executives expected a major AI vendor outage to significantly disrupt operations, while 71 percent said switching their primary AI vendor or model would be difficult. Doromal cited IBM watsonx Orchestrate as an open, hybrid enterprise agent management platform designed to manage agents regardless of where they were developed or which technology they use.

IBM Sovereign Core is intended for organizations seeking greater operational control through a customer-operated control plane built on open standards. Doromal said poor data management is the single most commonly cited barrier to effective AI governance, and that every AI model and agent sits downstream from the data it uses. He recommended testing governance processes through one high-impact use case before extending them across the organization. He said governance should be embedded in the workflow, not the calendar, adding that policy update cycles should be measured in days rather than quarters. The IBM IBV 2026 CEO Study found that 80 percent of Philippine CEOs surveyed said they were comfortable making major strategic decisions using AI-generated insights.

However, only 63 percent of Philippine executives surveyed said they had a clear vision of how AI would deliver a competitive advantage for their organizations. The study also found that 73 percent admitted the risk of falling behind was driving them to invest in technologies before fully understanding the value those technologies would bring. Doromal said the gap between investment and preparation makes governance a business concern, not merely a technical or regulatory requirement. He advised local organizations to work with technology partners that support skills transfer and strengthen internal capabilities, rather than leaving businesses dependent on external providers. He said governance maturity is not built in a single initiative, but is forged in the daily decisions that mitigate risks and accelerate value.

Organised by Eco-Business in partnership with the United Nations Development Programme, the inaugural Unlocking AI for Sustainability forum convened over 100 senior delegates to explore how AI can support sustainable development while managing its risks. AI technologies could add up to US$15 trillion to global GDP by 2030 by optimising trade, power grids and operational efficiency, including an estimated US$1 trillion for Asean economies, if properly deployed and governed, said UNDP. Edward Vrkić, Resident Representative for UNDP Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei Darussalam, said AI governance needs to account for stakeholders who lack the economic clout or infrastructure to manage and respond to the technology's risks. He said there is disparity between countries, but as concerningly, within countries, and that these are not just geographic but also demographic. He said this demands more inclusive design that ensures no one is left behind, highlighting how women are twice as exposed to job losses brought on by AI automation.

Jessica Cheam, Founder and CEO of Eco-Business, said Asean has a rare chance to rewrite the rules of its digital economy by putting people at the centre. She said the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, signed on 14 November and the first region-wide pact of its kind, is a step in the right direction by setting common rules for digital trade while helping the region's digital economy to grow to US$2 trillion by 2030. She said AI, digital rules and energy security are now on the same regional agenda, and that with Singapore taking over as Asean chair, this gives a real opportunity and a real responsibility to turn diverse AI provisions into practice across all 11 member states. Benoît Sauveroche, First Counsellor for Digital Transformation, Research and Innovation at the European Union Delegation to Singapore, said AI partnerships should look beyond investing in technological systems alone and into people and institutional and regional capacity as well. He said the most valuable innovation is innovation that people can trust, and that AI must be anchored in trusted infrastructure, sound governance, quality data, strong skills and a clear commitment to fundamental rights.

Sauveroche said the European AI Office, responsible for developing and enforcing AI guardrails, is developing the AI for Public Good initiative to leverage AI models. Leaders warned that the data centres and computing infrastructure needed to power AI place mounting pressure on electricity grids, land and water systems. Without deliberate policy choices, investment and capacity-building, AI could deepen existing technological and digital divides across and within countries. Vrkić also emphasised AI-driven gains in areas such as town planning, urban management and delivering greater efficiencies in basic services when well governed. The forum convened key decision makers to deliberate issues ranging from technological deployment, infrastructure investment, governance, energy and climate strategies.

stories.Headline: Austin ISD trustees adopt first AI policy with 18-month timeline for detailed rules
stories.Summary:
On Nov. 12, all eight trustees present on the dais voted to adopt Austin ISD's first-ever local policy on artificial intelligence, the Austin Chronicle reported on Nov. 19, 2026. The board acted after hearing multiple calls over the past several weeks from mostly parents to create some kind of districtwide policy on AI. The calls followed widely reported generative AI bans adopted in New York City, for pre-K through 8th grade, and in Los Angeles public school systems. AISD Board President Lynn Boswell told her colleagues at a Nov. 5 meeting that the district had been kicking this down the road for three years. Boswell said students are being impacted by this.

The policy gives the district an 18-month timeline to set more detailed rules about AI use for students, teachers and staff. Students can only use district-approved AI tools with teacher permission for classwork and must produce original work and properly credit sources, including AI tools used in creating the work. The superintendent is tasked with approving AI programs. The student policy gives an AI citation example: created with the assistance of Gemini and reviewed for accuracy and tone. In the policy agreement for staff, teachers cannot assign and/or require the use of AI tools outside of the list of district-approved tools and resources for classwork.

Trustee Arati Singh told the Chronicle that approved student uses of AI could include modifying text for those with different reading abilities, or coding to create games. Singh added that the new policy extends beyond students to teachers and staff within the district's central office, who could potentially use AI to find patterns in student outcomes and large datasets. Singh said school districts are already using AI to analyze student outcome data, help develop schedules, and to screen employee applications. Singh said she just hopes we don't lose the human touch in the process of adopting AI in the organization. Singh wrote to the Chronicle that she imagines at some point TEA and the State Board of Education will come up with better guardrails, and that until then her expectation is the district will fill in the gaps.

Amy Whiteaker, a science teacher in the district and parent of a middle and high schooler in AISD, said she does not want her students or her kids to think that AI will always have the answers and use it in place of their learning. Whiteaker said she does not want them to lose the ability to critically think, or to make decisions, or analyze data, or use reasoning. Ann Richards librarian Minda Anderson, who teaches media and research literacy, argued that a total district ban on generative AI for high schoolers isn't helpful and that students need situations to learn about the tool in a safe environment. Anderson said there's so little regulation on generative AI companies that we need to hold them accountable for the tools and services they're providing. Whiteaker told the Chronicle there have been incidents of students talking with Google chatbots, and the chat gives them advice for how to commit suicide, or the chatbot will empathize with them about how their parents are being unfair.

When Austin ISD blocked YouTube on elementary and middle school students' school-issued laptops this year, Whiteaker saw a noticeable difference in her classroom. Whiteaker told the Chronicle that during class students constantly were just watching ASMR and slime being created, and that it's very difficult to monitor 30 kids in the same room. Whiteaker said it's now less distracting, and therefore they're more into what they do in class. One way AISD is already piloting AI use in the district is by allowing students to take notes with Google's Gemini Notebook at the Ann Richards School, where Whiteaker teaches. Students can also use it to create AI-generated podcasts from those notes, Whiteaker told the Chronicle.

The district's future rules must address student understanding of and safeguards against potential harms of AI, including bias, cognitive surrender, and mental health risks, per the policy. The policy also adds bullying and harassment through the use of AI platforms to the district's disciplinary code. The student policy agreement reads that the student will not use AI programs to create harmful, explicit or intimidating content. Anderson noted that updates to software the district is already using, like Google Classroom, can include new AI features that fly under the district's radar. Anderson said we need to know about changes that they're making to their tools before our students are facing them.
