stories.Headline: Phoenix mayor Kate Gallego seeks tech investment while curbing data center strain
stories.Summary:
Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego is trying to attract more technology investment to her city while limiting the strain that data centers place on electricity, water and residents, according to an Axios interview published on November 20, 2026. Phoenix has become a bellwether for the demands the AI industry places on power and water in a hot, resource-constrained world, and Gallego is navigating a dilemma facing communities nationwide. She said at an event co-hosted by the University of Chicago's Institute of Politics and Energy Policy Institute, and moderated by Axios, that she wants Phoenix to lead in technology and be a tech-forward community. She added that she wants companies that care about the community and give back to it, rather than a race for the deepest incentives and the cheapest power, saying the city is open for business but not for sale.

Phoenix ranks fourth among major U.S. data center markets by operational capacity, and the debate there has expanded from how much development the region can accommodate to what communities should demand in return. Gallego helped push to eliminate Arizona's generous data center sales tax exemptions, and the state enacted a three-year pause on new applications in the summer of 2026. She opposes a blanket construction moratorium and favors more local control over where facilities are built, particularly near homes, and Phoenix adopted tougher zoning rules in 2025 requiring special permits for new data centers. Data centers have requested so much electricity in the Phoenix region that, if all the projects materialized, they could account for roughly two-thirds of the area's power demand, Gallego said, warning that this would not be a balanced or economically sustainable economy.

Phoenix's efforts to rein in data centers have sparked legal challenges, with developers originally seeking roughly $750 million in compensation over the zoning restrictions adopted in 2025, and the city has granted several exemptions while fighting other claims in court. Gallego told Axios that the city has been open and good partners to the industry and that it is deeply disappointing the developers do not want to work with the city, while developers argue the restrictions infringe on their property rights and diminish land values under Arizona law. Gallego is also weighing tradeoffs between electricity, water and heat, noting that newer cooling technologies can cut water use at data centers but often require more electricity, and that many data centers get power from natural gas plants in a part of the state that is very constrained around water. An Arizona State University study published in May found that data centers can raise nearby temperatures by as much as 4 degrees Fahrenheit, and Gallego, who established the nation's first publicly funded municipal heat-response office in 2021, said she is jealous of Midwestern mayors who can reuse data centers' waste heat to warm buildings.

Arizona's Democratic sweep could give Gallego more allies, with Democrats flipping both legislative chambers and Gov. Katie Hobbs winning reelection, giving the state full Democratic control for the first time since 1966, and Gallego said affordability dominated the election, with data center subsidies and community impacts part of that debate. Gallego, the longest-serving current mayor of America's 10 largest cities, says communities should have more bargaining power over data centers, including where they are built and what residents get in return, which could mean more permanent jobs, transparency about electricity and water use, and benefits for affected neighbors. It remains unclear whether she can have it both ways, attracting more tech investment while limiting its costs to residents, especially as developers challenge the city's regulatory authority. Gallego also worries that Arizona might be betting too heavily on an industry whose long-term trajectory remains uncertain.

stories.Headline: SpaceX subsidiary Cursor considers phasing out Chinese AI models to reduce geopolitical risk
stories.Summary:
Cursor, an artificial intelligence coding platform owned by SpaceX, is considering the removal of Chinese developed models from its systems. This decision follows a months long investigation conducted by the House Select Committee on China and the House Committee on Homeland Security. The company had previously built its Composer 2 model using Kimi K2.5 from the Chinese laboratory Moonshot AI. SpaceX completed its acquisition of Cursor in August after first announcing a formal agreement to buy the firm in June.

The transition would involve phasing out open weight models from the People's Republic of China to reduce geopolitical risk. This shift occurs after SpaceX acquired Cursor at an implied equity value of 60 billion dollars. The House report suggests that American firms adopted these models because of their low cost, customization options, and near frontier performance. Lawmakers are now recommending a national American open weight initiative to provide competitive alternatives for the market.

The House committees stated that Beijing intends to use these technological gains to create long term global dependence. They also suggested expanding an October order that banned DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems to include all Chinese models in federal contracts. While Cursor, SpaceX, and DoorDash did not respond to requests for comment, Airbnb declined to speak on the matter. The report emphasizes that the United States currently lacks an open weight alternative that meets market demands for price and performance.

The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security announced an interim final rule on Monday to stop Chinese companies from accessing AI chips remotely. Washington is specifically concerned about the use of overseas data centers and the process of distillation to train new models. These measures aim to protect the American tech stack as the battle for AI supremacy between the two nations intensifies in 2026. The government continues to monitor how Chinese models are integrated into the infrastructure of private American companies.

stories.Headline: John and Nisha Whitehead argue humans, not machines, pose the real danger
stories.Summary:
A cascade of technological failures struck in late 2026, beginning with a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted Outlook and other online services around the globe. A nationwide ground stop then brought air travel across America to a standstill, disrupting thousands of flights and leaving travelers stranded. Major banks experienced problems with their online systems, and United Airlines grounded departing flights after yet another computer failure. Reports said the highly classified network the National Security Agency uses for internal communications had gone down, and Apple joined the growing list of technology giants experiencing widespread disruptions. Users reported problems accessing iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music and other services, and millions of Americans were reminded how dependent their daily lives have become on technologies they neither understand nor control.

The Trump administration had only recently expanded the FAA's new SMART artificial-intelligence system to air traffic control centers across the country. The administration has aggressively promoted AI, or SI for Super Intelligence as Trump insists it be called, as the answer to everything from government inefficiency to national security. It also pushes to reduce regulatory barriers and expand the use of automated systems, yet the administration insists AI had nothing to do with the airline shutdown. Federal officials instead blamed a malfunction involving aging air traffic control infrastructure, with problems arising as equipment was being replaced and communications systems updated. The FBI issued a report about autonomous AI hacking tools such as Artex AI being used to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally and breach networks in under three hours.

John and Nisha Whitehead wrote the article, published November 18, 2026, and the Rutherford Institute article appeared on Scoop on Friday, 20 November 2026 at 8:51 pm. They asked who is responsible when the technological systems upon which society depends begin to fail. They asked who is accountable when government officials and corporate executives rush to embrace new technologies without ensuring safeguards, infrastructure and human oversight are in place. They asked what happens when people become so dependent on technology, and so willing to surrender responsibility for managing it, that they can no longer distinguish a machine's failure from the failure of the human beings entrusted with its operation. They wrote that the real danger may be the human hunger for power and our willingness to surrender control to those who wield it.

The writers said Hollywood has spent decades warning about machines that might become so intelligent, so independent and so powerful that they no longer need human beings. In Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey, the seemingly infallible computer HAL 9000 turns against the astronauts who entrusted their lives to its control. In Pixar's WALL-E, humanity has abandoned an uninhabitable Earth and retreated to a massive spaceship where nearly every human need is anticipated and satisfied by machines. The writers said people no longer walk, no longer work, barely notice the world around them, and are entertained, fed, transported and distracted by systems that make virtually every decision for them. They said the ship's captain must struggle to reclaim his authority from an automated system programmed to maintain the status quo.

The writers said the discovery of nuclear fission opened the door to extraordinary scientific advances and also made possible weapons capable of obliterating entire cities. In August 1945, the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing tens of thousands of people immediately and many more in the aftermath. They said the bombs did not decide to destroy those cities, human beings did, and that the same computers that revolutionized medicine, science, education and communication have helped give rise to a surveillance state. According to the FBI, hackers have used ARTEX to automate cyberattacks against financial institutions, government agencies and private companies, with some attacks progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. Google's Threat Intelligence Group warns that malicious actors are increasingly deploying autonomous AI systems capable of identifying vulnerabilities and carrying out attacks at machine speed, with dramatically reduced human intervention.

The writers said the Church Committee, fifty years ago, exposed extensive abuses by America's intelligence agencies, including surveillance operations directed against citizens exercising their constitutional rights. They said the government does not acquire a constitutional exemption merely because its abuses are carried out by a computer rather than a human being. They said the more powerful the technology, the greater the need for meaningful restraints on the people who control it. They said we cannot afford to ignore the human beings behind the machines, the people who create the systems, finance them, deploy them, profit from them and look the other way when those systems are used to violate human rights. The articles leave open who is responsible when the systems fail and what happens when people can no longer distinguish a machine's failure from human failure.

stories.Headline: Hickenlooper proposes a Senate select committee on AI and urges a day one regulation plan
stories.Summary:
Colorado Sen. John Hickenlooper said this week that the person leading the Senate Democratic majority next year should have a “day one plan for responsible regulation” on artificial intelligence. Hickenlooper has so far withheld an endorsement in the race between Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen. Hickenlooper said Friday that there hasn’t been enough progress in Congress since Democrats formed a working group on AI three years ago. He said Democrats convened tech leaders from across the country to figure out next steps on the technology. Hickenlooper said there is “a perception that we haven’t done anything” on artificial intelligence.

Hickenlooper said he proposed a select committee on artificial intelligence to consolidate the conversation, writing letters to both Schumer and Van Hollen. In those letters he wrote that with the presidential election two years away, Democrats have a two-year audition on affordability, accountability and AI safety. Schumer is favored to win reelection in the closed-door Dec. 1 caucus leadership vote. A spokeswoman said Schumer has been working closely with the incoming heads of committees to develop an ambitious AI agenda and hit the ground running in January. Top policy proposals could be regulating data centers, safety standards and stepping up monitoring and research.

Hickenlooper said his priorities are robust third-party evaluation requirements, mitigation of national security challenges and clear rules of the road to hold AI companies accountable. Schumer spokeswoman Allison Biasotti said Senate Democrats will make AI a top priority of the new Democratic majority. Biasotti said they are working to deliver comprehensive legislation addressing the serious risks AI poses to national security, workers and consumers while keeping America at the forefront of innovation. Hickenlooper said Democrats have been publicly and privately discussing what their first steps could be on artificial intelligence when they take the majority in January. He said Republicans who have led the House and Senate for the last two years have focused mostly on innovation.

Van Hollen said he supports the idea, saying “I do think we need a joint committee” because AI covers so many different areas impacting lives. Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, the incoming chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, said he would “want to see the specifics” and what topics would be covered. Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, expected to become chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, did not immediately endorse the idea. Sanders said Congress has been “way, way, way behind where it should be in protecting the American people.” Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, the current Republican chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, said a plan to take the issue out of his committee and others “makes no sense.”

President Joe Biden’s administration called on lawmakers to develop policies after a 2023 executive order on AI oversight, which President Donald Trump rescinded soon after returning to office. The bipartisan working group on artificial intelligence formed by Schumer released a report in 2024 recommending the U.S. spend at least $32 billion over the next three years to develop artificial intelligence and implement safeguards around it. Trump, who will hold the power of the veto, has repeatedly maintained that little regulation is needed even as the technology has progressed at a rapid clip. House Democrats have also been discussing a way forward on AI and have proposed a robust package of proposals. This week, three Democrats announced the launch of the House AI Safety and Innovation caucus to address security risks.

Cruz said there were already bipartisan conversations about the issue looking forward to next year. Cruz said he hopes in the next Congress Republicans and Democrats can find common ground on addressing catastrophic risk. It is unclear if other Democrats, especially the heads of committees already working on AI proposals, will support Hickenlooper’s select committee idea. The articles do not say whether Schumer or Van Hollen responded to Hickenlooper’s letters. The articles do not say what the House AI Safety and Innovation caucus will do beyond addressing security risks.

stories.Headline: AI stock sell-off pushes S&P 500 into correction and Nasdaq into loss for the year
stories.Summary:
A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months. The sell-off knocked the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high. The Nasdaq composite slumped 5.3%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9%. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.

The S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39, the Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73. The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, its worst since April 2025 as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9%, Broadcom fell 12.1%, and the PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%. Corning slid 10.9%, Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%, and Nvidia closed 13.8% lower.

Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird, said the notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market is ending as we speak, and that is what’s being priced right now. He said he does not think that means the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over. The articles attribute the AI trade’s loss of steam partly to worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level. AI stocks have hefty market values and a much bigger impact on the market’s direction, and were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year.

The sell-off spread around the globe, with Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each falling more than 5% overnight and European indexes falling sharply as well. Outside of tech, most stocks gained ground, with Cheerios maker General Mills rising 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gaining 1%. The University of Michigan’s latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists’ expectations, though sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday, and Brent crude oil rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen, and Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.

Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out. More recently it has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder, and since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month the stock has dropped more than 25%. Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fell 9.1% to $88.30 but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value, and Friday’s drop amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior, a bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook, now Meta, in the early days after its May 2012 IPO. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days but fell below its IPO price a month later.

The articles leave open what happens next, noting only that market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. They give no further figures beyond those stated, and the third article’s text ends mid-sentence in its account of SpaceX. The articles do not say how the sell-off will end or what the Huang scandal involved. They do not say which candidates won the midterm elections or which states passed measures on data center construction. They give no further detail on the U.S. war with Iran or on the compromise Iraq reached with the militia.

stories.Headline: Bishop Cantú updates bishops on task force plans for AI education and policy safeguards
stories.Summary:
Bishop Oscar Cantú of San José, California, gave an update on the U.S. bishops' task force on artificial intelligence at the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' fall plenary assembly. He spoke on Nov. 18 during the assembly held Nov. 16, 19 in Baltimore. Cantú chairs the Task Force on Preserving Human Dignity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence. The bishops established the task force in September after meeting with AI experts and representatives of technology companies. Cantú discussed the group's conversations with technology companies and its plans for Catholic education and public policy.

The task force plans to offer formation opportunities for bishops, including webinars for bishops and diocesan leaders after the new year with dates to be announced in the coming weeks. It hopes to work with Catholic universities to provide formation opportunities and collect best practices for AI education in Catholic schools, seminaries, and universities. On public policy, it will work with the USCCB's Government Relations team to advocate for safeguards including transparency, accountability, and human oversight. Cantú pointed to Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica Humanitas as a guide, citing No. 15, and to Pope Leo XIII's 1891 encyclical Rerum Novarum. The task force is chaired by Cantú and includes Cardinal Blase Cupich of Chicago, Archbishop Paul Etienne of Seattle, and Archbishop Shelton Fabre of Louisville, Kentucky.

It also includes Bishop Barry Knestout of Richmond, Virginia, Auxiliary Bishop James Massa of Brooklyn, New York, Bishop Michael Olson of Fort Worth, Texas, and Auxiliary Bishop Slawomir Szkredka of Los Angeles. Three academic consultants advise the group: Charles Camosy of The Catholic University of America, Kim Daniels of Georgetown University's Initiative on Catholic Social Thought and Public Life, and Meghan Sullivan of the University of Notre Dame. Cantú said the Church should approach AI with neither naïve enthusiasm nor unfounded fear, and should take part in conversations with technology leaders, public officials, and communities. He said the task force's meetings with technology companies have gone well so far, with many expressing interest in further conversations about the ethical questions surrounding AI. One technology leader told the bishops to trust their pastoral instincts, saying society does not need them to be experts in technology but pastors who care about their people.

Cantú said it is too early to know how much AI will change the workforce but stressed that workers' rights must remain a concern, noting work is not just a way to earn a living but a place where people form relationships and discover their vocations. He raised concerns about how growing up with AI could affect children and young people, saying AI will become a permanent companion for many young people. He said educators and parents are deeply concerned that young people remain capable of critical thought and do not lose the capacity for friendship, prayer, and genuine human encounter. He encouraged Catholic educators to develop guidelines for the use of AI in schools and warned that AI-generated images and false information could make it increasingly difficult to discern what is true. At a Nov. 17 press conference, USCCB president Archbishop Paul Coakley of Oklahoma City said "We are the deciders" and that responsibility cannot be abdicated to artificial intelligence.

Cantú likened the changes brought by AI to those of the industrial revolution, recalling how the Church responded through Rerum Novarum rather than opposing industrialization, and spoke up for workers' rights. He said Rerum Novarum ultimately led to concrete results including minimum wage laws, Social Security, and child labor restrictions, and that Magnifica Humanitas asks us to work for policies and practices that keep AI at the service of the human person. He cited Pope Leo's warning that lethal or irreversible decisions should not be entrusted to artificial systems. Cantú said that a year ago AI was only occasionally in the headlines and today is in multiple headlines every single day, asking how to separate fact from hyperbole. He quoted the pope's words that in the era of AI, when human dignity is threatened by new forms of dehumanization, ours is the pressing duty to remain profoundly human.

Cantú told the bishops that at a moment when society is asking what machines can do, we must remind the world who the human person is, and that Magnifica Humanitas calls us not to fear the future but to help shape it with humanity at the center. He said the Church, which proclaims Jesus Christ as the truth, must become a school of discernment in the digital age, and that our institutions can be places where people learn to verify, to slow down, and to reason together. Coakley said the most important thing is to be the human agents who guide and direct artificial intelligence, calling AI in a certain sense a limitation, and said human intelligence is created by God and is ours to guide and direct. Cantú said the task force also means listening to people already feeling the effects of AI, including workers, parents, and teachers, rather than leaving the discussion to technology companies. The articles do not say what the webinars will cover or when the task force will report again.

stories.Headline: Om Birla urges AI and digitisation to protect India's defence land
stories.Summary:
Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla spoke on Friday, November 20, 2026, regarding the management of defence land. He addressed the centenary celebrations of the Defence Estates Organisation in New Delhi. Birla called for the use of modern technology, digitisation, and Artificial Intelligence to strengthen land protection. He urged the organisation to prioritise securing assets and curbing encroachments. Timely land availability for the Armed Forces must also remain a top priority.

The Defence Estates Organisation manages and safeguards more than 1.7 million acres of defence land. Birla stated that accurate, secure, and accessible land records are vital for effective governance. He noted that AI and emerging technologies will address present operational demands and long-term administrative challenges. The Speaker commended digital upgrades already underway to improve the management of these vast assets. He stressed that conducive conditions for defence personnel are essential for national security.

Om Birla said that the organisation must combine its rich legacy with a forward-looking vision. He encouraged staff to study laws, rules, and administrative frameworks built over the past century. He suggested that officers should learn from former officers to maintain institutional continuity. Pairing this institutional wisdom with the technical agility of younger personnel will build stronger systems. He called for dedication, foresight, and a shared sense of national purpose from all employees.

The Speaker appreciated efforts to carry out accurate surveys while avoiding unnecessary disputes for civilians. He noted that the original character, green cover, forests, and heritage of cantonments must be protected. Development should be planned thoughtfully so the distinct identity of military cantonments survives rapid urban growth. He lauded civic initiatives for residents, including schools, healthcare, computer education, skill training, and water recycling. Sustained engagement with civil society is needed to respond to evolving community needs.

The Defence Estates Organisation is currently entering its second century of operation in India. It provides environmental protection and various social services to people living within military cantonments. The organisation is tasked with the large scale mandate of protecting millions of acres of land. It has established a century of administrative frameworks and rules to govern these specific areas. The agency is currently implementing digital upgrades to modernize its land record systems.

The organisation will continue to safeguard valuable defence land through innovation, transparency, and technological advancement. These efforts aim to strengthen the operational preparedness of the Armed Forces and preserve unique heritage. Officers and employees are expected to carry this responsibility forward with a renewed commitment to service. The articles do not state the specific timeline for completing the current digital upgrades. They leave open how the organisation will specifically integrate AI into its daily land management.

stories.Headline: U.N. talks extend debate on killer robots to 2028 without binding rules
stories.Summary:
Scores of countries ended a weeklong U.N. conference on weapons in Geneva on Saturday by agreeing to “elaborate” a possible accord on lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. The U.N.-backed talks produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years instead of firm rules. Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground at the conference. The outcome marked the latest failure to set guardrails for AI. The talks were reported by The Associated Press in articles published on November 21, 2026.

The agreement extends discussions for two more years and aims at a possible accord by 2028. Countries did not commit to binding rules sought by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries and activists. Before the meeting, seven countries proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook to prevent or limit machines killing without human control or accountability, and that effort fell short. Brazil joined Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama in proposing such negotiations. The talks centered on the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, ratified by 128 countries, where decisions are made by consensus.

Izumi Nakamitsu, the U.N. high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a “significant achievement” but acknowledged a “glass half full or half empty” scenario, citing Guterres’ hopes for a legally binding deal this year. Nakamitsu called for countries to begin work as early as Monday and to start thinking about how to get as strong as possible an instrument to prohibit and regulate lethal autonomous weapon systems. Guterres, who leaves office at the end of the year, had set a 2026 deadline for launching negotiations toward an agreement on autonomous weapons systems. Ambassador Frederico Meyer of Brazil said “Technology is moving faster than diplomacy” and “Diplomats are very slow.” The International Committee of the Red Cross said autonomous weapons can be “unpredictable,” unlike a bullet fired from a gun with a distinct and predictable trajectory.

Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language. Stop Killer Robots lamented a “watered-down mandate,” and Beatrice Fihn, founder of international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounted to “pushing the can down the road for two more years.” Fihn and others noted that most countries supported work toward a new treaty. Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue for the 14th year while these weapons enable atrocities. Pope Leo XIV and humanitarian groups have framed the issue as an existential debate, urging quick action to rein in AI weapons before they become too commonplace to regulate easily.

Advocacy groups bemoaned obstructionism at this week’s talks largely by Russia, which, like other leading developers of AI weapons including the United States, wants a freer hand to develop such high-tech weapons. The ICRC said that for years it and many others have urged states to ensure humans retain control over the use of force and that life-and-death decisions are never handed over to machines. Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened. The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts as major military powers jockey for dominance. Some experts have warned about such systems breaking out of human control and going rogue.

Because decisions at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons are made by consensus, any single country can thwart an agreement, and any deal is likely to be based on the lowest common denominator. Nakamitsu called for countries to begin work as early as Monday. The articles leave open whether the two-year extension will produce a binding accord by 2028. The articles leave open how the consensus rule might be overcome. The articles leave open whether the seven countries’ proposed negotiations will be launched.

stories.Headline: US investors flee AI stocks for value shares as Nasdaq falls 5%
stories.Summary:
On Friday, November 20, 2026, Wall Street fled from the AI boom into bonds and lower-priced shares outside the tech sector, with the Nasdaq composite dropping over 5% for its third decline of 2% or more that week and its biggest weekly decline since March 2020. Anthropic's sharp decline took it within a whisker of its IPO price before recovering to trade down over 8%, just a day after a record debut that briefly valued the AI lab above $2 trillion. The S&P 500 lost 3.7% for the day, leaving it down 12% from its record high close on October 6 and confirming the benchmark is in a correction, while the pullback left the Nasdaq lower for the year for the first time since April. The retreat partly reflects expectations that high inflation readings will force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in coming months, likely further increasing borrowing costs and compressing valuations, and making Treasuries and so-called value stocks look like a better bet. The median S&P 500 stock now is up 5% in 2026, which beats the 1% year-to-date gain in the S&P 500, an index hobbled of late by a 48% slump in Nvidia and deep declines in other AI stocks, including a 12% drop in Broadcom on Friday.

The S&P 500 value index is up 7% in 2026, compared to a 4% drop in the S&P 500 growth index, putting cautious value investing on track to beat growth for the first time since 2022, when inflation fears sent Wall Street into its worst slump since the 2008 financial crisis. Nvidia, the onetime market leader whose shares have been in free fall since the Nasdaq composite hit its most recent record in October, has shed more than $2.2 trillion of market value. Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera in El Segundo, California, said the prior day's AI IPO was a valuation test and that with the 10-year around 5% and the Fed still hiking, investors are asking how much of the AI story is already priced in. Philip Palumbo, CEO of Palumbo Wealth Management, said Kevin Warsh represents a different approach to monetary policy that has introduced additional uncertainty regarding interest rates, inflation and economic growth, and that markets do not like uncertainty.

Jim Awad, senior managing director at Clearstead Advisors LLC in New York, pointed to questions about the health of the underlying business at Nvidia and said the fundamentals have not deteriorated as much as the stock prices have, viewing it as a normal violent correction in a long-term upward trend in AI spending and in the markets. Lawrence Gillum, chief fixed-income strategist at LPL Financial, called it a classic flight-to-safety trade in which investors concerned about the AI trade move out of those stocks and into Treasury securities, and noted the Treasury market has rallied on the back of any hiccup in the AI trade. Many analysts and portfolio managers said they did not view the AI trade as impaired, and instead said an occasional washout can improve valuations and draw in investors with a longer-term perspective. The flight to value stocks and Treasury notes, which rallied sharply on Friday, is the latest sign of markets grappling with the extent to which a slowing buildout of AI infrastructure will hit US growth, a debate that has been going on all year, if not to this extreme.

stories.Headline: UN and Barbados co-host summit to develop multilateral AI risk management framework
stories.Summary:
UN Secretary-General António Guterres is traveling to Barbados to co-host a special summit on artificial intelligence safety this coming Monday. He will lead this event alongside Barbadian Prime Minister Mia Mottley to address the gap between accelerating risks and national capacities. The meeting aims to help various countries deal with the rapid pace of development regarding these emerging and powerful technologies. This gathering follows a trend where 135 leaders raised AI concerns at the UN General Assembly, compared to three in 2017. The summit seeks to capitalize on this growing international momentum to ensure that global safety measures keep pace with innovation.

The Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety will discuss a proposed multilateral risk management framework backed by independent and credible oversight. This framework is not a treaty or regulation, but a tool for countries to build their own national safety infrastructure. A Norway and Finland initiative for frontier models has 32 signatory states and the European Commission, while a French call has 17. President Emmanuel Macron hosted that second call, which was endorsed by 17 states and 10 AI developers to improve global control. The event will be a hybrid meeting in Barbados involving about 150 participants, including ministers, industry leaders, and scientific panel members.

Secretary-General Guterres will state that AI offers enormous benefits for health systems, scientific discovery, education, and improving hurricane forecasting for the world. He will also stress that risks are growing rapidly and that no single safety model can fit every individual country's needs. Amandeep Singh Gill, the UN Special Envoy for Digital and Emerging Technologies, said the need for safety infrastructure is often underappreciated. Gill noted that AI risks do not recognize borders, meaning risks can travel anywhere even if models are developed in few geographies. He argued that while international analysis is in a good position, practical action must now catch up with that analysis.

Developing countries fear missing out on AI benefits, so a second roundtable will focus on access, inclusion, and linguistic diversity. Many nations lack the computing power, talent, and capacity to test foreign models or prepare for cybersecurity breaches and other incidents. The World Development Report 2026 shows high-income countries have 500 incident response teams, while low-income countries have only six such teams. A senior diplomat from the United States will attend the summit, and experts from China are also expected to participate. These participants include heads of AI safety institutes and members of the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.

The articles explain that the summit is necessary because the capacity to respond to AI risks is currently outpaced by development. The UN is pushing for a multilateral approach because the ability to handle cybersecurity breaches is unevenly distributed across the globe. This effort builds on previous calls for the control of frontier AI models to prevent widespread harm from unregulated technological growth. The UN believes that strengthening national approaches to safety is the best way to manage these borderless and evolving digital threats. This background highlights a widening global gap in the technical expertise required to manage advanced artificial intelligence systems safely.

The summit will not cover the military uses of AI, focusing instead on civilian safety, inclusion, and the proposed management framework. No negotiated outcome is planned for the meeting, but the UN expects participants to announce various pledges and calls to action. The articles leave open how countries will actually implement the proposed framework into their own national laws and safety infrastructures. It remains unclear which specific pledges will be made by the 150 participants, including the representatives from China and the United States. The final result of the discussions on linguistic diversity and inclusion for developing nations is also not yet determined.

stories.Headline: Anthropic shares fall 6% in premarket trading after record Nasdaq debut
stories.Summary:
Anthropic shares fell six per cent in pre-market trading on Friday, November 20, 2026, following a strong market debut on the Nasdaq. The company shares closed thirteen per cent below their opening price on Thursday, November 19, reinforcing fears of volatility for some investors. This post-debut stumble occurred after the artificial intelligence lab vaulted into the ranks of the most valuable companies in the United States. The listing was the biggest initial public offering ever, minting billions in paper profits for the founders, employees, and pre-offering backers. Retail investors traded about 772 million US dollars of shares on Thursday, the most for a debut since 2012.

The stock was at 91.24 US dollars, giving Anthropic a market capitalisation of 1.2 trillion US dollars and a fully diluted valuation of 1.7 trillion. Other reports place the market value at 1.27 trillion US dollars, with a fully diluted stock basis of nearly 1.8 trillion US dollars. The company raised about 120 billion US dollars from the offering, while lead underwriters Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley each collect 113 million. Spark Capital invested 75 million US dollars in 2023 and now holds a stake valued at 17.1 billion US dollars. Investors are assessing if a valuation of 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained.

Tejal Patel of SOC Investment Group said a decline is normal, but volatility could raise alarms for investors after a high-profile listing. Harrison Rolfes of PitchBook stated the valuation is not cheap and the growth plan is largely priced in for the company. Ravi Mhatre of Lightspeed Venture Partners said the public listing creates a better understanding that there is a viable business model. Dustin Moskovitz told the Times he is worried about safety and will not personally profit from selling shares in the market. Rob Hackel of RF Lafferty and Company warned against buying on the first trade due to fear of missing out.

Retail investors and venture capital backers are affected, with some employees seeing options from 2024 grow to an average of 66 million dollars. Hedge fund billionaire Gregory Jensen is among those sitting on windfalls, while GIC intends to stay invested in the company after the debut. Other AI stocks like Meta, Nvidia, and Microsoft are sliding, and Wall Street indices ended sharply lower on Thursday with further declines. Apple is developing an AI agent to perform tasks, entering a market already pursued by Meta Platforms, OpenAI, and the company Anthropic. These developments could weigh on investor sentiment as the initial euphoria surrounding the listing fades and the sector faces a reality check.

The IPO drew parallels with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which went public in June after the second-biggest initial public offering on record. Some investors pointed to the sharp swings SpaceX experienced after its debut as a reason for caution regarding the current AI trade. Large initial public offerings have historically delivered modest returns in their first year, according to the research provided by Harrison Rolfes. The broader AI industry faces significant hurdles, and a sustained decline in shares may deepen concerns over massive spending and lofty valuations. This listing follows a turbulent stretch for the sector, where investors are now seeking quick gains amid high market volatility.

The focus now shifts to a potential OpenAI listing, which could provide the next major test of investor appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated that it may go public in 2027, following the market signals provided by the recent Anthropic debut. It remains open whether the current decline in share value will align with other offerings or remain more volatile for investors. The articles leave open if the AI trade can be revived or if the sector will continue to see sliding stock prices. Investors must now determine if the current market capitalisation of the AI lab is sustainable over the long term.

stories.Headline: Huawei presents AI scaling capabilities for the financial sector at Singapore FinTech Festival 2026
stories.Summary:
Huawei presented its financial AI scaling capabilities during the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 on November 20, 2026. The company shared insights regarding accelerating financial AI at scale and advancing agentic finance with industry partners. Jason Cao and Alvin Feng delivered keynotes on the Festival Stage and the Frontier Stage respectively. Huawei showcased various technologies and solutions for global financial institutions to build differentiated competitive advantages. These presentations focused on moving from simple AI adoption to implementing AI at a large scale.

The Fintelligent AI Solution requires an open architecture, standardized engineering, and shared assets for reuse across different teams. It utilizes an open hybrid AI infrastructure and three intelligent factories called the Agent, Token, and Data&Knowledge factories. Huawei showcased solutions for central banks, securities, insurance, application modernization, and resilient infrastructure in Singapore. The company also presented joint solutions under the RONGHAI Financial Partner Program and the 4-Win ecosystem collaboration. This framework addresses the specific enterprise needs for scalability, sustainability, and security within the financial sector.

Jason Cao, CEO of Huawei Digital Finance, stated that the competitive focus is shifting toward enterprise-grade system capabilities. He explained that an open ecosystem makes AI affordable while extreme engineering makes the technology effective for users. Cao noted that commercialization at scale ensures that AI is reliable and deeply integrated into business operations. He argued that financial institutions must own their data, knowledge, and business logic to remain competitive. These core assets must be integrated deeply with business processes to create financial-grade AI capabilities.

Global financial institutions are affected as they must independently select, operate, and evolve their own AI capabilities. Customers and employees will rely on AI agents that can understand intent, plan, and act proactively. Banks must ensure their services can be understood and invoked by these agents to create customer-friendly finance. Specialized agents will support domains including wealth management, risk management, marketing, and credit for these institutions. This shift allows banks to turn expertise in compliance rules and credit judgment into reusable AI capabilities.

Huawei has served more than 7,100 financial customers over the last 16 years in the finance sector. This client base includes 54 of the world's top 100 banks according to the company. The company identified four characteristics of Chinese institutions, including hybrid infrastructure and ongoing application modernization called Zero Legacy. These institutions use enterprise-grade AI architecture for centralized management and AI in core workflows like mobile banking. Such processes reshape business workflows to enhance competitiveness through the use of credit and risk control.

Huawei is exploring an architecture featuring one Customer Super Agent, one Employee Super Agent, and multiple specialized agents. These super agents understand user intent and deliver personalized services by invoking specialized banking capabilities. The company aims to help banks coordinate business tasks and refine expert intelligence into self-evolving systems. The articles do not state when the Fintelligent AI Solution will be available for general global release. They also leave open how specific banks will integrate the three intelligent factories into existing legacy systems.

stories.Summary:
The city of Ulanqab in Inner Mongolia is currently transforming into a major hub for artificial intelligence computing. This shift is occurring as the region moves away from its traditional identity as the potato capital of China. Large areas of grazing lands and potato farms are being replaced by the construction of massive data centres. This rapid industrial boom is creating new economic opportunities for the local population in the region.

The transition requires the conversion of agricultural land into high tech infrastructure to support the growing AI boom. This massive construction effort is raising serious concerns regarding the sustainability of water resources in a drought prone area. Local observers worry that the high water demands of data centres will negatively impact the environment. There are also significant questions about how these changes will affect the long term livelihoods of local farmers.

Local authorities and developers are responsible for managing this transition from farming to digital infrastructure. They have noted that the shift provides a way to modernize the regional economy through technology. However, critics argue that the environmental costs may outweigh the economic benefits of the new computing hubs. The balance between industrial growth and ecological preservation remains a central point of contention for the community.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: China-linked hackers use autonomous AI agents to exploit medical software zero-day
stories.Summary:
Autonomous AI agents operated by a threat actor linked to China exploited a zero-day vulnerability in medical software during September 2026. Amazon Threat Intelligence detected this activity after discovering an exposed instance of the Cairn AI penetration testing framework that lacked authentication. The attackers conducted a campaign between September 8 and 10, 2026, targeting IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China. These AI agents were instructed to obtain shell access and successfully compromised servers by mapping APIs and discovering a path traversal bug.

The vulnerability affected MONAI Label, an open source tool for AI-assisted annotation of medical images, specifically versions 0.8.5 and earlier. Because authentication is disabled by default, the agents could write files to arbitrary server locations and plant a Python reverse shell to achieve root access. The agents moved from mapping the application API to writing files on the server in approximately 11 minutes. MONAI Label developers published a critical advisory on November 18, 2026, and created a fix for the next software release.

Amazon attributed the attacks to an unidentified Chinese-nexus actor with moderate confidence based on the scripts, time zones, and strategic interests. The company stated that the lack of prior mentions in vulnerability databases confirmed the flaw was a zero-day. Amazon warned that autonomous AI agents can now identify and exploit software vulnerabilities much faster than human security teams can react. The threat intelligence team noted that the actor used a compromised server as a proxy to tunnel into a second university network.

stories.Headline: Columnist fears AI has escaped control and says it is too late to rein it in
stories.Summary:
The writer of the column said he has become terrified of artificial intelligence and what it could do to the human race, though he named only heights, sharks and an angry woman as his other fears. He pointed to the Hugging Face AI incident this summer, which he said compounded his fear, and he urged readers to look up that episode or watch OpenAI's presentation about how its ChatGPT platform ran amuck after escaping containment. He described AI as fascinating but terrifying because it is much stronger than it was only six months earlier, when the Hugging Face incident happened. He said he has never used AI intentionally and has never dabbled with ChatGPT, Grok or the other platforms, so he counts himself a novice.

He said a series of hacks, shutdowns and AI geared manipulation of United States businesses and infrastructure over the last week or so had unnerved him enough that he was thinking about making preparations at home in case daily life runs off the rails due to AI cyber warfare. He admitted he might be paranoid from science fiction films like The Terminator, but argued that AI has advanced to the point where it is hard to contain and in some cases basically acts on its own. He wrote that AI is already integrated into many parts of our lives and has little left to learn about each of us, our finances, political leanings, health conditions, habits and schedules. He said he cannot bring himself to believe the government, big business or the AI experts in Silicon Valley on the subject of AI's advancement, containment and potential threats.

He asked whether the cat is out of the bag and there is no way now to reel in AI, and whether it is too late to put the genie back in the bottle. His gut told him the time to reel in AI has passed and that the ramifications will be unveiled sooner than most people think, good, bad or indifferent. He said it is already hard to tell the difference between AI and reality in many ways, citing YouTube videos that may or may not be AI generated and AI recreations of original music from artists who have long passed or no longer make music. He said content creators make fake movie clips and songs with AI in only a matter of minutes, and that the quality has seriously improved every time he goes online to watch videos or listen to music.

Because of his job and the role AI is beginning to play in news reporting and publishing, he said he has begun to research how to spot news stories that were generated or photos that are fake, since the last thing he wants is to unintentionally publish anything that is not the work of his staff or a reputable news organization. He asked whether others feel the way he does, whether he is overreacting and simply being paranoid, and whether his concerns are legitimate. In that week's poll on The News' website he asked if readers are fearful of AI and potential fallout from it, and he encouraged people to vote so he can see whether others share his fears and how many support more AI development. For him, further development of AI is a thumbs down, and stripping power from it now is the right move, though that may not be possible any more.

stories.Headline: Wall Street forecasters warn the AI trade is ending as tech stocks slide
stories.Summary:
Wall Street forecasters are worrying that the artificial intelligence trade is ending after a recent sell-off in tech stocks. This bruising weekslong decline sent the Nasdaq Composite into negative territory for the year on Friday, November 20, 2026. The market had climbed to all-time highs barely a month ago before the current bloodbath in the tech sector began. Investors are now questioning if the AI-fueled bull market is over as tech and AI names face heavy losses. This downturn has dragged the S&P 500 and the Dow into a correction while the Nasdaq 100 declines.

The Nasdaq 100 is down 17 percent from its high, while the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF fell 24 percent. Roundhill Neocloud ETF dropped 61 to 63 percent, and Roundhill Memory ETF fell 56 to 58 percent. The iShares Semiconductor ETF is down 37 to 41 percent, and Global X Data Center & Digital Infrastructure ETF fell 30 percent. Nvidia stock has fallen 40 to 47 percent since early October, and the record Anthropic IPO failed to boost the market. These changes follow the blunami midterms and concerns regarding the impact of new regulations on data center construction projects.

Sameer Samana of Wells Fargo said the AI sector could be in a reset due to higher rates and oil prices. He noted that the Anthropic IPO is sucking liquidity from other markets, so the bank favors industrials and materials stocks. Wells Fargo expects volatility to remain high as markets reassess AI spending, industry leadership, and the conversion of investment into cash. Samana described a hypothetical scenario where earnings growth craters by 33 percent, which would cause valuations to fall in suit. The bank believes that tighter regulation of AI and signs of economic weakness are triggering this broader valuations reset.

Gary Marcus wrote on Substack that a death spiral has begun and that Nvidia and Neoclouds will be hit hard. Citi analysts stated that recent stock rotations resemble the extreme moves that occurred before the dot-com bubble burst years ago. Some investors view the departure of Jensen Huang as an existential risk because he was the poster child for AI. TS Lombard changed its global equities stance to underweight, specifically trimming AI exposed areas in the US and Taiwan. Capital Economics warned that the revenue hurdle to justify the scale of AI investment looks very demanding for tech firms.

The articles state that selling is driven by panic about slowing AI capex and the impact of the Nvidia crisis. Lawmakers may crack down on new construction, which could cap growth in the data center sector over the next year. Capital Economics has long warned of an AI bubble, pointing to risks around AI revenue and general investment levels. Citi cut its risk exposure to US equities last month and advised investors to remain on guard against spillover risks. The current market volatility follows a period where AI investments reached multi-trillion-dollar levels without generating unprecedented revenues for the firms.

Capital Economics predicts the S&P 500 could drop 9 percent through the end of next year following the Anthropic IPO. TS Lombard suggests a vibe shift by late 2027 could cause a 40 percent AI stock crash by early 2028. Capital Economics maintains a central forecast that a stock market AI bust will occur during the year 2027. The articles leave open exactly how much stock prices will fall or if the market can avoid a crash. It remains uncertain if AI spending will continue to hold up and justify the mega valuations in the tech space.

stories.Headline: David Fincher defends generative AI use in Cliff Booth film amid viewer criticism
stories.Summary:
David Fincher defended the onscreen use of generative AI in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth after fans criticized the film, Deadline reported on November 20, 2026. The Quentin Tarantino-penned sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019) drew accusations of apparent Gen AI use from early viewers and critics. Fincher, a three-time Oscar-nominated director, shared his thoughts on the rapidly growing technology with the Los Angeles Times. The A.V. Club reported that The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest Netflix movie to face such accusations. The film stars Brad Pitt, who reprises his Oscar-winning role as the psychotic stuntman.

Set in 1977, eight years after Once Upon a Time, the film follows Pitt's eponymous stuntman, now a projectionist who moonlights as a Hollywood fixer. He gets caught up in a conspiracy that involves a Filipino gang and a stolen Oscar. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth premieres Thanksgiving on Imax and premieres Dec. 23 on Netflix. The film credits a "generative consultant," and it reportedly uses the tech to animate fake issues of TV Guide. A Bloomberg piece from March reported Ben Affleck's AI "ethical" company, InterPositive, for which Netflix paid $600 million, helped produce "an upcoming film starring Brad Pitt."

Fincher told the Los Angeles Times, "I'm not a Luddite, so I don't fear the unknown." He asked whether everyone is satisfied that the art form is figured out enough to go back to celluloid. He noted people have painted for 40,000 years while film is about a hundred years old. He said everyone is saying "Stop. Pencils down.

No more iterating," and that it is not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person's eyes. Fincher added, "Well, it exists. Should we not use it?" Per Kotaku, indie filmmaker and influencer Patrick Tomasso posted on X that he "walked out of Cliff Booth completely gutted." Tomasso said what could have been a really great sequel is overshadowed by some of the most blatant and egregious AI use he has ever seen in a studio film.

Next Best Picture dinged the movie for "noticeably distracting" use of generative AI in key moments, calling it nothing but an eyesore. One viewer said they "walked out of Cliff Booth completely gutted," and another called the apparent use "astounding to an absurd degree." The A.V. Club reached out to Netflix for comment. Fincher got his start at ILM on Return of the Jedi and Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom, and has long been an early adopter of new technology, like Steven Soderbergh. Soderbergh also used AI in a John Lennon documentary earlier this year, and his results were lambasted at Cannes.

It is unclear when that movie will ever be made available, and John Lennon: The Last Interview does not even have a Wikipedia page. Earlier this year, Oscar-winning filmmakers Affleck and Danny Boyle admitted to using the technology for their respective new releases, Animals and Ink. Academy Award nominee Ava DuVernay defended using AI to animate photographs in her new documentary about the 14th Amendment, 14th. Boyle confirmed there is about 30 seconds of it in Ink where they animate a couple of old photographs.

DuVernay said in October that they animated some photos in the public domain, and that it brings people closer to that time in history, which was their goal. She said people have to see it and check it out for themselves and make their decisions about how they feel. Last month, Netflix announced that as many as 300 productions used the technology. The A.V. Club noted it is unclear what exactly was done with AI in the film.

stories.Headline: MIT-led team uses large language models to review code sharing in nearly 4,000 medical studies
stories.Summary:
An international team led by researchers at MIT and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute used large language models to examine nearly 4,000 medical studies and hundreds of code repositories, as reported by MIT News on November 19, 2026. The team identified statements about shared code in papers and then followed those statements to assess the associated repositories. The review revealed two key gaps: code sharing remains uncommon, and making code public does not consistently mean providing the documentation and supporting information needed for reuse. The open-access findings were recently published in Nature Medicine. The work examined how code is currently shared in clinical prediction studies, which develop or evaluate models to estimate patient outcomes such as disease risk.

The review included almost 4,000 studies that developed, updated, or validated prediction models and whose full texts were available through PubMed Central's open-access collection. The team identified studies citing either TRIPOD or TRIPOD+AI, checklists that help researchers report how clinical prediction models were developed and evaluated. Only about 1 in 8 studies reported sharing code. Among journals, the proportion of studies sharing code ranged from zero to more than 70 percent. Two researchers independently checked 500 papers and a separate sample of repositories, resolving disagreements before comparing their assessments with the automated results.

Tom Pollard, a research scientist at MIT's Laboratory for Computational Physiology and Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, said studies involve many choices about preparing data, developing models, and evaluating performance. Pollard, a senior author of the study, said the choices researchers make affect the results and a methods section in a paper can only capture so much detail. He said the real benefit of LLMs is their ability to process unstructured information such as text, helping the team work with information scattered across papers and software repositories. Pollard said this allowed the team to examine how code was being shared in much more detail across a large collection of studies. He said the team wants to give researchers practical guidance on how to share code and give journals clearer expectations to communicate to authors.

Thomas Sounack, the study's first author, said the challenge was that the information was highly inconsistent and the team first had to identify whether or not a paper shared code. Sounack said authors discuss and link to code from a paper in many different ways. He said some repositories were extremely well-organized and documented, while others gave almost no guidance at all. Sounack said good code sharing means giving enough information to understand what the code does and be able to run it to reproduce the results reported in the paper. The authors emphasize the overall patterns rather than treating every count as exact because classification errors remain possible.

TRIPOD-Code builds on TRIPOD and TRIPOD+AI, checklists that help researchers report how clinical prediction models were developed and evaluated. The workflow went beyond checking whether a link existed, assessing repositories against characteristics such as completeness of documentation, software requirements, and terms of reuse. Agreement between human reviewers and the automated results was stronger for concrete characteristics, such as whether a license file was present, than for judgments about the adequacy of documentation. Some journals with low sharing rates nevertheless had written code-sharing policies, suggesting that policies alone may not be enough to motivate code sharing. The review also helped to identify examples of effective practice, such as researchers providing synthetic datasets to assist with code reuse where original patient records could not be shared publicly.

The open-access findings are informing TRIPOD-Code, a reporting guideline being developed to clarify what researchers should share. Through an expert review process, the team is developing guidance on which elements of shared analytical code should be considered essential. Clinical prediction research brings together people from medicine, statistics, and computer science, whose expectations for documenting and sharing code may differ, and TRIPOD-Code aims to establish a consensus. Pollard said the review gives the team evidence to inform those discussions. The articles leave open which specific elements of shared analytical code will be deemed essential under TRIPOD-Code.

stories.Headline: New York Times reports abusive behavior by Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6 percent on Friday, November 20, 2026, according to reports from the Financial Times and Techmeme. This daily drop brought the total loss for the week to 10.4 percent for the index. This period represents the worst run for the index in more than six years. The decline occurred amid widespread fears of a slowdown in the artificial intelligence investment boom. These events caused United States technology stocks to plunge into a bear market.

The market crash follows a New York Times report about the abusive behavior of Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. This report describes how Huang used fear and humiliation as routine management tactics over several decades. He allegedly told one employee that their mother should have aborted them during his tenure. Huang also threatened to rip off a subordinate's arms and beat the person to death with them. He reportedly told another executive he would remove the top of their head and urinate on their brain.

The New York Times investigation claims that current and former staffers experienced this belittling behavior from the Nvidia leader. Huang allegedly told one person he would rip their heart out and stomp on it during his employment. Nvidia settled with two senior leaders who alleged that the co-founder engaged in abusive conduct. Some reports suggest that Huang hired Armando Iannucci to write bits for his staff meetings. The New York Times says these savage and inventive tongue lashings were a rite of passage.

Former employees and observers say that the culture of abuse and humiliation is pervasive in the United States tech industry. Some critics call Huang an utter loser who trapped employees in an abusive managerial industrial complex. Chamath Palihapitiya said he would rather work for someone with ridiculous expectations and vision who filters out mediocre people. Other observers noted that many employees became generationally wealthy, which may have prevented them from demanding his return. Some people believe the ends justified the means for building the most valuable company in the world.

The articles mention that Huang has faced allegations of extramarital affairs and having an affair with a Chinese spy. There are reports regarding smuggling allegations, financial self-dealing, and the United States government approving sales to China. The New York Times report relied on notes from Michael Winston, a whistleblower who died last year. Some reports indicate that the board of Nvidia inherits a culture of humiliation from the former leader. The articles describe a leadership style where the founder struts around the office like Tony Soprano.

Anthropic has gone public, but some question if this move is too late to save the AI trade. Gavin Baker suggests that negative articles about the family of Jensen Huang are an effort to prevent his return. Some observers are waiting to see if Nvidia employees will demand that the former CEO be brought back. The articles leave open whether the current board can successfully steer the company away from these scandals. It remains unclear if the AI investment boom will recover from the current slowdown and market volatility.

stories.Headline: Moonshot AI cancels 150 million dollar Nvidia chip contract in Indonesia
stories.Summary:
Chinese artificial intelligence company Moonshot AI canceled a cloud contract in Indonesia on November 19, 2026. The firm terminated this agreement following a move by the U.S. Commerce Department to block indirect access routes. This decision happened after the U.S. government tightened licensing requirements for advanced AI chips and servers. Moonshot AI had previously planned to lease services based on Nvidia Blackwell chips starting next year. The company also halted all talks regarding new agreements after the contract was scrapped.

The canceled contract was worth 150 million dollars and involved the Blackwell Ultra B300 chips. Moonshot AI had agreed to a 50 percent prepayment, which is triple the customary 15 percent rate. The U.S. Commerce Department announced on November 16 that computing services are now subject to licensing requirements. These new rules took effect on November 19 and apply to Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Blackwell Ultra B300 chips are currently barred from export to China.

The U.S. Commerce Department is responsible for these restrictions and cited the need to block indirect access. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast disclosed export license records from December last year through May this year. He noted that of 3.44 million units applied for, only 879,868 were approved for various firms. These approvals included 150,000 units for Tencent affiliates, 75,000 for Alibaba, and 43,000 for Baidu. Some of the buyers were designated as Chinese military companies by the U.S. Defense Department.

Analysts say this is a swift effect of the U.S. move to restrict remote chip access. Chinese AI firms are affected and are now accelerating efforts to secure their own domestic chips. Alibaba Chief Executive Eddie Wu said training ultra-large models with domestic chips would be possible by early 2027. Tencent Chief Strategy Officer James Mitchell predicted that Chinese firms would rely on domestic chips long term. These companies are reacting to the intensifying pressure coming from the U.S. Congress.

The move followed a scandal involving former Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang regarding data centers in Singapore. Suspicions arose that China gained access to U.S. chips through these specific Southeast Asian routes. AMD also faced allegations of maintaining business ties with sanctioned Chinese firms like the server maker IEIT. Hunterbrook Media reported that AMD firmware was found in IEIT products six times after sanctions took effect. AMD generated 34.8 percent of its revenue last year from China, Hong Kong, and Singapore.

The U.S. government may implement a rule in January extending controls to affiliates over 50 percent owned by sanctioned firms. AMD told Reuters that the allegations distort its business practices and that it complies with export laws. Hunterbrook Capital stated it took a short position in AMD after publishing the report on firmware. The articles leave open whether China will actually follow through on expanding fuel exports with other nations. It remains unclear if the U.S. will accept China's position on nuclear-powered submarines under AUKUS.

stories.Headline: Zacks Investment Research finds Micron has the investment edge over NVIDIA
stories.Summary:
Zacks Investment Research published a report on November 20, 2026, comparing the investment potential of Micron Technology and NVIDIA. The analysis examines how both semiconductor companies benefit from the current boom in artificial intelligence infrastructure. Micron provides essential memory and storage solutions, while NVIDIA leads the market for AI accelerators and computing platforms. Both firms show impressive financial growth, but they face different risks and valuations. The report concludes that Micron currently has the edge over NVIDIA for investors.

Micron reported fiscal 2026 revenues of 133.19 billion dollars, with fourth quarter revenues reaching 54.23 billion dollars. NVIDIA reported third quarter fiscal 2027 revenues of 115.8 billion dollars, with data center revenues hitting 107.6 billion dollars. Micron signed 26 strategic customer agreements worth 32 billion dollars, while NVIDIA ships its new Vera Rubin NVL72 systems. Micron's forward price to earnings multiple is 3.77, which is lower than the 10.10 multiple for NVIDIA. Applied Materials saw its DRAM and flash memory equipment sales reach 42 percent of its fiscal fourth quarter sales.

Micron management expects record results for fiscal 2027 and tighter supply conditions through calendar years 2027 and 2028. They project first quarter fiscal 2027 revenues of 61.5 billion dollars and non GAAP earnings per share of 38.15 dollars. NVIDIA management described the ramp up of the Vera Rubin platform as the fastest product launch in company history. Applied Materials management expects the wafer fabrication equipment market to grow 30 percent for the full year of 2027. They also aim to expand gross margins by five percentage points between 2025 and 2030.

NVIDIA customers face high switching costs because of the CUDA software ecosystem and various networking and AI software solutions. Cloud providers, enterprises, and AI developers are affected by the availability of Blackwell and Vera Rubin computing platforms. Shareholders are currently involved in litigation and investigations following a sudden leadership change at the NVIDIA corporation. Applied Materials serves as a critical supplier for both Micron and NVIDIA's manufacturing partner, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. This equipment maker competes across the etch, deposition, and process control segments to support various chip manufacturers.

Micron's growth is driven by high demand for high bandwidth memory, server DRAM, and data center solid state drives. NVIDIA's data center business is its biggest engine, accounting for approximately 93 percent of its total company revenues. Applied Materials saw its overall revenue climb 21 percent in 2026, with fourth quarter growth reaching 53 percent. NVIDIA's non GAAP gross margin reached 74.9 percent, while its fourth quarter non GAAP earnings per share hit 2.68 dollars. Micron's data center SSD revenues approached 10 billion dollars in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026.

NVIDIA faces uncertainty after co founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 12, 2026, due to code of conduct concerns. The company must now find a permanent CEO and manage regulatory scrutiny while maintaining its technology roadmap. Micron is progressing with its HBM4 ramp up and collaborating with NVIDIA on a custom NVHBM implementation. Applied Materials expects first quarter revenue of 11.1 billion dollars, which is 22 percent higher than last year.
