stories.Summary:
Akira Hayashi is campaigning for a global halt to advanced artificial intelligence development in November 2026. The twenty year old Tokyo native believes that the race for powerful AI could end in catastrophe. Meanwhile, sixteen year old Henrijs Dandzbergs founded a missile startup called Polemos Industries in late 2026. Dandzbergs won half a million dollars after joining the fall 2026 cohort of the Y Combinator accelerator. He aims to create precision guided missiles that are cheap to manufacture and resist jamming attempts.

The AI 2027 report warns that humans must act by 2027 to prevent AI from deceiving people. Such systems could threaten human survival through biological weapons or cyberwarfare, according to the 2025 online publication. Dandzbergs wants to lower the cost per kill using AI to optimize targeted killing of enemies. He attended Astra Nova, an Elon Musk linked school, and took a class from a NASA employee. His startup competes with defense companies like Anduril, Leidos, and CoAspire to build mass producible missiles.

Akira Hayashi says that artificial intelligence could kill humans in the near future and wants the world to change. He established a community focused on AI safety after enrolling as a student at the University of Tokyo. Henrijs Dandzbergs says his drive is a patriotic intention to protect American, Ukrainian, and European soldiers from threats. He believes autonomous weapons are an inevitable part of the future and wants to move with modern warfare. Harj Taggar, a YC partner, called Dandzbergs an exceptional person and expressed disbelief at his young age.

Fergus McKenzie Wilson, the Unicorn Mafia director, says Dandzbergs will eventually realize the emotional weight of killing people. Tom Karako of the Missile Defense Project says there are trade offs regarding reliability, payload, and range. Dandzbergs claims he is not sacrificing his childhood because this is the childhood he always dreamed of having. The startup's social media video, released November 5, showed missiles destroying a convoy of four military vehicles.

Hayashi became an AI doomer after reading Nick Bostrom's 2014 book, Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies, in high school. He spent time poring over internet forums and academic papers regarding the potential dangers of advanced artificial intelligence. Dandzbergs grew up moving between Spain, Australia, Indonesia, and Latvia before his family returned home during the pandemic. He previously won a London hackathon with teammates Kai Yang and Aleksandrs Tihenko by designing hardware circuit boards. This victory provided him with ten thousand dollars, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and O-1 visa assistance.

Dandzbergs hopes to showcase a prototype missile by the time the Y Combinator program finishes in December 2026. He has already developed the software system for guidance and is currently hammering out the hardware design elements. stories.Summary:
NATO is collaborating with OpenAI to integrate artificial intelligence into its cybersecurity operations, focusing on identifying software vulnerabilities and investigating suspicious activities across allied networks. The partnership involves NATO's Communications and Information Agency (NCIA), which provides technology and cybersecurity services to the alliance. OpenAI reported that NATO's core institutions access advanced AI models for cybersecurity, with monthly usage reaching up to 300 billion input and output tokens. These models support software reviews, suspicious activity investigations, and vulnerability validation. OpenAI's cybersecurity initiative, Daybreak, provides these capabilities and supports authorised vulnerability research and remediation.

The NCIA accesses AI models processing up to 300 billion tokens monthly for cyber operations, according to OpenAI. AI agents were tested in the Crossed Swords 2026 exercise by NATO's CCDCOE, held in Tallinn, Estonia, from November 2 to 6. The exercise gathered over 250 participants from more than 40 NATO and non-NATO countries, including military cyber operators, digital forensics analysts, and threat hunters. The exercise introduced a training stream where participants designed, deployed, and evaluated AI agents during simulated cyber operations. The CCDCOE noted that agents were incorporated into operational workflows alongside human operators.

Dr Dylan Browne, NCIA General Manager, stated that AI models can accelerate vulnerability discovery and help detect emerging threats. He added that NATO will assess model usage and operating costs as AI adoption expands. OpenAI facilitated the use of AI agents during a recent NATO cybersecurity exercise. The company reported that NATO's core institutions access advanced AI models for cybersecurity. OpenAI's Daybreak initiative supports authorised vulnerability research and remediation.

The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) used OpenAI models to identify four vulnerabilities in software across EU institutions, with fixes published for all four. A joint assessment by ENISA and CERT-EU reviewed 27 software codebases from EU institutions, identifying 220 potential security issues. At the time of publication in November, 88 issues had been assessed, with 95 per cent confirmed as genuine vulnerabilities. CERT Polska, Poland's national cybersecurity incident response team, used AI models to identify six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS. Two of these could be combined for unauthorised administrative access, and evidence suggested prior exploitation before MikroTik released security updates.

stories.Headline: CJ Olive Young plans AI-driven global expansion of its beauty platform
stories.Summary:
CJ Olive Young announced plans to use artificial intelligence to expand its beauty platform globally on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The company held its first technology conference, called define:OMNI, at Olive Young N Seongsu in eastern Seoul. This event showcased a model for shoppers who browse on phones, test in stores, and buy through apps. The retailer aims to elevate the shopping experience by taking its omnichannel model to international markets. It wants to become the first answer for any beauty question anywhere in the world.

The plan requires a borderless global platform, an intelligent supply chain, redesigned stores, a unified commerce platform, and agentic AI. The company operates 1,300 stores in Korea and has an app with over 10 million monthly active users. About 18 million members share a single membership, while the global online outlet has 6 million members. Foreign visitors have spent over 1 trillion won, or 750 million dollars, and the global mall grows 70 percent annually. The retailer opened a California store and a US online mall in May to replicate its network.

Chief Operating Officer Lee Jin-hee stated that technology is now at the center of every new business the company tries. She said the firm will transplant its Korean data and omnichannel know-how onto the global platform for customer services. Chief Technology Officer Kim Hwan explained that he moved the company to a multi-cloud setup to stop frequent outages. Chief Product Officer Lee Seung-hyo noted that technology should work so that customers never realize they faced any inconvenience. He highlighted that an in-house system now completes product translations within one day instead of several weeks.

The conference drew 500 industry officials, including Google architect Rajan Manickavasagam and Palantir Technologies Korea head Steven Kim. These speakers shared examples of how other retailers manage both physical stores and online channels to serve their customers. The AI agent Tiki is currently available to 1 million selected users to provide recommendations based on skin type. Shoppers are affected by a new unified cart that merges standard shipping, store pickup, and the Today Dream service. This Today Dream service launched in 2018 and helped lift online sales to more than 30 percent of total sales.

The company draws on skin diagnosis and purchase data along with more than 47 million customer reviews to power AI. It offers a Skin Scan service that recommends products and tracks changes, which is now available via a mobile version. The retailer is linking its product data with external AI services like Google Gemini and OpenAI's ChatGPT for users. The firm previously outsourced all product translation for overseas listings, which took several weeks per product before the new system. The company has already established a presence in the United States through its May launch in California.

Olive Young will now tailor its global mall to each country by supporting multiple languages and speeding up local delivery. The company plans to use AI to forecast demand at stores in Korea and overseas to improve its supply chain. It will expand the role of AI to help users compare different products and build their shopping carts automatically. The articles leave open how the company will adapt to specific local shopping habits in various different international markets. They do not specify the exact number of new California stores the retailer intends to open in the future.

stories.Headline: SEBI member KVR Murty says the regulator is preparing AI guidelines for capital markets
stories.Summary:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India is preparing to issue guidelines for the responsible use of artificial intelligence in capital markets, SEBI Whole Time Member KVR Murty said on Thursday. Murty spoke at a World Federation of Exchanges event in Mumbai. He said the guidelines will include disclosures and accountability requirements for related entities. He highlighted the growing role of AI in trading and investment decisions. He stressed the need for stronger regulatory oversight as autonomous AI systems become increasingly sophisticated.

Murty said AI is enabling ordinary investors to develop their own trading algorithms. He said an AI agent is given a goal, not a fixed set of rules, and can change how it trades as it learns. He asked how a strategy that rewrites itself can be approved. He raised concerns about millions of investors using agents built on similar models and data, potentially triggering simultaneous market exits. He said every agent, however intelligent, must be traceable, and someone must answer for what it does.

Murty said SEBI has already created a verification agency to examine risk and return claims made by investment advisers, research analysts and algorithmic trading providers. He said AI applications in market surveillance, compliance and fraud detection offer significant potential, although governance frameworks remain incomplete. He said India's Demat 2.0 pilot facilitated fundraising of Rs 1,025 crore by three issuers. He said bond and cash settlement took place simultaneously through central bank digital currency on a T+0 basis. He said what is needed is stronger governance, not faster adoption.

Murty urged market infrastructure institutions to invest in research and development, potentially through dedicated laboratories functioning as Securities Market Innovation Hubs. He said technology can strengthen investor trust but cannot substitute for it. He said the future of capital markets would be determined by their ability to support the real economy, maintain resilience and safeguard investor trust rather than merely increasing trading volumes. A Congressional Research Service report said the Securities and Exchange Commission has not issued regulations specifically targeting AI use in capital markets. The report identified unresolved policy concerns including accountability gaps when AI systems fail, risks from market concentration among a small number of AI developers, and potentially misleading "AI washing" disclosures.

The National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020, P.L. 116-283, Division E, defines artificial intelligence as a machine-based system that can make predictions, recommendations, or decisions influencing real or virtual environments. Common capital markets applications include investment management, algorithmic trading, robo-advising, anti-money laundering compliance and back-office productivity support. In April 2025, the Trump administration's Office of Management and Budget issued Memorandum M-25-21, directing agencies including the SEC to develop AI strategies and build an AI-ready federal workforce. The SEC issued its compliance plan in September 2025 and launched an AI task force in August 2025, reporting 60 internal AI use cases that year. The SEC withdrew a 2023 proposed rule addressing conflicts of interest associated with predictive data analytics in June 2025, along with other rules proposed under the previous administration.

As of October, the SEC had received petitions for rulemaking seeking mandatory AI governance and risk management disclosures in public filings but had not indicated whether it would pursue AI-specific rulemaking. The SEC's fiscal 2027 examination priorities continue to emphasize AI disclosures, AI-related risks and cybersecurity under existing securities laws. The Unleashing AI Innovation in Financial Services Act, H.R. 4801, sponsored by Rep. J. French Hill (R-AR), would establish AI innovation labs at the SEC and other financial regulators, allowing test projects to operate with relief from certain regulations. The bill was placed on the Union Calendar on June 24. The AI Act of 2024, H.R. 10262, sponsored by Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA), would have required the SEC to study AI's benefits and risks for capital markets, and the House Financial Services Committee referred it in November 2024, but it did not advance before the 118th Congress adjourned.

stories.Headline: Etsy sellers leave the site over a new policy that lets Etsy train AI on their content
stories.Summary:
Many longtime owners of shops on Etsy, the online marketplace known for its handmade goods, said this week that they had left the site over a policy change that they said leaves them vulnerable to exploitation by artificial intelligence companies. Language in Etsy's new terms, set to take effect on Dec. 16, says the company and its third party partners and vendors reserve the right to use sellers' content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies. The terms say that Etsy and its partners will use such technologies in part to improve the platform and keep it safe for users. The previous version of the terms did not include a clause about using content for artificial intelligence.

Aaron Millard, an illustrator, wrote in an Instagram post announcing that he was deleting the shop that he has run for nearly a decade, saying that selling on the platform now means letting Etsy train AI on artwork and resell that data to third parties with no way to opt out. He said his work took years to learn and create and that he would not let it be stolen. Kristen and Geoff Zephyrus, the founders of the home goods and stationery brand Cognitive Surplus, which has sold its products on Etsy for 13 years, also deleted their shop. In an Instagram post, they accused the company of claiming perpetual, free, boundless permission to not only train AI on their art, but also to resell the data for profit. Kristen Zephyrus said in an interview that for Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with human content is just unimaginably awful and that they do not want anything to do with that.

Etsy said it would revise its policy after hearing complaints from sellers. James Ossman said it will not use content to copy work or replace creativity, but will use it for safety, fraud checks and ads. The articles do not say when the revised terms will be published or what they will contain. The articles also do not say how many sellers have left the site or whether the deletions will affect the Dec. 16 effective date.

The situation involving Advanced Micro Devices stems from claims by Hunterbrook Media that company firmware was found in products from IEIT Systems. This server maker is part of the Inspur Group, which the US Commerce Department blacklisted in 2023, along with three other closely linked companies. Meanwhile, California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia to determine if advanced chips or confidential data reached China. This probe follows the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose shares plummeted 22 per cent after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a suspected spy.

Attorney General Rob Bonta stated that companies are prohibited from misleading their investors under corporate securities law. He is investigating whether the actions of Nvidia or its former leader violated California law by deceiving the public. Regarding the Nvidia leadership crisis, board chair Harvey Jones confirmed the company has no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang. Huang admitted to having affairs with subordinates and left the company last week, despite public campaigns for his return by leaders like Elon Musk. Megaspeed, a customer of Nvidia, denied that its operations were used to divert chips to China.

These investigations highlight a broader tension over whether Advanced Micro Devices will become the next target after the scandal surrounding Nvidia. Members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate if Megaspeed diverted hardware to Chinese entities. stories.Headline: Nvidia results and Anthropic IPO fail to ease AI concerns as S&P 500 closes in correction
stories.Summary:
Stocks ended their worst week in more than a year with a steep sell-off on Friday, as concerns about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom boiled over after building for weeks. The S&P 500 fell 3.7 percent on Friday and closed in correction territory, which is defined as a drop of 10 percent or more from its recent high and is a symbolic measure of investors’ souring mood. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slid 5.3 percent, a loss that erased its gains for the year and marked a grim milestone for an index holding many of the technology giants that powered the A.I. boom. Some investors had billed the past week as a referendum on artificial intelligence investments, with Nvidia reporting financial results and Anthropic debuting on public markets.

Despite Nvidia’s bumper profits and hefty initial demand for Anthropic’s shares, neither could dispel the wider concerns about the industry that investors had been stacking up for weeks. The concerns initially focused on whether future profits would justify A.I. companies’ rampant debt-fueled infrastructure spending, according to the report. The midterm elections increased the likelihood of new hurdles for data center construction, and recent earnings reports highlighted signs of supply chain constraints that could slow the growth of some businesses. The deepening leadership crisis at Nvidia also rattled investors’ confidence in what had been, until recently, one of the market’s highest flying stocks. Even Anthropic, only one day after its blockbuster I.P.O., could not escape the market malaise, with its shares falling 9.1 percent on Friday.

The sell-off was reported by Joe Rennison in The New York Times, with the article updated at 5:47 p.m. ET on Nov. 20, 2026. stories.Headline: China-linked hackers use AI agents to find zero-day flaw in medical-imaging software
stories.Summary:
Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a zero-day flaw in medical-imaging software. These agents gained root access to a university server during a campaign in September. Amazon Threat Intelligence reported the incident this week after reconstructing the intrusion. The attackers used an open-source framework called Cairn to run their agents. These agents worked with little direction to achieve the goal of shell access.

The flaw affects MONAI Label version 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup. This path-traversal weakness, CVE-2026-133968, allows unauthenticated users to write files outside the storage folder. It is rated 9.8 out of 10, which is a critical score. The software is used by research teams to label scans and train models. The vulnerability exists in the parts of the server that store images and labels.

Amazon Threat Intelligence said the agents mapped the interface and wrote files in eleven minutes. They stated the operator chose the targets while the agents selected the methods. Investigators tied the campaign to China with moderate confidence due to Simplified Chinese prompts. They noted the use of China Standard Time and targets likely of interest to China. However, they did not connect the work to a named group or government.

The attack affected one university server and potentially a second university network. Amazon believes the second network was broken into in the same way. The company noted that root access depends on how the service account is run. They stated there is no evidence that patient records or clinical systems were touched. The report also mentioned that the campaign included several failed operations.

MONAI Label is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework. The server runs with authentication off by default, allowing any network client to trigger writes. The attackers used a Python startup file and a training feature to gain root access. Amazon found the operator's Cairn control panel exposed on the internet without a password. This panel revealed the agents' prompts, task settings, and their run history.

Maintainers merged a source code fix on October 19 to force uploads into approved folders. A security advisory published this week says a patched version will arrive in a future release. The newest installable version remains 0.8.5, which dates back to the year 2024. Amazon suggests blocking untrusted network access and running the server under a limited account. It remains open whether other MONAI Label systems would yield the same root result.

stories.Headline: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims Claude helped him prove the Riemann hypothesis in Lean code
stories.Summary:
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the AI company Anthropic, claimed on Friday, 20 November 2026, to have discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis working with Anthropic's Claude AI. He published a statement on his website saying he believed he had, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution.

Alpöge has not published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of slop. He says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages. Instead he released a version written in Lean, a computer code mathematicians use to mechanically verify proofs as a series of logical steps in a process called formalisation. The process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, meaning the code compiles, it is considered proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt. Alpöge says the proof confirms the generalised Riemann hypothesis, which widens out the concept to different properties of prime numbers.

Alpöge wrote that it is natural to feel that this is an end, in his case a loss of a principal guiding light. He wrote that what he saw during the course of progress so amazed him that he believed it is one dawn across science of something far greater. He wrote that the precise timing is horrible and that if he could have, he would have finished this all much earlier. He says he spoke to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and determined that there was a constraint to respect before the announcement could be made. Anthropic listed on the stock market on 19 November, and Alpöge appears to suggest that he waited to announce the proof until after.

Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London said let's see if it compiles first, and that it might be a while before we find the relevant experts able to tell us the thrust of the argument. Buzzard said it probably will be true because Alpöge will have a huge amount of egg on his face if the Lean code doesn't compile or is deficient in some way. James McKee at Royal Holloway University of London said there are numerous results conditional on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and now those are theorems. McKee said most mathematicians believed, or the more cautious ones merely suspected, that GRH was true, so its proof will not be unsettling. McKee said what is both unsettling and tremendously exciting is the rapid progress in recent months towards automated proofs of significant mathematical results, and that it is both a wonderful time and a terrible time to be a research mathematician.

Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile, said that if the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial, something like a Rosetta Stone. Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind, said that if true, even from a first high level scan of the summary of the proposed argument, it is very plausible to him that the new ideas in the proof will open up brand new avenues of thinking in number theory. Andrew Sutherland, an MIT mathematician, told Scientific American today after he had independently compiled Alpöge's result in Lean that this is indeed an historic moment and that the world has changed. Sutherland said he knows there will be a wide range of reactions in the community, but to him this is a human triumph and a day for celebration. Sutherland said there is much work to be done to understand the mathematical details of the proof, that he can't wait to dig into them, and that perhaps the single most important step in the proof was building a machine that can think.

In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis, but that stopped short of a full proof. The first chink in the problem's armor appeared in October, when one of the proofs in OpenAI's massive dump of math results made significant progress on making sense of the primes. In July, Alpöge announced that the Jacobian conjecture, which academics have spent decades trying to prove was true, is actually false, giving a tiny, 216-character counterexample as proof. He and Tristan Buckmaster at New York University also announced that they had cracked three significant problems considered stepping stones to the Navier-Stokes problem, hours before OpenAI controversially revealed a full solution. Scientific American reported that Buckmaster implied in September that OpenAI had stolen his and Alpöge's work.

The process isn't without vulnerabilities, and the code and mathematics will need to be thoroughly checked by humans. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn't take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct. Scientific American called the story breaking news and said it will be updated. The Riemann result, if correct, doesn't have any immediate real-world applications, and it won't upend global banking or make the internet run faster. Sutherland once told Scientific American that an AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one he'd want to meet, and that if that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems.

stories.Headline: Alibaba trains next-generation Qwen AI model on in-house chips
stories.Summary:
Alibaba announced on Thursday that its next-generation Qwen AI model is being trained using in-house chips. This news came during the company's fiscal 2027 second-quarter earnings call. The announcement occurred amid an intensive roll-out of various Chinese AI models. Other major Chinese developers also released new products or updates during the past week. This shift moves competition toward cost, domestic computing adaptation, and post-training optimization.

The T-Head GPU roadmap includes the Zhenwu M890 launching this year and V900 and J900 mass production in 2027. Alibaba Cloud revenue from AI and compute services rose 53 percent, while AI product revenue reached 17.92 billion yuan. New U.S. rules from November 16 and November 19 restrict remote cloud access and overseas foundry production. TSMC and Samsung suspended shipments for nodes 16 nanometers or below, limiting Chinese firms to 28nm and 40nm. Licensing now applies to semiconductor exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand.

CEO Wu Yongming stated that domestic computing infrastructure is becoming the supporting base for full-stack AI technology. He said this base will carry workloads for Alibaba and its customers in inference, training, and agentic tasks. Wu noted that capacity expansion in 2027-28 will make the pace of long-term model iteration more controllable. The company revealed that its AI-related annual revenue will top 10 billion dollars. Alibaba also reported that total revenue in the third quarter rose 10 percent year-on-year.

Baidu released the Ernie 5.5 Flash Preview with 280 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window. Tencent's WorkBuddy agent topped 10 million daily active users and 100 trillion daily tokens. Zhipu AI released GLM-5.3, which improved coding capability by 50 percent over the previous GLM-5.2 version. Databricks data from November 2 shows GLM-series models account for over 60 percent of open-weight token usage. The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said U.S. measures infringe on rights and undermine global supply chain stability.

The U.S. Department of Commerce is investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company, for possible export control violations. Applied Materials previously paid a 252.5 million dollar penalty for illegal equipment exports to China via South Korea. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized Nvidia's internal controls, suggesting executives would be dismissed if Nvidia were a bank. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang denied allegations of chip diversion before his resignation. The U.S. government is now seeking to increase statutory caps on fines for violating export controls.

The U.S. Senate is considering semiconductor tracking mechanisms and congressional review of licenses for advanced AI chip sales. A defense bill scheduled for the end of the year may further restrict cloud computing and equipment exports. The Trump administration has shown internal disagreements between the Treasury and Commerce departments regarding the timing of rules. It remains open whether China will retaliate by restricting rare earth exports as it has done previously. Nvidia expects to maintain solid business performance because AI semiconductor demand continues to far exceed the supply.

stories.Headline: Chinese experts urge educational reforms to develop AI-ready talent
stories.Summary:
Scholars and industry leaders gathered at a recent talent forum hosted by the University of Hong Kong in Beijing to discuss innovation. These participants met to explore how universities and technology firms can better equip professionals and students for a workplace reshaped by artificial intelligence. This discussion occurred as 12.7 million college graduates prepare to enter the workforce this year amid high employment pressure. Rapid advances in the digital economy are currently shrinking traditional roles while creating new occupations that require advanced skill sets.

The transition requires a shift toward interdisciplinary talent and a stronger emphasis on foundational knowledge in mathematics, physics, and languages. This educational transformation aligns with the 15th Five-Year Plan for 2026 to 2030, which calls for the digital transformation of schooling. The plan also demands deeper coordination between talent development, science, technology, and education, alongside reforms to evaluation systems. Institutions must streamline existing curricula to nurture independent learning rather than simply adding more courses to heavy workloads.

University of Hong Kong vice-president Wang Yang stated that critical thinking and judgment can turn China's educational strengths into a tangible advantage. Tan Jianrong of Zhejiang University explained that fields like robotics require integrated expertise that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries. Assistant professor Li Hongyang noted that conventional academic grades often fail to capture rigorous thinking and the ability to spot research flaws. Duan Nan of JD Group emphasized that professionals need sound judgment and the skill to frame the right questions to steer technology.

The current context involves a marked improvement in research capacity, though geopolitical tensions continue to challenge international academic exchanges. Experts believe that humans must still assess whether artificial intelligence outputs meet real user needs and deliver practical outcomes. Wang Yang expressed optimism regarding continued scientific advances over the next 10 years despite these global challenges. Future efforts will focus on integrating these new skills into the broader national strategy for education and technology.

stories.Headline: AI sell-off wipes out Nasdaq gains for 2026
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq erased all its 2026 gains on Friday, November 20, 2026, as a global AI sell-off hit the markets. This decline happened during the second day of trading for Anthropic, the company that creates the Claude chatbot AI model. Investors questioned the huge sums of money being poured into AI buildout, causing the tech-heavy Nasdaq to lose trillions. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 5% from its value on January 1, while the S&P 500 fell 3.59%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 both ended the trading day in correction territory.

Anthropic raised 81.34 billion dollars in an IPO that valued the firm at 1.414 trillion dollars on Thursday. Its shares jumped 17% Thursday, but fell 9% Friday to 88.30 dollars, near the 83 dollar debut price. The Nasdaq lost 4 trillion dollars in market value this week, and the S&P 500 fell to 6,918.45. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to their lowest since mid-April, while the Nikkei and Kospi each fell 5%. The Stoxx 600 dropped 1.9% on Friday, and the FTSE 100 fell 5.1% over the week.

Neil Wilson of Saxo said there was relentless selling in tech as post-IPO euphoria gave way to reality. Chris Beauchamp from IG suggested Anthropic could be draining market liquidity as investors sell other shares to buy it. Daniela Hathorn of Capital.com stated that demand for AI remains strong but cannot overcome concerns about elevated valuations. Benedicte Lowe from BNP Paribas told CNBC that investors were panic selling to judge if AI enthusiasm had peaked. Binky Chadha of Deutsche Bank called the market very oversold and said that growth and earnings remained strong.

Nvidia fell 14% after California served a subpoena regarding semiconductors in China, while SanDisk fell 14% and Micron fell 12%. Broadcom and AMD also fell between 12% and 14%, and SoftBank shares in Tokyo dropped 14.5% on Friday. The University of Michigan survey through November 16 showed that those with the largest stockholdings reported declining personal finances. Bitcoin dropped below 60,000 dollars for the first time since July, and gold had its worst week since March. The VIX fear gauge topped 30 for the first time since March, reflecting high levels of market anxiety.

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on November 12, and CFO Colette Kress became the interim chief executive officer. President Donald Trump threatened a tremendous tax on United States companies that build their data centers in foreign countries. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said on Thursday that the central bank will need to raise interest rates again. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5%, and the dollar reached a 19-month high due to inflation fears. SpaceX had to raise the yield on its 32 billion dollar debt sale to 8.3% recently.

The Federal Reserve will meet on December 9, and futures put the odds of a December rate hike at 95%. The chair of the Taiwan stock exchange pledged to ensure stable capital markets and reassure investors in Taiwanese companies. Analysts remain divided on whether this is a temporary sentiment shift or the start of a larger bear market. The articles leave open whether the S&P 500 will fall another 10% or more after this correction. It remains unclear if AI companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions in current investment spending.

stories.Headline: Ubisoft launches Motherbrain subsidiary to develop AI game masters and smart NPCs
stories.Summary:
Ubisoft announced on November 20, 2026, that it has launched Motherbrain, a dedicated subsidiary focused on developing proprietary generative AI technology for gameplay, according to a report in The Verge. The new unit was established as a dedicated subsidiary focused on AI for gameplay innovation, supporting all game creators in developing groundbreaking experiences, Ubisoft said in its earnings report that day. GamesIndustry.biz reported on November 21, 2026, that the subsidiary consists of the team behind Ubisoft's generative AI project Teammates, which began playtesting last year. Ubisoft said the subsidiary is currently focused on developing smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds.

Ubisoft said Motherbrain aims to serve creators globally, both within Ubisoft's Creative House ecosystem and beyond, and to form partnerships with selected technology actors. CEO Yves Guillemot added that Motherbrain aimed to empower creators and open up new possibilities for richer, more immersive and engaging player experiences. The launch comes as Ubisoft laid off 166 staff at its Montreal and Quebec studios, eliminating production and support roles to ensure resources were aligned with current production priorities and business needs. As GamesIndustry.biz understands, the cuts accounted for less than 4% of the studios' total headcount and included members of Vantage Studios.

Ubisoft said that as its portfolio evolves, its production needs are changing, requiring it to adjust the size of some teams to ensure resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs. The articles do not say who at Ubisoft is directly responsible for Motherbrain beyond Guillemot's statement and the company's own announcements. The Verge reported that Motherbrain is working on an experience called Teammates, which Ubisoft first revealed last year. GamesIndustry.biz reported that Ubisoft's H1 results showed a 16.5% decline and that the company merged two Creative Houses.

The articles do not say what happens next for Motherbrain beyond its stated focus and partnership aims. GamesIndustry.biz noted that the launch comes amid the layoffs and that Ubisoft's Q2 net bookings came in above guidance thanks to the Assassin's Creed Black Flag remake. The articles do not say whether the layoffs and the new subsidiary are connected beyond their shared timing in the same earnings period. No further details on Motherbrain's staffing, funding or timeline were given in either article.

stories.Headline: Google donates Agent Substrate, gVisor and OpenRL to the CNCF
stories.Summary:
Google donated Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, placing two core components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance, TechGig reported on Nov 20, 2026. The donation also includes OpenRL, Google's open-source reinforcement learning orchestration project, according to both articles. InfoQ reported on Nov 20, 2026, that Google announced the donation of Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF. The move is intended to address securely executing untrusted, AI-generated code and managing compute overhead from agents that frequently pause and resume. Together, the projects target different layers of agent infrastructure, from isolated code execution to managing agent lifecycles and coordinating large-scale training workloads.

Google estimates that agents can spend 90-95 per cent of their time idle while still holding important state, including memory, files, repositories, and active sessions. Agent Substrate separates agent state, called actors, from compute resources, known as workers, and actors retain state including filesystem contents, memory, and execution context. Workers provide reusable, pre-warmed execution environments drawn from shared Kubernetes pools, and when an agent resumes, Substrate assigns it to an available Worker and restores its previous state. According to Google, this approach lets agents resume in under 500 milliseconds without creating a new Kubernetes Pod for every execution, and it reduces pressure on the Kubernetes control plane. Google's gVisor provides an additional isolation boundary through a user-space application kernel that intercepts system calls and handles them within its own isolated environment, and Agent Substrate also supports Cloud Hypervisor microVMs for hardware-level virtualisation.

Google argues that conventional Kubernetes workloads and AI agents have fundamentally different execution patterns, because a traditional application typically starts, serves requests, and continues running. An AI agent, however, may execute code for a few seconds before waiting for model inference, an external API, or human approval, according to Google. Google says keeping every agent in a dedicated Pod wastes resources, while scaling to zero introduces delays when environments must be reconstructed. Google states that large-scale agent evaluations can overwhelm Kubernetes control planes when thousands of short-lived execution environments are repeatedly created and destroyed. Google's stated goal is to establish an open foundation for agentic applications, much as Kubernetes helped standardise container orchestration.

InfoQ reported that other providers are addressing similar challenges through technologies such as Kata Containers, Firecracker, and dedicated sandboxing platforms. Google's contribution is to combine secure execution with an agent-aware orchestration model and place the resulting technologies within an open ecosystem, according to InfoQ. AI agents routinely execute generated shell commands, install packages, and interact with external tools, and treating this code as trusted creates significant risks, particularly when multiple agents share infrastructure. gVisor reduces the exposure of the underlying host while retaining much of the efficiency associated with container-based execution, and Agent Substrate gives platform teams flexibility to select an appropriate isolation boundary without changing the overall agent lifecycle model. The articles state that AI agents need their own secure, stateful, and efficiently managed execution infrastructure beyond conventional Kubernetes workloads.

Kubernetes was designed around long-running applications and relatively stable workloads, according to InfoQ. Agentic systems introduce more dynamic execution patterns, where environments must be created, suspended, restored, and isolated at much greater frequency. The announcement reflects a broader shift in cloud-native infrastructure patterns, the articles state. By donating these projects to the CNCF, Google is helping establish the foundations for that next layer of cloud-native computing, InfoQ reported. The articles describe the donation as addressing emerging challenges in securely executing untrusted, AI-generated code and managing substantial compute overhead from frequently pausing and resuming agents.

The articles do not state when the CNCF will accept the projects, how the foundation will govern them, or what licence terms will apply. They do not say whether OpenRL will be managed alongside Agent Substrate and gVisor or separately within the CNCF. The articles give no timeline for CNCF review, no comment from CNCF officials, and no details on how existing Google users will be affected by the transfer. They do not state how the projects will be maintained, who the maintainers will be, or whether other companies will contribute. The articles leave open how the move will change Google's own agent infrastructure and what adoption the projects will see under vendor-neutral governance.

stories.Headline: Digital.ai launches Release 26.3 to bring governed AI agents into enterprise delivery
stories.Summary:
Digital.ai launched Release 26.3 on November 20, 2026, according to SD Times, and TechGig published its report on November 21, 2026 at 05:00 AM IST. The release elevates AI agents to first-class citizens alongside human developers and automated pipelines, the company announced. Digital.ai said the update integrates agentic workflows directly into established compliance and governance frameworks. The company unveiled the upgrade as a way to solve the tension between innovation and control in enterprise delivery. TechGig reported that the release aims to address that same tension by embedding agentic workflows in governance.

Release 26.3 allows probabilistic AI agents to operate in harmony with deterministic automations such as security scans and testing, according to the announcement. It ensures humans stay in the loop whenever policy demands it, the articles state. DevOps Agent Orchestration integrates context-aware AI agents into existing delivery flows, keeping every dynamic action fully auditable and compliant. The Release MCP Server lets developers and coding agents initiate, analyze, and optimize release pipelines directly from AI environments like Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex. Release Assistant is a native AI companion designed to help release managers diagnose pipeline failures, optimize release velocity, and streamline troubleshooting.

Derek Holt, CEO of Digital.ai, said enterprise software delivery in the AI era combines AI agents, people and automation as companies accelerate their agentic journey from coding to delivery. Holt noted that customers need those three to work seamlessly together across all delivery pipelines. He said Release 26.3 brings the power of agents and AI into harmony with traditional DevOps automation and human judgement across all delivery targets. Holt listed those targets as mainframe and data centers, cloud and containers. TechGig reported that Holt noted customers need AI agents, people, and automation to work seamlessly together across all delivery pipelines.

SD Times reported that as artificial intelligence shifts software development into hyperdrive, enterprise delivery pipelines face potential risks from AI agents inserting themselves into production environments. The article said those agents can take ungoverned actions on code and workflows. According to the announcement, organizations no longer have to choose between velocity and security. The release is available starting today, and existing users can immediately upgrade their current templates to integrate AI capabilities across legacy infrastructure and modern cloud platforms. With a flexible bring your own model approach, enterprises can use Digital.ai's hosted infrastructure or connect their own internally approved AI models.

The article said the release allows probabilistic AI agents to operate in harmony with deterministic automations while keeping humans in the loop when policy demands it. stories.Headline: Virginia Tech launches an interdisciplinary AI minor for students in every major
stories.Summary:
Virginia Tech launched a new interdisciplinary artificial intelligence minor in summer 2026, and the program is designed to prepare students in every major for careers in an AI-powered future. The minor teaches technical foundations while encouraging students to evaluate AI’s social impacts and wrestle with questions of ethics and policy. Christine Julien, head of the Department of Computer Science, led a group of collaborators from across the university in developing the program. She said that regardless of major, today’s students are entering a workforce where AI will be part of nearly every profession. Students in the minor learn the technical foundations of AI, examine ethical and social consequences, and explore how the technology intersects with fields in the arts, social sciences, business, and humanities.

The result is not simply technical training, because the minor is intended to give students the conceptual foundation to ask better questions about AI’s impacts. One such class is “The Skeptic’s Guide to AI,” which Benjamin Jantzen first taught last fall. He expected a classroom filled mostly with humanities students, but nearly every student was a first-year engineering major. Julien said the goal is to ensure Virginia Tech graduates understand how these technologies work, how to evaluate them critically, and how to apply them responsibly in their own fields. Jantzen said being a skeptic means asking whether what people are told about AI tools is literally true and whether the tools can do what they say they do.

He said it also means uncovering the assumptions behind those claims and considering what may be gained or lost, because there are always trade-offs with any technology. He said that for democracy to work, people have to understand what they are being asked to accept and what they are being asked to give up, and that demands scrutiny and the work of the skeptic. The articles describe AI as offering enormous potential to accelerate scientific and social innovation, with Virginia Tech work that includes uses designed to speed drug discovery, unravel the secrets of DNA, protect consumers from scams and identity theft, and support the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission to double scientific productivity. The articles also say AI raises concerns about related job losses, economic uncertainty, and the environmental and natural resource costs of operating systems. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the minor’s launch.

stories.Headline: At an AI Tipping Point - University of Pennsylvania
stories.Summary:
Karen Detlefsen recently challenged her philosophy students to write four letters to a classmate using different levels of artificial intelligence assistance. This exercise occurred during the Fall/Winter 2026 semester at the University of Pennsylvania to explore if AI can think like philosophers. Detlefsen wanted her students to contemplate whether machines can truly create and what it means to be human. The technology now permeates many facets of modern life, including social media, elections, and the military. In September 2026, AI solved a decades-old problem regarding equations that govern how fluids move.

The University of Pennsylvania led a natural language processing revolution in the early 1990s through several different academic fronts. Mark Liberman directed the Linguistic Data Consortium to annotate language datasets in English, Chinese, and Arabic for machine learning. Mitch Marcus led the Treebank effort at Penn Engineering to train computers to split sentences into phrases independently. Today, many U.S. city and state governments have hired Chief AI Officers to manage these emerging technologies. John Lapinski is now starting a new initiative to bring these various government leaders together for collaboration.

Michael Horowitz, a Professor of Political Science, says that AI will inevitably reshape society and more advances are coming. He believes the main question is who can adopt the technology most effectively and safely in the future. Charles Yang explains that large language models are essentially fancy versions of predictive typing that solve sequence prediction problems. John Lapinski states that governments across the world will eventually step in to decide how AI is used. Lapinski also notes that AI cannot be used when a task requires zero error, such as NBC returns.

Political campaigns and the military are affected by AI, as are people receiving information through the media ecosystem. Horowitz notes that autonomy in weapons, like radar-guided missiles used since the 1980s, requires human responsibility for force. Lapinski worries that AI could create synthetic public opinion data to mislead voters before the 2028 presidential election. He mentions a fake polling company that recently tried to proliferate fake results through the media ecosystem. The general public and experts agree that regulating artificial intelligence is a good idea, though methods remain unclear.

Alan Turing pondered whether machines could think as far back as the 1950s, long before the current AI movement. Charles Yang studied the science of cognition as a PhD student at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He notes that children learn from 5 million words yearly, while large language models use billions or trillions. Unlike the steady progression of AI, children often make more mistakes as they learn new words and grammar. AI has moved from niche academic journals to headlines in The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal.

Experts are currently figuring out how to use AI responsibly and what safeguards to put in place for data centers. The U.S. military experiments with AI but lags in adoption due to the tests required for operating procedures. Some scientists are still trying to understand how simple predictions become complex ideas, which remains a complete mystery. AI is prone to hallucinating made-up information, and policies may become obsolete quickly because the technology moves so fast. The articles leave open how the world will eventually regulate AI and if machines can truly be creative.

stories.Headline: MIT researchers constrain chaotic AI models with hard physics limits
stories.Summary:
Researchers with MIT’s Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems have found a way to introduce physics-based restrictions on machine learning models of chaotic systems. The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in a paper by MIT graduate student Sunbochen Tang and MIT professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis. The work was published on November 20, 2026, and reported by David Chandler of LIDS. The approach enforces energy dissipation as a hard constraint so predictions cannot grow without limit. The team is making the information freely available.

The model learns an energy-like function along with a boundary where chaotic behavior should be confined. A projection layer adjusts how the model predicts the system will evolve and enforces energy dissipation as a hard constraint. Outside the boundary the energy-like quantity must decrease, drawing the simulated system toward the bounded region. The team tested the approach on physical systems ranging from simple textbook cases to highly complex multidimensional systems. The paper, titled “Learning dissipative chaotic dynamics with boundedness guarantees,” and open-source code are accessible online at PNAS.

Sapsis, a professor of mechanical engineering and LIDS affiliate, said lack of guarantees for a bounded response has always been a major obstacle for data-driven models of complex nonlinear systems. Azizan, the Hayes Associate Professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society and a principal investigator in LIDS, said tiny differences in starting conditions can lead to dramatically different outcomes. He said chaos does not mean anything can happen and that these systems often remain bounded, and their models should be too. Tang, a doctoral student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and LIDS, said the model learns an energy-like function and a boundary, and a projection layer enforces energy dissipation.

Tang said previous attempts imposed penalties or incentives during training, with no guarantee the model satisfies the constraints at test time. He said capping predictions, for example at 100 degrees for temperature, could restrict the model from representing complex features learned from data. Azizan said the fundamental difference is hard constraining versus soft constraining, and the output is always physically consistent even for a new case. He said data is not as abundant for many physical systems, so physics-constrained approaches can help because the physics is another source of information. Tang said the approach is readily applicable to a wide range of neural network architectures.

The models are used in climate and weather, industrial processes, aeronautics, and hydrology. In fluid dynamics, turbulent flows can disrupt air travel, reduce the efficiency of wind turbines, and affect fuel economy of vehicles. In weather forecasting, the chaotic nature of atmospheric dynamics makes accurate long-term predictions difficult. The team plans to continue testing the approach on ever-larger systems and is trying to see how well it would work on data-driven models of realistic weather systems. Azizan said the projection layer is modular, model-agnostic, and can work with different neural network architectures.

A follow-up work this year by members of the team was presented at the Learning for Dynamics and Control conference and won the conference’s Best Paper Award. Azizan said trustworthy and reliable AI needs more than evidence that a model usually works, and for high-stakes applications you need guarantees about properties that must always hold. He said the team established one such guarantee, boundedness, and the broader goal is to make principles part of how AI models are built, not just how they are tested. Azizan said he hopes other researchers and practitioners will build on the projection layer and test it on larger and even more complex problems. The articles do not say when the follow-up work was presented or what it found.

stories.Headline: UVA President Beardsley outlines plan to use AI while keeping human judgment central
stories.Summary:
On Friday, UVA President Scott Beardsley sent an email to the University community outlining his vision for the role artificial intelligence will play at UVA. The note was published November 20, 2026, by University News under the headline that Beardsley charts the University's future in artificial intelligence. Beardsley says UVA will harness the potential of artificial intelligence across the University while prioritizing responsible use and human judgment. The photo accompanying the article is by Lathan Goumas of University Communications. Beardsley joined colleagues in the Contemplative Sciences Center for a symposium on AI and Human Flourishing.

UVA offers more than 100 AI-focused courses per year and AI instruction is embedded in all 12 schools. UVA researchers have advanced AI and large language models for more than three decades. UVA is investing in computing power through the new Fontaine Computing and Innovation Center and spearheading the Commonwealth AI Initiative. The initiative unites universities, industry, government, and nonprofits to establish Virginia as a source of trusted, responsible AI expertise. The work takes place at the first data science school in the country and at the LaCross Institute for Ethical AI in Business at the Darden School of Business, which will soon host a conference.

Beardsley said UVA will not outsource consequential decisions to machines, and that AI will support human judgment, not replace it, in classrooms, labs, clinics, and offices. He said the goal is graduates with technical literacy in AI who can question it, critically interpret it, and know when to set it aside. He said the most successful universities will pair the newest technologies with the oldest methods of teaching and learning, including the Socratic seminar, the blue book, oral exams, and the argument defended aloud. He said faculty will continue to decide what resources students may use in coursework and the technologies permitted in their classrooms, and must be clear about expectations whether they embrace AI, restrict it, or take a hybrid approach. He said students are bound by the Honor Code and are leading the discussion on upholding Honor in the age of AI.

Beardsley said UVA's Information Technology Services already offers embedded AI tools such as Microsoft Copilot Chat and Google Gemini in the Academic Division, though many in the community are paying for licenses to additional tools. He said UVA is committed to providing equitable access and exploring frontier AI platforms, and will share more information soon. He said AI is shaping nearly every profession and is a trillion-dollar industry, and that UVA is building infrastructure to track AI's effects on the workplace in partnership with employers, recruiters, and alumni. He said UVA will adapt curricula, bolster career services, and partner with AI-related companies to hire students and collaborate with faculty on research. He said four standing University committees on AI, for teaching and learning, research, operations, and policy and use, will advise as the work unfolds.

Beardsley wrote that AI has been around for decades and has been part of the development of the internet, social media, and broadband communications, and that the emergence of agentic AI is accelerating the pace of transformation. He wrote that UVA was founded on the belief that education should serve the public good, especially in moments of rapid and profound change. He wrote that scholars and stakeholders have been advancing the understanding of AI for years and confronting the hard questions it raises for society. He wrote that UVA has backed that purpose with sustained investment in AI spanning research, institutes, infrastructure, and partnerships with leading companies. He wrote that Jefferson founded the University on the belief that people learn best through genuine human relationships built on discussion and debate.

In the coming weeks, interim Provost Brie Gertler will share updates on AI applications in the Academic Division, and Dr. Mitch Rosner will share updates with UVA Health. Beardsley wrote that UVA will pilot AI with care across its operations and will continuously reassess and adapt as the technology advances at exponential rates. He wrote that no one has a crystal ball. He directed readers to AI@UVA and to the faculty-led AI Exchange@UVA podcast for an interview with him and others. The article does not say what the updates from Gertler and Rosner will contain.

stories.Headline: NMSU receives DARPA award for solution to AI trust issues - New Mexico State University
stories.Summary:
Two New Mexico State University professors are leading one of only 10 teams in the country receiving grants to work on one of the biggest challenges in artificial intelligence, which is how to build an AI you can trust with life-or-death decisions. Son Tran, an NMSU computer science professor and department head, and Stylianos Vasileiou, an NMSU assistant computer science professor, received a $600,000 grant over two years through a special research area under the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. That program is called CLARA, short for Compositional Learning-And-Reasoning for Automated Complex Systems Engineering, and it is a fundamental research program designed to tightly integrate artificial reasoning and machine learning components to create high-assurance machine intelligence. Their proposal carries the title "SPARTA: Splitting-based Polynomially-bounded Automated Reasoning with Tensorized Adaptation," and NMSU is working with two other research groups, one led by Chitta Baral from Arizona State University and the other by Yuliana Lierler and Jorge Fandinno from the University of Nebraska at Omaha.

The team's goal is to develop high assurance and broadly applicable methodologies for combining Automated Reasoning and Machine Learning, according to the article. Tran said integrating these branches of artificial intelligence will provide the speed and flexibility of machine learning with verifiability based on artificial reasoning proofs that have strong logical explainability and computational tractability. He said the team will focus on developing efficient and scalable approaches to combine machine learning approaches with logic programs, and such systems will provide explanations for their answers, which is a key difference compared to contemporary machine learning systems. Vasileiou said AI generally splits into two camps, one great at spotting patterns quickly and the other great at following strict logic, and combining them gives you the best of both worlds. He said you are getting an AI that can think fast on its feet while still showing its work in a way humans can verify and trust.

Right now, building an AI that is safe enough for critical jobs takes massive amounts of custom engineering, and CLARA aims to create one universal foundation that is rock-solid, mathematically proven, and ready to adapt to almost any complex problem. The program aims to build a reliable, plug-and-play AI engine that can be reused across dozens of high-stakes industries without needing to be rebuilt from scratch every time. The article names Minerva Baumann, a media relations officer, as the contact for the story and lists the College of Arts and Sciences, artificial intelligence and computer science among its tags. The release date for the announcement was Nov. 20, 2026, and the article does not say what happens next beyond the two-year grant and the work with the partner groups.

stories.Headline: UConn president Maric calls for breaking silos to grow Connecticut's AI economy
stories.Summary:
Hundreds of people gathered at Rentschler Field in East Hartford on Thursday, Nov. 19, as UConn held its annual Economic Impact forum. The event was entitled “Powering the AI Economy for Connecticut Towns.” It was the third consecutive year for the forum, held in Storrs in 2024 and Stamford in 2025. Connecticut leaders from government, academia, and industry attended. UConn held the forum in the club level of Pratt & Whitney Stadium at Rentschler Field.

The forum explored how Connecticut’s established strengths support continued growth and the roles each sector must play. UConn’s annual economic impact to Connecticut has grown to $13 billion, supporting 60,000 jobs and returning $19 for every dollar the State invests, according to Reka Wrynn, UConn’s associate vice president of budget and planning. The forum marked Radenka Maric’s first public remarks since the UConn Board of Trustees announced plans to extend her presidency. Anthropic, the company that created AI platform Claude, went public on Thursday, closing at $97.17 a share for an evaluation of about $1.76 trillion. According to the Wall Street Journal, it was largest IPO in history.

UConn President Radenka Maric said the state must break through silos that obstruct collaboration. “It is not only what technology can do for us, it is how we enhance our collaboration,” Maric said. Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz led a standing ovation, saying she joined Gov. Lamont in excitement that Maric will continue her tenure. Bysiewicz said the state has a distinct advantage and does not need to build an economy around AI from scratch.

“UConn is one of our state’s most important economic assets,” Bysiewicz said. David Bergman, associate dean for faculty and research for the School of Business and special advisor for AI to the provost, said the forum’s timing was appropriate given Anthropic’s record-setting IPO. Hartford Mayor Arunan Arulampalam said the city seeks to work with a set of hiring institutions that rivals any city in the country. “Our goal is to have a workforce that is among the most prepared for the technology of tomorrow of any workforce in America,” Arulampalam said.

Lindsay DiStefano, UConn’s vice president for research, innovation, and entrepreneurship, highlighted the Grant Trails heat map, which demonstrates research impact town-by-town through Connecticut. Assistant Professor Wei Ren of the College of Agriculture, Health, and Natural Resources led the UConn proposal that earned a highly competitive Genesis Award. The program is federally funded by the Department of Energy to double the country’s scientific productivity by funding AI-related research projects. The DOE granted $525,000 for a project that uses AI to study how water and other fluids move underground.

DiStefano said the winner comes from an area vital to the mission of a land grant university and the state. The forum included expert panels on how UConn is teaching responsible use of AI to students and building partnerships with organizations throughout the region. Several students presented individual research topics, including crumbling foundations in Connecticut, weight stigma in social media, and inventions. Bysiewicz addressed Connecticut’s modern “industrial revolution,” with economic transformation as business adapts to AI, quantum computing, biotech, and advanced manufacturing.

She said the state has a proven legacy of companies, an educational network, and governmental infrastructure to meet challenges. She said the state needs to make innovation an engine of broad-based economic opportunity. Arulampalam explained how the capital has built opportunities out of what already was in place, seeking not to create a new “Silicon Valley or Cambridge.” He said the city is seeking to foster opportunities to work with employers and colleges to create hands-on opportunities for students.

stories.Headline: Engineers, Clinicians Partner to Advance Human Health with AI
stories.Summary:
Engineers at the University of California, Davis are working with clinicians on artificial intelligence tools meant to detect Alzheimer's disease earlier, expand care options for survivors of sexual assault and improve results for patients awaiting corneal transplants. The projects are funded by AI and Health Seed Funding Awards from the Center for Information Technology Research in the Interest of Society and the Banatao Institute, known as CITRIS, which aim to strengthen interdisciplinary connections between schools and colleges across UC Davis and UC Davis Health and to establish the university as a leader in AI-enabled healthcare technology research. The awards followed a matchmaking mixer for engineers and clinicians held in November 2025 and co-hosted by the UC Davis AI Center in Engineering, or AICE, with CITRIS, the Healthy Aging in a Digital World initiative and the Clinical and Translational Science Center as partners. That event produced six awarded seed grants, including the three co-led by engineers.

For the Alzheimer's project, Chen-Nee Chuah, the Child Family Professor in Engineering in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, is developing an AI model that can pick up early signs of the disease from a patient's speech, working with Michelle Cohn, a postdoctoral scholar in linguistics, and Alyssa Weakley, an assistant professor of neurology. The team is examining conversational interviews with older adults from the UC Davis Alzheimer's Disease Research Center Corpus, which is annotated with patients' cognitive status such as mild cognitive impairment or late-stage Alzheimer's, to train a model to identify biomarkers of cognitive impairment by analyzing how a patient sounds and their manner of speech. The team has completed the datasets needed to train the large language model on acoustic and linguistic features of cognitive impairment in older adults, and the National Institutes of Health has given the researchers a boost to develop an AI-enabled remote monitoring system to detect health issues in older adults, which will directly support the early detection work. The project will culminate in a real-world pilot deployment within a local senior living community.

Josh McCoy, an associate professor of computer science, is leading a project to develop a trauma-informed, AI-powered chatbot that can connect survivors of sexual assault with appropriate social and health support services, with Jessica Draughon Moret, an associate professor at the UC Davis Betty Irene Moore School of Nursing, as co-lead. The private chatbot aims to expand access to and simplify the process of seeking care, and the pair are working to ensure it is informed by human-centered design and built on expert consultation with survivors. The team has a prototype for the platform, called CARE-COMPASS: Community Assistance and Resource Engagement, and is currently in the refinement and user feedback phase, with the goal of seeking additional funding from the National Institutes of Health for further development and broader use. Separately, Hamed Pirsiavash, a professor of computer science, is co-leading a project with Mark Mannis, a distinguished professor of ophthalmology and vision science, to develop an AI-powered evaluation system for donated corneal tissue, joined by Min Zhao, a professor of ophthalmology and vision science, Ana Sandoval Castellanos, a postdoctoral fellow in the Laboratory for Cell Nanoengineering, and several medical students.

The cornea team has been working with Sierra Donor Services, a non-profit donor procurement organization serving the Northern California and Northern Nevada regions, to source a curated dataset of microscopy images of corneal tissue, and through self-supervised learning the system uses computer vision and machine learning to distinguish between healthy and abnormal tissue. The goal is to reduce clinicians' workload from hours to minutes when evaluating tissue and to minimize variability in the quality of donated tissue, and the project's next step is to test the AI model with larger sample sizes. Sam King, a professor of computer science and director of CITRIS at UC Davis, said an engineer can build a model that scores well on a benchmark and still fails in a clinic because the team does not know which errors matter to a patient, while clinicians know but cannot build these systems alone. He said the technology is improving faster than those partnerships are forming, and the awards exist to close that gap by putting engineers and clinicians on the same problem before design decisions are made. The awards dovetail with the AICE's AI and Health research area, which accelerates discovery by facilitating conversations between engineers and clinicians, and through AICE's partnership they are helping realize CITRIS Health's mission to encourage innovations in technology that improve health outcomes and increase access to medicine.

stories.Headline: Anthropic spends $3.4 billion on Caterpillar gas turbines for off-grid AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Anthropic spent 3.4 billion dollars on gas turbines to power its artificial intelligence data centers in the United States. This massive transaction was finalized in late September between the corporate leadership of Anthropic and the company OnePWR Solutions. The AI developer took over an equipment order queue that OnePWR had placed with Caterpillar Inc. two years earlier. By assuming these manufacturing slots, Anthropic avoids supply chain constraints that would otherwise delay access to heavy-duty generator hardware. This deal represents the largest single purchase of power generation equipment ever executed by an artificial intelligence firm.

The Anthropic Off-Grid 1.7GW Power Generation and Data Center Initiative requires 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty, gas-fired generation equipment. This commitment includes hardware fabrication, balance-of-plant engineering, and site construction works for the project located in the United States. The buildout requires high-pressure natural gas piping, heavy structural steel, concrete foundation footings, high-grade copper wiring, and specialized acoustic cladding. Technical needs include gas pipeline interconnections, step-up substations, on-site fuel storage, SCADA microgrid controls, and direct liquid cooling interconnections. Design contractors are integrating high-efficiency natural gas turbine sets with specialized cooling modules and modular power blocks.

Anthropic PBC is the developer responsible for this initiative and is using it to secure a dedicated electricity supply. The company wants to maintain execution velocity across its multi-hundred-billion-dollar compute pipeline while preparing for an initial public offering. By becoming a power plant owner, the firm avoids utility grid interconnection backlogs that can delay projects by several years. This strategy ensures uninterrupted operational uptime for next-generation foundation models by skipping the reliance on public utility transmission upgrades. The company is taking direct control of its energy supply chain to keep gigawatt-scale training clusters running.

Industry analysts identify utility grid interconnection backlogs as the single largest constraint on modern data center deployment today. Major cloud operators are increasingly deploying self-generated natural gas power systems to secure reliable electricity while waiting for upgrades. The program will support thousands of specialized engineering, fabrication, and heavy civil construction jobs during the buildout phase. At peak, construction employment is estimated at more than 3,500 workers across mechanical, electrical, pipeline, and civil trades. Once operational, the project will support over 450 permanent jobs for electrical engineers, data center technicians, and plant operators.

The deal occurs during a global competition for high-density computing infrastructure, including SK Hyper's pursuit of 350 billion dollars. This shift reflects a broader trend where AI developers move from being grid customers to owning their own power. The project combines high-density AI data center infrastructure with distributed natural gas power plant infrastructure to bypass grid bottlenecks. These systems are designed for base-load and peak-shaving operations to deliver continuous, utility-scale electricity to off-grid campus locations. The initiative aims to accelerate deployment schedules and drive large-scale equipment manufacturing employment within the United States.

Deployment is organized into three phases, starting with Caterpillar delivering initial natural gas generator sets to designated installation sites. Engineering teams will then perform civil integration by connecting microgrid switchgear, step-up transformers, and fuel supply pipelines. Finally, on-site power units will energize live server clusters without grid reliance to complete the operational commissioning process. Phased hardware deliveries will run through 2027 and 2028 to reach the total continuous capacity of 1.7 gigawatts. The report leaves open the specific campus site coordinates and the final completion date for the full fleet.
