stories.Headline: Nvidia weighs cutting its over $100 billion AI investment push under interim CEO Colette Kress
stories.Summary:
Nvidia is considering a reduction in its artificial intelligence investment strategy. This shift follows a scandal and the resignation of former Chief Executive Jensen Huang. The company has previously spent enormous sums of money in the AI market. Wall Street and Silicon Valley are now watching the flow of capital. Observers want to know who will be hit first if funding stops.

The total investment portfolio exceeds 100 billion dollars across labs, power producers, and cloud firms. Nvidia held 48 billion dollars in eight listed companies as of September 30. These include a 10 percent stake in CoreWeave, plus investments in Nebius Group, Intel, and xAI. On November 19, Nvidia committed 10 billion dollars for shares in the Anthropic initial public offering. It also guaranteed 105 billion dollars for an Ohio data center project for SB Energy.

Interim CEO Colette Kress spoke during an earnings call on November 17. She stated that she takes pride in the company's role in supporting the industry. Kress said the firm will stick to its principles when evaluating future investment deals. She noted that much work remains to determine the right types of investments. These comments suggest a change from the approach used under Jensen Huang.

Critics describe these financial arrangements as circular financing because recipients use funds to buy Nvidia chips. This structure means that trouble at one party can spread to other companies. Investors who sold Nvidia shares also unloaded stock in related companies. The combined market value of eight listed portfolio companies fell 820 billion dollars since October 6. OpenAI is affected as it agreed to lease capacity from the Ohio data center.

Nvidia participated in venture deals totaling 220 billion dollars this year, which is 27 percent of global investment. The company made large bets on private firms including OpenAI and Anthropic. These deals boosted demand for Nvidia chips and made the firm a financial center. Nvidia holds exclusive rights to supply chips during the first half of the Ohio project. The AI ecosystem depends heavily on this vast financial support.

Long term supply agreements and lease obligations rose to 518 billion dollars from 85 billion dollars last year. Nvidia must meet these sizable purchase commitments over the coming years despite any management changes. The company will continue to evaluate whether specific investments are right for its future. The articles leave open how the new management will scale back its investment. It remains unclear which specific partners will lose financial support first.

stories.Headline: Akamai turns away AI infrastructure deals as power limits constrain capacity
stories.Summary:
Akamai Technologies is turning away some potential AI infrastructure business because of limited power availability, Chief Financial Officer Ed McGowan said at an event hosted by RBC software analyst Rishi Jaluria, MarketBeat reported on Saturday, November 21, 2026. The company has signed $14 billion in large deals this year, McGowan said. He said its pipeline is the largest he has seen in its history. Demand comes from enterprises, foundation-model developers, startups and other AI companies. Power constraints make it difficult to take on additional large projects requiring capacity in 2027.

McGowan said power is the most important and scarcest element today, and that availability should improve in the second half of 2028 and into 2029. Akamai closed a $2.5 billion offering the prior week and is funded for its committed deals without returning to debt markets through 2028, Jaluria said, and McGowan confirmed that. McGowan said Akamai has investment-grade ratings from Fitch and Moody's, while S&P downgraded the company. He attributed the difference to the agencies' assumptions about future leverage and growth. He said Akamai expects to deleverage over the next two years as it pays down debt and expands EBITDA margins.

McGowan declined to set a firm date for a sustainable return to positive free cash flow, saying faster cloud infrastructure growth would require more capital spending before revenue arrives. Depending on the pace of growth, he said, the company could reach that point in 2028 or later. He said three large customer projects expected to start in the fourth quarter are now generating revenue. Data center construction, customer-specific fit-outs and equipment issues can affect the precise date revenue begins, he said, calling it spreadsheet risk. Asked about an approximately 13% internal rate of return calculation for a large infrastructure contract, McGowan said Akamai included data center fit-out and network connection costs, as well as spare capacity, in its analysis.

McGowan said those costs could be shared as other customers are added to the same facilities. He said the calculation assumed revenue only for the contract's duration, although the company may be able to continue using the equipment afterward. He described the return as a floor, noting that a customer committing to a deal of that size receives Akamai's best pricing. McGowan said Akamai sees substantial demand for CPUs alongside GPUs in AI applications and will supply the hardware customers need. He pointed to potential uses for its distributed infrastructure in latency-sensitive applications, including robotics and other forms of physical AI.

Akamai is already supporting workloads from central cloud to the edge, including post-training work, McGowan said, but does not plan to build gigawatt-scale facilities for large-scale model training. Its development work includes making applications easier for customers to run without specifying the underlying hardware. In security, McGowan said AI-related bot activity is increasing demand for bot management tools, although traffic volume does not translate directly into revenue. Customers are also seeking broader web application firewall coverage, he said. McGowan described security as a healthy, recurring-revenue business but stopped short of predicting an acceleration in its growth rate.

Akamai acquired cloud provider Linode in March 2022, and McGowan said the company has since more than quadrupled the revenue it acquired in that transaction. McGowan said Akamai's own rising third-party cloud costs, along with customer requests to run their code on Akamai's platform, helped prompt its entry into the broader compute market. He said Akamai would continue to consider acquisitions, while weighing potential deals against returns from investing in its fast-growing cloud infrastructure business. McGowan said the company's financing needs after 2028 would depend largely on how quickly it chooses to grow. Akamai provides cloud computing, cybersecurity and content delivery services through Akamai Connected Cloud.

stories.Headline: NHAI deploys AI dashcam analytics to detect road damage and track contractor repairs
stories.Summary:
The National Highways Authority of India is deploying an artificial intelligence-powered analytical tool to assess road conditions, identify damage to roads and pavements, communicate the information to contractors, follow up on the complaints and ensure that the issues are rectified. NHAI officials announced the system during a series of technical sessions at the 85th Indian Roads Congress in Hyderabad on November 20, 2026. Dashcam Analytics systems have been mounted in patrol vehicles to monitor highways for infrastructure-related issues. The system captures geotagged, high-resolution photographs of road conditions, pavements and road signage and uploads them to a dashboard, where each photograph is uniquely numbered. The system then communicates the information to the relevant contractor, who proceeds to rectify the issue, and NHAI officials described it as an end-to-end detection to rectification system.

Key road conditions identified by the system include potholes and road rutting, which refers to the formation of depressed surfaces on the road. Other issues identified include edge dropping and uneven road shoulders, streetlights that are not working, signage, and gaps in road medians. The Indian Roads Congress also deliberated on whether India could take a lead in road safety globally. Samrat Valani, vice-president of Development, Operations and Customer Experience, North America, Transurban, made a case for a clear mandate to halve road deaths by 2030, in line with the Stockholm Declaration on road safety adopted in 2020. He emphasised the need for a strong framework based on the four Es of education, engineering, enforcement and emergency care, along with political will and evidence that the initiatives were working.

Sharing examples of road safety interventions from across the world, Valani said that data show that in India, 54,000 people who did not wear helmets lost their lives last year. Citing the case of Vietnam, which he described as a motorcycle country, he said a government-led awareness programme at around 100 schools had increased helmet use from 36% to 69% in one year. As the programme continued, they saw in the next year that the usage dropped to 50% and stabilised at around 57%, and he said the point was not the number of injuries but the helmet use and the ability to count, because when you count, you get to know the effectiveness of the programme. Touching upon the importance of quick incident and accident detection, leveraging technology to respond to incidents and clearing them as quickly as possible, he said that in the US, for every minute an incident remains on the roadway, the likelihood of a secondary accident increases by 2.8%. Informing road users, creating awareness and measuring outcomes, adopting a fair approach by issuing warnings, particularly in cases of speeding, followed by firm enforcement, and using data to prevent crashes are important metrics, he said.

stories.Headline: Rep. Vince Fong introduces bipartisan bill to place private AI experts inside CISA
stories.Summary:
Representative Vince Fong introduced a bipartisan bill on November 20, 2026, to strengthen cybersecurity in the United States. This legislation follows several widespread technical outages that have recently impacted various systems across the entire country. The Bridging Resources for Innovative Defense and Government Expertise in Artificial Intelligence Act would authorize the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to collaborate with private professionals. This bill calls for a pilot project involving about 100 private sector workers to serve within the CISA. It also requires a semi-annual report on the status of the program and ways the agency could improve it.

Republican Representative Vince Fong of Bakersfield stated that communities and critical industries are struggling to keep up with a surge in AI-related cyberattacks. He noted that attacks in the Central Valley have targeted water systems, hospitals, and schools to steal sensitive data. Fong argued that bringing in private sector specialists ensures that national experts have the tools needed to modernize systems. Democratic Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey co-authored the bill and said that adversaries are using AI to attack American networks.

He claimed that the agency on the front lines of defense does not have enough capacity to keep pace. Gottheimer stated that the act is a common sense fix to help the agency hunt intruders and patch vulnerabilities. The bill follows a nationwide plane ground stop and outages impacting the National Security Agency and Microsoft Outlook. Other affected entities include Apple, United Airlines, and multiple banks that experienced technical failures.

These events highlight the vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure that the new legislation aims to address through private sector expertise. The bill must be approved before the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency can begin collaborating with the private sector AI professionals. The legislation aims to stress-test AI tools before they are exploited by adversaries to protect national security. The articles do not state when the bill will be debated or if it has passed.

stories.Headline: Dan Ives views recent AI sell-off as a generational buying opportunity
stories.Summary:
Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives discussed a significant artificial intelligence sell-off during a CNBC interview on Friday, November 21, 2026. He described this recent downturn as one of the most disconnected technology crashes he has witnessed since starting his career in the late 1990s. The market experienced a sharp swing in investor expectations, causing the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF to drop over 6 percent. Meanwhile, the iShares U.S. Technology ETF fell nearly 7 percent during the same trading session.

This volatility requires investors to look past current political uncertainty and concerns regarding chip export restrictions to China. Ives believes the market is incorrectly pricing stocks as if the AI revolution will not happen, despite the cycle being less than 15 percent complete. He noted that demand for chips from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Nvidia Corp. remains so high that new orders might not be filled until the end of 2028. Furthermore, he stated that roughly 75 percent of data center projects have already received the necessary permits.

The Yorkville Ives partner argued that the current market sentiment is an overreaction to spending concerns and a political backlash against data center expansion. He characterized the situation as a white-knuckle roller-coaster moment but maintained that the broader technology bull market remains intact. Ives suggested that this period represents a generational opportunity to buy winning companies before the market realizes its mistake in eighteen months. He believes the infrastructure boom will eventually benefit financial services, industrials, and energy companies.

The current turbulence follows a blue tidal wave of political opposition that acted as a gut punch to technology investors. While retail sentiment on Stocktwits remained bearish toward the S&P 500 ETF, some indices showed recovery in after-hours trading. The Invesco QQQ Trust ETF rose 1.53 percent, and the SPDR S&P 500 ETF gained 1.11 percent. Ives expects the long-term potential of the industry to eventually outweigh these temporary shocks.

stories.Headline: TSMC suspends advanced chip orders for Chinese design firms amid tighter export controls
stories.Summary:
On November 19, Reuters reported that TSMC tightened restrictions on certain Chinese semiconductor design companies. The company suspended manufacturing orders using 16nm technology or more advanced nodes. These actions occurred as export controls evolved toward manufacturing capacity and advanced packaging. The restrictions target the entire AI supply chain rather than individual chips. This shift happened during a period of extraordinary demand for AI infrastructure.

Affected Chinese customers are generally limited to older 28nm and 40nm manufacturing processes. This limitation applies provided their products do not require advanced packaging or incorporate HBM. TSMC can no longer use the previous technical verification process for these specific designers. Advanced chip orders are now presumed to fall under export controls unless authorizations exist. These rules apply to companies operating across Taiwan, China, Southeast Asia, Europe, and the United States.

The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security introduced an interim final rule on November 16. This regulation targets overseas data centers providing substantial computing capacity to restricted foreign entities. Regulators stated that restricting physical exports may be insufficient if users obtain remote access. They are concerned with who ultimately accesses the computing capacity that advanced chips provide. Compliance now involves monitoring beneficial ownership and cross-border computing arrangements for cloud providers.

Chinese semiconductor designers are the primary entities affected by these new manufacturing restrictions. They face challenges in rebuilding an entire ecosystem including domestic foundries and memory technologies. Using older nodes increases electrical power consumption, silicon area, and system integration complexity. NVIDIA, AMD, and smartphone manufacturers may absorb the capacity left by canceled Chinese orders. These high performance computing customers represent a shift in TSMC's potential customer mix.

TSMC reported October 2026 consolidated revenue of approximately NT$586.9 billion, a 59.7 percent increase. Revenue for the first ten months of 2026 increased 43.3 percent over 2025. NVIDIA announced expanded manufacturing commitments on November 17 with Foxconn, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Kinsus, Amkor, SPIL, and TSMC. The Vera Rubin NVL72 platform and Vera CPUs began volume shipments during the third quarter. These products leverage CoWoS technologies and TSMC's 3nm and 5nm nodes.

NVIDIA provided multibillion-dollar funding to SPIL for expanded advanced packaging operations in Taiwan. The company also made substantial prepayments to Amkor for expansion in South Korea and the United States. OSAT providers and equipment suppliers must now demonstrate the traceability of their delivery networks. The articles leave open whether these restrictions will produce temporary or permanent shifts. Future developments over the next twelve months will determine the final impact.

stories.Headline: Solidigm reports $8.7 billion net profit in first nine months of 2026
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix's enterprise NAND subsidiary Solidigm and its controlling entity reported KRW 11.56 trillion, or about $8.7 billion, in net profit during the first nine months of 2026, according to The Herald Business. That figure was roughly 42 times the KRW 277.4 billion the same business reported a year earlier. The subsidiary's revenue reached KRW 21.96 trillion, about $16.5 billion, over the nine-month period, nearly quadrupling from KRW 5.61 trillion, or about $4.2 billion, a year earlier. Its net assets climbed to KRW 12.61 trillion, roughly $9.5 billion, and the $8.7 billion represents reported net profit rather than the subsidiary's valuation.

Solidigm specializes in enterprise solid-state drives built using NAND flash memory, which provides the persistent storage needed to retain large volumes of information. SK Hynix had been reviewing a U.S. listing of Solidigm with an anticipated fundraising target of approximately $10 billion, but the company suspended its IPO review on Oct. 23. Solidigm's controlling entity, formerly SK Hynix NAND Product Solutions, was renamed HYAICO on Oct. 30 and restructured as a holding company. The Herald report said the two entities' operations and financial results are nearly identical, and it estimated that HYAICO's full-year net profit could exceed KRW 17 trillion if the current pace continued, an extrapolation rather than company guidance.

CEO Kwak Noh-Jung explained in the company's third-quarter results announcement that the listing was originally intended to raise external capital for Solidigm's production expansion and reduce SK Hynix's investment burden. After reviewing market conditions, management concluded that proceeding would not deliver the originally anticipated outcome. Investors should watch whether enterprise SSD demand and profitability remain strong as AI data-center capacity expands, and how SK Hynix funds Solidigm's next production investments without an IPO. The question is how durable the NAND business's contribution will be if memory supply catches up with demand.

stories.Headline: Yunhong Han and co-authors present ReactNexus, a generative framework that maps reaction networks from reactants alone
stories.Summary:
A paper posted to arXiv on 21 November 2026 by Yunhong Han and 18 other authors describes ReactNexus, a generative framework that produces transition-state candidates directly from reactant graphs without requiring products to be specified in advance. The framework then predicts the chemical species those candidates connect and refines the resulting pathways using a reactive machine-learned potential to guide exploration of the reaction network. Its models were trained on a quantum-chemical database of 130 million structures drawn from 1.1 million reaction records, covering 11 elements and multiple charge and spin states. The authors say the work shows how generative models can extend mechanistic analysis to increasingly complex reaction mixtures.

On held-out reactions, 93.6% of the generated candidates refined to valid transition states at the density functional theory level, and 83.3% connected the supplied reactants to distinct products. Across decomposition, complex rearrangements and organocatalysis, ReactNexus showed how competing mechanisms shape product formation and uncovered pathways that previous studies had missed. In a multisite nucleophilic aromatic substitution, it identified diarylation products that explained LC-MS signals which had initially gone unassigned, with the structural assignments supported by NMR after isolation. ReactNexus also predicted an additional product family that was not detected under the initial conditions, and later experiments at higher temperature provided LC-MS evidence supporting its formation.

The authors frame the work as a response to a specific difficulty, noting that automated saddle-point searches can explore from reactants alone but their computational cost rises sharply as competing pathways accumulate across successive steps. They also observe that machine-learning approaches to transition state generation typically require predefined products, even though identifying those products is a central goal of exploration. ReactNexus is presented as a way around both constraints, generating candidates from reactants and then refining the pathways with the reactive potential. The abstract highlights the potential of generative models to extend mechanistic analysis to increasingly complex reaction mixtures.

The paper is titled Generative discovery of chemical reaction networks, and its author list runs from Yunhong Han and Gaopeng Ren through Chenru Duan and Qiyuan Zhao. The work was posted on arXiv along with a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, and the posting carries the standard arXivLabs notice describing that framework for collaborators who develop and share features on the site. That notice states that individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have accepted values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and that arXiv works only with partners who adhere to them. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the higher-temperature experiments already reported.

stories.Headline: Tristan Harrison urges comms teams to ask six questions before commissioning AI video
stories.Summary:
The article is a set of six questions for PR and comms teams to ask before commissioning AI video, written by Tristan Harrison, who spent years in PR agencies before running a production company that combines AI with live action and traditional filmmaking. He says the Christmas season ended the theoretical stage of the AI advertising debate, pointing to the backlash over Dior's animated holiday short and to Very, which was upfront about combining CGI with AI-assisted animation and achieved its highest-ever pre-launch audience-testing score. He also notes that the IAB has updated its industry framework on AI transparency and disclosure and that the EU AI Act's transparency rules are already in force. His conclusion is that audiences are not necessarily against AI, since they want good creative and honesty about how it is made, and that AI video is a reputational decision for comms teams rather than only a creative or production one.

The six questions cover who is actually making the film and who is responsible for the final cut, since the software is not an acceptable answer, and where AI genuinely adds value, since it is not always quicker or cheaper and the technology should serve the idea. They also cover approval points, because a small change such as a shirt going from green to red can mean rebuilding an entire sequence, and Harrison describes getting clients to approve static AI-generated frames before animation and asking for a PPM meeting as with traditional film making. Ownership is the fourth question, covering likeness rights, consent, synthetic voices, music licensing, the tools used and ownership of the finished assets, with the warning not to assume a supplier's software licence covers the brand's intended use. Disclosure is the fifth, which he says should not be an awkward conversation after the film is finished, since not every AI-assisted production task requires a public label but nobody involved should be left guessing, and discussing it only at launch is too late. The sixth asks whether the supplier can deliver beyond the demo, with advice to see completed client projects rather than showreels and to find out how revisions are handled when AI does not deliver what was expected.

Harrison gives one example from his own experience, a brief involving precise eye movements that proved difficult to control with AI, where an actor and a camera would have been simpler. He says the best approach might be fully AI-generated, live action or a hybrid, and that suppliers should be asked why they recommend a particular route and whether they considered the alternatives. He describes comms teams as often the last line of defence for a brand's reputation and says that with AI video they should also be the first people asking the right questions. The article ends with an invitation to sign up for the publication's free twice-weekly editorial alert and to register for free analysis on techniques and campaigns in the PR sector.

stories.Headline: Salt Security finds 77 percent of firms using AI see agents act outside authorized behavior
stories.Summary:
Salt Security reported on November 19 that 77 percent of organizations using or exploring AI saw agents act outside authorized behavior. This finding came from a poll of 500 C-suite professionals conducted by Censuswide from September 10 to 18. The respondents included 250 leaders from the US and 250 from the UK. These professionals worked at organizations with 50 or more employees. Most executives, specifically 92 percent, would still allow agents to take some independent action.

The poll found 64 percent of leaders restricted, delayed, or canceled AI projects over regulatory, governance, or security concerns. While 97 percent of AI users keep agent inventories, 19 percent admit these lists are not consistently updated. Salt sells tools to discover agents, MCP servers, and APIs to monitor runtime behavior and govern connections. Other surveys show different results, such as a 49.8 percent rate from Salt's October 13 report. EMA reported 65 percent of agents acted outside scope, while CSA found 53 percent exceeded permissions.

Salt co-founder and COO Michael Nicosia stated that executives give agents authority over money, data, code, and customer relationships. He argued that governance cannot be a one-time approval process for these systems. Nicosia said organizations need continuous visibility into what every agent can reach and actually does. He believes a static inventory or single sign-off is a weak foundation for governance. This view contrasts with Microsoft, which points to identity, permissions, and policy controls.

The CSA survey affected 445 IT and security professionals and was fielded in September and November 2025. Illumio and Sapio Research polled 1,100 decision-makers in 10 markets, finding 26 percent of agents connected without approval. EY surveyed 202 senior AI executives at US public companies with at least one billion dollars in revenue. Their data showed 26 percent of organizations using agentic AI cannot detect unauthorized internal agents. These various figures reflect different respondent groups, denominators, and definitions of unauthorized action.

The articles note that agents often inherit access through existing APIs, identities, and applications across separate teams. This relates to the mid-1970s least privilege concept by Jerome Saltzer and the 1988 confused deputy problem by Norm Hardy. The UK National Cyber Security Centre warned in December 2025 that language models are inherently confusable deputies. Salt Labs also found that the Manus platform, based in Singapore, was vulnerable to hidden email prompts. TechRadar reported on October 2 that Manus fixed this issue after JavaScript ran in the runtime.

Next, buyers should ask five questions about who answered, the denominator, what counted, the timing, and who paid. The articles leave open whether control belongs at the moment access is granted or during agent runtime. They also leave the exact definition of an AI agent open, as no standard definition exists. It remains unclear how serious the incidents were for the 77 percent of firms. Finally, the reports do not state exactly how many projects were affected by governance concerns.

stories.Headline: SpaceX sells $32 billion in bonds through a trust to buy Nvidia chips for its data centers
stories.Summary:
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) sold $32 billion of bonds through a trust set up to buy Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) chips on Thursday, with the largest piece paying investors a yield above 8%. The sale was reported by The Motley Fool on Friday, November 20, 2026, and the stock was down 6.7% as of 11:39 a.m. ET on Friday. The bonds are part of a more than $40 billion financing package SpaceX announced in October. The largest piece, about $25.2 billion, was priced at a yield of 8.259%.

The average yield on high-grade U.S. corporate debt was 5.95% that day, and bonds considered "junk" were yielding an average of 8.3% that day. To try to keep the debt off its books, the financing runs through a separate entity, a trust that sells the bonds, buys the chips, and leases them to SpaceX. Functionally, SpaceX is still the one borrowing, and its quarterly lease payments are what pay the bondholders back. The loans are secured by the chips in the same way a mortgage is secured by a home, and if SpaceX ever defaulted, the lenders' fallback would be to repossess the GPUs and sell them. The chips, destined for SpaceX data centers, are expected to start arriving in January.

The AI unit nearly tripled its sales between Q2 and Q3, growing revenue from $2.6 billion to $7.6 billion. According to reporting from The Financial Times, the lenders involved wanted guarantees that SpaceX would keep the financed chips on terra firma, apparently worried about the logistics of repossessing chips circling the Earth at about 17,500 mph. It is not clear if the lenders were able to get anything binding in the final documents, but SpaceX says these chips are for its "terrestrial compute build-out." CFO Bret Johnsen said in the company's October financing announcement that SpaceX is seeing "less than one year payback periods" on its infrastructure investments. The business spent $16.4 billion in capex in its Q3, the lion's share of the company's overall $19.6 billion capex spend.

The Motley Fool's Johnny Rice wrote that he is still skeptical long-term and does not think the payoff will hold up. Similar maneuvers are increasingly common across the AI data center market as companies look for ways to deal with ballooning debt balances. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Nvidia and Space Exploration Technologies. Johnny Rice has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The stock was down 6.7% as of 11:39 a.m.

stories.Headline: EU AI Act amendment delays high-risk rules but adds new prohibitions and enforcement powers
stories.Summary:
The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, entered into force on 27 July 2026 and amends the AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, on a number of points. It is widely described as a postponement, and in one important respect it is, because the obligations for high-risk AI systems will now apply later than originally planned. That description is incomplete, however, because much of the AI Act already applies and the Omnibus also introduces new prohibitions and stronger enforcement tools. The note by Logan & Partners sets out the main changes and what they mean in practice for companies that develop, procure or use AI systems in the European Union. The AI Act is not a future regime, since its first provisions have applied since 2 February 2025.

Since 2 February 2025 the practices prohibited under Article 5 have been unlawful, including manipulative or deceptive techniques, social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images, and emotion recognition in the workplace and in education, subject to limited exceptions. Infringements may lead to fines of up to EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Providers of general-purpose AI models have been subject to Chapter V since 2 August 2025 and must maintain technical documentation, put in place a copyright policy and publish a summary of the content used for training. The Commission's power to fine these providers has applied since 2 August 2026, and the transparency obligations in Article 50 have also applied since that date. Users must be informed when they interact with an AI system, synthetic content must be marked in a machine-readable format, and deepfakes must be disclosed.

Under new Article 111(4), providers of generative AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026 to comply with the marking obligation in Article 50(2). The requirements and obligations in Sections 1 to 3 of Chapter III will apply from 2 December 2027 to the systems listed in Annex III, which covers areas such as recruitment and workforce management, creditworthiness assessment, risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, education, biometrics, critical infrastructure, law enforcement, migration and the administration of justice. They apply from 2 August 2028 to AI systems that are safety components of products, or are themselves products, covered by the EU legislation listed in Annex I, such as medical devices, toys and lifts. The recitals explain that the postponement responds to the late availability of harmonised standards and to delays in setting up national authorities, and the legislator chose fixed dates. The Omnibus does not link application to the publication of standards, so companies should not plan on the assumption of a further extension.

The transitional rule in Article 111(2) has also been adjusted, so high-risk systems placed on the market or put into service before the relevant application date fall within the AI Act only if their design is significantly changed after that date. According to the recitals, this assessment is made per type and model, and systems intended for use by public authorities must in any event comply by 2 August 2030. The Omnibus adds two prohibitions to Article 5, which apply from 2 December 2026, the first covering AI systems that generate or manipulate realistic intimate images or sexually explicit content of an identifiable person without that person's explicit consent and the second covering AI-generated child sexual abuse material. Under new Article 5(1a), a provider may be caught even where its system was not designed for this purpose, where such output is a reasonably foreseeable outcome that can be reproduced without significant technical modification and the system lacks adequate safeguards to prevent it.

A deployer, by contrast, is caught only where it uses the system for the purpose of generating such material, so providers of general-purpose image and video generation tools should review their technical safeguards. Article 25 now specifies the information, technical access and assistance that an initial provider must give to the party that becomes the provider of a high-risk system, and it also requires written agreements with suppliers of AI models, tools and components. A breach of these obligations may now be fined up to EUR 15 million or 3% of turnover under new Article 99(4)(da). At EU level, the AI Office has obtained exclusive competence over certain AI systems, including systems based on a general-purpose AI model where the model and the system are developed by the same provider, and AI systems that constitute or are integrated into very large online platforms or search engines, with some exceptions.

The AI Office now has inspection powers and may impose periodic penalty payments. Article 4 on AI literacy now requires providers and deployers to take measures to support the AI literacy of their staff, and it states expressly that no specific level of literacy has to be guaranteed. SMEs and the new category of small mid-cap enterprises may provide technical documentation in a simplified form and apply a quality management system proportionate to their size, and where they are fined, the lower of the fixed amount and the percentage of turnover applies. New Article 4a allows providers of high-risk systems to process special categories of personal data where this is strictly necessary to detect and correct bias, subject to specific safeguards, and in exceptional cases the same possibility extends to deployers of high-risk systems and to providers and deployers of other AI systems and models.

The Commission has published draft guidelines on classification under Article 6, the consultation closed in July 2026 and, at the time of writing, the final guidelines have not been adopted. Article 6(3) allows certain Annex III systems to be treated as not high-risk, for example where they perform only a narrow procedural or preparatory task, but this exception never applies to systems that perform profiling. Providers relying on it must document their assessment before placing the system on the market and register the system. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Study finds European Union uses AI Act to seek global influence through governance
stories.Summary:
Vasiliki Koniakou published a scholarly investigation in Information Systems Frontiers on November 21, 2026. The study evaluates if the European Union can gain global influence through its Artificial Intelligence Act. This research examines the act as a domestic framework and a geopolitical instrument. The author uses legal analysis and policy review to assess the rulebook. The study focuses on a strategy called leadership through governance.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 establishes a risk-based scheme for a market of 450 million consumers. Article 5 prohibits social scoring, untargeted facial scraping, biometric categorization, and workplace emotion recognition. High-risk systems under Article 6 and Annexes I and III require continuous risk management and human oversight. Article 27 mandates Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments for certain public or high-impact sectors. Article 50 requires machine-readable markings for synthetic content and biometric categorization.

Koniakou says the Union uses its single market to compensate for lacking frontier models. The author states that strategic intent is designed into the legal and administrative architecture. The researcher argues that the act functions as a sociotechnical regime reshaping corporate workflows. Koniakou notes that compliance might become superficial documentation rituals without technical integration. The author concludes that European influence is currently spreading in a diluted, terminological form.

The study notes the United States leads through capability and dominant private technology firms. China pursues leadership through state-directed plans and national champions to align research. Multinational corporations are affected by the Brussels Effect to avoid inefficient separate production pipelines. Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon, Cohere, and Mistral AI signed a 2025 code. Meta declined participation, while xAI endorsed only the safety chapters of the code.

The Union lacks native digital platform giants and private venture capital despite strong research. This situation is described as the European Paradox where science fails to reach commercial supremacy. The 2020 White Paper on AI and 2021 Coordinated Plan provided the foundational intent. The High-Level Expert Group defines Trustworthy AI as being lawful, ethical, and technically robust. The act targets machine learning opacity, system autonomy, and algorithmic inscrutability.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 deferred high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028. This amending statute added prohibitions against child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate imagery. Article 99 allows fines up to 35 million euros or 7 percent of turnover. The AI Office has exclusive authority over foundation models in very large online platforms. The articles leave open if foreign firms have permanently integrated European ethical norms.

stories.Headline: Dutch court bans BYD Ti7 SUV sales in EU for infringing Land Rover Defender design
stories.Summary:
A preliminary relief judge at the district court in The Hague barred the sale of the BYD Ti7 SUV in the European Union on November 20, 2026. The court ruled that the seven-seat vehicle infringes upon the design rights held by Jaguar Land Rover for the Land Rover Defender. This legal action followed the launch of the Ti7 in China under the Fangchengbao brand during 2025. The judge determined that the distinctive and characteristic elements of the Defender are reflected in the design of the BYD model. This decision came during summary proceedings rather than a full trial to address the immediate design conflict.

The injunction takes effect one week after the ruling because BYD currently lacks concrete plans to place the vehicle on the market in the European Union. Until the legal case is resolved, BYD is prohibited from producing the Ti7 at its new factory in Hungary, which was scheduled for mass production early next year. The court stated it had no jurisdiction over the UK affiliate of BYD, meaning the order does not reach Britain. JLR filed the suit after BYD listed the Ti7 on its UK website with deliveries planned for January 2027. Media reports highlight the boxy flat-roof shape, squared-off wheel arches, and upright proportions as key points of contention.

BYD stated that it strongly disagrees with the ruling and maintains that the Ti7 resulted from its own independent design work. The company intends to appeal the decision and will pursue every available legal avenue to challenge the ban. Jaguar Land Rover, which is owned by Tata Motors, stated that proceedings are ongoing and that the company protects its intellectual property. JLR declined to provide further comments beyond these statements regarding the current status of the litigation. The Defender remains a critical asset for JLR, with more than 100,000 units sold worldwide in 2025.

This unusual early ruling occurs as BYD expands its presence, with European sales doubling to over 280,000 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026. According to ACEA data, BYD has recently outsold other major manufacturers including Ford, Tesla, and Nissan in the region. Major automakers rarely sue over design rights in Europe, making this specific court decision a rare occurrence in the industry. The outcome of the appeal will determine if BYD can eventually bring the Ti7 to the European market. The legal battle highlights the growing tension between established European brands and expanding Chinese automotive firms.

stories.Headline: Google ties school access to AI tools as administrators gain opt-out control
stories.Summary:
Google announced on Nov. 3 that students using its classroom software will lose access to Google Search if their school administrators opt out of the company's artificial intelligence tools altogether, according to Associated Press reporting cited by Newstalk KZRG. The decision follows Google's move in August to activate its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students using Google Classroom. Google said it will no longer automatically enable AI tools for K-12 student accounts, and administrators will be able to individually enable or disable tools including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Google Search, with the features off by default until administrators turn them on. Because Google's Search tools are integrated with AI, schools that choose not to use AI will also lose access to Google Search through those student accounts.

The policy could affect school districts across southwest Missouri, southeast Kansas, northeast Oklahoma and northwest Arkansas, where schools rely on digital platforms, Chromebooks and online search tools for everyday instruction. Google says about 150 million students and teachers worldwide use Google Classroom, and many students rely on school-issued Chromebook computers. Google Vice President and General Manager of Education Chris Phillips said the company believes schools should have control over AI in classrooms and the ability to manage how the technology is used. The company also said it is updating Search to better support learning, including offering step-by-step guidance through problems rather than simply providing quick answers to assignments.

Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan criticized the decision, arguing Google is using its influence over school technology to encourage AI adoption. Josh Golin, executive director of children's advocacy group Fairplay, also criticized the policy, arguing that schools should consider privacy-protective alternatives to Google and encourage more substantive research methods. Missouri's U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley joined Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut in sending a letter to Google CEO Sundar Pichai demanding answers about AI integration into school technology. The senators set a Nov. 2 deadline for Google to respond to nine questions, including why AI features were made the default in some school settings, what research the company has conducted into AI's effects on children's mental and emotional well-being, and how the company responds to concerns raised by teachers, parents and school administrators.

Google's Nov. 3 announcement addressed changes to its AI settings for school administrators, but did not directly respond to the senators' letter or address all nine questions. The debate continues over whether AI should be a tool schools choose to implement or a technology they must accept to maintain access to services students already rely on. School systems nationwide are navigating how to incorporate emerging technology while maintaining safeguards for students and preserving educators' authority over classroom instruction. For schools across the four-state region, the discussion could ultimately center on whether districts retain the flexibility to decide how students access information, what technology they use and how AI fits into the learning environment.

stories.Headline: Shield ranks on Deloitte Technology Fast 500 for second straight year
stories.Summary:
Shield, a communications risk management solution for financial institutions, was named to the Deloitte Technology Fast 500 for the second consecutive year, according to an announcement published on November 19, 2026. The annual ranking recognizes the 500 fastest-growing technology companies in North America, and the company said the placement follows its recognition as a Visionary in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Digital Communications Governance and Archiving. Shield also ranked among the three highest-scoring vendors across six use cases in the accompanying Gartner Critical Capabilities for Digital Communications Governance and Archiving. The company said this marks its third consecutive year of recognition in both reports since the category was established.

The recognition reflects demand from financial institutions that are replacing fragmented legacy archiving and surveillance systems while regulatory requirements continue to tighten, Shield said. The company said its AI-native platform gives firms full visibility and control over communications data across its entire lifecycle, and its AmplifAI suite reduces alerts requiring manual review by 77.3% while accelerating investigations resolution by up to seven times. Shield said its BI Insights tool turns raw surveillance data into trackable metrics covering alert trends, review coverage, reviewer productivity and operational performance. The company also said its modern archive, included in Forrester's 2026 Information Archiving Platforms Landscape, reduces storage costs by up to 50% and eliminates archive export and exit fees.

Shiran Weitzman, CEO and co-founder of Shield, said the growth reflects a fundamental change in what financial institutions expect from communications compliance technology. He said some firms are moving away from decades of fragmented legacy infrastructure, while others have invested in modernization but have not realized the transformation they were promised. Weitzman said both groups want to move beyond managing systems and start managing risk more intelligently, and he described the company's goal as building a next generation of compliance where trusted data, agentic intelligence and human control work together. He said the second consecutive Deloitte recognition reflects the trust customers place in that vision and the dedication of the team.

Shield said it recently introduced native capture of Microsoft 365 Copilot and Claude interactions for archiving, surveillance and investigations, and its MCP Server lets institutions securely access surveillance intelligence through supported AI tools while maintaining existing governance and access controls. The company said it will continue investing in AI innovation, modernizing communications risk management and strengthening partnerships with leading financial institutions as it expands its global footprint. Shield said its ambition is to set a new standard for communications compliance in which trusted data, intelligent automation and human judgment work together. The company said it believes readiness must be continuous so institutions have the intelligence, agility and control to handle whatever comes next.

stories.Headline: CalCPA launches Spark to teach 75 accounting students client and people skills
stories.Summary:
The California Society of CPAs launched a leadership development program called Spark, part of a broader ecosystem named Leader Lab 360 that was introduced in June 2026, and its first cohort brought together 75 students from campuses across California, ranging from Fresno State to schools in Los Angeles and the Bay Area, including community colleges. The program was described in a November 2026 article by Miklos Ringbauer, founder of MiklosCPA and the 2026-27 board chair for CalCPA, who said the effort focuses on skills that rarely appear on an exam but show up in every client meeting. Those skills include interviewing, personal branding, networking and follow-up, client communication and navigating the first day on the job, and five virtual sessions build the foundation for an immersive capstone in Sacramento. At that capstone, participants turn learning into action through real-world challenges, professional networking and hands-on advocacy at CPA Day at the Capitol, and Ringbauer said those in-person days are where a group of students becomes a cohort and where mentoring relationships begin.

Ringbauer argued that as artificial intelligence takes on more routine work such as data entry, reconciliations and spreadsheet organization, emerging professionals have an opportunity to engage in higher-value work earlier than in the past, when young accountants spent years on administrative and compliance tasks before moving into client relationships and advisory work. He said communication, critical thinking, adaptability, collaboration and relationship-building will become even more important as AI becomes more capable, and that the human connection is at the heart of the profession. He acknowledged that such abilities are sometimes called soft skills but said that term undersells their importance, because the ability to communicate, build trust and exercise judgment complements technical expertise rather than ranking below it. He also said accounting has adapted to technological change before, as paper ledgers gave way to spreadsheets and spreadsheets gave way to cloud-based systems and sophisticated analytics, with each transformation changing the work CPAs do without eliminating the need for trusted professionals.

Ringbauer, who teaches federal taxation at Orange Coast College, said he cares that Spark reaches community college students and that education should give students the foundation and confidence to solve problems they have not yet encountered. He said the question is not simply whether AI can perform accounting tasks but how professionals are prepared to work alongside it, and he described the responsibility as making sure the next generation of CPAs is ready for that transformation. He said a CPA license can be a foundation for far more than traditional accounting, including entrepreneurship, leadership, advisory work, innovation and public service, and that the future of accounting will require professionals who understand both technology and people. The article does not say what happens after the first cohort or give further details on future sessions.

stories.Headline: Yes Bank tightens AI cyber defences and delays fintech payouts
stories.Summary:
Fintech platforms have been hit as collateral damage while Yes Bank strengthens its defences against AI-driven cyberattacks, sources told Inc42 on November 21, 2026. The cybersecurity upgrades at Yes Bank are disrupting workflows and delaying payouts at payment service providers, according to those sources. One fintech executive said his platform faced issues ever since Yes Bank sent an email noting the bank was implementing enhanced precautionary measures to safeguard transactions. He was subsequently informed that the bank was making changes to its banking APIs, which was delaying settlements. These changes are impacting payment processing and settlement timelines for some businesses that rely on banking APIs to move funds.

Another industry insider said the issues began to crop up after the Reserve Bank of India issued directives to banks and other financial institutions to bolster cybersecurity defences. According to that source, the RBI directions came after the recent cyberattack on the State Bank of India, referring to the data leak at the bank in October. The RBI is also said to have directed banks and other financial institutions to ensure customer funds are not impacted by the growing wave of AI-assisted cyberattacks. Inc42 has reached out to Yes Bank for a comment on the matter. This story will be updated upon receiving their response.

CERT-In issued an advisory dated November 21 flagging that malicious actors were using AI-driven cyberattacks to undertake unauthorised transactions at technology service providers handling government-linked payment processes and platforms handling vendor payouts. CERT-In said attackers altered business records or approval relationships and then used legitimate payment processes to approve fraudulent transactions. The watchdog did not elaborate on how much money had been funneled out. CERT-In said the reported incidents involved cyberattackers misusing business applications and workflows rather than direct exploitation of payment APIs alone. As per CERT-In, these attackers used trusted systems to process unauthorised transactions and exploited gaps in verification and reconciliation of changes to business records.

CERT-In identified techniques used by attackers, including automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems, services and possible attack paths. It listed rapid preparation and modification of exploits for known vulnerabilities, including through analysis of software updates and related technical information. It also cited use of multiple agents or automated workers to undertake reconnaissance, privilege discovery and other intrusion tasks in parallel. CERT-In noted modification of scripts, requests and attack steps in response to errors, blocked attempts or information returned by targeted systems.

It also flagged use of valid credentials, legitimate administrative functions, trust relationships and external infrastructure to gain further access. CERT-In directed government entities to identify and restrict accounts and integrations that can approve payments or change payment-related records. It recommended independent certification for high-risk changes to payment records and called on banks to reconcile critical business data maintained by service providers against authoritative records. It called on the TSPS to restrict administrative accounts and control-plane privileges.

CERT-In also directed fintechs to review unusual activity and monitor changes to payment-related business records. Multiple Indian crypto exchanges continue to grapple with delays in processing withdrawals due to disruptions at their banking partners. Coinbase India had paused all withdrawals last week before partially resuming payouts, citing an outage at its banking partner. CoinDCX, facing similar issues, claimed upgrades at most of its partner banks were delaying processing of INR withdrawals.

Zebpay said payouts were taking longer than usual because of a technical disruption at its banking partner. Earlier yesterday, Razorpay told customers it had to delay merchant settlements temporarily due to a technical issue at a partner bank, and the IPO-bound unicorn later reinstated the service hours later. The development comes on the same day CERT-In issued its alarm over unauthorised transactions at technology service providers for banks and other financial institutions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Cognizant executive says legacy systems absorb up to 80% of banks IT budgets
stories.Summary:
Ashish Bhatnagar, Head of Banking & Financial Services for Cognizant in the UK & Ireland, gave a Q&A to FinTech Magazine published on November 20, 2026, about how banks can turn legacy systems into an AI advantage. He said legacy technology is a major constraint on banks' modernisation efforts. He said legacy systems can absorb up to 80% of banks' IT budgets through simple maintenance. He said many of these systems support critical services and contain decades of business rules and institutional knowledge. He said it can be difficult to scale or transition to new technology.

He said architecture reviews, risk assessments and security approvals were designed to provide essential control but often cannot scale with the volume and pace of a major transformation programme. He said this produces late-stage delays, fragmented delivery and a reluctance to experiment. He said fear of failure can create paralysis, because if a new system fails it can affect whether people can pay bills or access their money. He said in the UK alone banks spend an estimated £3.3bn (US$4.3bn) annually managing core legacy systems. The article states core banking management and maintenance consumes an average of 24% of UK banks' IT budgets, nearly a quarter.

He said the true cost of legacy extends beyond licence fees, upgrades and system run rates to substantial below-the-line costs from additional employees and the specialist knowledge and manual processes required to keep systems operating. He said every hour and pound devoted to maintaining ageing infrastructure cannot be used to improve customer experiences, introduce new products or integrate AI. He said legacy environments can make banks less attractive to scarce technology talent. He said governance, security and regulatory controls are indispensable in banking but the processes used to apply them can become bottlenecks. He said the answer is not to weaken oversight but to embed it into delivery from the beginning.

He said security, compliance, data permissions and usage rights should be designed into the architecture and supported by repeatable, automated controls. He said an AI-ready bank has moved beyond isolated pilots and created the conditions to deploy AI securely, responsibly and at enterprise scale. He said that requires infrastructure capable of supporting AI, accessible contextual data, and robust permissions and governance built into the architecture from the outset. He said the bank also needs a culture that permits controlled experimentation, supported by the right engineering, data and AI skills.

He said AI readiness means AI becomes part of how the organisation operates, not simply another tool, and can support complete workflows while meeting security, compliance and customer expectations. He said existing systems often contain valuable assets including business rules, customer context, historical data and institutional knowledge. He said AI can help surface and apply that intelligence while accelerating modernisation itself. He said AI-driven automation, predictive DevOps, automated testing and self-healing systems can improve productivity and reduce the burden of technical debt.

He said banks can then modernise in controlled stages, focusing investment on the value streams that matter most and minimising disruption to critical services. He said this approach creates value sooner, makes transformation decisions better informed and frees up resources for further innovation. He said leaders should first reduce structural friction by identifying where legacy complexity, manual controls and approval bottlenecks create drag, then simplify or automate them. He said teams should second organise delivery around value streams, focusing on complete customer or business outcomes rather than isolated technology components.

He said this improves delivery speed and reliability, increases straight-through processing and prevents risk, security or architecture issues emerging late. He said banks should third build intelligence from existing systems, using AI to extract value from the data, business rules and institutional knowledge already embedded in their estates, with security, compliance, permissions and responsible-AI controls designed in from the outset. The article lists Cognizant's partners as Microsoft, AWS, Google Cloud, Temenos and ACI Worldwide, and says Cognizant and ACI Worldwide demonstrated ACI's BASE24-eps card-processing platform running at scale on AWS, processing more than 4.6 million transactions without failure in performance testing. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Walmart reports 25% rise in global ad revenue as AI tools and connected TV deals gain traction
stories.Summary:
Walmart reported on November 20, 2026, that its global advertising revenue rose 25% in the latest period, while U.S. ad sales climbed 37%, according to a Simply Wall St article published on Yahoo Finance. Management tied the advertising gains to recent moves in connected TV, including acquisitions involving Vizio and Vibe.co, and the retailer also highlighted new AI powered retail media tools and conversational commerce features as part of its advertising push. The article said Walmart runs a global network of stores, clubs, websites and apps that generate vast shopper data, which gives its advertising unit a direct line to purchase behavior across consumer retailing. The piece was described as general in nature and produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St.

The article said the 25% advertising jump feeds into a broader pattern its research has tracked, and it noted that its analysis turns up one warning sign for Walmart as well. It framed the ad rise as fitting Walmart's narrative that higher margin businesses such as advertising, marketplace services and memberships gradually matter more to earnings than low margin store sales, and it said the main factor that has to go right is continued growth and profitability of those alternative profit pools. The article also said the news sharpens a key risk already flagged in that narrative, that regulators are scrutinising Walmart's use of AI and digital pricing, and that tighter rules on how Sparky or digital shelf tools work could slow the profit streams investors are now cheering. It pointed readers to a full story suggesting a $129 fair value for Walmart.

The article did not name any Walmart executive or provide direct statements from the company, attributing the advertising figures and the connected TV and AI details to management and the retailer generally. It said the advertising surge gives bulls fresh evidence that the ad unit is not just an add-on but a material earnings contributor that differs from traditional retailers such as Target or Costco. It also said that to judge what the headline really means for Walmart, readers need a clear view of where its mix of low margin retailing and higher margin services is heading over time, which it said is exactly what a narrative tries to spell out. The article stated that Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned and that the piece does not constitute a recommendation to buy or sell any stock.

The context the article gave is Walmart's effort to build higher margin income streams alongside its store sales, with advertising, marketplace services and memberships expected to matter more to earnings over time. It said the advertising gains were supported by AI tools and connected TV deals and described the ad unit as increasingly material rather than incidental. The article did not say what happens next beyond inviting readers to add Walmart to a watchlist and get alerts as these catalysts play out, and it noted that its analysis may not factor in the latest price-sensitive company announcements or qualitative material. It also said the article does not take account of readers' objectives or financial situations.

stories.Headline: Performativ links bank staff AI assistants to client records under existing permissions
stories.Summary:
Performativ connected AI assistants used by bank staff to client and portfolio records on November 19, 2026. This release allows employees to query business systems using tools like ChatGPT and Claude. The company used the Model Context Protocol to create these links for existing clients. This update is specifically for bank staff and not for the bank clients themselves. The service is off by default and requires a firm to enable it.

The system uses the Model Context Protocol to link assistants to records hosted in the EU. Administrators decide who can use the service, and each employee uses an individual login. Existing Performativ permissions apply to every user, and the company logs every request for audit. The platform connects to more than 150 custodians and supports over 1,500 advisors. It manages more than 100 billion euros in client assets across its broader platform.

CEO Albert Geisler Fox stated that the current release is for staff at client firms. He described letting bank clients query their own portfolios through AI assistants as a future ambition. The company says this setup prevents staff from manually copying client data into outside assistants. Performativ claims these controls ensure security and regulatory compliance for the firms using the service. The company says the system keeps data access tied to the firm's existing rules.

The service affects relationship managers, portfolio managers, back office teams, and compliance staff. Relationship managers can use the tool to create briefings that compare portfolio progress with projections. Portfolio managers can examine performance and risk alongside the advice a client previously received. Compliance teams can review risk profiles, regulatory status, and recent changes to client records. These workflows use data including meeting notes, account activity, and the identities of responsible advisors.

The MCP capability builds on governed agent workflows introduced with Custom Agents in November 2025. Performativ provides a platform for portfolio management, customer relationship management, compliance, and reporting. The company aims to move AI queries into the assistants that employees already use. This builds on the existing platform where firms manage their client relationships and records. The new version changes where staff can ask questions about their business data.

The next step is the ambition to let bank clients use their preferred AI assistants. This future direction would allow clients to ask about portfolios under the bank's controls. The articles do not state when this client facing feature will be released. They do not provide the specific adoption numbers for the new MCP service release. It remains open how many firms have enabled the service since November 19.

stories.Headline: Delaware court fines partner personally for filing unverified GenAI output but spares his firm over its AI policy
stories.Summary:
The Delaware Court of Chancery sanctioned a senior partner personally under Court of Chancery Rule 11 for filing a brief containing unverified GenAI output, in Leiske v. Kidd, C.A. No. 2025-0426-CDW (LWW), on November 13, 2026. The underlying proceeding concerned advancement, and on January 22, 2026, the plaintiffs filed an answering brief opposing the defendants' exceptions to a Magistrate in Chancery's final report. Five days later, the defendants' reply brief pointed out that the brief contained fabricated quotations, inaccurate citations and hallucinated legal propositions. The following day, the plaintiffs' lead counsel, who had signed the brief, filed a letter acknowledging that a GenAI tool had been used and submitted a corrected brief.

The letter attributed the failure to catch the errors to an oversight during a paralegal's cite-check, but the corrected brief removed quotation marks around the nonexistent quotes while retaining the inaccurate descriptions of the underlying cases. When defence counsel wrote to the court identifying the remaining misrepresentations, the plaintiffs' counsel responded by faulting opposing counsel for failing to "meet and confer" before alerting the court and insisting that the cited authorities were real and supported the arguments advanced. After resolving the exceptions dispute on the merits, the court issued an Order to Show Cause concerning the GenAI issues, which directed both the signing partner and his law firm to explain why sanctions should not be imposed under the applicable court rule and the court's inherent authority. The partner and the firm filed detailed affidavits, and the court determined the matter without an evidentiary hearing. The court emphasized that the use of GenAI in legal practice is neither forbidden nor inherently problematic, and that these tools offer substantial benefits and efficiencies, but they must be used with the care required by the court's Rule 11 and the Delaware Lawyers' Rules of Professional Conduct, including ensuring the accuracy of every authority and citation presented to the court.

Under Court of Chancery Rule 11(b)(2), an attorney who presents a paper to the court certifies that, after an inquiry reasonable in the circumstances, its legal contentions are warranted by existing law. The court said that "[a]n attorney's signature on a court filing is not a procedural formality; it is a certification to the tribunal," and that a fake quotation or a fabricated legal synthesis generated by an algorithm is not "existing law," so presenting unverified GenAI output violates the rule. Rule 11(c)(1) provides that, absent exceptional circumstances, a law firm must be held jointly responsible for violations committed by its partners, associates or employees. Drawing on Rule 5.1(a) of the Delaware Lawyers' Rules of Professional Conduct and the American Bar Association's Formal Opinion 512, the court asked whether the firm had made reasonable efforts to put in place measures giving reasonable assurance of compliance. The court concluded that it had, because the firm had barred the use of unapproved GenAI tools in March 2023, formed a working group in 2024 to evaluate tools and study ethical guidance, and adopted a comprehensive GenAI policy in July 2025 requiring an experienced lawyer to review GenAI output for accuracy and completeness.

The firm had also developed an accredited ethics training program that over 200 employees had completed by January 2026, and the court said the firm "did the right thing" and should not be sanctioned for an individual lawyer bypassing those controls. The signing partner, as Chair of his firm's AI subcommittee, had been piloting a GenAI tool that was not approved for general firm use, yet he used that tool to draft and condense arguments in the brief. He then delegated cite-checking to a junior lawyer and a paralegal and filed the brief without personally verifying the authorities, and the court held that the duty of candour and the obligation to conduct a reasonable inquiry under Rule 11 are personal and nondelegable. The court held that a senior lawyer who signs a brief cannot disclaim responsibility for unverified GenAI output where the lawyer knowingly introduces text generated by GenAI into a draft, and the signatory must ensure that the underlying authorities have been reviewed and that those authorities actually support the propositions for which they are cited.

The court rejected the argument that it was sufficient that the cases cited were real or that the overarching propositions were arguably consistent with general principles of law, noting that GenAI tools not only invent case names but also fabricate plausible-sounding quotations and stretch real decisions to stand for propositions they never addressed. The court stated that counsel has an affirmative duty to review the underlying authorities and correct the errors if GenAI errors are detected, and that "[i]t is not enough to remove quotation marks and leave a fabricated legal synthesis in place." As to the sanction, the court weighed the partner's initial deflection of blame and the retained mischaracterizations against his subsequent acceptance of full responsibility, sincere contrition and long record of practice before the court. It imposed a fine of US$2,500, consistent with fines in comparable proceedings, and given the nondelegable nature of the duty, the partner was required to pay it personally.

Additional mandatory continuing education was considered redundant, since the lawyer had already completed several GenAI ethics programs and led internal training. The court noted that GenAI tools are now widely used in everyday legal practice and can assist with drafting, condense and refine written material, and outline arguments in a fraction of the time it would otherwise take. At the same time, courts across North America have been faced with a steady stream of briefs and factums containing fabricated cases, invented quotations and mischaracterized holdings, and the question is no longer whether such errors will attract judicial scrutiny but what happens when they do. The article states that although this is a Delaware decision, the reasoning will resonate with litigators and their firms in any jurisdiction where courts are confronting the same problem.

It states that a lawyer who signs a factum or other document citing authorities owns every citation in it, and reliance on a cite-check by others will not shift that responsibility, particularly where the signatory knows that GenAI-generated text was used. It states that verification must go beyond confirming that a case exists and requires reading the authority to confirm that any quotation is accurate and that the decision supports the proposition for which it is cited. For law firms, the article states, the decision underscores the value of a clear GenAI policy, verification requirements, restrictions on unapproved tools and documented training for members of the firm. The article states that its content is intended to provide a general guide to the subject matter and that specialist advice should be sought about specific circumstances.
