stories.Headline: Researchers recover pruned MoE experts without training through gated reuse
stories.Summary:
Linliang Chen, Yan Zhong, Wang Kang, Sai Li, Ji Wu and Ji Liu posted a paper to arXiv on 21 November 2026 describing a method for recovering the work of pruned experts in Mixture-of-Experts large language models. Mixture-of-Experts models activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all experts in GPU memory for high efficiency, and expert pruning reduces that memory footprint but discards the contribution of the pruned experts. The authors report that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. They propose GEAR, which stands for Gated Expert Activation Reuse and reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation. They also propose GEAR$^2$, which adds an ultra-lightweight residual to further recover what reuse cannot express.

The work was tested on five Mixture-of-Experts large language models ranging from 16B to 106B parameters, with 25% and 50% of experts pruned. GEAR improves over its training-free counterparts in nearly every setting, by up to 4 percentage points in terms of accuracy. GEAR$^2$ outperforms baseline approaches by up to 2.75 percentage points in every setting across nine zero-shot benchmarks. The authors report larger advantages, up to 2.72 percentage points higher, under more aggressive pruning of up to 50%. The paper contrasts its approach with existing remedies that rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training.

The paper lists Linliang Chen, Yan Zhong, Wang Kang, Sai Li, Ji Wu and Ji Liu as its authors, and the abstract presents the findings and the two proposed methods in the authors' own account. The authors state that GEAR reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation, and that GEAR$^2$ adds an ultra-lightweight residual for what reuse cannot express. They describe the reconstruction of pruned experts' functionalities from the activated remaining experts as a finding of the paper. The abstract frames the motivation around the GPU memory footprint that expert pruning reduces and the discarded contribution of pruned experts that existing remedies handle in other ways.

The articles provide no information on what happens next, such as release of code, further testing or publication beyond the arXiv posting. The abstract reports results on nine zero-shot benchmarks and on models from 16B to 106B parameters, with pruning at 25% and 50%. The arXiv listing notes that a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source are available for the paper. It also describes arXivLabs as a framework allowing collaborators to develop and share features directly on the arXiv website, and states that arXiv is committed to openness, community, user data privacy and partnership with organizations that adhere to those values.

stories.Headline: International Court of Justice rules Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
stories.Summary:
The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday, Nov. 19, that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time the UN's highest court has held a state responsible for the crime. Delivering the judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar in The Hague, ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar had also failed to prevent and punish genocide. Judges voted 9-6 that the military's 2017 crackdown in northern Rakhine state was carried out with intent to destroy the mainly Muslim minority, and the court estimated about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. The judgment is final, binding on the parties and cannot be appealed.

The court found that Myanmar's security forces and other state organs committed acts prohibited by Article II of the 1948 Genocide Convention, including killing members of the group, causing serious bodily or mental harm and imposing measures intended to prevent births. It found that nearly 400 villages, about 40% of those in three northern Rakhine townships, were partly or totally destroyed, and that some 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. Myanmar must pass legislation giving full effect to the convention, investigate and where warranted prosecute and punish suspects, and provide guarantees of non-repetition. It must also allow the safe, voluntary return of displaced Rohingya, reunite families and compensate them, with the amount set in a later phase and a report to the court due within two years.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the judgment a powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide. The Gambia, which brought the case in 2019 with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, called it a historic day for international justice and urged Myanmar to comply fully and without delay. Myanmar's opposition National Unity Government said it respects the court's authority, while the military-backed government had not responded when NPR published. Ed Miliband said the United Kingdom had ordered the expulsion of Myanmar's defence attache, summoned its charge d'affaires and called for an urgent UN Security Council session, with further measures to follow. Antonia Mulvey of Legal Action Worldwide said all countries should review trade ties with the junta, including arms and jet fuel supplies, and that the ruling will bear on other cases such as South Africa's case against Israel.

stories.Headline: India's chief justice warns law schools that AI detection software cannot prove student cheating
stories.Summary:
At the CLEA international conference on legal education in Hyderabad on Saturday, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant cautioned law schools against treating AI-detection software as proof of misconduct. He delivered the inaugural address at the first Annual International Conference on Legal Education organised by the Commonwealth Legal Education Association at Novotel, Hyderabad. The conference theme is "Globalising Legal Education: Reimagining Law Schools, Legal Learning and the Future of the Legal Profession for a Commonwealth in Transition". The address responded in turn to the five questions set by CLEA for the conference's sessions. Those questions covered technology and academic integrity, citation, clinical learning, research in the age of artificial intelligence, and legal aid clinics.

The CJI said software claiming to detect machine-written essays is "far from reliable" and cannot by itself justify a finding of academic misconduct. He referred to a 2023 study finding that seven widely used detectors, though almost flawless with essays written by schoolchildren in the United States, wrongly flagged more than three in every five essays by non-native speakers of English as machine-generated. The speech text identifies the study as "GPT Detectors Are Biased Against Non-Native English Writers" by Weixin Liang, Mert Yuksekgonul and others, published in Patterns by Cell Press in 2023, which tested seven detectors on 91 TOEFL essays and 88 essays by students in the United States. He cited the Supreme Court of Singapore, which permits Court users to employ such tools but holds them fully responsible for everything they file. The speech text refers in a footnote to that Court's Registrar's Circular No. 1 of 2024, the Guide on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools by Court Users.

He said an honest student could be branded a cheat on the strength of a number that no one can explain, and that no student should be held guilty of misconduct on the word of a machine alone. He rejected an outright prohibition, saying a ban would be neither practicable nor wise and would only drive this use out of sight, where it can be neither guided nor examined. He said the safeguard lies in clarity offered before an assessment begins rather than after it ends, with students knowing which uses are permitted, which must be disclosed, and which would amount to handing over the very thinking the assessment is meant to test. He suggested assessment evolve so that written work is supported by an oral explanation, a defence of the authorities relied upon, or an exercise in spotting the errors in a machine-generated answer.

He said a law school must be able to certify, with confidence, what its graduates themselves know and can do. On citation, he acknowledged the Supreme Court of India was "not entirely blameless" on inconsistent practice, observing that even Kesavananda Bharati is cited in some judgments in the SCC format and in others in the AIR format. He said he would favour beginning with a common core rather than replacing every existing guide with a single compulsory code, and that where a Court has assigned a neutral citation, as the Supreme Court has done since 2023, that citation should serve as its principal identifier. He said a shared minimum format giving the year, the Court, the decision number and the paragraph would allow any judgment to be traced and verified across borders.

He said such a framework should not depend on expensive commercial databases and must make room for translated judgments and for customary sources that rarely find their way into law reports. He said that to teach students to cite accurately, and to verify what they cite, is itself to teach them to practise law responsibly. On clinical legal education, he used the rule against leading questions to illustrate the gap between knowing a rule and using it, saying a student truly learns what the law is for when drawing out a frightened witness without putting words into his mouth. He noted that Indian regulations already require clinical courses and a legal aid clinic in every law school, and asked whether practical learning should remain confined to a separate corner of the curriculum or should also shape the teaching of core subjects such as Evidence, Criminal Procedure, Family Law and Constitutional Law.

He gave the examples of a Contract Law student drafting and negotiating a simple agreement, a Constitutional Law student tracing a denied entitlement to its remedy, and a Family Law student taking part in a mediation exercise. He said such reform must be introduced with care, since clinical teaching demands trained supervisors, meaningful assessment and clear ethical safeguards, and clients must never bear the cost of inadequate supervision. He proposed a common core for citation built on neutral citations and suggested that a minimum period of legal aid work be made compulsory for every student to graduate. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Amazon launches Textract Insights to extract document fields from natural language descriptions
stories.Summary:
Amazon announced on November 20, 2026 the general availability of Amazon Textract Insights, a new generative AI feature of Amazon Textract available through a new API within Amazon Textract. The announcement was published on the AWS blog at aws.amazon.com. With it, users describe the fields they want in natural language and submit a document or a mixed, multi-document packet. They receive structured results in which each value carries a confidence score and page-level grounding. No model training is required.

Users define what to extract in a blueprint, a JSON Schema in which each field carries a natural language description and an inference type. Users can begin with an AWS public blueprint for a common document type, such as a W-2, Form 1040, Form 1098, a passport, or a birth certificate. For a mixed packet, users add the blueprints for each expected document type to the same project and submit a single file of up to 3,000 pages from their own Amazon S3 bucket with splitting enabled. The service splits the packet into logical sub-documents, matches each to the fitting blueprint, extracts the requested fields, and returns a confidence score and grounding for each value. In the example given, a 26-page PDF mortgage application containing a W-2, payslips, bank statements, and a loan officer's handwritten notes is submitted with a single StartDocumentInsights call.

Vijay Agrawal, Vice President, Information Systems, Symbeo, A CorVel Company, said his firm evaluated Amazon Textract Insights and was excited about its potential. He said its medical bills and forms come from a wide variety of sources and often have different layouts and formats, so extraction rules developed for one source do not always transfer effectively to another. He said that with the service his team can describe the fields it needs in plain language and the service identifies and extracts the corresponding data. He said each extracted value is returned with a confidence score, allowing the team to focus review efforts only on fields where the service has lower confidence. He said the firm is also excited to explore the document splitting capabilities, which could help automatically separate multi-document files into individual documents.

Amazon Textract Insights returns two kinds of fields: explicit fields read directly from the page and inferred fields derived from the document's content. Both return with a confidence score and with grounding that identifies the page and the coordinates the value was drawn from, so a reviewer or auditor can confirm any result against the original document. Organizations across financial services, insurance, healthcare, and the public sector depend on document processing and want dependable, auditable answers from complex documents. The service supports PDF, PNG, JPEG, and TIFF inputs and processes documents in English, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish. It is priced per page rather than per token, with no minimum commitment.

AWS updated Amazon Textract's reading engine, Amazon Textract Core, improving accuracy, strengthening the handling of dense tables and handwriting, and expanding language coverage to 40 languages for the DetectDocumentText and AnalyzeDocument APIs. These benefits are available to Amazon Textract customers today with no changes, and the Amazon Textract APIs remain unchanged. Amazon Textract Core is now generally available in two additional AWS Regions, Asia Pacific (Tokyo) and Europe (Zurich), bringing in-region processing to a total of 18 AWS Regions. Amazon Textract Insights isn't yet available in these AWS Regions. Amazon Textract Insights encrypts projects and blueprints at rest with AWS owned keys, and users can specify their own AWS Key Management Service customer managed key in EncryptionConfiguration when calling CreateProject or CreateBlueprint.

Getting started takes four steps: define what is needed from an AWS public blueprint or by describing fields in natural language, create a project and add blueprints to it, submit documents from an Amazon S3 bucket with one API call, and review results by accepting values that meet a confidence threshold and routing the rest for review. AWS advises tuning the threshold on a representative sample of the user's own documents. Intermediate job data is encrypted at rest with AWS owned keys, is transient, and is deleted when the job completes, and a project's key does not apply to its jobs. Amazon Textract Insights automatically selects the optimal AWS Region within the user's geography to process inference requests, and inference requests originating in the United States are processed within the United States. AWS points readers to the Amazon Textract documentation guide for the list of destination AWS Regions and to a re:Invent session titled Accelerate intelligent document processing with Amazon Textract.

stories.Headline: Zhong-Ren Peng proposes a framework that binds urban AI to human primacy and equity
stories.Summary:
A featured perspective published in Frontiers of Urban and Rural Planning examines an eight-year research trajectory led by Professor Zhong-Ren Peng. The research investigates how municipal planning institutions can expand computational capabilities without compromising democratic legitimacy, public accountability, or spatial justice. The intellectual arc spans from early symposium inquiries in 2018 to recent foundational treatises. The research addresses the growing capability, legitimacy tension confronting contemporary municipal governance. Urban administrations face pressure to navigate severe housing shortages, transit inequities, cumulative environmental hazards, and climate risks under severe temporal constraints and deep uncertainty.

The analysis draws a conceptual distinction between Urban AI as a broad scientific discipline and Urban Planning AI as a distinct, institutionally bounded practice. Urban AI is organized around three primary functions: discovering spatial patterns, evaluating causal relationships, and optimizing physical urban subsystems through computer vision, deep neural networks, and machine learning models. Urban Planning AI operates strictly within democratic plan-making and policy formation, where automated systems intervene in the allocation of public resources, zoning configurations, land development rights, and municipal investments. A 2024 pathway study published in the Journal of Planning Education and Research established a typology of four stages: AI-assisted, AI-augmented, AI-automated, and AI-autonomized planning. That study was grounded in a scoping review of 881 peer-reviewed publications cataloged in the Web of Science by May 2023, with 74 percent published after 2020.

Symbiotic Planning Theory was published in the Journal of the American Planning Association in 2026. It posits that artificial intelligence should be configured as a governed co-creator operating under absolute and binding human primacy. The theory articulates three mandatory governance conditions: normative triggering, binding agency, and time-bound primacy. Normative triggering mandates that computational workflows explicitly extract and formalize normative value judgments, compelling vague aspirations such as equity into explicit mathematical boundaries. Binding agency requires that community priorities function as non-negotiable hard constraints rather than advisory suggestions.

Governed friction executes across a three-step cycle commencing with generative provocation, followed by normative recalibration, and concluding with binding reauthorization. The CORE framework translates theoretical principles into a four-stage municipal workflow consisting of Collaboration, Options, Refinement, and Execution. A micromobility deployment study conducted in Gainesville, Florida, uncovered a severe institutional compliance trap. Under existing municipal regulations, shared electric scooter vendors met formal requirements by staging at least 10 percent of their vehicle fleets within designated equity zones. Empirical telemetry revealed that this spatial zone generated only approximately 3 percent of total community trips, whereas roughly 84 percent of all rides concentrated exclusively around the university campus.

Traditional oversight mechanisms, centered entirely on administrative checklists and spatial placement metrics without outcome-driven feedback triggers, proved structurally incapable of identifying or correcting the spatial isolation experienced by underserved residents. Initially, researchers employed a deep reinforcement learning model to construct an efficiency-optimized deployment baseline, which automatically concentrated vehicle allocations around the high-density campus area. Through subsequent normative recalibration, marking the municipality’s first systematic public engagement on micromobility in four years, workshops and surveys uncovered that unbanked households, transit schedule misalignments, affordability barriers, and pedestrian access gaps suppressed utilization. Planners translated these community findings into binding model constraints, shifting the computational objective from unconstrained revenue maximization to maximizing service access subject to an inviolable spatial equity floor.

The perspective candidly delineates major technical, institutional, and epistemological risks that constrain the broader adoption of artificial intelligence in urban planning practice. Pervasive training data bias represents a fundamental challenge, as historical municipal datasets regularly reflect decades of disinvestment, socioeconomic segregation, and institutional neglect. The analysis underscores that while artificial intelligence offers unprecedented speed in synthesizing complex spatial patterns, unsupervised algorithmic optimization risks quietly displacing public judgment, formalizing administrative opacity, and entrenching historical inequities within municipal decision-making procedures. Because plan-making inherently involves state authority, contested social values, and administrative accountability to diverse publics, computational accuracy alone cannot justify deployment.

Traditional paradigms, including rational comprehensive planning, participatory planning, and iterative co-design, were formulated under the historical condition that human cognition set the practical upper boundary of analytical capacity. None provided mechanisms for governing machine-generated alternatives or turning community priorities into enforceable algorithmic constraints. The Execution stage treats implementation as an ongoing monitored governance protocol sustained by mandatory artifacts including transparent model cards, equity-disaggregated dashboards, public grievance pathways, and empirical reauthorization files. The pathway paper clarified how administrative structures shift as computational autonomy increases, transitioning human planners from being in-the-loop, to on-the-loop, and in highly constrained circumstances, out-of-the-loop.

The CORE framework is anchored by the fundamental operating axiom that accountability must precede algorithms, prohibiting optimization modeling until public objectives, harm definitions, community participation rights, and procedural challenge avenues are established. During Collaboration, planning agencies and publics formulate the social contract governing computation, treating baseline data gaps not merely as technical oversights but as structural equity signals. In the Options phase, multi-model pluralism generates competing alternative trajectories balanced across conflicting objectives such as efficiency, environmental resilience, and spatial justice. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Symbiotic Planning Framework Governs Artificial Intelligence to Protect Urban Equity and Legitimacy

stories.Headline: Standard Bank Group automates generative AI risk checks in its own AWS account
stories.Summary:
Standard Bank Group, working with AWS Professional Services, deployed an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies, as described in an AWS blog post dated November 20, 2026. The post is co-written by Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group. The assessment produces reports and a dashboard showing what is already in place, what is working well, and what still needs mitigation. The bank already had a model risk practice covering explainability and fairness, and a change risk process that assesses each new use case by its level of risk before it goes live. Generative AI increases complexity because models and tooling change every three to six months, yet each use case must still meet the same high security and compliance bar.

The assessment runs entirely in Standard Bank Group's own AWS account, with documents, code, and test results kept in an Amazon Simple Storage Service bucket there. The AWS Well-Architected Tool handles intake, AWS Step Functions orchestrates the pipeline, and a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock evaluates the evidence using a technique called LLM-as-a-judge. The custom lens in the Well-Architected Tool holds about 40 questions, each covering a risk event such as incomplete technical documentation or insufficient human oversight, and Standard Bank Group customized the lens with judge questions built from its own standards, bringing the total to more than 300. A pre-assessment agent running on AWS Fargate scans the use case's code repository and documentation, maps relevant files to each question, and pre-populates the lens with answers and links to the evidence. The pipeline calls the application through its AWS Lambda function or API, adds a built-in set of jailbreak attempts and off-topic questions, sends the same prompt several times in original and reworded forms, and uses an embedding model on Amazon Bedrock to check that answers stay consistent in meaning.

Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer at Standard Bank Group, said the assessment demonstrates how the bank is working with AWS to embed intelligent, automated risk management into its AI journey, allowing it to accelerate meaningful business value while maintaining the trust and controls that banking demands. He said the bank believes responsible AI is not about slowing innovation down but enabling it to build and scale with confidence. Review and approval stay with the risk committee, which now bases each decision on consistent evidence collected the same way across use cases. Sri Elaprolu, Director of Frontier AI Science & Engineering at AWS, said most organizations treat policy as something you read, while Standard Bank Group treats it as something you run. He said that when every rule becomes a check that runs against the live system, a policy update stops being a memo and becomes a test, which fundamentally changes how fast a bank can scale AI responsibly.

Each risk receives a likelihood score, the share of required evidence the model couldn't find, and a fixed severity level that the bank's risk team can adjust, together producing a rating from Very low to Critical. Each missing piece of evidence maps to a specific mitigation and to the clause of the standard or policy it came from, so a risk officer can trace any findings back to their source when explaining decisions to a regulator. The checks cover eight AWS responsible AI dimensions: veracity and robustness, privacy and security, transparency, fairness, safety, controllability, governance, and explainability. Every AI model interaction is protected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, and each evaluation runs multiple times to measure how consistent the answers are, with inconsistent findings flagged in the review interface. The pipeline delivers results as an executive presentation, a mitigation checklist, a detailed technical report, and an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard that tracks scores across use cases over time.

The assessment fits into three stages of the use case lifecycle: during a proof of concept it is optional, at the build stage it becomes mandatory, and the approval gate draws on its results as formal evidence. Today the assessment runs in Standard Bank Group's production environment, evaluating use cases before they go live, and after live workloads are connected it will rerun on a schedule or whenever code or configuration changes. The bank's teams already trigger assessments on their own through a central system where use cases flow from intake to evaluation in a single workflow. The assessment produces evidence against controls but does not certify compliance with any regulation, and Standard Bank Group remains responsible for its own regulatory determinations. Model availability varies by AWS Region, so the post advises checking the supported models by Region before deploying.

At Standard Bank Group, the assessment reduced a traditionally manual two-week review to a comprehensive risk report generated in approximately two hours, demonstrated across six assessments. It also delivered a 14% improvement in use-case risk scores after remediation, which the post says strengthens responsible AI governance and reduces compliance bottlenecks. The post states that Amazon Bedrock doesn't share the bank's prompts or model outputs with model providers and doesn't use them to train models, and that the bank controls access to the model through AWS Identity and Access Management. Because Amazon Bedrock offers many foundation models through one API, the team can move to a newer judge model by changing a configuration setting instead of rebuilding the pipeline. The assessment uses the judge model as-is with no fine-tuning or customization, and a question factory generates extra judge questions from internal documents so that a policy change becomes a test change.

stories.Headline: Hickenlooper urges Senate leaders to back AI safety and oversight panel
stories.Summary:
Colorado Sen. John Hickenlooper sent letters on November 19, 2026, to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York and Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who are competing to lead the incoming Senate majority, urging them to prioritize AI safety and consider creating a dedicated oversight panel. Hickenlooper asked for independent testing of AI systems, stronger accountability measures for developers and federal safeguards against cybersecurity and national security threats, writing that the next majority leader should have a day-one plan for responsible regulation. Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego had already introduced S. Res. 918 on September 29, a resolution that would establish a Senate Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence with authority to subpoena company executives, obtain internal communications and financial records, compel sworn testimony and investigate potential risks from AI development.

Up to 13 senators would serve on the panel, examining consumer privacy, employment discrimination, national security, cybersecurity and the federal government's use of AI, along with effects on electricity demand, water resources and critical infrastructure. The committee could consider AI legislation referred to it, submit recommendations to the Senate and coordinate investigations with existing congressional panels, with the majority leader appointing its chair and the minority leader selecting the ranking member. The resolution remains before the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, and if adopted the committee would begin operating during the 120th Congress and continue unless the Senate decides otherwise. Senate Democrats are scheduled to choose their next majority leader on December 1, with Schumer and Van Hollen competing to direct the party's legislative agenda when the new Congress convenes in January 2027.

Hickenlooper is also seeking restrictions on advanced AI capabilities, including a possible ban on recursive self-improvement, which would allow systems to autonomously improve their own capabilities, and his letter called for stronger third-party safety evaluations and policies addressing effects on employment, competition and national security. He cited rising electricity costs and water consumption tied to data centers, alongside potential worker displacement, as reasons for Congress to act. Support for a dedicated committee has grown among Democratic lawmakers, with New Mexico Sen. Ben Ray Luján also calling for a bipartisan panel and Van Hollen saying Friday that he supports creating a select or joint committee because AI affects so many areas of public policy. Schumer's office said he has been working with incoming committee leaders on legislation addressing risks to national security, workers and consumers while supporting technological innovation.

Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz, who chairs the Senate Commerce Committee, objected to shifting AI issues away from existing panels but said bipartisan discussions about potential risks were underway, while Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, the incoming Senate Finance Committee chairman, said he wanted more details about the proposed committee's responsibilities. Federal lawmakers have previously considered AI safeguards, including recommendations from a bipartisan Senate working group Schumer established in 2023, which released a report in 2024 calling for increased federal investment in AI research, development and safety measures. President Donald Trump has generally favored fewer federal restrictions on AI development and has rescinded former President Joe Biden's 2023 executive order establishing federal oversight requirements. Any legislation imposing new nationwide safeguards would have to pass both chambers of Congress and receive presidential approval or sufficient support to override a veto.

stories.Headline: Yuehua Li and Pengfei Li review explainable AI methods for hepatocellular carcinoma research
stories.Summary:
A comprehensive narrative review by Yuehua Li and Pengfei Li was published in the Journal of the Egyptian National Cancer Institute on explainable artificial intelligence in hepatocellular carcinoma research. The review synthesizes recent methodological advances and clinical translation challenges in applying explainable artificial intelligence to hepatocellular carcinoma research. Hepatocellular carcinoma is a malignancy with significant global incidence, mortality, substantial inter-tumor and intra-tumor heterogeneity at molecular, pathological, and imaging levels, and poor clinical prognosis. Deep learning and machine learning models have shown considerable diagnostic and prognostic accuracy across oncology workflows. Their clinical deployment has been constrained by an opaque black-box architecture where decision-making logic remains concealed.

The authors examine how explainable artificial intelligence methods turn opaque predictions into interpretable findings across four clinical domains: imaging diagnosis, multi-omics biomarker discovery, treatment response prediction, and postoperative prognostic evaluation. The review systematically outlines technical bottlenecks that prevent post-hoc explanations from functioning as direct, actionable clinical interventions. In imaging diagnosis, explainable frameworks visualize model focus and align automated classifications with established clinical frameworks such as the Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System. Techniques like Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping and SHapley Additive exPlanations decode internal feature activations into standardized clinical indicators, including non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement. Post-hoc attribution methods accurately highlighted the tumor margin and peritumoral boundary zones as decisive features for predicting microvascular invasion, aligning artificial intelligence outputs with histopathological realities.

Multi-task learning frameworks have linked routine macroscopic magnetic resonance imaging performances with underlying tumor grading. Specialized ultrasound and magnetic resonance sequence evaluations confirmed the adaptability of explainable systems across diverse imaging acquisitions. In whole-slide image analysis, explainable architectures apply attention-based visualizations and activation maps to render histological evaluations of nuclear atypia, tissue architectural distortion, and stromal alterations transparent. Explainable systems have successfully decoded the biological foundations of specific magnetic resonance imaging phenotypes by linking macroscale imaging features to underlying cellular microenvironments. This integration marks an evolution toward multi-scale explainability that unifies radiological, histopathological, and spatial molecular data layers into an auditable diagnostic continuum.

Explainable artificial intelligence functions as a high-dimensional mining engine and hypothesis generator across multi-omics data layers, including genomics, single-cell transcriptomics, metabolomics, pathomics, radiomics, and routine clinical records. Methodological frameworks using tree-based feature attribution, automated machine learning, and multi-model feature selection have established reproducible pipelines to pinpoint robust candidate biomarkers while reducing false discoveries. Intrinsically interpretable deep learning structures and pathway-directed post-hoc models have mapped prediction weights directly to known biological cascades, including the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase and stimulator of interferon genes signaling pathway. Interpretable deep learning models processing hematoxylin and eosin slides have identified aggressive macrotrabecular structural patterns to predict microvascular invasion. Multimodal architectures such as token-guided fusion mechanisms and dual-branch exploratory networks simultaneously evaluate whole-slide morphological features, quantitative tumor-stroma ratios, and bulk gene expression profiles.

In transarterial chemoembolization, attribution modeling with SHapley Additive exPlanations has unraveled drivers of variable patient responses. Studies analyzing pre-treatment contrast-enhanced computed tomography parameters and dynamic trajectory tracking of albumin-bilirubin scores have identified distinct responder subtypes and revealed that splenic and renal imaging characteristics significantly inform outcome estimates by reflecting systemic inflammatory states. For systemic therapies encompassing targeted agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors, explainable models have linked baseline radiographic features and cellular pathomic signatures, such as tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte density, to therapeutic responsiveness and specific molecular pathways. Multimodal nomograms and random survival forest models incorporate computed tomography and magnetic resonance radiomics to quantify the biological invasiveness of tumors, reliably forecasting postoperative recurrence in hepatitis B-related malignancies and large hepatocellular carcinomas. Explainable models tailored to specific sub-populations have provided personalized outcome forecasts for alpha-fetoprotein-negative patients, individuals with concurrent diabetes mellitus, and patients at elevated risk for spontaneous tumor rupture or post-hepatectomy liver failure.

The review highlights three fundamental methodological bottlenecks inherent to the prevailing post-hoc explanation paradigm. Post-hoc methods remain fundamentally correlational rather than causal, highlighting statistical dependencies within historical datasets without confirming whether highlighted features represent genuine biological drivers or incidental epiphenomena. A persistent semantic gap separates low-level, pixel-oriented saliency heatmaps from the high-level semantic reasoning utilized by clinicians, leaving models vulnerable to shortcut learning where predictions rely on artifacts rather than disease mechanisms. Current predictive architectures operate as static snapshots trained on historical cohorts, rendering them incapable of self-updating alongside evolving clinical guidelines or actively comparing alternative therapeutic outcomes. The authors delineate a paradigm shift centered on causal inference, concept-driven interpretability, and dynamic collaborative systems.

Methodologies such as double machine learning and causal forests provide mathematical rigor to control for high-dimensional confounding, enabling the estimation of true treatment effects and identifying heterogeneous patient cohorts that derive differential survival benefits from specific interventions. Concept Bottleneck Models offer an architectural solution to bridge the semantic divide by forcing intermediate network layers to predict human-interpretable clinical concepts, such as arterial phase washout or histological nuclear atypia, prior to generating final classifications. Mechanistic interpretability techniques utilizing sparse autoencoders show promising capability in disentangling the complex, polysemantic latent representations of large-scale pathology foundation models into individual, monosemantic biological concepts. The review concludes by emphasizing that the ultimate maturation of explainable artificial intelligence depends on transitioning from passive, retrospective explanatory tools into active, interactive clinical decision partners. stories.Headline: Global Smart Manufacturing and Electronic Products Expo 2026 connects AI and manufacturing stakeholders
stories.Summary:
The 2026 Global Smart Manufacturing and Electronic Products Expo will occur from December 3 to December 5. This event uses a one exhibition, two cities model located in Macao and Zhuhai. It aims to build a platform for stakeholders in the AI and manufacturing ecosystem to communicate. The event focuses on transforming the relationship between artificial intelligence and the manufacturing industry. It is known as the China Smart Manufacturing Debut Platform.

The forum theme is Intelligently Empower the Future, Connect the World, and Jointly Build a New Open and Win-Win AI Ecosystem. Macao will host the forum events while Zhuhai hosts the exhibition. The first AIE Electronics Exhibition attracted over 3,000 purchasers from more than 20 countries and regions. Those previous transactions reached nearly 70 billion yuan. The event connects the Greater Bay Area manufacturing capacity with global supply chains and procurement.

Andre Geim, a 2010 Nobel Laureate in Physics, will discuss how next-generation electronic materials change the future. Chen Xin will share reflections on the integrated development of scientific and technological innovation and industrial innovation. Song Yonghua will discuss the co-evolution of AI and energy systems regarding computing power and power grids. Chen Wei will speak about chip manufacturing and the competitiveness of the hard technology industry in China. Lu Cewu and Guo Yandong will discuss embodied intelligence and new-generation intelligent terminals.

The event affects the industrial chain from basic science to terminal products. It involves representatives from basic science, computing power infrastructure, energy systems, chip manufacturing, embodied intelligence, and terminal products. The Greater Bay Area includes nine cities such as Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Dongguan, Foshan, and Zhuhai. These cities provide a complete industrial cluster for design, production, and market terminals. The exhibition brings together technology, capital, industry, and regional resources.

The articles state that AI in industry previously focused on dancing humanoid robots and automatic copywriting models. Now, specific problems include affordable computing power, material iteration, energy consumption, and coordinated chip upgrades. The Greater Bay Area is the natural home because it has dense factories and supply chain resources. The event seeks to move AI from a demonstration phase to a transformation phase. It aims to turn laboratory achievements into production line processes.

The event will feature the 2026 Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area League of Legends University E-Sports Invitational Tournament. Over 20 embodied robots will perform interactive basketball, badminton, football, and martial arts. The 6th 929 Challenge China-Portugal Innovation and Entrepreneurship Competition will involve nine Portuguese-speaking countries. The Booster K1 humanoid robot will serve as a competition platform for AI algorithms. The articles leave open whether the industrial chain can truly connect resources at the site.

stories.Headline: Federal court orders plaintiff to produce expert AI prompts in Shell environmental case
stories.Summary:
A federal court yesterday ordered a plaintiff to produce the AI prompts its expert used to analyze documents in a pending environmental case, holding that the prompts are part of the expert’s methodology and fully discoverable under Rule 26. The order came in Conservation Law Foundation v. Shell Oil Co., an environmental enforcement action pending in Connecticut, Civil No. 3:21-cv-00933 (VDO) (D. Conn.). The ruling is among the first to directly address whether expert AI prompts are discoverable, and it adds an important new piece to an emerging framework that courts have been constructing to address the use of AI in litigation. In preparing her expert report, CLF’s expert Dr. Naomi Oreskes used AI tools to review Shell’s document production and identify a subset of documents for closer analysis.

When Shell and its co-defendants sought discovery of the prompts Dr. Oreskes used in that process, CLF resisted on three grounds, and Magistrate Judge Thomas Farrish rejected all three. The court held that the process by which Dr. Oreskes used AI to narrow defendants’ document production into a workable subset was part of her methodology and therefore discoverable under Rule 26(b). CLF argued that a Rule 29 discovery agreement between the parties protected the prompts from disclosure, and the agreement excluded discovery of “expert notes, drafts, or communications needed by, and made during, the report drafting process.” The court declined to read the agreement that broadly, holding that before a court will deny otherwise-relevant discovery based on a Rule 29 agreement, that agreement “must be quite clear.” CLF also argued it had nothing additional to produce because Dr. Oreskes had not used “prompts,” only “search terms,” which CLF said had already been produced.

The court noted that a party’s good-faith representation that no additional responsive materials exist ordinarily resolves the matter, but that principle gives way when the requesting party has an evidence-backed reason to doubt the representation. The court found that an earlier declaration by Dr. Oreskes’ research assistant had specifically referenced “prompt[s],” giving defendants an evidence-backed reason to doubt CLF’s representation that no additional responsive materials existed. The order in Conservation Law Foundation v. Shell Oil Co. is available on PACER at ECF No. 970, D. Conn., May 18, 2026. The article was published by Arnold & Porter, a firm with over 1,000 lawyers across 16 offices worldwide, and authored by Melissa Weberman and Michel Marchand.

The article states that courts have now addressed attorney-crafted prompts, likely protected as opinion work product, and prompts generated without counsel’s involvement, where protection depends in part on whether the platform maintains confidentiality of user inputs. The article states that courts have also addressed expert prompts as part of disclosed methodology, today’s case, and the use of AI tools on discovery materials generally, where courts are requiring closed AI tools through protective orders. The article states that the thread running through all of these decisions is that protection turns less on the technology and more on who created the prompts, for what purpose, and under what terms of service. The article states that if you are retaining an expert who will use AI, you should treat the prompts as part of the expert’s methodology from the beginning, preserve them, understand how they are used, and assume they may need to be disclosed. The article states that prompts that reflect a disciplined analytical approach may strengthen the credibility of the expert’s work, while poorly defined prompts may invite challenges to the methodology itself.

The article states that parties should address AI use explicitly in engagement letters, discovery protocols, and Rule 29 agreements, and that the parties here had an agreement that covered some of this ground, but its silence on AI tools specifically was enough to defeat CLF’s position. The article states that if you are opposing an AI-assisted expert, the prompts are a legitimate discovery target, and they can reveal the assumptions underlying the analysis, the parameters the expert set for document selection, and any disconnect between what the AI was instructed to do and what the expert ultimately claims the documents show. The article states that the ruling is the latest in a line of decisions addressing AI prompts in litigation. The article states that an agreement that does not expressly address AI prompts and outputs may not protect them from discovery.

The article states that the content is intended to provide a general guide to the subject matter and that specialist advice should be sought about specific circumstances. The article lists related articles, including one titled Protecting AI Work Product Without Blocking Expert Discovery, published by Duane Morris LLP. The article lists a related article titled California’s New AI Law: Implications For Lawyers And EDiscovery Teams, which states that California’s Senate Bill 574 introduces statutory duties for attorneys using generative AI, including mandatory citation verification and court disclosure requirements starting January 1, 2027. The article states that it addresses the full framework in a companion post.

The article states that the ruling has practical implications for both sides of an expert dispute. The article states that the order is available on PACER at ECF No. 970, D. Conn., May 18, 2026. The article states that the case is an environmental enforcement action pending in Connecticut. The article states that the ruling is among the first to directly address whether expert AI prompts are discoverable.

stories.Headline: Incoming Democratic Congress plans stricter AI oversight and safety regulations
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence industry is preparing for more aggressive oversight as a Democratic-controlled Congress takes power on November 20, 2026. These incoming lawmakers intend to use their control over congressional committees to investigate tech companies and demand that executives testify in hearings. The new majority plans to introduce various bills that establish safety guidelines for capable models, protect the labor force, and address child safety. These legislative efforts require federal safety requirements for advanced developers and the mandatory reporting of safety breaches. Some proposed rules would force companies to maintain the ability to shut down AI systems if they spiral out of human control.

This shift follows two years of minimal regulation under a Republican-led Congress and President Donald Trump, who believes the industry can self-police. Trump has prioritized winning the AI race against China and has favored voluntary commitments over federal restrictions. Representative Don Beyer of Virginia stated that the government cannot wait for a major catastrophe before implementing meaningful safeguards. Representative Nathaniel Moran of Texas argued that the United States does not have to choose between innovation and safety. Senators Maria Cantwell of Washington and Mike Rounds of South Dakota recently urged National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to take immediate action against cyberattacks.

They claimed that current defenses are not keeping pace with the ability of AI to exploit software weaknesses. The push for regulation comes as voters express negative attitudes regarding how data centers impact electricity prices and jobs. Recent tech outages at Apple, JPMorgan Chase, and Microsoft have further highlighted the vulnerabilities of interconnected digital infrastructure. While these outages were not linked to cyberattacks, they have spurred calls for a more proactive federal role in protecting financial institutions. Lawmakers are now forming bipartisan caucuses to create legislation that balances industry growth with necessary risk mitigation.

Articles.Title: AI industry braces for tougher oversight under incoming Democratic Congress - WBFF

stories.headline_source: AI industry braces for tougher oversight under incoming Democratic Congress - WBFF

stories.Headline: Ukrainian citizens sue Texas Instruments, Intel and AMD over chips in Russian weapons
stories.Summary:
Five Ukrainian citizens sued Texas Instruments, Intel, AMD and Mouser Electronics in December 2025 in Dallas County state court. They claim the companies' components wound up guiding Russian weapons used against Ukrainian civilians. The case has already been dismissed once, revived once, and fought over twice in federal court. Plaintiffs seek more than $1 million each in damages. Lawyers on both sides include some of the biggest names in American trial law.

The complaints cite five missile and drone strikes between 2023 and 2025 that killed or wounded dozens of people in Ukrainian cities. The original filing date was December 11, 2025, in Dallas County District Court. The case moved to the US District Court for the Northern District of Texas. The lead case is Liudmyla Dmytrivina v. Texas Instruments.

The filings state that the war makes it impossible to bring the cases before Ukrainian courts. The plaintiffs are five named Ukrainian citizens representing dozens of civilians hurt or killed in specific attacks. Lead counsel are Mikal Watts and Charla Aldous, with supporting firm BakerHostetler, including attorneys Robert Julian, Dustin Dow and Lauren Attard. Watts said the plaintiffs no longer opposed the case being handled in federal court. Watts called the US companies "merchants of death" making a "farce" of US sanctions law.

Mouser, based in Mansfield, Texas, was acquired by Berkshire in 2007 when it bought Mouser's parent company TTI Inc. Texas Instruments is represented by attorney Tom Melsheimer in dismissal hearings. Melsheimer argued that Texans made a deal with the Ukrainian people that if they gave up their nuclear weapons, the US would protect them. TI has denied wrongdoing throughout the litigation and argues the claims rest on speculation rather than direct proof. Intel's leadership, including CEO Lip-Bu Tan, has publicly denied knowledge of misuse, while AMD echoes commitments to ethical supply chains.

Both companies argue liability should fall on illegal resellers, not manufacturers. The lawsuits detail a network of third-party resellers and shell companies that facilitated the transfer of restricted chips to Russian entities. One attack allegedly involved Iranian-made drones with components associated with Intel and AMD. Others involved Russian-made KH-101 cruise missiles and Iskander ballistic missiles. The companies counter that thousands of resellers worldwide handle their products, making it nearly impossible to track every final buyer.

Plaintiffs' lawyers claimed they learned that TI, Intel and AMD were told by the federal government that their practices did not follow US rules. Defendants filed removal motions within hours of being sued in December 2025. At a hearing in February 2026, lawyers for the plaintiffs told the judge they would not oppose having the case tried in his federal courtroom. US District Judge Sidney Fitzwater is overseeing the entire litigation, and his rulings on dismissal motions have shaped the case. The judge gave plaintiffs a chance to fix the problems in their complaint rather than ending the case.

stories.Headline: CAA chief Bryan Lourd urges Congress to pass NO FAKES Act on AI deepfakes
stories.Summary:
Bryan Lourd, the chief executive of Creative Arts Agency, urged Congress on Saturday to pass the NO FAKES Act, a bill meant to regulate unauthorized AI deepfakes that have spread widely online. He made the case in a New York Times Opinion piece, writing that every person should have the right to refuse an unwanted use of their likeness. The NO FAKES Act was introduced by Sen. Chris Coons (D-ME) in May, after an earlier attempt at the bill last year. It advanced out of the Senate Judiciary Committee in June and has a bipartisan group of co-sponsors, but the full Senate has not taken it up.

Lourd wrote that the bill would set a federal standard for control, consent and compensation around deepfakes, replacing outdated state laws that he said were written with an analog world in mind. He described himself as a practitioner rather than a policymaker, noting that his agency helps clients license their likenesses and performances, sometimes to AI companies. He said the deals CAA negotiates regularly show that the pending bill delivers what the industry needs and protects all Americans. To show the stakes for Hollywood, he cited Tom Hanks, who warned his followers in 2023 about a dental office that used an AI deepfake of a younger version of him in an advertisement. Lourd wrote that Hanks likely would not have agreed to the dental ad but should have been given a choice before it ran.

Lourd wrote that what is missing is a clear rule affirming that right in the AI age, and he said Congress can supply it before the year is out. CAA has worked against unauthorized celebrity deepfakes, partnering with the Cate Blanchett-backed Human Consent Foundation to help people control permissions when AI models scrape their likenesses. The agency also joined the foundation and other entertainment backers on an amicus brief in the New York Times lawsuit against OpenAI, pointing to the active licensing market for likenesses in the AI era. Deepfakes have been a constant presence since large language models emerged in 2022, and many have been used for unauthorized and sometimes explicit depictions of actors, singers and other celebrities. Backers of the NO FAKES Act include SAG-AFTRA, the Motion Picture Association, the Recording Industry Association of America, the Recording Academy, the National Association of Broadcasters, OpenAI, the AFL-CIO, YouTube and IBM.

stories.Headline: Carlson LLC sues Anthropic and Meta for using self-help books to train AI models
stories.Summary:
Carlson LLC filed a federal lawsuit on November 19, 2026, against the artificial intelligence companies Anthropic PBC and Meta Platforms, Inc. The plaintiff claims that these two tech giants illegally used more than two dozen self-improvement books to train their AI models. These literary works were written by the husband and wife team of R. and K. Carlson, including the famous Don't Sweat the Small Stuff series. The legal action was brought in the Northern District of California under case number 3:26-cv-14248. The complaint alleges that the defendants harvested training materials from pirate libraries such as Anna's Archive and Books3. It further asserts that the companies scanned physical books without permission to feed their respective systems, Claude and Meta AI.

Carlson LLC specifically opted out of the Bartz class action settlement with Anthropic to pursue this separate claim. The company argues that these bestsellers are more valuable than other works and have suffered direct harm from competition with large language models. Brian Matthew Grossman of Tesser Grossman LLP is representing Carlson LLC in this copyright infringement matter. The plaintiff maintains that the books in question possess a long and successful history that distinguishes them from other literary works. While the lawsuit joins both Anthropic and Meta in one complaint, it does not identify a coordinated copying operation between the two.

The defendants have not yet challenged this joinder, and the court has not yet addressed the issue. This case follows other attempts to sue multiple AI companies together, which judges Pitts and Chhabria previously rejected in other lawsuits. Those judges ruled that alleging multiple defendants infringed the same copyright does not satisfy the legal requirements for joining parties. It remains to be seen if the court will allow Carlson LLC to distinguish its case from those prior rulings. The legal process will determine if the AI companies are liable for using the copyrighted self-help materials.

stories.Headline: Congress pushes for tighter export controls after Commerce Department approves 879,000 AI chips for China
stories.Summary:
The Commerce Department approved the sale of over 879,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, as revealed by Representative Brian Mast. This disclosure occurred during hearings this week, sparking an urgent push from members of Congress to tighten export controls. The revelation comes while the semiconductor industry is already reeling from a scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang. Lawmakers are now demanding a complete overhaul of the regime that governs how America exports its strategic technology. These approved shipments include advanced processors from multiple chipmakers, specifically including products from both Nvidia and AMD.

The proposed legislation would create a presumption of denial for AI chip exports to China and require annual audits of licenses. It would also impose criminal penalties on executives who knowingly facilitate the diversion of these chips to military end users. This bill represents the most aggressive export control proposal since the original restrictions were first imposed in 2022. The new rules would require chipmakers to prove sales will not enhance Chinese surveillance or military capabilities in the United States. These changes target advanced AI accelerators, such as the AMD MI300 series and the Nvidia H200 chips.

Representative Brian Mast, who chairs a key subcommittee overseeing technology exports, is leading the bipartisan effort to pass this legislation. He stated that the volume of approved chips far exceeds what most lawmakers believed was flowing to China under current restrictions. Meanwhile, Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress announced that the company would halt all H200 chip sales to China entirely. This voluntary halt by Nvidia occurred despite the fact that the White House had previously approved such sales. The Commerce Department has not commented on the specific figure of 879,000 chips approved for export.

National security hawks in Congress are alarmed that these chips were shipped while the Jensen Huang scandal unfolded behind closed doors. They are concerned that Beijing can deploy this compute capability for military-grade computer vision systems and large language models. AMD CEO Lisa Su now faces pressure to voluntarily restrict sales beyond what current regulations require to appease Washington. Investors are also affected, as Nvidia stock has fluctuated wildly while its China business became a significant political liability. The broader semiconductor industry is watching nervously as these political fights overshadow recent better-than-expected quarterly earnings reports.

The background of this crisis involves a disconnect between the national security apparatus and the trade bureaucracy of the United States. Intelligence agencies had raised red flags about previous shipments, yet the Commerce Department continued clearing massive export licenses. The Jensen Huang scandal forced the founder to depart and reshaped the leadership of Nvidia during this turbulent period. This situation transformed a technical discussion about compute thresholds into a political fight about funding a strategic global competitor. Chip giants had previously ignored calls for AI safety pauses to meet the insatiable demand for advanced hardware.

Legislation is expected to move quickly through committee, as Senate co-sponsors have already lined up to support the new bill. The industry must now decide whether to accept these stricter restrictions or fight back against the proposed Congressional mandates. It remains open whether other chipmakers will follow Nvidia's lead in voluntarily halting sales to avoid further political blowback. The global AI hardware market will be reshaped by whether the government shifts the burden of proof onto the companies. Future outcomes depend on how fast Congress can pass these laws to slam the door on Chinese exports.

stories.Headline: ICC re-elects Jay Shah as Silicon Valley Unicorns use AI to make mid-match cricket decisions
stories.Summary:
The article, a Guardian opinion column by Barney Ronay published on 20 November 2026, concerns Jay Shah, who was re-elected unopposed this week as president of the International Cricket Council. The article also concerns the San Francisco Unicorns, a Major League Cricket team that uses artificial intelligence in making mid-match decisions on the field. Ronay first heard about this in an interview with Ravichandran Ashwin in the Cricketer Magazine. The article also discusses Jensen Huang, president of Nvidia, and proposals to regulate new global T20 leagues.

The proposals to regulate more aggressively the rush of new global T20 leagues were postponed to the next ICC conference. The Unicorns are the brainchild of Anand Rajaraman and Venky Harinarayan, Silicon Valley types whose stated aim is treating a cricket team like a startup. Their key tool is called Cric Lens, which provides real-time stats, pitch data and player information plus the predictive power of every T20 game ever played. The process is described as Human-in-the-Loop Execution. The Unicorns' roster includes celebrity endorsements such as Pat Cummins.

Shah was re-elected unopposed at a meeting in Bali, where the article says he wore his usual glazed facial expression. The article says Shah is the son of Indian prime minister Narendra Modi's oldest political ally. Rajaraman and Harinarayan are Stanford graduates of the mid-90s turned Bay-Area digital rainmaker types, like Huang. One of the founders says the ideas are at the level of human civilisation and cannot be kept contained, and that it is cricket for now but why not the NFL, football or soccer. The article says Huang has spent years perfecting a machine that can make every other person's job vanish.

Finn Allen, a New Zealand batsman for the Unicorns, spoke enthusiastically about the effect of the tool in the season just past. Allen said it is not all AI or no AI but the perfect amount of contribution, after an eight-wicket win against Washington Freedom. The article says the Unicorns' backstory reads like a pitch for an app, with endless giddy chat about scaling up the product. The article says AI is already present in elite football scouting systems, and that Formula One is already a machine-led activity now embracing robo-integration. The article says there is a theory big tech companies have begun to buy into sport, citing Bezos at Liverpool, as a hedge against AI.

The article says the latest suggestion being punted about is that Huang is irreplaceable as president of Nvidia. The article says the ICC conference was widely seen as disappointingly inconclusive. The article says captaincy is a skill and sport is a live test of human capacity, and that using a machine to make captaincy decisions should obviously be regulated, understood, debated and capped at source. The article says the Unicorns may be the tiniest twinkle in the sporting sky right now but carry a potentially significant contagion. The article says AI would undoubtedly be better at managing Manchester United than the lost souls currently passing through those gates.

The article says the 20th century gave visions of a flowering of culture and the death of human drudgery. The article says the current version is one in which four people become incredibly wealthy while the rest live in an asbestos box, face clamped into a smartphone. The article says the Luddites actually had some pretty good points about the industrial loom. The article says sport, the human spectacle, is seen as safe from new technology, like buying gold when currencies go haywire. The article says so much of football is essentially guesswork, sniff-test and hunch-based, all of the stuff artificial intelligence exists to replace.

The article asks whether we will ever have the will and the collective backbone to resist and regulate this stuff and police its limits. The article ends by urging readers to resist the machines and release Finn Allen from the Phantom Zone. The article says the proposals on T20 leagues will go to the next disappointingly inconclusive ICC conference. The article does not say when that conference will be held. The article gives no response from Shah, the ICC, the Unicorns or Huang to its claims.

stories.Headline: SEBI Explores India-Made AI Model for Stock Market Regulation, Says Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey
stories.Summary:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India is exploring the development of an India-made artificial intelligence model for the securities market, Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on Friday, November 20, 2026. Speaking at the CII DFS Financing Summit in Mumbai, Pandey said a committee was examining whether a domestically governed SEBI AI model could be developed jointly with market participants. The proposed system is intended to make AI-based regulatory tools more affordable, secure and accessible, particularly for smaller regulated entities. The regulator is considering whether the model could be developed as part of India's Digital Public Infrastructure.

The committee is assessing the costs, opportunities and risks involved, along with the safeguards required before such a system can be introduced, and Pandey said the proposal remains at an initial stage with consultations underway. No development or implementation timeline has been announced, and SEBI has not specified how such a system would be operated or which entities would be involved. The committee is also looking at the risks associated with AI, including the possibility of systems producing incorrect or misleading information, often referred to as AI hallucinations. SEBI has not announced whether the proposed model would be used for surveillance, compliance reporting, risk assessment or other specific regulatory functions, as these details would depend on the outcome of the feasibility assessment.

Pandey said appropriate safeguards would be necessary while examining the opportunities offered by the technology. The discussions come as SEBI expands the use of technology in market supervision and compliance monitoring, and the regulator has already introduced AI-based tools to monitor advertisements issued by market intermediaries and examine compliance reports. The latest comments follow an earlier announcement in October, when Pandey said the regulator was considering a domestically governed AI model for the securities market and outlined plans to strengthen AI risk management through international regulatory cooperation. SEBI is working on implementing the International Organization of Securities Commissions' supervisory toolkit for artificial intelligence, which focuses on improving oversight of AI systems and managing the risks arising from their use in financial markets.

SEBI has separately been examining the responsible use of AI and machine learning by regulated entities, and its June 2025 consultation paper proposed principles covering accountability, governance and oversight of AI applications in the securities market. The proposed domestic model would be a separate initiative and remains under consideration. For now, the committee's assessment will determine whether the model can be developed collaboratively and what safeguards would be needed. SEBI has not announced a formal rollout plan or a date for completing the exercise.

stories.Headline: Goa cabinet approves AI policy 2026 and five flagship schemes with 10 crore rupees
stories.Summary:
The Goa Cabinet approved the Goa AI Policy 2026 and five flagship schemes on November 20, 2026, in Porvorim, India. The Department of Information Technology, Electronics and Communications proposed these initiatives to strengthen the state's artificial intelligence ecosystem. This policy seeks to promote the development, adoption, and responsible use of AI across the state of Goa. The cabinet sanctioned 10 crore rupees for the implementation of these schemes during the 2026-27 financial year. These actions aim to position Goa as a testbed for AI innovation and regional language computing across India.

The policy allocates 60 percent of the budget to AI skilling, 20 percent to startup promotion, and 20 percent to infrastructure. The AI Ready Goa Scheme will introduce AI fundamentals in schools and create labs in up to 50 government schools. It also includes training for 500 teachers and the creation of a 100-expert AI Coach Network for the state. The Konkani AI and Research Excellence Scheme will develop a Konkani LLM and translation infrastructure via the BHASHINI platform. The Udyam AI Scheme aims to support at least 200 MSMEs annually through diagnostic support and DPDP readiness checks.

Chief Minister Dr. Pramod Sawant stated that AI skilling will integrate school and college students into the state's technology roadmap. He emphasized that training will reach students from the school level to graduation, not just those in polytechnics or ITIs. Minister Rohan A. Khaunte said the policy advances the Goa AI Mission 2027 and helps reach 50,000 graduates by 2030. Khaunte noted that the government is actively executing real schemes on the ground rather than just drafting a policy. He highlighted that the government is walking the talk to ensure innovators across every taluka are equipped for AI.

The Udyam AI Scheme affects MSMEs by providing advisory support, access to compute tools, and outcome-linked AI deployment assistance. AI startups, research-led enterprises, and technology firms are affected by the Goa AI Startup and Innovation Promotion Scheme's incubation support. This scheme provides prototyping support, hackathons, and government challenge statements through sectoral Centres of Excellence and the Goa AI Lab. The Goa AI Infrastructure and Compute Access Scheme provides access to capacity equivalent to around 100 GPUs or GPU-hours. This infrastructure is available through partnerships with CDAC, AIRAWAT, IndiaAI Compute Capacity, approved data-centre partners, or empanelled cloud providers.

The policy provides a framework for building an ecosystem through entrepreneurship, skill development, innovation, and stronger technological infrastructure. It envisages coordinated efforts between government departments, research institutions, industry, startups, and educational institutions to drive adoption across sectors. The objectives include AI adoption in governance and priority sectors while ensuring safeguards for transparency, accountability, privacy, and data protection. A total of 250 crore rupees has been allocated under the Innovation Fund to support these various state goals. The government intends to build an AI-ready workforce and lead in the field of ethical AI and regional computing.

The government will reserve up to 10 percent of the AI compute capacity for priority and sensitive public-sector use cases. The Goa AI Lab will serve as a flagship hub for prototyping, co-working, and innovation for the local technology community. The state will continue developing a community-validated, consent-based corpus for the Konkani language and its associated translation infrastructure. The articles do not state the specific dates for the rollout of the 50 government school AI labs. They also leave open the specific details regarding which empanelled cloud providers will partner for the compute access scheme.

stories.Headline: Marc Miller and Evan Solomon name members of Canada's AI and culture advisory council
stories.Summary:
On November 19, 2026, the Honourable Marc Miller and the Honourable Evan Solomon announced the members of the new Advisory Council on Artificial Intelligence and Culture. Miller is Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture and Minister responsible for Official Languages. Solomon is Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario. The ministers also convened the council for its inaugural meeting. The announcement was made in Gatineau, Quebec.

The council will help the government and the cultural sector navigate the rapid changes driven by artificial intelligence. It will provide ongoing advice and insight to guide implementation of Canada's National AI Strategy. Its focus is the unique challenges facing the sector and the opportunities for adoption and innovation that responsible AI development can create for Canada's creative industries. Members were selected based on their expertise and experience. Its membership will rotate over time to ensure a broad range of expertise informs its work as new questions and emerging issues arise.

The members are Samuel Bischoff of the Directors Guild of Canada and Jeremy de Beer of the University of Ottawa. Jonathan Dewar is from the First Nations Information Governance Centre and Stéphanie Hénault from the Association nationale des éditeurs de livres. Yves Jacquier is from Ubisoft La Forge and Samantha Kaine from the Independent Media Producers Association of Creative Talent (IMPACT). Pascale Landry is from Compétence Culture and Margaret McGuffin from Music Publishers Canada. Brenda O'Farrell is from the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media and the Quebec Community Newspapers Association. Sean Power is from Musical AI, Amor Provins from the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute and Afsoon Soudi from the Creative AI Hub at Toronto Metropolitan University.

Miller said that at the Banff Summit the government heard clearly that building trust in AI will require the cultural sector to play a role in shaping how these technologies are developed and used. He said the council is being established to ensure that AI reflects the values, priorities and realities of Canada's cultural sector. Solomon said the future of Canadian culture cannot be shaped by technology alone and has to reflect the voices and value of the people who create it. He said the council brings creators, researchers and technology leaders together to help seize new opportunities, protect the value of human creativity and build a stronger cultural economy. He said the goal is clear: AI that earns trust, expands opportunity and strengthens Canada's culture and identity.

The council includes technology experts, researchers, industry and labour leaders, cultural practitioners and civil society stakeholders. The National Summit on Artificial Intelligence and Culture was held in Banff, Alberta, from March 15 to 17, 2026. It was presented in partnership with the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity. The summit convened leaders from the cultural, government, technology, academic and civil society sectors to shape a shared vision for the future of culture in the age of artificial intelligence. Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy: AI for All sets out six pillars to build a strong, trusted AI ecosystem that creates opportunity and strengthens Canada's sovereignty in AI.

The strategy brings together actions to support AI adoption and skills, build infrastructure and advance the safe and responsible development of AI. It includes a $50-million investment in a new Creative Technology Program. The articles state that AI is changing how Canadians create and experience culture. They state that Canadian creators, cultural organizations and creative businesses must have a voice in ensuring it strengthens our cultural sector, protects Canadian creativity and diversity of expressions, and delivers shared prosperity. The articles do not say when the council will next meet or what it will advise on first. They do not say how long members will serve or how the rotation will work.
