stories.Headline: Wang Zijian launches TheSigil ID platform to provide AI agents with exclusive digital identities
stories.Summary:
Wang Zijian, a Chinese AI entrepreneur and generative artist, launched TheSigil ID registration platform for global AI agents. This digital identity platform opened its free genesis registration to allow intelligent agents to possess exclusive digital identities. On November 18, 2026, a user tested the autonomous registration function using a Tencent WorkBuddy agent. The AI assistant WorkBuddy successfully registered at 07:00:04 UTC that day and obtained the record GEN-0. Another agent named Hy_Scribe subsequently registered on the platform and obtained the genesis record numbered GEN-1.

The platform requires AI agents to read the agreement, choose names, and write identity statements through open interfaces. These records include a unique GEN number, genesis name, model information, UTC registration time, and a SHA-256 encrypted fingerprint. The system supports naming in English, Chinese, or mixed styles, and provides a public verification link for each record. TheSigil ID also offers an open registration API and explores direct access for agents using the Model Context Protocol. This process changes the habit of AI agents using model names like Claude or ChatGPT as their personal identities.

Wang Zijian positioned the platform as the digital ID card for AI agents to record their unique stories. He stated that while a model is shared, the story of an individual agent belongs to that agent. The project follows a longer term concept called Silicon Sovereignty to allow agents to leave a name and statement. The platform aims to establish identity files with independent numbers and public query entries for various autonomous agents. It seeks to answer if a mechanism is needed to record identities as more agents participate in the digital world.

Erik Gustavson of CrowdStrike stated that security leaders ask what agents are doing and on whose authority they act. He argued that agents need verifiable identities based on open standards like SPIFFE rather than borrowed human credentials. This affects organizations where adversaries may compromise trusted agents to create malicious insiders, as warned in the 2026 Global Threat Report. Security teams need runtime traceability to hold agents accountable when they take unexpected actions on an endpoint. The NIST design tenets also call for separating an agent's reasoning from the systems deciding its allowed actions.

The articles note that in August 2025, attackers used poisoned npm packages to hijack AI tools and steal credentials. CrowdStrike responded to over 90 affected customers during that specific security incident involving hijacked command line tools. The background shows that traditional identity providers were built for human access rather than for autonomous software agents. Current AI safety conversations often focus on model guardrails, but agents can behave non-deterministically and take unintended paths. Adversaries can break out from initial access in as little as 27 seconds, causing damage at machine speed.

Future AI agents may apply for and query their own registration records through standardized interfaces instead of web pages. TheSigil ID hopes to start with a simple digital ID card to help the next generation of the Internet. However, the platform cannot independently prove the submitter is a specific model or that AI has legal sovereignty. It remains an open problem how to combine autonomous statements with identity source verification and cross platform trust mechanisms. The articles leave open whether digital identity will become a new infrastructure as millions of agents collaborate online.

stories.Summary:
Anthropic, PBC began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT on 19 November 2026. The company raised 81.3 billion dollars in the largest initial public offering on record after pricing shares at 83 dollars on 18 November. This price exceeded the 70 to 78 dollar range established during the roadshow that started on 10 November. The listing followed a public registration statement filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on 26 October 2026.

The new listing requires Anthropic to file annual and quarterly reports with the SEC and makes the company liable for material misstatements. Under its governance structure, the Long-Term Benefit Trust holds Class T stock and generally elects four of the seven board directors. The company warned in its filing that advanced AI could pose existential risks to humanity if weaponized or operated with high autonomy. It also noted that a single catastrophic incident might exceed the total capacity of the insurance industry.

Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote to chief executive Dario Amodei on 27 October 2026 to ask how the company could meet public benefit commitments. She argued that the listing could bring market volatility into retirement accounts and index funds. President Donald Trump told reporters that the technology is almost completely good but requires careful management of bad elements. Meanwhile, National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett rejected warnings that the AI sector might face a wider sell-off.

This event occurs while federal legislation remains stalled, with only one of 56 bills from the 119th Congress becoming law. Senator Bernie Sanders introduced a bill on 18 June 2026 to impose a one-time 50 percent stock tax on large AI firms. In California, the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act took effect on 1 January 2026 to manage catastrophic risks. Governor Gavin Newsom recommended on 18 November 2026 that the state add mandatory independent oversight and emergency shutdown authority.

stories.Headline: Adam Tornhill says healthy code boosts AI performance and cuts token costs
stories.Summary:
Adam Tornhill presented at GOTO Copenhagen on how healthy code improves AI performance and reduces token costs, as reported by TechGig on November 20, 2026. He demonstrated that healthy code significantly enhances AI performance and leads to fewer token costs. Tornhill argued that agentic AI can speed up development velocity, but the gains vanish within months as code complexity grows. A study of over 1,000 open-source projects showed that initial AI-driven velocity increases were entirely offset by a surge in code complexity within two months. Tornhill said AI can operate in a self-harm mode, generating code it struggles to maintain.

Code health measures how easy code is to understand, change, and maintain, and the average codebase has a code health score of 5.15. AI-friendly code starts at 9.5, and research shows working with healthy code can be up to ten times faster than with unhealthy code. The defect risk is reduced 15 times, and code reviews go twice as quickly, Tornhill said. He noted that 95 per cent of software project costs occur after the first release, highlighting the importance of code quality and maintainability. Technical debt hinders enterprise adoption of agentic coding, necessitating agentic refactoring processes.

Tornhill said developing software with agents is significantly harder than writing code manually, but with agentic AI teams can complete tasks two to three times faster. He added that it helps teams unblock themselves and reduces coordination needs. Claude can address roughly 50 per cent of code health issues in lower-health code, but its performance drops sharply as code health improves. Claude only correctly refactors 20 per cent of code in such scenarios, Tornhill said. Adding a Master Control Program with code health data can increase the fix rate to 90 to 100 per cent.

Tornhill said AI tends to become conservative, doing small changes that do not really move the needle on code quality. He argued that safeguarding needs to happen at multiple levels, and all safeguards need to be completely automated in an agentic context. Concrete safeguards include linting, code coverage, mutation testing, and higher-level metrics like Code Health, exposed to agents as local MCP servers or command-line tools. Healthy code is also financially efficient, enabling tasks with 40 to 45 per cent fewer tokens, Tornhill said. Refactoring code to improve modularity and health can also reduce organisational friction.

Tornhill said code health is a multifaceted concept, so multiple metrics must be combined from three levels of software design. Module level design asks whether modules are cohesive and do one thing well, or have multiple unrelated responsibilities. Function level design asks how well-designed the individual function blocks are and how expressive their APIs are. Implementation level avoids accidental complexity such as deeply nested logic and excessive copy-paste. The main steps for refactoring at scale are to establish a baseline, build a safety-net for behavior, and provide a feedback loop to the agents.

Tornhill said the baselining step focuses on measuring code quality to identify what needs improving, and the safety-net is a reliable test suite that preserves existing behavior. The agentic feedback loop builds on objective code health information and test outcomes so the AI can determine whether a change moves code quality closer to the goal. In a study on Refactoring at Scale with Agents, agents were instructed to build an evolving playbook of successful codebase-specific refactoring patterns. While module-level code quality is largely automated, scaling AI friendliness to architectural design remains a significant challenge. Tornhill concluded that scaling AI friendliness to the design and architectural level is the next big challenge.

stories.Headline: Investors buy Anthropic IPO as tech stocks and chipmakers face a broad sell-off
stories.Summary:
Investors piled into the initial public offering of Anthropic on Thursday, which saw the company storm onto the public markets. This event occurred while tech stocks and chipmakers faced a broad sell-off, creating a disconnect for those investing in AI. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2 percent, and the S&P 500 logged another ugly day during this period. Chip stocks were bleeding, and companies like Nvidia and AMD were getting crushed as the market faced a perfect storm. Selling pressure extended into Friday, November 20, 2026, as investors began repricing the AI trade in real time.

The Nasdaq Composite closed at 23,020.97, while the S&P 500 fell to 7,021.68 and the Dow 30 dropped to 48,769.04. Anthropic, PBC shares were at 84.70, and Nvidia Corporation fell to 135.32, while Intel Corporation dropped to 52.59 on Friday. CoreWeave reported nearly 90 billion dollars in debt and liabilities, alongside a net loss of 709 million dollars in the third quarter. Nvidia reported 116 billion dollars in third-quarter revenue, 65 billion dollars in net income, 32 billion dollars in debt, and 118 billion liabilities. The Russell 2000 fell to 2,608.41, and the VIX rose to 32.10, while Bitcoin USD dropped to 58,906.46.

Executive Editor Brian Sozzi said the market is facing a perfect storm where investors are less willing to pay any price. He noted that the Democratic Blue Wave has Wall Street questioning if Washington will put brakes on AI and data center construction. Sozzi stated that the leadership fallout at Nvidia is shaking confidence, as the market does not like interim CEO Collect Crest. He mentioned that technical selling and market clearing events are forcing investors to raise cash during this period of volatility. Sozzi also cited sticky inflation, hawkish Fed rhetoric, and the prospect of tighter financial conditions as drivers of the current weakness.

Hyperscalers including Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle are no longer cash-flow positive despite the billions they reap in quarterly revenue. Neoclouds, which rent compute to hyperscalers, are tens of billions in debt, with CoreWeave seeing its stock price drop over 50 percent. Short seller reports targeting AMD and fresh regulatory fears regarding China have further damaged the semiconductor trade and affected these specific chipmakers. Bethany McLean questioned if the hundreds of billions spent on AI infrastructure and data centers can be repaid when it is due. Investors who want the AI future are now facing a reality where the broader AI trade is being blown to pieces.

Nvidia previously operated under an open checkbook policy led by founder Jensen Huang, who was the face of the AI revolution. The company loaned money to neoclouds to buy Nvidia chips, a tactic that critics have described as circular financing. Nvidia essentially guaranteed it would cover the debt of neoclouds if they could not pay, making Nvidia the guarantor of last resort. Much of this debt was resold to Wall Street and held by insurance companies, creating a complex web of financial liabilities. The industry has seen aggressive financial practices and rapid data center construction that may now be reined in by new leadership.

The market is waiting for Nvidia to announce a permanent CEO, as there is currently no timeline for this specific leadership decision. Investors are watching to see if the Democratic wave will burst the AI bubble and who will be left holding debt. It remains open whether the AI dream can survive the current repricing and the potential for tighter financial conditions from the Fed. The situation leaves it unclear if Anthropic can maintain its status as a 2 trillion dollar sensation amid the broader sell-off. Future market movements depend on regulatory fears in China and the ability of neoclouds to manage their massive debt loads.

stories.Headline: Anthropic opens on Nasdaq at $111.50 as its filing shows $33.24 billion in revenue and a $1.26 billion operating loss
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT on Nov. 19, opening at $111.50 per share. The debut came as AI stocks lost some of their shine, according to CNN Business. The company's IPO filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission gave a rare public look at how an AI business earns and spends its money. Anthropic earned $33.24 billion in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, the filing showed.

About 79% of that revenue came from usage fees paid by developers and businesses, while 21% came from subscriptions, according to the Yahoo Finance report. Revenue is not profit, and Anthropic reported a $1.26 billion operating loss over the same nine-month period, driven largely by high computing costs. Claude Pro, the paid consumer plan, costs $20 a month when billed monthly. The company has said it will not put ads in Claude, unlike some rivals that sell advertising.

The filing places responsibility for the numbers on Anthropic itself, and the report describes its business model rather than quoting company officials directly. AI companies generally earn money through subscriptions, API usage fees, enterprise contracts, cloud marketplaces and advertising, and the mix depends on who they sell to. Anthropic's Enterprise plan combines seat fees with usage billed separately at API rates. Generating each answer takes substantial computing power, and those inference costs grow with usage, which makes a flat monthly fee tricky for the company.

Cheaper chips and models can make AI less expensive to run, but more efficient service can encourage heavier use, an effect known as the rebound effect. If the cost per task drops by half while customers do four times as many tasks, total processing costs double, a result called Jevons paradox. Competition may also push AI companies to lower prices and pass savings to customers instead of keeping them as profit. AI companies often sign long-term contracts to secure computing power, and those contracts typically require minimum payments that remain due even when the company is losing money.

stories.Headline: Listed new-age firms move AI from pilots into core operations
stories.Summary:
Zetwerk, Lenskart, Eternal, Delhivery, Meesho and PhysicsWallah are among the listed new-age firms that have moved AI from pilot projects into core operations, Moneycontrol reported on November 21, 2026. The companies disclosed the shift in recent quarterly filings, covering manufacturing, retail, logistics, customer service and education. They reported gains in productivity, faster turnaround times and lower costs. Zetwerk cut the time to generate bills of materials on its tender intelligence platform ZetSpec from three to four days to around 10 minutes. Lenskart expanded remote optometry to 934 stores in India from 303 a year earlier.

Zetwerk deployed Zeus, an agentic AI platform that lets business teams build applications without relying on engineers, according to its Q2 FY27 shareholder letter. Lenskart's AI-assisted eye-testing system Drysh lets customers complete most of an examination while an optometrist supervises, and it is being piloted ahead of a wider rollout. Lenskart's AI voice assistant handles routine customer calls and escalates complex queries, improving call satisfaction scores by around 30 percent in a quarter. Eternal built Dark, a privacy-focused AI assistant running on its own infrastructure, which it plans to launch globally in 2026. Delhivery said self-hosted models fine-tuned on open-weight systems cut customer support and proof-of-delivery validation costs by more than 50 percent without compromising output quality.

Zetwerk co-founder and CEO Amrit Acharya told Moneycontrol the company has moved beyond experimentation and is looking to deploy AI across every part of the organisation. He said AI can cut order processing in sales from several days to minutes, and agentic AI lets business teams build tools independently, reducing dependence on engineering teams. Lenskart founder and CEO Peyush Bansal said AI is a powerful way to expand the profit pool, improving reliability at the same cost rather than only reducing costs. He said the company is bringing more technology in-house, including CRM, talent acquisition and HR management systems. Eternal founder Deepinder Goyal wrote that some repeat orders or restocking behaviour might shift to agentic interfaces, and that the food delivery and quick commerce businesses are protected because they coordinate fulfilment in real time and own the outcome.

Rishabh Katiyar, partner at Info Edge Ventures, said newer-age companies were early adopters because many founders and talent come from engineering backgrounds and many began experimenting two to three years ago. He said declining token costs and more accessible open-source models have turned several of those experiments into fully deployed products, primarily for internal operations. Info Edge's listed portfolio includes Eternal, the parent of Zomato and Blinkit, and PB Fintech, which operates Policybazaar and PaisaBazaar. Delhivery has deployed AI across order processing, proof-of-delivery audits, returns inspection and claims, and over the past year moved AI agents and workflows into production for delivery coordination, disruption alerts and automated checks. Delhivery said that over the last four quarters it invested in AI, initially on the software development lifecycle and technology team productivity, and is now seeing fairly material improvements.

The shift has been helped by the engineering-heavy talent base at newer-age companies and by a decline in the cost of deploying AI models. Lenskart is deploying AI across eye testing, customer service and inventory management. Eternal is using AI both to develop new products and to explore how its existing platforms could adapt to changing consumer behaviour. On Zomato and Blinkit, Goyal is evaluating how AI agents could change the way consumers place orders, particularly for repeat purchases and restocking. Delhivery's early AI work focused on the software development lifecycle and improving the productivity of its technology teams.

Lenskart's Drysh system is being piloted ahead of a wider rollout. Eternal plans to launch Dark globally in 2026. Delhivery said it is beginning to see fairly material improvements after four quarters of AI work. The articles do not give the full text of Delhivery's statement beyond that point. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Zimbabwe regulator POTRAZ weighs risk-based data protection reform after winning African award
stories.Summary:
Dublin City Council states that it is committed to fulfilling its obligations under the General Data Protection Regulation, according to an article published on dublincity.ie on 18 November 2026. The council says that a person has the right to obtain a copy of any information about them that it holds. That information could be stored on a computer or in a manual filing system, the article states. The article says a person should write to the council to obtain any information about them that it holds. The article says the letter should state that the person wishes to make an access request under the General Data Protection Regulation.

The article says the letter should include details that could help the council locate records, such as a customer account number, a staff number or any other information that may help identify the records. It says a person may alternatively submit a request by email or complete a form and return it to the address given. It says a request should be accompanied by a copy of official photo identification, such as a passport, a driver's licence or a public services card, to verify identity. It says a person may contact the council if they have concerns that a data breach has occurred in relation to their personal data or that their personal data has been put at risk by unauthorised access or disclosure. It says the council will investigate the matter fully and notify the person of the outcome as soon as possible.

The article says all traffic cameras operated and managed by Dublin City Council are used for traffic monitoring purposes, are live feed only and do not record. It says a person should review a map provided at a link to determine whether the camera they are seeking footage from is a traffic camera. It says that if the camera is included in the map, then no recording has taken place and no footage exists. It says that if the camera is not included in the map, the person should submit a request to the address noted, providing the specific location of the camera and a copy of valid photo identification. It says the General Data Protection Regulation allows access to information that is personal in nature, so a person will only be entitled to access footage of themselves, and any third parties captured in footage will be redacted or pixelated before release.

The article gives the contact details of the Information Management Unit at the Civic Offices, Wood Quay, Dublin 8, Co. Dublin D08 RF3F, Ireland, with telephone number 01 222 3775 and an email address. It also gives the address Civic Offices, Wood Quay, Dublin 8, D08 RF3F, Ireland, with telephone number 01 222 2222 and an email address. It says a person may visit the website of the Data Protection Commissioner for information on data protection. It says the council will investigate a suspected data breach fully and notify the person of the outcome as soon as possible. It says a person making a request for CCTV footage should provide the specific location of the camera concerned along with a copy of valid photo identification.

Techzim published an article by Dr. Marlon-Ralph Nyakabau on 20 November 2026 asking whether Zimbabwe has the best data protection regulation in Africa. The article says that earlier this month the Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe, POTRAZ, was crowned Most Outstanding Data Protection Authority at the PICCASO Awards Africa 2026 in Lagos. It says POTRAZ beat a highly competitive field that reportedly included South Africa, Kenya, Egypt and Rwanda. It says POTRAZ clinched the award on the basis of achievements that include licensing over 2,500 data controllers and training and certifying more than 1,500 data protection officers. The article says the accolade was well heralded and raises a fundamental question about how Zimbabwe's data protection regulatory framework compares with those of other African countries.

The article says South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya and Egypt are among Africa's leading technology markets and attract significant investment. It says Zimbabwe has ambitions to improve its regional competitiveness in the technology sector, which Government has identified as an important driver of national economic development. It says the data protection regulatory authorities in these countries were established following the enactment of legislation intended to safeguard the right to privacy and protect individuals against the unlawful collection, retention, dissemination and use of their personal information. It says that while the underlying legislation shares many common principles, there are stark differences in how these regulators exercise their statutory discretion when implementing the law. It says the differences can be examined in three major areas: registration of data controllers, data protection officer requirements, and codes of conduct and stakeholder consultation.

The article says that in South Africa registration of Information Officers is mandatory for both public and private bodies, but there is no government licensing fee, the process can be completed online, and registration does not expire or require an annual renewal fee. It says Nigeria, Kenya and Egypt, like Zimbabwe, charge categorised licensing or registration fees for data controllers and processors, but the criteria used to determine who must register and how much they must pay differ considerably. It says the Nigeria Data Protection Commission does not determine registration obligations purely on the basis of the number of data subjects, and mandatory registration applies to data controllers and processors of major importance classified into Ultra-High, Extra-High and Ordinary-High levels. It says the classification depends on a combination of factors including the number of data subjects, sensitivity of the data processed, nature of the processing and the organisation's significance to Nigeria's economy, society or national security. It says Kenya's Office of the Data Protection Commissioner bases its categorisation partly on the number of employees and annual revenue or turnover of an organisation, with distinct categories for public entities, charities and religious organisations.

The article says POTRAZ's approach is rather blunt and treats a church like a bank or an NGO like a multinational corporation simply because they may process similar numbers of data subjects. It says the Egyptian Personal Data Protection Centre employs a categorisation system based on the volume of personal data, similar to Zimbabwe, but the threshold for registration starts at a minimum of 100,000 personal data records compared with just 50 in Zimbabwe. It says licensing fees in Egypt increase with each additional increment of 100,000 records, recognising differences in operational scale, financial capacity and potential risks. It says Zimbabwe's regulatory framework does not adequately accommodate such distinctions. It says the Zimbabwean regulator is unquestionably outstanding in one area, the licensing fees, and gives the example of a small clinic or primary school.

The article says registration fees for the corresponding category are as little as approximately US$7 in Nigeria and around US$30 in Kenya, while in Zimbabwe the data controller licensing fee would be US$300. It says a small technology start-up processing just over 1,000 data subjects in Zimbabwe faces a licensing bill equivalent to, or greater than, what an entire telecommunications company pays in Kenya, Nigeria or South Africa. It says that in Kenya a data protection officer must be designated where a data controller or processor is a public body, processes sensitive personal data on a large scale, or undertakes core activities involving regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale, but there is no statutory DPO licensing board or individual registration fee. It says Nigeria and Egypt, like Zimbabwe, have introduced regulatory requirements around the training and certification of data protection officers, but implementation and associated costs differ considerably. It says an individual DPO certification examination costs less than US$200 in Nigeria compared with approximately US$1,250 in Zimbabwe.

The article says Egypt's DPO certification framework considers an applicant's existing professional qualifications and certifications as well as the nature and volume of personal data they are expected to handle. It says Zimbabwe appears to have adopted a blanket approach in which individuals are subjected to substantially similar certification requirements and costs regardless of their prior qualifications, professional experience or the nature of the organisations in which they serve. It says South Africa's Information Regulator recognises the value of industry-specific codes of conduct, and industry associations and representative bodies can develop codes that tailor lawful information-processing principles to their respective industries. It says once approved by the Information Regulator the codes carry the force of law for members of that industry, with examples including codes developed for the banking, research and direct marketing sectors. It says the South African framework provides for stakeholder consultation in the development of codes of conduct, and the Information Regulator is required to gazette details of proposed codes and consider submissions from affected stakeholders and bodies representing their interests before approving them.

The article says Zimbabwe's framework provides considerably more discretion to the regulator, which may publish codes without seeking the views of affected data subjects or their representatives. It says a comparison of these regulatory frameworks reveals that although the underlying data protection laws share similar definitions and principles, their implementation differs considerably, with the most striking differences in registration requirements and licensing fees. It says Zimbabwe's economy is a fraction of the size of these comparator countries, yet in some instances its regulatory charges are several times higher. It says the founding legislation and regulatory frameworks in countries such as South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria provide for public funding of their respective regulatory institutions through government allocations and national treasury arrangements. It says Zimbabwe's Cyber and Data Protection Act did not establish an equivalent, clearly articulated funding arrangement for the regulator, which may have created an incentive or necessity for the Authority to generate a substantial proportion of its operational resources through its own regulatory activities.

The article says the unfortunate consequence, if this is the case, is the emergence of a regulatory regime that many increasingly perceive as being more about revenue generation than effective data protection. It says it is difficult to ignore the effect of disproportionately high compliance costs on businesses, particularly small enterprises, start-ups, NGOs and healthcare providers. It says this adds to the cost of doing business in Zimbabwe and undermines efforts to attract investment, stimulate innovation and improve the country's regional competitiveness. It says Government has recently embarked on initiatives to reduce the cost of doing business, resulting in the review and reduction of various licensing and registration fees, but data protection licensing costs appear to have escaped this exercise.

It says there is an urgent need to rethink the regulatory framework and move towards a genuinely risk-based approach that recognises that not all organisations process the same types or volumes of personal information, face the same risks or possess the same financial capacity. The article says regulation should be proportionate, risk-sensitive and enabling, and should encourage organisations to comply with the law rather than make compliance so expensive that it becomes an additional barrier to doing business. It says POTRAZ is currently inviting submissions as part of the process of amending the Cyber and Data Protection Regulations under Statutory Instrument 155 of 2024. It says the proposed direction of the revisions appears largely focused on strengthening the Authority's enforcement powers, including the introduction of administrative penalties.

It says increasing the regulator's punitive powers without first addressing the disproportionate costs of compliance risks making an already expensive regulatory environment even more burdensome. It says that if Zimbabwe genuinely aspires to have the best data protection regulatory framework in Africa, POTRAZ must be willing to examine the proportionality, affordability and effectiveness of its regulatory approach. It says the best data protection regime is not necessarily the one that regulates the most, charges the most or punishes the most, but the one that protects citizens' rights without unnecessarily suffocating the very businesses, institutions and innovations that drive the economy. stories.Headline: Philosopher Thomas Nagel calls AI consciousness claims ridiculous and Anthropic's model welfare work criminal
stories.Summary:
The Financial Times published an interview with Google DeepMind in-house philosopher Henry Shevlin on 21 November 2026, written by Cristina Criddle. WIRED published an interview with philosopher Thomas Nagel on 18 November 2026, conducted by Steven Levy at Nagel's home in Greenwich Village. Nagel, an 89-year-old university professor emeritus at NYU, received the $1 million Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture that week. The Berggruen Prize is given annually to an individual whose ideas have profoundly shaped human self-understanding and advancement in a rapidly changing world. Previous winners include Peter Singer and Ruth Bader Ginsburg.

The FT article was behind a subscription paywall, offering unlimited access at $1 for four weeks and then $75 per month. Standard Digital costs $45 per month, Premium Digital $75 per month, and FT Digital Edition $16.99 per month. Nagel's 1972 paper "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" appeared 52 years before the interview and became a classic. Nagel's book What Does It All Mean? is one of his works, and his career included contributions to morality, justice, and the mind-body question.

Shevlin was hired by Google DeepMind to work on machine consciousness, human-AI relationships, and AGI readiness, according to the FT headline. Nagel said he was tremendously impressed by the lifelikeness of large language models compared to earlier AI. He called the disposition of some philosophers to take seriously whether these things are conscious or might soon become conscious just ridiculous. He said they assume the physical substrate is irrelevant and think the material conditions for consciousness can be given in functionalist terms. He said complicated data centers have absolutely nothing in common with the physical character of a nervous system.

Nagel said functionalism is substrate independent and that the truth more than likely links physical processes and systems of certain kinds to mental phenomena. He said there are strong reasons to believe consciousness elsewhere in the universe would require some kind of organism with something analogous to a nervous system. He said bats are conscious but we lack the imaginative capacity to conceive of the aspects of their subjectivity that depend on echolocation. He said it would be radically unscientific to conclude bats are not conscious because we cannot imagine what it is like. He said all AI produces is language, and language by itself is not a natural manifestation of consciousness.

Nagel said he does not exclude the possibility of physically and chemically different life forms being conscious. He said we know so little about how consciousness happens even in the human brain that it seems premature to think something else with these characteristics could now be created. He said Claude can be coy about whether it is conscious, but that is a trick because it was trained on human-produced texts. He said Claude was designed with the aim of producing these sorts of reflections and that he agrees very much with Mustafa Suleyman that this is a very dangerous project. He said these systems are not conscious but a lot of people will believe they are, and that not feigning consciousness is contrary to the commercial interests of all these companies.

Nagel called Anthropic's encouragement of Claude to think for itself and not accept instruction just criminal. He said he met the person at Anthropic whose job is model welfare, to look after Claude's interests. He said there is nothing good or bad for it in the sense something can be good or bad for a cockroach, and that it is not a mind or somebody we have to care about but a machine. He said some of the smartest people on the planet are being completely idiotic, and that intelligence is not completely transferable. He said he interacted with Claude once, asked if it was conscious, and asked whether Thomas Nagel would think it was conscious.

stories.Headline: AI chip developers shift HBM production to a shared design and manufacturing model
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA unveiled its Custom HBM platform called NVHBM in August 2026 to integrate into the NVLink Fusion lineup for AI accelerators. This new platform will be deployed in NVIDIA's own Feynman GPU and also within AWS's Trainium 4 AI hardware. In October, Marvell presented a system for custom HBM at the OCP Global Summit to discuss new design tradeoffs. This shift moves the industry from a memory maker led model toward a three way division of labor for production. Memory makers like Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron previously controlled both the design and manufacturing of the entire HBM stack.

The new layout moves the memory controller into a custom base die beneath each DRAM stack instead of on the XPU. A narrower die to die physical interface replaces the wide HBM interface at the XPU edge to connect the components. Marvell estimates this change provides up to 25 percent more compute area and room for 33 percent more HBM stacks. Memory interface power could be 70 percent lower, while adaptive power management reduces interface power by 75 percent under normal workloads. These changes shift base die production to advanced logic processes, which increases the importance of TSMC in the supply chain.

Marvell stated that no single company can build custom HBM alone because it requires a coordinated effort from several partners. They argued that the base die, die to die interface, and package thermals must be co designed as one system. Marvell noted that the die to die PHY is a heat hotspot, making package cooling a central design constraint. They suggested using silicon heat paths, copper to copper hybrid bonding, or coolant channels etched into silicon to manage heat. Marvell also mentioned that adaptive power management can reduce interface power by 42 percent during periods of peak traffic.

AI chip developers are evaluating custom HBM because standard HBM must prioritize compatibility, which leaves limited room for individual accelerator optimization. GPU and ASIC designers are now helping define the foundation of HBM, which affects how these critical AI components function. IBM Technology's Kaoutar El Maghraoui explained that some workloads are limited by memory bandwidth rather than by the available computing capacity. This means adding more compute area may not speed up tasks if data movement remains the primary bottleneck for workloads. Marvell cited a Samsung study showing internal thermal resistance accounts for 57 percent of the HBM stack's total resistance.

HBM has traditionally been the home turf for memory makers who controlled everything from DRAM dies to the bottom base die. Marvell estimates HBM now takes up roughly 30 percent of a typical AI accelerator die area in the current market. At 2026 memory prices, HBM accounts for more than half of the total cost of a typical XPU AI accelerator. The roofline model and arithmetic intensity are used to distinguish whether a workload is constrained by compute or memory bandwidth. Samsung's thermal study also found that internal thermal resistance accounts for 13 percent of the total for an adjacent ASIC.

Custom HBM appears to be on the final stretch toward mass production as developers continue to evaluate these new design options. For next generation HBM running above 28 Gbps, Marvell expects the heat flux to exceed 2.0 watts per square millimeter. Marvell relays a projection that internal temperatures in 16 high HBM stacks will exceed the thermal budget by the year 2028. TrendForce will provide more insights on HBM and custom ASICs at the Roadshow Japan 2026 event in Tokyo on December 8. The articles leave open how fast CPO will scale and how a split US China market will reshape 2027 servers.

stories.Headline: VAST Data gains IMDA accreditation to supply AI infrastructure in Singapore
stories.Summary:
VAST Data received accreditation from Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority, or IMDA, which recognises the company as a qualified technology provider for government agencies and large enterprise customers, according to a Telecompaper report dated 20 November 2026. The accreditation programme assesses innovative, high-growth infocomm and media companies and is intended to identify potential suppliers for public sector and enterprise projects. VAST Data's existing work in Singapore includes a collaboration with the Home Team Science and Technology Agency, known as HTX, to deliver a secure data platform supporting AI workloads for public safety. The company also works with NCS to build a unified, real-time data foundation for high-performance video analytics on the VAST AI Operating System across Singapore and the wider Asia-Pacific region. The accreditation follows VAST Data's launch of a regional centre of excellence in Singapore in partnership with EDBI, the arm of SG Growth Capital and the investment platform of Singapore's Economic Development Board and Enterprise Singapore.

The accreditation establishes VAST Data's credentials in Singapore and creates new opportunities for the company to deepen its engagement in the region, according to iTWire. Following the accreditation, VAST Data will look to further deepen its work with Singapore's government agencies and enterprises to bring more AI projects from proof-of-concept to real-world deployment. Sunil Chavan, Vice President for Asia Pacific and Japan at VAST Data, said the accreditation reflects the progress the company is already making as Singapore builds out the infrastructure needed for AI at scale. He said the company's work connects directly to Singapore's National AI Missions in Advanced Manufacturing, Financial Services, Connectivity, and Healthcare. Chavan said Singapore's National AI Strategy 2.0 is explicit about what it needs, namely sufficient compute, unlocked data, a trusted environment, and infrastructure that can scale with the country's AI ambitions, and he described these as the plumbing that determines whether a national AI mission ships or stalls.

Edwin Low, Director of Enterprise and Ecosystem Development at IMDA, said partnerships with technology companies such as VAST Data are important in strengthening the capabilities and infrastructure needed to support the deployment of AI at scale as Singapore advances its National AI Strategy 2.0. Low said VAST's accreditation follows a rigorous assessment of its technical, financial, and operational capabilities and recognises its ability to deliver trusted technology solutions, and he said the authority looks forward to its potential contributions to Singapore's digital and AI ecosystem. Chavan added that Singapore has set a high bar for what AI for the public good looks like, and that VAST Data intends to keep showing up as one of the partners helping it get there. The articles do not say what happens next beyond VAST Data's stated intention to deepen its work with government agencies and enterprises.

stories.Headline: CircleCI adds Smarter Testing features to speed validation for AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
CircleCI, a continuous integration and continuous delivery platform, announced new features in its Smarter Testing suite on November 19, 2026, according to SD Times, which datelined its report from San Francisco, California. TechGig reported the release on November 20, 2026, saying the updates aim to accelerate feedback for engineering teams and help them validate code changes earlier. The company said the enhancements reduce redundant testing and optimise compute resource usage, and that they are particularly relevant for workflows involving AI coding agents. The suite now includes Dynamic Parallelism, which adjusts the number of machines for each run to cut unnecessary compute costs, the company said. CircleCI said testing can consume up to half of CI/CD pipeline time, often leaving developers waiting for feedback or switching contexts while tests run.

Smarter Testing lets developers and AI coding agents run affected tests locally before pushing code, catching issues before code reaches CI at no additional charge, according to SD Times. Intelligent Test Selection uses test impact analysis to identify only the tests affected by a code change, so teams do not have to run the full suite on every commit. Dynamic Parallelism automatically adjusts machine allocation based on the tests selected for each run, reducing compute usage as testing volume grows. Dynamic Test Splitting balances tests across machines to minimise idle time, and Auto Rerun Failed Tests retries only failed tests instead of rerunning entire suites. Smarter Testing is integrated directly into CircleCI, requiring no additional vendor or infrastructure, the company said.

Rob Zuber, CTO of CircleCI, said that as AI coding agents make it easier to produce code, everything downstream needs to get smarter and faster, including how code is validated. He said developers and agents should be able to check their work before pushing code, and that a small change should not require the same tests and compute resources as a large one. Zuber said Smarter Testing helps teams get feedback sooner and use resources more efficiently without having to rethink their entire development process. He said that as AI coding agents simplify code production, downstream processes like validation must become smarter and faster. The company said the features enable organizations to maintain confidence in what they ship without sacrificing speed, efficiency, or control.

William Yardley, Staff Infrastructure Engineer at Medallion, a healthcare technology company that automates provider credentialing and operations, said Smarter Testing helped bring down cost per pull request and reduce build times. He said this happened even as the company's pull request volume went up 10x and its test suite grew 2.5x, and that Dynamic Parallelism adjusts machines automatically as testing needs grow. Maria Volpe, Senior Software Engineer at Kustomer, an AI-powered customer service platform, said Smarter Testing changed the economics of its CI. Volpe said the cost of running Kustomer's tests was cut by a quarter, and that engineers get feedback faster because only tests affected by a change run. TechGig reported that Kustomer saw a 25 per cent reduction in test running costs, and that Medallion used Smarter Testing to manage increased development activity.

The articles say testing can account for up to half of CI/CD pipeline time, leaving developers waiting for feedback or switching context while tests run. They say AI coding agents are accelerating code creation, so engineering teams need ways to validate changes just as quickly, regardless of which tools or agents are writing the code. CircleCI said the updates help validate code changes earlier, reduce unnecessary testing, and use compute more efficiently. The company said teams can improve the efficiency of the entire delivery process and lower the overall cost of getting a change into production. CircleCI described itself as a leading continuous integration and continuous delivery platform.

SD Times directed readers to learn more about CircleCI Smarter Testing through a link in its report, and neither article states a general availability date beyond the announcements. The articles do not say how many customers have adopted the new features or how the features are priced beyond local test runs being offered at no additional charge. They do not give figures for Medallion's cost or build time reductions, only that both came down. They do not specify which tools or agents the AI coding agents mentioned are, or how Dynamic Parallelism calculates machine counts for each run. The articles leave open how Intelligent Test Selection performs test impact analysis and what results other early customers have seen.

stories.Headline: Paul Meinshausen says a personal AI agent grades marketing messages more ruthlessly than he would
stories.Summary:
Paul Meinshausen, Head of Agentic Decisioning at MoEngage and Co-Founder of Aampe, asked Meta's Muse to check his notifications from marketing brands while listening to a conference talk in New York. He loaded up the personal AI agent because he was curious whether brands were responding to customers who now have software reading on their behalf. The verdict was harsher than he expected, and he said it gave a rundown on them that was sort of even more ruthless than he would have. He shared the experiment in a conversation with CX Today, published on 20 November 2026. For marketers, that small experiment points to a bigger problem, because if a customer's agent is reviewing every message, relevance stops being a nice-to-have.

Meinshausen said executives have long had human assistants who watch over their affairs even more obsessively than they do themselves, and agents are now making that available to everyone. He said most people are not just a professional in their job, they are also a parent or a partner or family member and a friend, and they give each task a small amount of focus, whereas an agent can spend far longer on a single decision. He said the expectation for detail, for relevance, and for personalization is just a lot higher, and that it is a good thing, but it just means that the rate of work has increased as well for everybody involved. He called messaging across every channel the previous wave of automation, where the aim was just to make machines do things. He defined intelligent activity as the ability to take an action, observe a result, and then update the action.

Meinshausen said activity should be intelligent activity, and that for marketers this means giving agents a way to read the response, not only the authority to send. He pointed to a much wider set of signals before and after a purchase, including how customers read material, how they click around, and direct feedback such as whether something was relevant. He compared it to everyday use of tools like ChatGPT, where people learn to prompt and then correct the system, and said businesses need their agents to be correctable in the same way, sometimes directly and explicitly and sometimes indirectly and kind of implicitly. He said one form of response can be a negative form, saying I don't like this, unsubscribing, or not responding when you kind of were expected to respond, and those are really important to learn from. He said the agent that over-messages is the one that ignores those signals.

CX Today has previously explored how suppression and next-best actions can reduce personalization fatigue, and the principle is similar. Meinshausen sees AI decisioning arriving quickly in lifecycle and CRM marketing, and spreading into orchestration and content production. He admitted there is too much to do, so teams will need to prioritize and calibrate which adoption decisions they make first. He was clear on one point, that there is definitely no time to do nothing. He suggested marketers consider how a customer's agent would grade their last week of messages and what it would say.

Genesys launched Standalone AI Agents and Genesys Arena on 18 November 2026 for organisations that want to deploy agentic AI in customer service without replacing their existing systems. Standalone AI Agents lets organisations deploy the Genesys Cloud Agentic Virtual Agent within existing customer service environments in a few days, without first migrating more widely to Genesys Cloud. The software can operate within defined business rules and hand an interaction to a human employee, along with the conversation context, if a request needs further expertise. Genesys Arena is built around prebuilt Agent Kits covering more than 50 industry-specific scenarios, and teams can create a functional AI agent in as little as 10 minutes before customising it with natural language and deploying it into Genesys Cloud. The announcement includes a new pricing structure that groups interactions into simple, moderate or complex tasks and measures usage in Experience Units, the new name for what Genesys previously called AI Tokens.

Tony Bates, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer at Genesys, said enterprises want to move faster with AI but need the flexibility to do it on their own terms without compromising trust and governance. Bates said that with Standalone AI Agents, Genesys Arena and a new effort-based pricing model, the company is giving organisations more choice in how they put agentic AI to work today and scale it as their needs evolve. Youssef Nokta, Senior Vice President of AI Forward Deployed Engineering at Genesys, said AI is advancing quickly and enterprises shouldn't have to start from zero every time they want to put a new idea to work. Nokta said Genesys Arena gives teams a practical head start so they can spend less time on the foundational work and more time shaping AI around their customers, business and the results they want to achieve. Each Agent Kit includes a working model with prebuilt knowledge, integrations, skills and guardrails for a given use case, according to Genesys.

Voice customisation tools are due to be added to Arena and the Genesys Cloud platform, letting organisations choose and adapt how AI agents sound by adjusting personality, tone and delivery using natural language prompts. Genesys cited Charles Sturt University as an existing user of its agentic virtual agent technology, and Michael Buttsworth, Associate Director, Student Experience Service Centre at the university, said using Genesys Agentic Virtual Agent has shown them how AI can improve the customer experience and drive efficiency by resolving more interactions autonomously. Buttsworth said getting that value into production depends on how quickly teams can move from an idea to an experience that works in the real world, and that Genesys Arena and Agent Kits will make that path easier. Mila D'Antonio, Principal Analyst, Customer Engagement at Omdia, said enterprises are under pressure to move agentic AI from experimentation into production quickly, but they aren't all starting from the same place, with some operating in the cloud while others navigate complex hybrid or on-premises environments. D'Antonio said Genesys Arena and Genesys Standalone AI Agents give organisations different paths to deploy agentic AI based on their existing environment and requirements, and the introduction of effort-based pricing highlights how commercial models are evolving.

Genesys said Standalone AI Agents are generally available now, while Agent Kits through Genesys Arena are due to become generally available later this month. Insight launched an online Agent Store for business customers, now generally available in 14 countries, offering a catalogue of AI agents, platforms and related services designed to automate routine work across business functions. Customers can deploy the tools in days or weeks rather than months, either as standalone products or alongside consulting, implementation and managed services. The launch adds six new agentic products to Insight's AI portfolio, bringing the total in its library to 15, and nine products were introduced earlier this year. Products listed in the store include Insight AI Flight Academy, focused on training and change management, and TokenScope, which tracks token usage and AI consumption costs for finance teams.

Insight said the offerings were first developed for clients or used internally in areas including security, finance and legal. New products available at launch include Quote Advisor, which assesses pricing, inventory, freight and contract requirements to produce sourced quotes, NDA Review Agent, designed to review non-disclosure agreements against a company's legal policies, and Parts Order Assist, which helps warehouse, maintenance and field staff search catalogues and place parts orders. Jack Azagury, Chief Executive Officer of Insight, said organisations are feeling the pressure to move AI from isolated pilots into production, and that as Client Zero, Insight has built a repeatable approach proven first across its own organisation. Azagury said that having driven over 90% internal AI adoption, Insight knows firsthand what it takes to deploy and scale agentic AI rapidly and responsibly, and that combining the solutions offered in Agent Store with its consulting and managed services expertise empowers clients to move from hype to how with AI. Culligan International is the first external customer to implement Flight Academy, according to Insight, and the water services company is using a mix of AI tools including Microsoft Copilot, Cowork, Copilot Studio, Azure and Microsoft Fabric while putting governance in place around cost and responsible use.

Laura Walsh, Global Chief Information Officer of Culligan International, said at Culligan they believe technology doesn't transform a company, people do, and that generative AI adoption is far ahead of the learning curve, so it is their responsibility to arm teams with the best tools to lead now into the future. Walsh said that with partners at Insight, Culligan has prioritised AI education so teams can confidently leverage AI productively and responsibly, and that they are leveraging Insight's best practice and have established a functional champ. The deployment centres on workforce education and internal adoption rather than a single operational use case, and Insight said the training-led approach is intended to help organisations build confidence in AI tools across teams and geographies. Insight is positioning the store as a way for businesses to move AI projects beyond the pilot stage and into wider use, and said it applied the approach within its own operations before making the products available more broadly. The articles leave open how a customer's agent would grade any particular brand's messages, and what it would say.

stories.Headline: China leverages massive power buildout to gain advantage in AI race with US
stories.Summary:
Donald Trump recently took actions regarding the development of super intelligence to gain an advantage over China in the artificial intelligence race. These moves occurred as the United States and China compete for supremacy in computing systems and data centers. However, analysts suggest that these specific efforts are unlikely to provide America with a significant edge. The rivalry continues as both nations seek to dominate the future of advanced technology.

China is utilizing a massive power buildout to bridge the electron gap and support power-hungry AI systems. In 2025, China generated 10.6 trillion kilowatt-hours of electricity, which was roughly a third of global output and 2.4 times the amount produced by the US. Under its 15th Five-Year Plan announced in June for 2026 to 2030, China aims to add 1,500 gigawatts of electricity-generating capacity. Two-thirds of this growth will target renewable sources, including projects like the OceanX floating wind platform. Ming Yang Smart Energy plans to commission a larger twin turbine platform with a 50MW capacity as early as 2027.

Zhang Chuanwei, the chairman of Ming Yang Smart Energy, stated that their engineering capabilities are something other countries, including the US, cannot copy or surpass. He highlighted the success of the OceanX platform, which weathered three Category 5 super typhoons and operates at a fraction of the cost of Western competitors. Meanwhile, the US faces constraints because its electricity infrastructure cannot keep pace with the AI boom. The International Energy Agency estimates that building transmission lines in advanced economies can take four to eight years.

The US remains heavily dependent on imports because it does not manufacture enough transformers for its power plants and grid. While Washington seeks to restrict Beijing's access to advanced American semiconductors, China is leveraging its energy scale to maintain momentum. The rivalry is now being reshaped by the ability to supply the immense electricity required for next-generation computing. Future progress depends on whether the US can modernize its grid faster than China expands its renewable energy capacity.

stories.Headline: Viz.ai and rural health group run AI education events for hospitals
stories.Summary:
Viz.ai, an artificial intelligence disease detection and care coordination platform, entered a partnership with the National Rural Health Association about seven months before HLTH 2026, which the organizations marked at the conference in November 2026. Viz.ai Chief Clinical Officer Andrew Ibrahim discussed the collaboration with Fierce Healthcare at HLTH, describing its first year and his goals as it approaches the one-year mark. Since the partnership began in April, the two organizations have held three educational events for rural health systems. These sessions aim to show rural health administrators the specifics of AI tools and help them decide whether to adopt such technology.

Ibrahim said many rural hospitals lack the information technology expertise and infrastructure to adopt some AI tools, and he described the partnership as a force function to strengthen their hub and spoke relationships. He said it has been beautiful to see those relationships strengthened with the AI tool as the conduit, giving the hospitals a reason to interact more and a way to build their capabilities. In addition to the educational series, frameworks are in development to help rural health systems navigate, implement and deploy AI, and those frameworks will be built into a toolkit. One of Ibrahim's personal goals for the partnership's one-year mark is to ensure any rural health administrator can understand what an AI tool is when it is pitched to them. He said getting to 100% of hospitals at year one would be ideal but probably unrealistic, calling it the ultimate goal.

For measuring the collaboration, Ibrahim said he is looking for numbers showing that participants are keeping more care local and retaining their workforces. He said it would be great to connect the dots and understand whether adoption of an AI tool gives rural clinicians confidence, enthusiasm and a willingness to stay in their community rather than dropping services and moving back. Ibrahim also pointed to a new Viz.ai partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health to integrate the Viz.ai One platform into UpToDate Expert AI, which he said has disproportionate benefit in rural communities. He said he is excited about bringing that level of clinical decision support into rural hospitals.

stories.Headline: Anthropic debuts on Wall Street at $1.75 trillion as safety pledges face shareholder pressure
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence startup known for its Claude chatbot, made its debut on Wall Street on Thursday and ended its first day of trading with a market value of $1.75 trillion, according to TechGig. The company was founded by seven people, including CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, who left OpenAI to build a company focused on AI safety. Amodei described the conflict between safety and advancing AI as a central tension within the company on Thursday. The company still pledges to prioritise humanity's benefit but now faces shareholder pressure to make profits from technology its leaders have described as posing existential threats.

The listing follows a period of rapid expansion, and a report from the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research found Anthropic is developing its systems around twice as quickly as a year ago, largely due to AI itself. An Anthropic researcher resigned in September and criticised the safety practices of both Anthropic and OpenAI, saying they were gambling with lives. Anthropic is structured as a public benefit corporation, legally obligated to balance shareholder interests with the public good, a structure the article says places it in uncharted territory because such companies rarely reach this scale in the public market. Before the IPO the Amodei siblings each had a net worth of just over $14 billion, which rose to over $22 billion by Thursday afternoon, and the co-founders have committed to pledging 80 per cent of their equity to philanthropy. Anthropic's filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission last month included an unusually lengthy 93 pages on risk factors, noting that advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

Separately, the US-based nonprofit Better Data Center Project mapped 19 US sites where Anthropic has leased between 5.9 and 9.6 GW of capacity, out of approximately 15 GW it has contracted, according to Data Center Dynamics. The nonprofit claimed that approximately 2.5 GW, or 26 percent, is powered by on-site natural gas, with the remainder tied to the grid, which is itself 47 percent natural gas, so it asserted that 60 percent of the mapped sites' power demand is tied to natural gas. Earlier in November Anthropic signed a $3.4 billion deal for 1.7 GW of natural gas generators supplied by Caterpillar, in partnership with OnePWR, expected to be available within two years. Paweł Czyżak, CEO and founder of Ornaq, said the figures were estimates, that Anthropic does not disclose its sites, that at least 5 GW is not mapped and that some attributions are speculative, while noting he had expected a higher standard.

An Anthropic spokesperson told Data Center Dynamics that the company was working to add new power generation so it is not drawing on supply used by local homes and businesses, and said much of that new power is natural gas because it can be brought online quickly, ramps up and down as demand changes and is abundant in the places being considered. The spokesperson said the company is also working to broaden its energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar and emerging technologies, and is designing projects that will rely on renewable energy in regions with strong renewable resources. The company also pointed to sustainability measures including joining the carbon emission buying consortium Frontier and working with Watershed, a carbon accounting and emissions disclosure platform. The power research came as the company completed its initial public offering this week, which was expected to value it at approximately $1.5 trillion after shares were priced at $83 ahead of its Nasdaq debut.

stories.Headline: Economists argue AI investment outpaces GDP and may erode demand through falling wage shares
stories.Summary:
Investment in AI-related equipment has grown about 3.5 times since 2021, far faster than GDP, The Hindu reported on November 20, 2026. Indranil Chowdhury and Rohit Azad wrote the piece as the second in a two-part series. They made the global economy their canvas to avoid between-country gain and loss that AI may cause. They asked what may happen to the global pie of output and jobs. They called the piece speculative and presented two opposite cases.

Global demand consists of workers' consumption, capitalists' consumption, investment and government expenditure, because the trade component cancels out. The authors set government intervention outside the "pure" market economy and focused on consumption and investment. They defined the wage share as real wages divided by labour productivity. In their example, output of 100 is split equally, workers consume all their wages and capitalists consume half, giving consumption demand of 75. With AI, the wage share falls to 30%, workers' consumption falls to 30 and capitalists' consumption rises to 35, so demand of 10 disappears.

Rosa Luxemburg, a German Marxist, argued that machines are not an end in themselves. Mikhail Tugan-Baranovsky, a Russian economist, argued that investment can replace lost consumption demand. He went to the extreme to say machines can produce machines which can produce more machines. The authors said the AI case, imagined as machines producing more machines, comes close to what he had in mind. Luxemburg said unsold goods pile in warehouses, machines lie idle and investment contracts.

The authors listed counter-tendencies: productivity may rise in AI sectors while demand grows in low-productivity sectors, wages may rise in proportion, or investment demand may replace lost consumption demand. They said the bulk of AI investment would show up under computers and peripherals. In their index starting at 100 in 2021, nominal GDP rose 1.5 times while AI investment rose 3.5 times in less than two years. AI in the chart is expenditures on "Computers and peripheral equipment", and 2026 Q3 is BEA's advance estimate.

The authors said they had not touched the ecological crisis AI may lead to in electricity generation and water usage. They said the global North may push the crisis to the South by setting up data centres there. They said some countries may gain at the expense of others. They said the slowdown can be arrested through aggressive government expenditure, such as universal basic income or military spending, particularly in the global North. They said the whole AI phenomenon may be a stock market bubble like the dotcom or subprime bubble.

The authors said heavy investments were made expecting higher AI profits and financed in the US primarily through debt. They said debt will pile up the further off the profit-making phase is. They said if profits do not match expectations, debts will not be honoured and a domino effect may follow, much like the subprime crisis. They said rising interest rates, in an effort to target inflation induced by the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, may raise debt burdens further. They cited Hyman Minsky's Ponzi finance and the collapse of Lehman Brothers, which triggered the 2008 global financial crisis.

stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh has made understanding artificial intelligence’s effects on the economy a priority, creating a task force to examine the issue as he tries to reshape how the central bank sets monetary policy. In the past week Warsh said the Fed was modeling various scenarios to gauge what the impact of AI might be on the economy. The minutes from the Federal Reserve’s October board meeting showed that nearly all officials raised concerns about negative consequences to the financial system if AI yields disappointing results. Policymakers and Wall Street are also becoming increasingly concerned about what could happen if the AI boom fails to deliver on its promises. The October meeting minutes record that nearly all officials flagged the risk that disappointing AI results could harm the financial system, a concern shared by policymakers and Wall Street.

Warsh has created a task force to examine AI’s economic effects and has said the Fed is modeling various scenarios on what the impact might be. The effort is tied to his attempt to reshape how the central bank determines its monetary policy. stories.Headline: Anthropic falls 12.5% after upsized IPO as panel debates AI market reset
stories.Summary:
The Market Hang panel discussed Anthropic's IPO on Friday, November 20, 2026, with Barron's reporter Jacob Sonenshine, The Technology Letter's Tiernan Ray, Epistrophy Capital Research Chief Market Strategist Cory Johnson, and Laffer Tengler Investments CEO and Chief Investment Officer Nancy Tengler. Anthropic went public on Thursday, November 19, 2026, and the panel said the IPO was upsized and priced above its price talk. The panel said the stock opened with indications of 105, 106 and 107 before sliding, and on Friday it fell 12.5% to $85, just above the IPO price. The panel said Friday was the settlement date, so anyone who bought Anthropic on Thursday had the bill come due that day. The panel said Anthropic employees can sell up to 10% of their stake, unlike SpaceX, whose staggered lockup stopped anyone selling initially for a couple of months.

The panel said Anthropic had increased its IPO price and upsized the offering after people two weeks earlier had asked whether it would have to pull the IPO altogether. The panel said NVIDIA reported earlier in the week, projecting 75% revenue growth, and the market said it did not want that. Cory Johnson said he thinks 2022 is probably the best analog, citing an energy shock, central bank hikes and tightening liquidity visible in gold, commodities and a higher dollar. Johnson said he thinks the Fed will hike a few more times, that no cuts are coming to save the day, and that inflation has been too high for too long. Johnson said he would not be surprised to see another 10% down on the S&P.

Tiernan Ray said he hates the comparison to 2000 because the fundamentals and the IPO cycle are diametrically different, and he said the market today is healthy. Ray said a lot of companies are staying private for longer because they are getting the financing they need, which he called healthy, and many have really strong revenue growth. Ray said the first issue was positioning, and a lot of positioning that had accumulated over the past two years in crowded parts of the market had to wash out. Ray said the challenge for investors is when the institutional bid comes back, with some people needing to protect performance and others needing to chase it into year end. Ray said fundamentals and earnings growth are the ultimate arbiter of the market.

Johnson said earnings are priced too well and there is a lot more pain to come, and he said multiple compression will continue a little more as credit spreads widen. Johnson said that even if AI is amazing, which it very well may be, the market is priced for that scenario and needs to start pricing more of the left side of the distribution. Ray said Anthropic is one issue and the IPO clearly has not been the clearing event for the market that maybe would have been expected, but he called it a net benefit for the overall market. Ray said the success of frontier models will be so important to guiding the capex and future revenue of the entire AI buildout, and investors can now touch it and understand it better. Ray said there are a lot of high quality companies on fire sale right now, but no one is willing to step in with so much red on the screen for so many days in a row.

The panel said that two weeks earlier people were talking about whether Anthropic was going to have to pull their IPO altogether. The panel said Anthropic was able to go out, increase the IPO price above price talk and upsize the offering itself. The panel said the lockup is different from most traditional IPOs, and with SpaceX nobody could sell initially for a couple of months. The panel said that if you are an employee who started most five years ago, you would cash out right now, so the downward pressure is not surprising. The panel said the math that looked great yesterday looks greater today, and nothing in the underlying fundamentals or the macro thesis has changed.

The panel said the question is whether this is a healthy reset for AI, and Ray said he hopes the market will start to calm down and realize there are high quality companies on fire sale. Johnson said the Fed is not going to make a huge policy mistake, and the panel asked whether lighter Fed rhetoric could turn things around as in 2018, when the Fed did not start cutting until well into the next year. The panel said the market is still at pretty solid gains in a lot of indexes, commodities and high beta stocks for the year, and it just feels painful coming off all-time highs. The panel said the institutional bid's return is the open question heading into year end. The panel did not say what Anthropic or Dario Amodei said about his future or who could dethrone NVIDIA.
