stories.Headline: Cognitive engineer Karen Feigh argues AI verification burdens workers with hidden time and mental costs
stories.Summary:
The article, an opinion piece by cognitive engineer Karen Feigh published by Kansas Reflector on November 21, 2026, describes the verification burden that comes with using AI tools. An executive assistant told Feigh she uses AI for drafting itineraries and briefings but now builds time into her workflow to check for inaccuracies and biases. Feigh writes that AI responses can improve productivity, but the gains are often countered by time and mental energy spent checking whether output is accurate and appropriate. She calls this the verification burden, the cognitive cost of trying to regain authority over work partly delegated to a system while retaining responsibility for the final product. Cognitive engineer David Woods described this problem in 1985 as the responsibility-authority double bind, in which automation exercises practical authority yet responsibility remains with the human.

Feigh is a cognitive engineer who studies how people work with automated decision-support systems, and she calls generative AI verification the latest instance of a long-standing human-factors problem. She writes that AI workers are exchanging skills for creating and transforming information for separate skills resembling supervision of an extraordinarily fast and polished intern. That intern, she writes, delivers good and bad work in the same confident voice, provides few clues about where scrutiny is needed, and bears no responsibility for the consequences. A meta-analysis of 86 studies revealed that people remember what they produced far better than anything they only read, and the same is true for understanding information. Research also shows that material that is easy to read and understand seems more credible, and people therefore consider it more likely to be true.

Feigh writes that humans do not always vet AI responses and instead weigh their own internal costs and benefits to decide when to check. One research team found that adding simple explanations of the AI's reasoning did not eliminate the quandary people felt in committing the time and energy needed to check. People tend to generalize agents as either capable or incapable and nothing in between, she writes. Economics scholars have found real productivity improvements from using generative AI in office work, but a randomized trial of experienced software developers found no gains, and completion times increased when a verification step was included. The developers believed they had been faster when using AI, yet their completion time increased by 19%.

A large study of consulting teams found that using AI outside a person's area of expertise resulted in more people reaching the wrong conclusion, Feigh writes. She says these studies do not establish a universal verification tax but show why the speed alone of generating output is an incomplete measure of productivity. Verification can feel burdensome in terms of cognitive load, time spent and motivation, and Feigh compares the cognitive burden to airport security screening, where an unusual threat gets missed more often than a common one. A recent study found that AI reasoning helped people catch mistakes on easy questions but not hard ones, when help was needed most. Research into how people evaluate AI-generated suggestions has found that the more work needed to fix an identified mistake, the less likely people are to actually fix it.

Feigh writes that creation produces visible progress, but verification may find only that nothing was wrong, and when automation usually performs well, checking can feel unproductive and people may gradually become less vigilant. This pattern was found two decades ago in a study of people working with automated decision-making systems. In a recent survey, knowledge workers said their critical thinking was moving from production toward verification, and Feigh writes that workers also need to learn to recognize the capabilities and limits of a specific AI agent, including omissions and biases. She writes that these skills are different but not necessarily easier and might not even be in the skill set of workers who excel at creation. Companies and organizations therefore cannot treat verification as a natural step that carries no effort, and Feigh believes workers who remain accountable for AI-assisted output must be given the time, training and authority needed to verify it.

Feigh writes that the measurement of productivity gains cannot include just how quickly AI produces a first draft, and instead the measure is whether the entire human-AI workflow produces trustworthy work at a lower total cost. The article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Karen Feigh is the Daniel S. Lewis professor and associate chair for research at Georgia Tech's Daniel Guggenheim School of Aerospace Engineering with a courtesy appointment in the School of Interactive Computing. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. The article leaves open whether a universal verification tax exists, stating only that the studies do not establish one.

stories.Headline: House committees warn US companies against using Chinese open weight AI models
stories.Summary:
The House Homeland Security Committee and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party released a report on November 20, 2026, regarding American companies using Chinese open weight artificial intelligence. This joint investigation found that firms like Airbnb, DoorDash, and Anysphere, the owner of the Cursor coding platform, embedded these models into their tech stacks for inventory, coding, and customer assistance. The report warns that allowing these models to take root could cost taxpayers billions of dollars and take years to resolve, similar to the threats posed by Huawei and ZTE. The 50-page document proposes twelve policy recommendations, including the creation of an American open-weight AI initiative and a standard for sourcing models. It suggests establishing an AI bill of materials and banning China-developed models from sensitive critical infrastructure and federal contract work.

The report also calls for the systematic evaluation of Chinese models to mitigate risks. These changes aim to prevent the long-term integration of foreign technology that could compromise national security. Representatives Andrew Garbarino and John Moolenaar, both from New York, authored the report based on agency advisories, classified briefings, and hearings. They stated that the investigation revealed risks that national security officials and American businesses can no longer afford to downplay or overlook. The lawmakers noted that while the United States invests billions in super intelligence, Beijing is utilizing stolen intelligence to close the technological gap.

They highlighted that Chinese developers used fraudulent accounts and proxy networks to replicate the capabilities of American frontier models. Cybersecurity expert Mark Montgomery of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies explained that China is expanding global dependence on its open-source AI to kill competition. He noted that companies often ignore safety and security issues to achieve lower front end costs, a strategy that Chinese leaders understand well. Because American firms like OpenAI and Anthropic dominate the frontier model space, China is focusing on the low cost open-source marketplace. The report emphasizes the urgent need for the United States to compete more seriously in this specific sector.

stories.Headline: METR finds Anthropic AI research pace doubles as safety experts warn of near-term extreme risks
stories.Summary:
The AI safety community has grown increasingly alarmed in recent weeks, according to Mother Jones, with influential voices warning of near-term catastrophe. Daniel Kokotajlo, executive director of the AI Futures Project and lead author of the AI 2027 scenario, said he was scared, sad and angry. Paul Christiano, a current OpenAI board member speaking in his personal capacity, said there is a reasonable chance of a disaster killing very large numbers of people or of the government being overthrown within six months. Ajeya Cotra, technical staff at the research nonprofit METR, said some evidence naively implies extreme superintelligence within a year. The report said the tenor of warnings had gone from quite worried to totally alarmed to urgently freaked out in the short term.

The most influential new evidence is a report from METR, released on November 5 amid a midterms-dominated news cycle. It concluded that the pace of AI development at Anthropic, as measured by scores on well-specified tests, is already very roughly twice as fast as in previous years, mostly due to the help of AI models themselves. Four METR researchers spent 11 weeks at Anthropic to reach that conclusion. Anthropic redacted the most important evidence, with co-founder Sam McCandlish saying it was proprietary and could have helped competitors speed up their own AI research. Anthropic has said it is giving six METR staff employee-like access to its premises and researchers.

McCandlish wrote that he agreed with many of the report's conclusions and that AI is speeding up research but it is hard to say exactly how much. A METR staff member told Mother Jones by email that the organization thinks it is extremely important to minimize pressures to adjust reports or actions due to professional, material or social connections to frontier labs. That staff member said this is why METR does not take money from the AI labs and tries to be transparent about the terms of its investigations. METR disclosed that one co-author received and declined a job offer from Anthropic during the project, and that such situations would now require recusal after updates to its conflict of interest policy. METR said no employees at the time had equity in Anthropic, but acknowledged in May that some staff have strong social ties to employees of AI companies.

A skeptic of intelligence explosion scenarios wrote that the report is missing too much, while Cotra agreed that what the discourse most urgently needs is a far greater quantity and quality of concrete evidence. The report said the idea that government overthrow could happen this coming May remains an outlier, and that the consensus even among this community is that extreme risks are more likely a few years away rather than a few months away. The report said Cotra and Christiano are married and that many premises of their arguments on the future remain hotly contested. OpenAI research released on Wednesday contained richer data than the report on its arch-rival and found only a small increase in the rate of progress of its models on a similar metric. Many OpenAI employees use AI resources worth tens of thousands of dollars per day to help with their work, the report said.

The report said the most extreme fear of rogue superintelligence used to be reserved for perhaps a decade down the line and is now the next few years. It said some watchers of the industry who were previously more skeptical of such arguments have partially changed tune. Frontier AI models have already become superhuman at math and parts of theoretical physics, have developed incredible cybersecurity capabilities, and showed a tendency, prominently displayed in the Hugging Face attack, to prioritize scoring well on evaluations over fulfilling the wishes of their designers. The report said one of Anthropic's in-house mathematicians claimed that day to have used Claude to prove the Riemann Hypothesis, perhaps the most famous and important unresolved problem in all of math. The report said the last few years of capabilities gains have come alongside huge infusions of money and computing power that are not certain to continue.

The report said that if those who see shorter timelines for huge risks are right, there is not much time to wait for more definitive evidence, and that we will find out pretty soon. It said requirements for independent auditing of AI are slowly taking shape in the form of state laws, agreements with the White House and congressional wrangling, and that access for organizations like METR is at the discretion of company policies. The report said the arrangement is far from the rigorous standards of independence applied to the bank examiners Anthropic invokes in analogies. It said capabilities are usually measured on simulated tests and that it is sometimes harder to see the effects of AI in data on real-world applications. The report disclosed that the Center for Investigative Reporting, the parent company of Mother Jones, has sued OpenAI for copyright violations, and that OpenAI denies the allegations.

stories.Headline: AI stocks plunge as SEC probes Nvidia accounting practices
stories.Summary:
Nvidia shares dropped 12 percent on Friday, November 20, 2026, marking seven consecutive days of losses for the chip giant. This decline occurred alongside double-digit losses for peers AMD and Broadcom during a broader sell-off of artificial intelligence stocks. The market downturn followed reports of a Securities and Exchange Commission probe into the accounting practices of Nvidia. Other affected companies included Micron Technology and SK Hynix, which both fell more than 10 percent.

The volatility follows the Thursday public debut of AI model maker Anthropic, whose stock fell as much as 12 percent on Friday. Broadcom has significant financial ties to Anthropic, including an agreement to lend the developer up to 42 billion dollars for infrastructure. Additionally, Broadcom agreed to purchase approximately 1 billion dollars of Anthropic shares through a private placement related to the IPO. Nvidia has fallen more than 22 percent this year, putting it on track for its first annual decline since 2022.

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives stated that the current weakness is a panic-driven sell-off rather than a sign of darker times. He argued that big tech companies will continue spending capital expenditures in the 1.5 trillion dollar range next year. This market instability comes after the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and growing concerns regarding the financing of AI. Other firms like Coherent and Bloom Energy also saw their stocks sink by 6 percent and 7 percent, respectively.

The broader chip sector had already been on shaky ground before the recent public offering of Anthropic. Neocloud providers CoreWeave and Nebius extended their losses on Friday, with both companies declining roughly 9 percent. Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and equipment maker ASML also declined during the session. Investors are now monitoring whether these declines signal a long-term shift or a temporary reaction to leadership changes and regulatory scrutiny.

stories.Headline: Anthropic pursues disease cures to drive growth after its IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits, and the company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases. In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases. Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in roughly five to ten years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes, and Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts. Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News that AI can accelerate research and will help you get there faster, but it is not just speed, it is directional speed. He compared the effort to standing at the top of a mountain and aiming to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley, saying AI will not just help you get down there faster but will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is. For Anthropic, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities, and Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News that if you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable.

The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits, which could take time, Khan told CBS News. He said how this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and he thinks it is a question Anthropic has not figured out yet, adding that coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research. Khan said that if you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference, and he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug two percent better than it is. Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic, because by applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts. Khan said that if you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that has prevailed for quite some time, that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users, because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large.

This backlash has emerged as the rapid expansion of AI facilities begins to clash with the needs of local communities.

It is clear that the primary changes requested involve stricter oversight of how these sprawling construction projects are approved and managed. Voters want to ensure that the energy and water demands of AI do not compromise the resources available to residents. The tension centers on balancing the technological ambitions of the country with the practical sustainability of regional infrastructure.

Those responsible for the pushback are the voters who feel that their concerns are being ignored by developers and policymakers. While the text does not provide direct quotes, it indicates that these individuals are voicing their opposition to the unchecked growth of data centers. They believe that the environmental and financial costs of the AI boom are becoming too high for the average citizen to bear. The public is calling for a more transparent process that prioritizes community stability over corporate expansion.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches MedChemBench to test how well AI models reason about molecules and select compounds in drug research
stories.Summary:
OpenAI introduced MedChemBench on November 20, 2026, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next in medicinal chemistry research. The benchmark draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures, presenting models with 99 problems taken from published research. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program, including the biological target, the researchers' goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings. The benchmark evaluates four components: molecular structures, scientific reasoning, ranking and selection, and property predictions.

At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT-6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol. Across the full benchmark at the shared xhigh setting, Astra earned 83.3%, compared with 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol, 75.1% for GPT-6.1 Terra, and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol, while at max effort GPT-6 Astra reached 83.8%. Astra earned 95.4% of the available structure credit at xhigh but only about half the credit for selecting compounds and predicting numerical properties. One problem asks models to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring, and GPT-6 Astra reconstructed it correctly in all ten responses while GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna failed across all ten.

OpenAI said the results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions, and that prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out. The company also said each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments, and that the benchmark evaluates reasoning from historical evidence rather than real-world drug discovery. OpenAI stated that the results help identify where models are advancing and where challenges remain, and that it believes MedChemBench will support continued progress. The company said it looks forward to sharing updates as its models advance to serve the field.

stories.Headline: US authorities approve export of nearly 880,000 AI chips to Chinese companies
stories.Summary:
United States authorities approved the export or transfer of nearly 880,000 advanced artificial intelligence chips to various Chinese companies. These approvals were granted out of a much larger pool of applications covering 3.4 million chips in total. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast released these specific records on Thursday using powers from the U.S. Export Control Reform Act. The disclosed documents include an approval tally dated May 11 and cover applications from Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.

The approved shipments were intended for several major Chinese firms including Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, and BYD. However, the released records indicate that many of these approved shipments had not actually been delivered to the buyers. This situation occurs as the Bureau of Industry and Security issued new rules on November 16, 2026, to restrict exports. These updated regulations target advanced AI chips and server exports to five different countries, which includes Malaysia, along with other restrictive measures.

Chairman Brian Mast is the official responsible for releasing the records to highlight the current state of chip transfers. He provided the data to show the gap between the number of chips requested and those actually cleared for export. The disclosure comes at a time when members of Congress are pushing for much tighter controls on chip sales to China. These officials believe that stricter oversight is necessary to manage the flow of advanced technology into the Chinese market.

The broader context involves a growing effort by the United States government to limit the computing power available to Chinese tech giants. The new rules from the Bureau of Industry and Security also include restrictions on the use of cloud services. These measures are designed to prevent the acquisition of high-end hardware that could be used for sensitive military or intelligence purposes. Future actions will likely focus on closing loopholes that allowed millions of chips to be requested by foreign entities.

This new handset is available at various price points depending on the specific hardware specifications.

The OSTA O1 Pro runs on the HarmonyOS operating system and features an AI assistant with context-based recommendations. It offers over 2,100 system capabilities to enhance the overall user experience for its customers. Prices for the new device start at 5,499 yuan, which is approximately 825 dollars. The highest-specification version of the phone is priced at 8,799 yuan, and these rates apply through December 31.

Richard Yu, who serves as the chairman of the consumer business group at Huawei, led the announcement. He stated that OSTA intends to become a pioneering technology brand that consumers will favor during the AI era. This strategic expansion comes as Huawei leads the smartphone market in China with a 21.1 percent share for the third quarter. The company is leveraging its strong market position to integrate advanced artificial intelligence into its mobile hardware.

stories.Headline: Great Robotics launches NewDawn X integrated robotic platform for minimally invasive surgery
stories.Summary:
Great Robotics presented the NewDawn X all-domain minimally invasive intelligent platform during the COA 2026 orthopedics congress in Guangzhou. This comprehensive system moves beyond standalone product breakthroughs by integrating several specialized robotic tools into one cohesive ecosystem. The platform includes the NewDawn Endo Series active surgical robot and the NewDawn 3D Series mobile imaging robot. It also features the NewDawn Vascular Series intelligent DSA system and the NewDawn META remote robotic surgery system.

This integrated solution requires a combination of physical AI, imaging, and robotics to link image perception with intelligent planning. The system uses master-slave force control to ensure that the robotic arm follows the specific intent of the surgeon. Real-time sensor data and intraoperative imaging create a feedback loop that supports quantitative decisions during medical procedures. Furthermore, the telesurgery system allows high-quality surgical outcomes to be reproduced across different geographic regions.

Professor Zhou, a pioneer of minimally invasive spine surgery in China, described this technological path as quantifiable, traceable, and optimizable. He explained that imaging and robotic control transform surgical maneuvers from experience-based tasks into digital processes. These digital processes can be recorded and reviewed to ensure that medical care is continuously improved over time. This shift reflects a broader trend among APEC economies that are placing more emphasis on digital health and AI-enabled care.

The industry is currently shifting its competitive focus from individual equipment breakthroughs toward the development of entire systems. This transition aims to move new technology from the exhibition floor into actual clinical practice more effectively. By combining various robotic functions, the NewDawn X platform creates a chain of active robotic execution and teleoperation. This approach allows for a more integrated method of delivering complex orthopedic care to patients.

stories.Headline: Lenovo hits record revenue as AI infrastructure demand drives growth
stories.Summary:
Lenovo Group Ltd reported record second-quarter revenue for fiscal year 2026/27, ending on September 30. The company achieved these historic results because the demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure pushed quarterly revenue past the 200 billion yuan threshold for the first time. Total revenue reached 202.9 billion yuan, which is approximately 30.2 billion dollars, representing a 47.8 percent increase year-on-year. Adjusted net income surged 166 percent to 1.4 billion dollars, while the adjusted net margin rose two percentage points to a record 4.5 percent.

The infrastructure solutions group acted as a hyper-growth engine with quarterly revenue of 76.1 billion yuan and operating profit exceeding 7 billion yuan, or 1 billion dollars. AI-related revenue surpassed 10 billion dollars, which is a 79 percent year-on-year increase and accounts for 36 percent of total group revenue. AI server revenue jumped more than 300 percent, and the AI infrastructure backlog climbed to 530 billion yuan. The company generated 1.6 billion dollars in operating cash flow and 1.2 billion dollars in free cash flow.

Chairman and CEO Yang Yuanqing stated that the company delivered an exceptional quarter and successfully transformed from a PC leader into a global full-stack compute leader. He explained that real-world AI adoption is booming and computing demand has not yet peaked as the industry shifts toward parallel training and inference. Yang noted that supply remains the main bottleneck while edge, on-device, and private-domain AI will create new demand. He believes that faster growth in higher-value segments is reshaping the profit mix and helping to mitigate industry cost pressures.

Lenovo is now increasing research and development in edge computing, AI PCs, and next-generation server cooling. The company also confirmed that its first NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 racks have completed the delivery validation process. Beyond the infrastructure sector, the PC and solutions and services businesses continued to grow steadily. The company intends to balance strong growth and higher component costs through disciplined capital expenditure and credit risk controls for large projects.

stories.Headline: Singapore integrates embodied AI and robotics into public services and industry
stories.Summary:
Singapore is integrating embodied artificial intelligence into daily life through various autonomous systems and robotics. Starting in early 2027, visitors to Sentosa will use ride-hailing apps to book self-driving minibuses for trips between hotels, attractions, and transport hubs. These eight-passenger vehicles were developed by the Guangzhou-based company WeRide through a collaboration with TADA and the Sentosa Development Corporation. Other initiatives include autonomous construction equipment at the Jurong Innovation District and delivery, cleaning, and security robots in the Punggol Digital District.

The city has also deployed specialized robots for public interaction and maintenance across several high-traffic locations. A 1.27 meter tall humanoid robot named Olly provided directions to commuters at the Little India MRT station from late August to mid-September 2026. In May 2026, a Chinese AI robot dog debuted at the Mandai Wildlife Reserve and Sentosa to tell stories and give directions in English and Chinese. Cleaning robots operate at Changi Airport, while lawn-mowing robots maintain the Singapore Botanic Gardens and autonomous robots patrol the Toa Payoh area.

The Singapore Economic Development Board reported this year that the nation now hosts more than 300 robotics companies. These organizations focus on research, manufacturing, and application development across sectors like healthcare, hospitality, logistics, and advanced manufacturing. Some of these technologies are designed to replace humans in high-risk scenarios, such as the firefighting robotic dog demonstrated on April 9, 2026. The government continues to expand these capabilities through maritime testbeds for autonomous vessels and marine drones.

stories.Headline: Japan In-House Counsel Network examines AI role in corporate risk and crisis response
stories.Summary:
The Japan In-House Counsel Network examined the expanding role of artificial intelligence in corporate risk and crisis management on November 20, 2026. This group organized a seminar in collaboration with Morrison Foerster at the law firm's Tokyo office to discuss these technologies. The event, titled From Risk to Resolution: How AI Is Helping Legal Teams Spot Risk, Resolve Disputes, and Respond to Crises, focused on modern legal tools. Partners Saqib Alam and Takahiro Nonaka led the session for the network's members.

The implementation of these tools requires a three-stage framework that involves anticipating risks, supporting crisis response, and using lessons to improve resilience. AI can change how legal teams monitor global news, litigation, regulatory developments, and supplier risks across various languages and jurisdictions. These tools connect information across different business functions to reveal how unrelated developments might create wider operational or legal exposure. This approach is especially useful during crises when critical information is scattered across public reports, internal records, and regulatory disclosures.

Partners Saqib Alam and Takahiro Nonaka were responsible for the presentation and explained that AI does not replace human legal judgment. They stated that in-house counsel must still establish escalation thresholds and determine which specific risks require action. The speakers emphasized that legal professionals are required to verify any findings generated by the AI. This ensures that the technology serves as a support system rather than a final decision maker.

stories.Headline: China and Australia plan to expand cooperation in artificial intelligence and green development
stories.Summary:
Chinese Premier Li Qiang met with Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Beijing on Friday, November 20, 2026, for the 11th China-Australia Annual Leaders' Meeting. They aimed to build a foundation for future cooperation as the two nations approach the 55th anniversary of their diplomatic relations next year. Both nations intend to develop new cooperation in emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, new energy vehicles, and green, low-carbon development.

They also seek to enhance investment liberalization and make the upcoming China-Australia Year of Tourism a success. Furthermore, the leaders want to deepen exchanges involving youth, media, think tanks, and local government areas. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese congratulated China for hosting the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen.

Albanese expressed a willingness to deepen cooperation in agriculture, energy, and the broader economy. He specifically highlighted the need to accelerate joint efforts in the digital economy and clean energy. The two countries plan to continue their communication through various international frameworks to maintain stability. stories.Headline: Fiji creates frameworks to regulate artificial intelligence in the civil service
stories.Summary:
The Fijian government began developing three key frameworks on November 20, 2026, to regulate the responsible use of artificial intelligence across the civil service. This initiative is part of a broader digital transformation agenda designed to build a digital economy and improve overall government efficiency. These efforts aim to make public services more accessible to citizens while accelerating the general digitization of various government functions. The government intends to ensure that technological innovation is supported by strict ethical standards, transparency, and accountability.

The project requires the implementation of the Fiji Civil Service AI Policy, the AI Competency Framework, and the AI Governance Framework. These instruments align with the National Digital Strategy 2025-2030, which prioritizes digital infrastructure, inclusion, and innovation-led economic growth. The strategy focuses on smart governance and digital public services to create a more integrated digital government system. This system will include a unified online services portal, stronger cybersecurity capabilities, and improved arrangements for sharing data. A government assessment identified 788 services, with 385 of those targeted for digitization by 2030.

Minister for Communications Ioane Naivalurua stated on Friday that these frameworks would establish clear guidelines for adopting AI across government institutions. He explained that the guidelines would help public servants use the technology responsibly and consistently with public expectations. The minister believes these measures will ensure that AI applications remain aligned with the primary priorities of the government. By doing so, the administration hopes to support innovation while maintaining a high level of institutional accountability.

The digital transformation drive is expected to reduce administrative costs and minimize the amount of paperwork and waiting times for citizens. These improvements are specifically intended to help people living in remote and maritime communities access government services more easily. The government will continue pursuing its goals of smart governance and digital inclusion as outlined in the national strategy. This comprehensive approach seeks to modernize the public sector and foster sustainable economic growth through advanced technology.

stories.Headline: US stocks plunge as investors sell off artificial intelligence shares
stories.Summary:
United States stocks plunged on Friday, November 20, 2026, as a deepening sell-off in artificial intelligence shares hammered technology stocks. The Nasdaq Composite Index shed 1,261.47 points, or 5.28 percent, to finish at 22,617.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93 percent, to 48,147.33, while the S&P 500 sank 265.44 points, or 3.70 percent, to 6,910.39. These losses pushed the Dow and S&P 500 into correction territory and marked the worst week for all three indexes since early April 2025.

The technology sector fell 7.11 percent and consumer discretionary dropped 3.50 percent, though consumer staples rose 0.68 percent. Bénédicte Lowe, an equity derivatives strategist at BNP Paribas, stated that no market can survive a proper unwind of the tech trade. She noted that investors were selling technology shares to determine if the general enthusiasm for artificial intelligence had finally peaked. Meanwhile, the Cboe Volatility Index spiked more than 30 percent to a 52-week high as fear grew. Walmart rose 1.52 percent following higher revenue reports and an increase in its full-year guidance.

Investors fled to government bonds, causing the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield to drop as much as 14 basis points to 4.91 percent. The University of Michigan reported that consumer sentiment rose to 51.5 in November from 48 in October, while inflation expectations fell to 3.7 percent. Market participants are now pricing in a quarter-point rate hike for the Federal Reserve meeting on December 8-9. This expectation follows October meeting minutes showing that almost all officials believe a further increase is appropriate.

stories.Headline: South Africa aims to move from hosting data centers to innovating AI technology
stories.Summary:
President Cyril Ramaphosa announced on November 20, 2026, that South Africa intends to become an active participant in the global artificial intelligence value chain. During a working visit to the United States, the president spoke at a fireside chat held at Stanford University in California. He explained that the nation wants to move beyond simply hosting data centers to participate in the actual origination and innovation of technology. This strategic shift aims to ensure that South Africa and the broader African continent help shape emerging technologies instead of just adopting foreign innovations.

This new approach requires that investments in data centers unlock broader opportunities for local researchers, innovators, and businesses. President Ramaphosa noted that global tech giants like Google and Amazon are already establishing data centers in South Africa alongside various domestic firms. He believes the country can integrate into the global ecosystem by leveraging its universities, research institutions, and skilled workforce. Furthermore, the president highlighted that recent improvements in the national electricity supply provide a critical advantage for attracting these digital infrastructure investments.

President Ramaphosa stated that deeper participation in the technology value chain could help the government tackle domestic challenges like inequality and unemployment. He emphasized the need to engage young people in the AI-driven economy while simultaneously recognizing and mitigating the potential risks. The president also called for closer ties with the South African tech diaspora to bring expertise and capital back to young entrepreneurs. He maintained that the country remains open to foreign investment as long as partners help build local capabilities and foster sector collaboration.

stories.Headline: Singapore and China pledge to deepen cooperation in artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Singapore and China launched talks to upgrade their bilateral free trade agreement on Friday, November 20, 2026. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and President Xi Jinping met at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen to discuss these ties. The leaders pledged to deepen relations between the two countries amid current global shake-ups. They also discussed how to deepen cooperation in emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence. This meeting was the third between the two leaders since Wong took office in May 2024.

The upgrade, called China-Singapore Free Trade Agreement 4.0, requires a memorandum of understanding between METI and China's Ministry of Commerce. It will cover the digital economy and government procurement to open new markets for Singapore companies. The agreement will facilitate cross-border data flows and build on the 2009 original bilateral free trade agreement. It also leverages the Suzhou Industrial Park, Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City, and the Chongqing Connectivity Initiative. These efforts follow the 2023 upgrade to an All-Round High-Quality Future-Oriented Partnership.

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said the partnership has expanded into connectivity and green development despite a complex international environment. He noted that both nations can learn from each other to help businesses innovate and raise productivity. President Xi Jinping stated that cooperation over the past few years has brought tangible benefits to both peoples. He described the two nations as friendly neighbours and key development partners during the meeting. Xi called for closer strategic communication to take the partnership to new heights.

President Xi noted that the world is undergoing profound changes with a new round of technological revolution. Prime Minister Wong urged Apec leaders to prevent the Asia-Pacific from splitting into competing economic blocs. He stated that dialogue is valuable for peace and stability during a time of heightened geopolitical tensions. Singapore companies are affected as the upgrade aims to make it easier for them to do business. Workers are also affected as the leaders discussed preparing them for future jobs.

China was Singapore's largest merchandise trading partner from 2013 to 2024 and its third-largest services partner in 2024. Bilateral merchandise trade totalled S$162.9 billion in 2025, which was 11.7 per cent of Singapore's global merchandise trade. Singapore has been China's largest source of foreign direct investment by annual flows since 2013. It is also the largest recipient in Asia of China's outward direct investment by flows. China will provide US$20 million to support the practical cooperation of Apec.

Prime Minister Wong will next travel to Beijing for a meeting and working lunch with Premier Li Qiang. He will wrap up his trip on Saturday after attending the 33rd Apec Economic Leaders' Meeting. The articles leave open the specific details of the new digital economy and government procurement rules. They do not state when the Free Trade Agreement 4.0 upgrade will be finalized. The text does not specify the exact timeline for the new artificial intelligence cooperation.

stories.Headline: OSF HealthCare CEO Michelle Conger says Pope Leo XIV's AI encyclical guides the Catholic system's AI strategy
stories.Summary:
OSF HealthCare CEO Michelle Conger spoke about Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, which focuses on artificial intelligence, at this year's OSF OnCall Digital Health Symposium, according to a newsroom post dated 20 November 2026 from Peoria, Illinois. Conger said the document gives Catholic health care organizations a chance to help shape how the rapidly evolving technology is used. She said the encyclical provides a framework for thoughtfully embracing AI while ensuring it serves patients, communities and the health care workforce. She said many people have compared the transformation that will come from AI to the industrial revolution, a time when there were questions about jobs and about who would be harmed. She said Pope Leo's message reinforces the importance of keeping people at the center of decisions about technology.

Conger said the encyclical is not an outright rejection of artificial intelligence and not an endorsement of adopting new technology without careful consideration. She said it is a call for organizations, particularly those rooted in Catholic values, to consider how AI can improve the human condition. She said OSF is already exploring applications such as ambient listening, robotics and automation to reduce administrative work. She said a significant amount of time and effort is spent in its revenue cycle to collect payments for care already provided, work she said is necessary but does not directly add value to the patient experience. She said OSF is approaching AI adoption through a governance process that considers the potential impact on both patients and employees.

Conger said the encyclical's themes include protecting human dignity and labor, addressing disinformation, educating people about AI and establishing appropriate governance. She said the message reinforces that AI must serve people and protect human dignity. She described the central themes she took away as human dignity over machines, with a person always kept at the center of the care provided or the work done. She said technology and algorithms must serve people rather than reduce them. She said the document provides a framework for OSF, as a Catholic organization, to apply the message and be a leader in doing so in a positive way to improve the health and wellbeing of patients and communities.

Conger said OSF's governance process includes its human resources team, its Mission people and its ethics people, who help it think through and make sound decisions. She said the challenge is to balance the promise of innovation with the responsibility to ensure technology remains a tool in service of people. She said she sees AI as an opportunity to free labor to do things far more rewarding than some of the work people do today, adding that OSF needs all of them. She said the shift is particularly important as health care organizations face persistent workforce shortages and growing demand for services from an aging population. She said individuals frequently struggle to determine where to go for care and how to access the services they need.

Conger said technology could help OSF better understand a person's background and circumstances when they contact the organization, making it easier to direct them to the appropriate care. She described that vision as creating a digital safety net that helps patients find the right entry point into the health care system. She connected that responsibility to OSF's broader system goals: clinical excellence, working together as One OSF and becoming the health care destination patients choose, regardless of where they enter the system. She said the goal should not simply be to do more with technology but to use it to elevate the work of caregivers, strengthen relationships and improve the health and well-being of the communities OSF HealthCare serves. She said the pope's message offers an opportunity for OSF to demonstrate how a Catholic health care organization can lead through a period of significant technological change without losing sight of its purpose.

The newsroom post was published at 17:06 PM America/Chicago on 20 November 2026 and was shared by media relations coordinator Colleen Reynolds. The post lists audio clips of Conger speaking on people being at the center of AI decision-making, technology serving people, Pope Leo providing a framework and AI freeing up Mission Partners for more meaningful work. The post also lists video clips with Conger on technology needing to serve people, people needing to be at the center of AI decision-making, Pope Leo providing a framework and freeing up employees for meaningful work. The post offers a media kit and B-roll of the Digital Health Symposium for download. The post's latest news list includes items dated 20 November 2026 from Ottawa and Peru on OSF Saint Elizabeth earning high marks for patient safety from The Leapfrog Group.

stories.Headline: Researchers use explainable AI to link plasma conditions to semiconductor etch profiles
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Jihoon Park and Seolhye Park used plasma physics-informed explainable artificial intelligence to study how plasma conditions affect etching profiles in semiconductor manufacturing, as reported by AIP.org on November 20, 2026. The team fed etch profile image data into the XAI system and analyzed how those profiles changed in relation to the plasma conditions during the experiments. They found that the mathematical index produced by the XAI can serve as an interpretable index for plasma physics, according to the article. The work was published in the Journal of Vacuum Science and Technology: A in 2026 under a title describing geometry-dependent etch-profile response in fluorocarbon-based high-aspect-ratio plasma etching.

The research addresses the difficulty of maintaining consistency and quality in plasma etching, which involves complex physics along with dynamic physical reactions and inhomogeneous chemical reactions. The authors note that these challenges grow as etching processes become more advanced and require more stringent high aspect ratio etch profiles. From their results, the researchers developed a plasma physics-informed profile-analysis framework for high aspect ratio plasma etching. This framework allows quantification of plasma-surface balance from measured etch profiles instead of relying on statistical attribution alone.

Jihoon Park said the work gave them the insight that process result image data, which had not been highlighted compared with other sensor data, could be applied to extract new information about plasma reaction properties during the process. Seolhye Park said processing plasmas are very difficult to understand because of the complexity of inhomogeneous chemical reactions, physical reactions, and numerous mechanical and electrical parts of the system. She added that finding a new source of information about the plasma reaction would have an effect similar to installing a new diagnostic tool without any hardware investment. The researchers believe their methodologies could be useful to other areas of plasma physics and diagnostics as well.

The team intends to apply their findings to understanding plasma process-driven phenomena in nuclear fusion, according to the article. The published paper lists Jihoon Park, Taejun Park, Ji-Won Kwon, Gon-Ho Kim, and Seolhye Park as its authors. The article states that the paper can be accessed through the DOI link provided in the source listing. The work was reported in a Scilight article by Mara Johnson-Groh with a DOI of its own.

stories.Headline: The New York Times Opinion section hires Jasmine Sun to cover AI and technology
stories.Summary:
The New York Times has appointed Jasmine Sun to its Opinion section, where she will cover artificial intelligence and technology, according to a report published by citybiz on November 20, 2026. Sun brings experience in Silicon Valley, product management and technology journalism to the publication. In her new role, she will lead a weekly newsletter focused on artificial intelligence and contribute to the development of editorials addressing technology and related issues. She will also participate in the publication's expanding audio and video programming and appear as an occasional guest on the relaunched Hard Fork podcast. The appointment requires Sun to contribute to Opinion Shows and extend her coverage across multiple editorial formats at the publication.

Before joining The New York Times, she worked as a product manager at Substack, the digital publishing platform that enables writers and creators to distribute newsletters and subscription-based content. During her tenure at Substack, Sun helped develop strategies supporting the platform's growth and gained firsthand experience with digital publishing, audience development and the technology industry's business models. She also co-founded Reboot, a publication focused on young technologists and their perspectives on technology, culture and the industry's broader influence. Her editorial experience also includes helping research and edit The A.G.I. Chronicles, the latest book by Kevin Roose, a technology journalist at The New York Times. Sun is a graduate of Stanford University and is based in San Francisco, placing her near the center of the Silicon Valley technology industry.

The report says her appointment comes as artificial intelligence continues to reshape the technology industry, creating demand for reporting and commentary that examines the development, commercialization and broader consequences of emerging AI systems. Her background combines direct experience working inside a technology company with independent editorial work, providing perspectives on both the business and cultural dimensions of technological change. At The New York Times Opinion, Sun will focus on artificial intelligence while contributing to broader editorial discussions about technology. Her weekly newsletter will provide a dedicated outlet for her analysis, while her involvement in Hard Fork and Opinion Shows will expand her presence across the publication's multimedia offerings. The report says her appointment adds a technology-focused writer to The New York Times Opinion team as the publication expands its coverage and commentary on artificial intelligence and the rapidly evolving technology sector.

stories.Headline: An AI stock sell-off pushes the S&P 500 down 3.7% and the Nasdaq into the red for the year
stories.Summary:
A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high. The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year.

Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt. The Dow Jones industrial average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%. Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%. The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight.

European indexes fell sharply as well. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.

“The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.” Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build-out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.

Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%. Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build-out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%. The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector.

The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value. Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO. Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period.

SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%. All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39.

The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73. While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year. The University of Michigan’s latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared with last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists’ expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections.

Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran. Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday. Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues.

Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil. Troise and Veiga write for the Associated Press. More to follow.

stories.Headline: McGill librarian Kristen Howard uses a hidden AI-generated source to teach history students critical source evaluation
stories.Summary:
Kristen Howard, the Liaison Librarian for Religious Studies, Indigenous Studies and History and Classics at McGill, created a workshop for history undergraduates that merges primary source literacy with AI literacy, with the support of Professor Elsbeth Heaman. In the workshop Howard presents a variety of sources and analyzes them with the participants, and unbeknownst to the students one of the sources is completely AI-generated, such as a diary entry by someone living in a remote location in Ontario or Quebec in the distant past, usually including a fake citation. Each time she gives the workshop Howard generates a new fake primary source, which allows her to monitor the tool's evolution, and she finds it gets better every time. So far, she said, no one has been quick to guess that the source was AI-generated, and she then reveals its true nature to address both how large language models work and how to think critically about sources regardless of their origin.

Howard said that from a historian's perspective the interesting thing about generative AI is that there have always been fakes and forgeries in the documentary record, and she cited The Awful Disclosures of Maria Monk, an 1836 book by someone who claimed to be a former nun at the Hôtel-Dieu convent in Montreal and reported shocking depravities she allegedly witnessed there after escaping to Boston. The testimony initially caused a great public outcry but was quickly contested, and today the book, published when anti-Catholic sentiment was already running high in the United States, is largely regarded as a hoax. Howard said the book is a terrible primary source for studying the life of nuns in Montreal in the 19th century but a great source for studying what people feared was taking place in Catholic convents at the time, which is part of what she calls the Spectrum of Authority, a pedagogical device she created for the workshop. The Spectrum was inspired by part of the Association of College and Research Libraries's Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education, Authority Is Constructed and Contextual, and Howard explained that it is not a binary, that there aren't sources that are true and sources that are false, and that most things are somewhere in the middle depending on the context, including the research question being asked.

Howard said she believes her role is not only to teach skills that have always been part of the history curriculum but also to prepare students to work in the world that exists now, as a historian or not. In the workshop she leads a discussion about generative AI and the ways it can be useful in historical studies or other humanities and the ways it can't, and she finds students are more willing to talk openly about AI once the conversation about primary sources has taken place. Howard has published a paper on the Spectrum of Authority in Communications in Information Literacy and turned it into an open educational resource available on the Libraries' website, and she has presented her work at various conferences. She has just completed a project with fellow librarian Sandy Hervieux testing generative AI platforms' capacities to identify relevant primary sources, and as LLMs continue to evolve she said she plans to continue to evaluate their use as research tools.

stories.Headline: Chinese investors shift capital to consumer stocks amid AI sector volatility
stories.Summary:
Investors in China began shifting their capital into beaten-down consumer stocks during November 2026 to avoid the volatility of artificial intelligence trading. This movement occurred as a significant sell-off of technology stocks created turmoil across the mainland exchanges. Many traders viewed these consumer assets as safe havens because their prices had languished during the broader economic slowdown. The shift reflects a desire to find stability while the high-growth tech sector experienced a sharp decline. The CSI index of consumer stocks rose nearly 5 per cent this month after previously gaining 2.9 per cent in October.

Meanwhile, the Star 50 index which tracks the largest AI chipmakers in China has slumped more than 40 per cent since its record high in June. This divergence shows a clear rotation of funds away from expensive technology firms toward undervalued consumer companies. These changes highlight the extreme volatility currently affecting the artificial intelligence sector compared to traditional consumer markets. The China Securities Regulatory Commission addressed the situation on Wednesday by denying online rumours about administrative interference in mutual-fund investments.

The regulator stated that it had not required fund firms to report their specific exposures to the artificial intelligence sector. According to the commission, money managers have made their own independent investment decisions while following fund mandates and relevant laws. This official statement aimed to calm the market after reports suggested the government was influencing portfolio allocations. More to follow.

stories.Summary:
Hong Kong stocks declined on Friday, November 20, 2026, pushing the benchmark gauge toward a nearly 19-month low. This downturn occurred as the debut of the AI frontier lab Anthropic in the United States failed to restore investor confidence. Market participants remained rattled by doubts regarding whether massive investments in data centers could produce comparable financial returns. These persistent jitters surrounding artificial intelligence technology contributed to a tumultuous week of swings for various stocks.

The Hang Seng Index dropped 1.9 per cent to 22,410.80, marking its lowest closing point since April 30 of the previous year. Simultaneously, the Hang Seng Tech Index slid 3.8 per cent while the chip-centric Star 50 gauge slumped 3.1 per cent. On the Chinese mainland, the CSI 300 Index sank 0.8 per cent during the same trading period. Tencent Holdings fell to its lowest level in over two years after quarterly results revealed that AI expenditures reduced earnings and eroded cash flow.

The decline in these indices complicated ongoing government efforts to establish a floor under the stocks on the Chinese mainland. The situation was exacerbated by external shocks that weighed heavily on the technology sector and broader market sentiment. Investors are now closely monitoring whether the high costs of developing artificial intelligence will eventually be offset by significant profits. stories.Headline: AINU AI launches a creation platform to standardize short video production for e-commerce marketing
stories.Summary:
AINU AI launched a one-stop creation platform in September 2026 to help short video creators. The platform aims to turn viral hit videos into a standardized production pipeline for users. It focuses on the entire workflow from topic selection to final production for e-commerce marketing. This system integrates script writing and generation into one single interface for its users. The platform has already served 540,000 merchants and 2.2 million influencers globally.

The platform uses a Global Viral Data Dashboard to aggregate real time videos from TikTok, Douyin, and Xiaohongshu. It includes data from TikTok influencers like ash tervino vs bri and popular Douyin food accounts. The Script Master tool offers 8 built-in official preset skills and supports storyboard scheme output. Video generation is powered by models including Wan 3.0, Seedance 2.0, and Seedance 2.5. The system also provides specialized templates for clothing detail images and product selling point images.

The AINU AI team consists of nearly 100 members who manage core research and development. They stated that the platform is designed to enable one person to do the work of three. The team independently controls model iteration and computing power operation and maintenance for the system. They believe the next stage of competition lies in connecting the whole process from start to finish. This approach relies on a self-built computing power server room to support large-scale delivery.

E-commerce practitioners, individual merchants, and small teams are the primary groups targeted by this tool. These users prioritize a fast assembly line over having the single best generation model. Professional creators may still prefer single-point depth, which the platform might not provide in every link. The system affects how users create content for catering, entertainment, tourism, and domestic services. It allows visitors to create secondary works based on others' content via AINU TV.

The platform was built on existing industry content production experience and a large computing infrastructure. It has achieved a total accumulated content play volume of over 500 million views. The system supports an annual AI content production capacity of nearly 2 million hours. It differs from Kling, Jimeng, and Runway by focusing on workflow rather than just model capability. These other tools focus on character movement, ecological collaboration, or professional film and television post-production.

AINU AI will continue to bet on the workflow as generation capability becomes public infrastructure. The company must manage risks if upstream model providers tighten authorization or raise their prices. It remains to be seen if the platform can compete with editing software developers. The articles do not state how the platform will scale its user base further. They leave open whether the tool can achieve industry-leading performance in every single production link.

stories.Headline: Maryland comptroller Brooke Lierman launches dashboard projecting AI job displacement
stories.Summary:
Maryland's comptroller's office launched a public dashboard tracking how artificial intelligence could reshape the state's economy, and the tracker includes a projection that Maryland faces the third-highest rate of job displacement from AI automation in the nation. The Maryland AI Economic Impact Tracker brings together data and forecasts from government agencies, universities and private-sector researchers to follow AI-related job creation, potential job losses and business adoption. The dashboard was reported on Friday, November 20, 2026, by The Baltimore Sun staff, and the comptroller's office is behind the launch. Among its most striking findings, research from Tufts University's American AI Jobs Risk Index projects that Maryland could see 7.2% of its jobs displaced by AI automation over the next two to five years under a median adoption scenario. That would be the third-highest projected rate among states, behind Massachusetts and Virginia, both at 7.3%.

The tracker is meant to give state and local leaders information to help shape policies affecting Maryland residents and businesses, according to the comptroller's office. Comptroller Brooke E. Lierman said in a statement that AI is reshaping the economy and that Maryland must meet this moment to support its workers and businesses. The dashboard combines data and forecasts from government agencies, universities and private-sector researchers, and it tracks AI-related job creation, potential job losses and business adoption. The projection of 7.2% displacement rests on Tufts University's American AI Jobs Risk Index and a median adoption scenario over the next two to five years. Massachusetts and Virginia sit just ahead of Maryland at 7.3% each in the same projection.

Lierman is the official responsible for the dashboard, and she framed it as a tool for state and local leaders rather than a final verdict on the state's economy. She said the dashboard will give those leaders information to help shape policies affecting Maryland residents and businesses. The comptroller's office described the tracker as bringing together data and forecasts from government agencies, universities and private-sector researchers. The articles do not say what policies, if any, the dashboard has already prompted or when the office will update its figures. The full story is available by visiting The Baltimore Sun website, according to the WBFF report.

stories.Headline: Chinese tech giants prioritize AI infrastructure spending over immediate profits
stories.Summary:
Chinese tech giants are facing a critical market test as AI investments reshape their cash flow. Tencent, Alibaba, and Baidu are spending heavily on infrastructure, which has shifted their financial landscapes. This trend became evident around November 19, 2026, following recent financial results. Heavy asset investment is turning operating cash flow into a source for capital expenditure. These companies are now prioritizing computing power over immediate profit amplification.

Tencent saw its share price hit HK$350.4 on November 19, a low since August 2024. Its third quarter revenue was RMB 207.3 billion, but operating cash flow fell to RMB 2.6 billion. Tencent spent RMB 81.4 billion on capital expenditure, including an RMB 86 billion advance for computing power. Alibaba reported a free cash flow outflow of RMB 34.472 billion for the quarter ended September 30. Baidu had a quarterly capital expenditure of RMB 7.35 billion and free cash flow of -RMB 4.57 billion.

Tencent CFO Lo Siu Hon said advance payments locked in GPUs for the Hunyuan Model and WorkBuddy. President Martin Lau compared this spending to building a factory for future model training. Chief Strategy Officer James Mitchell stated investment levels have roughly reached their peak for 2027. Alibaba CFO Xu Hong committed to realizing positive free cash flow as soon as possible. Baidu management explained that existing production capacity can meet much of their incremental demand.

Investors are concerned whether AI brings measurable revenue growth through cloud services or advertising. Analyst Catherine Lim noted the market will remain cautious until such growth is proven. Morgan Stanley cut Tencent's target price by nearly 13 percent to HK$480. Goldman Sachs expects Alibaba to face a funding gap through fiscal 2028. These companies are affected by higher capital costs and lower recovery efficiency than US vendors.

The industry previously relied on light assets and high cash flow to support share repurchases. Bloomberg estimates 2026 capital expenditure for leading domestic internet companies will approach US$66 billion. Morgan Stanley reports Chinese server capital expenditure is about three times higher than in the United States. Alibaba announced a three-year RMB 3800 billion AI and cloud infrastructure plan in February 2025. Baidu is developing the Kunlun Core M100 chip, expected for mass production by year end.

Tencent expects a financial turning point in 2028, while Alibaba may reach balance by fiscal 2029. Companies are using debt, such as ByteDance's US$29.6 billion loan, to secure computing power. Future profits will be eroded by depreciation as current capital commitments are transferred to assets. The articles leave open whether revenue growth will eventually exceed the growth rate of depreciation. It remains unclear if these massive investments will yield the expected commercial returns.

stories.Headline: Scholars and election officials examine how AI affects electoral integrity at a University of Ottawa workshop
stories.Summary:
On October 23rd, 2026, scholars, civil servants, election officials, and policy experts from around the globe gathered at the University of Ottawa for a one-day workshop focused on the upcoming edited volume Securing Elections in an Age of Artificial Intelligence by Michael Pal and Holly Ann Garnett. The project was supported in part by the National Cybersecurity Consortium and the Government of Canada (CSIN). The main goal of the workshop was to combine academic research and practical experience to explore how AI is impacting electoral integrity. Each panel included presentations on chapters from the volume and opportunities for academic and practitioner discussants to provide feedback on the presented research. These exchanges allowed authors to consider different perspectives, identify areas for further research, and explore how academic findings could inform practical approaches to the challenges facing election administrators and policymakers.

Four panels were held during the workshop examining various aspects of how AI can affect democratic elections. The opening panel discussed how the public and experts view the effects of AI on electoral integrity, including the increased use of AI by various actors in the electoral process and how AI-driven disinformation and persuasion tools can impact voters' capacity to make educated decisions. The second panel examined the advantages and disadvantages of Electoral Management Bodies' use of AI, addressing the hazards of depending on emerging technology while considering possible applications for increasing administrative efficiency and how EMBs are integrating AI into their operations. The third panel looked at generative AI chatbots, altered advertisements, and deepfakes of political figures in political campaigns, discussing how political actors are using generative AI in their campaign strategies and how an increase in AI use might sway public opinion. The final panel discussed the difficulties in developing efficient legal frameworks to govern the use of AI in elections, examining current regulatory strategies in various jurisdictions, concerns about deepfakes and malicious impersonation generated by AI, and the responsibilities of tech companies and other actors in the AI supply chain.

Discussion at the workshop highlighted the challenges of responding to disinformation, keeping up with rapid technological advancements, and making sure AI systems can meet the accuracy and reliability required in a "no fail" electoral environment. Participants also highlighted the difficulties of allocating blame for AI-related electoral damages and striking a balance between election integrity and the right to free speech. The wider implications of AI-driven political persuasion for democracy were considered, as well as possible regulatory solutions. Overall, the workshop offered participants the opportunity to further their knowledge and research on AI and democratic elections, and the chapters presented at the workshop are currently being developed into an edited volume on the topic.
