stories.Headline: Review authors link AI tools to supply chain resilience through agility and governance
stories.Summary:
A structured narrative synthesis of 75 studies published between 2015 and 2025 was published in Discover Artificial Intelligence. Adel Aazami, Amirhossein Hassani, Nadun Karunarathna, and Sebastian Kummer conducted the review. It examined how artificial intelligence can enhance supply chain resilience. The synthesis covered predictive analytics, machine learning, deep learning, digital twins, and robotic process automation. The review linked these tools to operational risk management.

The review covered literature published from January 2015 through December 2025. Database searches were executed through January 2026 across Emerald, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. The query combined three Boolean concept clusters covering supply chain contexts, artificial intelligence technologies, and resilience outcomes. The authors disclaimed compliance with PRISMA 2020 reporting standards because intermediate retrieval counts, database-specific search logs, screener counts, and inter-rater agreement statistics were not archived. Critical appraisal followed a qualitative, Joanna Briggs Institute-informed framework evaluating objective clarity, methodological adequacy, evidence validity, analytical transparency, and alignment between data and conclusions.

The authors assigned qualitative evidence weights of High, Medium, Low, and Limited support rather than numerical scores. They stated that artificial intelligence represents an enabling capability rather than a standalone operational remedy. They concluded that realized supply chain resilience depends on continuous co-evolution between technical capabilities, dynamic sensing and seizing routines, and verifiable institutional governance structures. They advised managers to sequence digital investments by establishing data quality, integration pipelines, and workforce analytics literacy before acquiring advanced predictive algorithms. They encouraged industry consortia and policymakers to develop standardized transparency protocols and secure data-pooling frameworks.

The synthesis found that research rose from fewer than 10 publications per year between 2015 and 2018 to more than 40 publications annually between 2023 and 2025. Research concentrated on demand forecasting and inventory management, while empirical investigations of supplier relationship management and deep-tier supplier vulnerabilities remained underrepresented. Conceptual frameworks, model-driven proposals, and simulation-based studies dominated the corpus, while longitudinal investigations and cross-industry empirical evaluations in live operational environments remained scarce. The authors noted that model opacity and black-box algorithms provoke algorithmic overrides during high-stakes crises. They also noted that disruptive crises are rare and poorly documented, generating a cold-start training problem that degrades algorithmic reliability.

Global logistics networks connect suppliers, manufacturing facilities, and consumer markets through cross-border flows of materials, capital, and data. Lean inventory and Just-in-Time principles removed safety stocks, backup sourcing channels, and redundant capacity across lower operational tiers. Modern networks face compounded shocks including the COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical conflicts, and extreme climate events. Traditional risk management relied on historical probability distributions and static redundancy buffers. Many enterprise networks lack end-to-end visibility across lower supplier tiers.

The synthesis developed an organizing conversion architecture uniting the Resource-Based View, dynamic capabilities theory, and institutional governance frameworks. Agility and adaptability operate as intermediate organizational pathways converting technological inputs into realized resilience. Digital readiness and governance maturity function as independently necessary boundary conditions. Explainable artificial intelligence functions as an operational requirement providing local decision rationales alongside global feature priorities. The articles leave open the intermediate retrieval counts, database-specific search logs, screener counts, and inter-rater agreement statistics.

stories.Headline: Algerian professor Fayçal Djeridane presents AI cancer screening project with Laghouat as potential pilot region
stories.Summary:
Professor Fayçal Djeridane presented the prospects of an ambitious AI-assisted cancer screening project at the 1st National Forum of Oncology Experts, held on November 5, 6, 2026, at the Chahid Mohamed Rezoug Cancer Center (CLCC) in Laghouat, Algeria. The forum gave particular attention to the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence in developing predictive and adaptive oncology during its scientific discussions. Djeridane is an internationally recognized Algerian expert in artificial intelligence and medical imaging and a member of the High Council of the National Scientific Community Abroad. His presentation highlighted the potential of emerging technologies in cancer screening and introduced the prospects of the project. The province of Laghouat could be selected as a pilot region for the AI-assisted cancer screening project.

The project would require defining the targeted cancers and eligible populations and establishing clearly structured screening pathways. It would require ensuring the availability of appropriate diagnostic infrastructure and training healthcare professionals. It would require validating algorithms in the Algerian population and protecting and securing medical data. It would require regularly evaluating diagnostic performance and project outcomes. The article was published on OncoDaily on November 20, 2026, and was authored by Abderrahim Djellaoui, MD, an Assistant Professor in Medical Oncology in Laghouat, Algeria, and medically reviewed by Vahe Grigoryan, MD, Editorial Director.

The article states that the aim is not to replace the expertise of radiologists or oncologists but to provide them with complementary tools. It states that a model designed using data from other countries does not necessarily guarantee the same level of performance in the Algerian population. It states that local validation is therefore a fundamental step before any large-scale implementation. It states that the approach requires close collaboration between oncologists, radiologists, biologists, epidemiologists, engineers, and data scientists. It states that artificial intelligence alone cannot solve all the challenges of cancer screening.

The article states that screening programs face challenges including the growing volume of medical imaging examinations, the availability of specialists, reporting delays, variability in diagnostic performance, and geographical inequalities in access to healthcare. It states that AI could offer applications including AI-assisted identification of suspicious lesions and improved analysis of mammograms and other medical imaging examinations. It states that applications also include characterization of certain radiological abnormalities, standardization and optimization of image interpretation, and support in identifying patients who require further diagnostic investigations. It states that the involvement of the Laghouat Cancer Center and its oncology team provides a particularly relevant clinical environment to support the initiative. It states that the project highlights the importance of collaboration between scientific experts, specialists in emerging technologies, and healthcare professionals.

The article states that cancer remains one of the major public health challenges worldwide and that early detection remains one of the key factors in improving patient outcomes and reducing cancer-related mortality. It states that AI is progressively emerging as a promising technology with the potential to transform medical practice, particularly in medical imaging, screening, risk assessment, and clinical decision support. It states that Algeria is also embracing this wave of innovation. It states that predictive oncology involves integrating clinical, biological, histopathological, molecular, and radiological data to better understand cancer behavior. It states that the combined analysis of these data could eventually help identify profiles associated with an increased risk of cancer, improve prognostic assessment, and contribute to predicting treatment response.

The article states that the potential selection of Laghouat as a pilot region opens up interesting prospects for exploring the integration of these emerging technologies into the Algerian healthcare system. It states that the Laghouat pilot project could provide an opportunity to develop a national experience in evaluating artificial intelligence tools applied to cancer screening. It states that such cooperation could also encourage the emergence of national research projects and contribute to strengthening Algeria's scientific expertise. It states that the transformation must be part of a structured strategy based on clear clinical objectives including improving access to screening, reducing diagnostic delays, addressing geographical inequalities, and improving patient outcomes. The article does not state whether the project has been approved, funded, or scheduled.

stories.Headline: Gallup finds frequent AI users report no change in meeting time
stories.Summary:
Gallup surveyed 21,648 U.S. employees and found that among the 32% of respondents who use artificial intelligence a few times a week or more, most reported no savings in meeting time. In that group of frequent users, 52% said they spend less time gathering information and 47% said they spend less time writing. But 83% said their time in meetings has not changed, and 78% reported no change in the time they spend collaborating with coworkers. The survey also found that 82% of frequent AI users spend about the same amount of time working with customers or clients.

The results suggest that while artificial intelligence speeds up some tasks, other parts of workplace life may be essentially AI-proof, and meeting time is the clearest example. A 2024 survey by the scheduling platform Reclaim.ai found that employees spend nearly 15 hours a week in meetings on average, which is roughly 37% of a standard workweek. Nearly two-thirds of frequent AI users, or 65%, said their roles require about the same mental effort as before, while 21% reported expending less mental effort and 14% said their work has become even more demanding. Among frequent users, 21% said they now spend more time reviewing and correcting work, and the same percentage reported spending more time learning new skills and tools.

Among employees at organizations that have adopted AI, just 29% told Gallup the technology has raised expectations for how much work they should complete in a day. Frequent AI users are more likely to feel pressure, however, since 36% said AI has raised expectations for their output and 33% said they felt pressure to use the technology to keep up. The survey's results suggest that AI is replacing routine tasks while creating new responsibilities, which may explain why even frequent users find their jobs have not gotten easier overall. Although meeting time has dropped from its pandemic-era peak, studies show that meetings still eat up an extraordinary amount of the typical worker's schedule.

stories.Headline: Anthropic launches the largest initial public offering in history on the Nasdaq
stories.Summary:
Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT on November 19 US time. This event set the record for the largest initial public offering in global history. Founder and CEO Dario Amodei led the company through this process. The company was founded less than six years ago.

The offering price was set at 83 dollars per share the day before going public. Shares issued increased from 825 million to 980 million, totaling 813.4 billion US dollars. This resulted in a fully diluted valuation of approximately 1.5 trillion US dollars. The company's prospectus shows steep revenue growth and astronomical computing power infrastructure commitments.

Dario Amodei is the 43-year-old founder and CEO who leads the company. He warned in an article that AI is becoming powerful at an unprecedented speed. Amodei stated that humanity's ability to control these systems may have fallen behind. He believes machines might one day surpass humans in almost all tasks.

The market is scrutinizing the company and waiting for its next moves. Amodei previously clashed with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman over security guarantees and organizational governance. He had requested that the security team have veto power over new product releases. These negotiations failed, leading Amodei and six colleagues to leave OpenAI in December 2020.

Amodei previously worked at Baidu on speech recognition with Andrew Ng's team in 2014. He co-authored the January 23, 2020, paper on Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models. He also led the GPT-3 project, which launched on May 28, 2020, with 175 billion parameters. His research focus shifted after his father, Ricardo, died from hepatitis C in 2006.

Amodei now calls for setting speed limits for the progress of artificial intelligence. He continues to focus on the challenges of software and performance engineering. The articles do not state the specific future products Anthropic will release. They leave open how the company will manage its massive infrastructure costs. They do not specify the current status of the security veto debate.

stories.Headline: PAHO publishes guidance on reinforcement learning in health AI
stories.Summary:
The Pan American Health Organization presented a new publication on 20 November 2026 in Washington, D.C., titled "Reinforcement Learning in Artificial Intelligence for Health: Opportunities, Risks, and Implications for Policy and Practice," which examines the opportunities, risks, and implications of reinforcement learning in artificial intelligence for health systems. The document provides guidance for policymakers, health authorities, technical teams, and health professionals so that they can better understand the potential of this technology and promote its responsible implementation. Reinforcement learning represents a step forward toward AI systems capable of supporting decisions that evolve over time, because it enables the identification and adjustment of strategies based on feedback from previous decisions. In health systems, where clinical and public health decisions are often part of continuous processes, this capability opens up new possibilities for improving care and operations.

The publication states that this approach can help optimize treatment sequences, support the care of people living with chronic conditions, improve the allocation of health resources, and develop public health interventions that adapt to changing epidemiological and operational conditions. It highlights that the potential of these technologies depends not only on their technical capabilities but also on the institutional conditions that support their implementation. One of the main challenges is preventing these systems from reproducing or amplifying inequalities embedded in historical data, and their adaptive nature means they require validation, monitoring, and continuous evaluation mechanisms to identify potential risks to safety, equity, and quality of care. The document emphasizes the importance of high-quality data, interoperable digital infrastructure, appropriate governance frameworks, and technical and institutional capacities.

The publication also underscores that human oversight must remain an essential component, ensuring that AI-generated recommendations strengthen, rather than replace, the judgment of health professionals and decision-makers. This approach aims to foster innovation without compromising patient safety, equity, or the protection of fundamental rights. The publication is part of PAHO's ongoing efforts to advance the digital transformation of the health sector in the Americas and to promote the development and use of safe, equitable, and people-centered artificial intelligence technologies. PAHO offers the full publication for download in English and invites interested readers to subscribe to a mailing list for updates on publications, activities, and resources related to artificial intelligence and digital health.

stories.Headline: Jeff Bezos co-leads Prometheus to build an AI engineer for physical design
stories.Summary:
On November 17, 2026, at the Semafor "Silicon Valley and the World" Summit in Menlo Park, California, Jeff Bezos appeared jointly with physicist Vik Bajaj. Bezos is now co-founder and co-CEO of the AI startup Prometheus. It is the first time he has returned to a CEO role since handing over Amazon in 2021. Bezos invested in the project at its seed stage at the end of 2024. He said on stage that the project is advancing so fast he "could not just sit on the sidelines and watch".

Prometheus has about 250 employees and has raised approximately 14.5 billion US dollars in total capital. Its valuation has soared to 41 billion US dollars. The company disclosed a 6.2 billion dollar first round in November 2025 and a 12 billion dollar round in June 2026. It was incubated at the Foresite Labs incubator in 2024 under the early code name FL2024-008 INC. Shareholders include JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, DST Global and ARCH Venture Partners.

Bezos denied that Prometheus is building humanoid robots or chat-focused large language models. He said the goal is an "Artificial General Engineer", abbreviated AGE. He said, "You can't learn engineering just by reading." He said locking six top physicists including Newton, Einstein and Maxwell in a room to build a toaster would likely leave them at a complete loss. Bajaj, a former Google X core executive and Stanford University School of Medicine professor, said specialized division of labor is already inevitable even in pure language models.

Bezos said Prometheus's system can finish analog chip, radio equipment or valve designs that take an engineering team of 10 to 20 people 6 to 9 months in 12 hours. Blue Origin has privately tested the tool on two projects. An engineer who worked on the Mars Helicopter at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory used one prompt to redesign it, and the model converged to a coaxial counter-rotating configuration highly similar to the real craft. Bezos said of proprietary enterprise data, "never share it, and strictly prevent it from leaking out".

Bajaj said Prometheus uses its self-developed multi-physics field simulation system to generate high-quality synthetic data. The company leased a plant of about 9,300 square meters in the former American Steel Industrial Park in West Oakland, California in August 2026. It has offices in San Francisco, London and Zurich. Kyle Kosic, co-founder of xAI, joined in early 2026 to lead computing power infrastructure. In November 2025 Prometheus acquired General Agents, an agent AI lab co-founded by Sherjil Ozair.

Bezos said the global physical manufacturing industry is worth tens of trillions of US dollars and "it is impossible to build a walled garden here". He said Prometheus will invest directly in some traditional enterprises empowered by its tools. Asked about merging Amazon, Blue Origin and Prometheus, he said, "That's a funny idea, there is nothing to announce". Amazon invested an additional 25 billion US dollars in Anthropic in April 2026 in exchange for a 1 trillion US dollar cloud spending commitment.

stories.Headline: Louisville Public Media CEO Kenya Young says staff review all AI use and journalists write its stories
stories.Summary:
Louisville Public Media published a statement of its practices on artificial intelligence on November 20, 2026, and its President and CEO, Kenya Young, issued a message the same day explaining how the organization uses AI and how it does not. Young said LPM had been watching the technology closely and planning for the changing landscape, and that AI is part of the organization's new three-year strategic plan under its priority of Digital Transformation and Adaptability. The plan says LPM will adopt AI tools with clear ethical standards that increase efficiency and responsiveness, freeing staff capacity for higher-value work. Young said LPM is in the beginning stages of adapting to AI and is exploring, experimenting and in some cases already using AI tools for work behind the scenes. Young said the tools are used for tasks such as transcription, research and data analysis, and that anything LPM uses AI for is reviewed and checked by a person.

She said LPM does not use AI to write its stories, that its journalists source stories, conduct interviews and write the news, and that this will not change. She said LPM does not use AI to choose the music listeners hear, does not play AI-generated music on air, and will not use AI to replicate anyone's voice or to alter real audio, photos or video. Young said hosts and music staff decide what plays on WFPK and WUOL, and that staff own the final result of whatever AI helps with. Young said technology companies, including AI companies, have invested heavily in journalism and media in recent years, and that LPM has received support from some of them, including the Google News Initiative and the OpenAI Foundation's People-First AI Fund. She said the organization's ethics and independence policy states there is no connection between its funding and editorial decisions, and that donors have no direct access to the newsroom, programming or those who make content decisions.

She said that holds for technology companies too, and that their support comes with no influence over what news LPM covers or what music it plays and no commitment to any company's products. Young said media companies across the country are cutting staff, and some have tied those cuts directly to their increased use of AI, while data centers are going up in communities, particularly in Kentucky. She said AI is undoubtedly changing how people work and navigate their days, and that a generation ago the internet changed the media landscape, in some ways for the better and in others for the worse. She said LPM will keep innovating, experimenting and evolving, guided by its standards and ethics, and that the most important theme in its strategic plan is trust. She said trust has to be earned every day, with every concerto on WUOL, every new artist on WFPK and every local story on WFPL.

stories.Headline: California political candidates use AI to create fake images for election advertising
stories.Summary:
Political candidates used artificial intelligence to create fake images for election advertising in California. These campaigns used the technology to stand out on the air and online. Many of these ads appeared during the current election year. Some candidates depicted themselves as heroic figures or fought massive robots. Other images showed candidates kowtowing to rich fat cats and bloodthirsty crowds.

Researchers at the Wesleyan Media Project found campaigns spent over 137 million dollars on AI ads by mid-October. Republican groups accounted for about 80 percent of those messages. Steve Hilton appeared as a gladiator with Xavier Becerra and Gavin Newsom in a coliseum. Spencer Pratt depicted himself as Batman, while a San Diego school board candidate used a fake bake sale. These ads appeared on platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and X.

Ramesh Srinivasan is a UCLA professor of information studies who hosts the Utopias podcast. He said AI can now automatically create content that targets voters based on their psychology. Srinivasan stated that people lack disclosure regarding when content is AI generated. He believes this is pernicious because it removes a common basis of reality. He is working with the U.S. Congress and state Senate to require watermarks.

A female school board candidate in San Diego called an AI image of her sexist. Srinivasan noted that the president used AI to show himself healing a patient resembling Jon Stewart. He said voters cannot always tell the difference between AI and human created content. This lack of distinction may influence whether people vote or for whom they vote. He believes this is a problem for a functioning democracy.

The articles mention the Cambridge Analytica story from the last 10 years regarding psychological targeting. That organization used data brokers and credit card records to influence people. Srinivasan noted that Big Tech companies may have censored content during the Biden administration. He mentioned that these companies seemed to bend the knee at the inauguration. He argues that technology should expand human abilities rather than replace them.

Srinivasan wants to rein in AI companies to ensure they pay people for their data. He believes regulation can direct innovation to accompany social and economic progress. The articles leave open whether a leader will emerge to protect democracy in 2028. It remains unclear if platforms will adhere to basic standards of disclosure. The future of collective governance depends on whether people share a common reality.

stories.Headline: DeepSeek introduces usage limits to manage high computing costs and server stability
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek introduced usage limits for its AI services in November 2026 to manage high costs. This decision affected users who relied on the platform for companionship, consulting, and psychological healing. Many heavy users expressed distress over the potential loss of their extensive chat histories. Some people spent more than ten hours a day interacting with the AI. These users now face a shift away from unlimited free access.

The new rules stop the resumption of inactive conversations older than seven days. Single inputs are now compressed to a limit of about 40,000 words. A daily usage cap now triggers a server busy prompt when quotas are exhausted. These changes target the App and web versions used by ordinary people. The platform aims to recover HBM memory occupied by idle sessions.

DeepSeek has not issued a direct statement, but reports suggest this was a last resort. The company faced multiple service failures, including slow responses and high generation delays. Technical logic shows that long conversations accumulate KV cache in GPU memory. This resource mismatch caused queuing and stuttering during periods of peak traffic. Reallocating memory helps the platform serve active users more efficiently.

Heavy users feel these limits acutely because their deep contexts step on the quota edge. Some affected individuals have started charging fees to help others connect to the API. Many users are now actively asking DeepSeek to implement reasonable payment options. They want to pay for higher computing power priority and longer conversations. These users view the limits as a unilateral relationship downgrade.

Computing power costs have risen, with H100 contract prices increasing 65 percent by October 2026. In the first quarter of 2026, over 300 small AI companies ceased operations. Seed round financing in the domestic AI sector fell 11 percent year on year. Pure API startups struggled because they lacked computing power stockpiles or traffic ecosystems. This environment makes the old premise of infinite capital subsidies unsustainable.

Doubao now uses a layered structure where heavy functions require payment to cover free ones. OpenAI launched ChatGPT Ads on August 31, 2026, reaching a 1 billion dollar revenue run rate. The industry is shifting from a scale first strategy to a unit economic model. It remains unknown if small platforms can replicate the advertising success of OpenAI. The articles leave open how DeepSeek will retain users after these limits.

stories.Headline: Meta AI funds LSU project that uses color-coded alerts to monitor infants breathing through artificial airways
stories.Summary:
Meta AI partnered with the LSU system on November 20, 2026, to launch five projects aimed at solving various healthcare challenges. One specific initiative called Eyes-On focuses on assisting infants who rely on artificial airways to breathe. This project functions as a specialized baby monitor for infants with complex or technology-dependent medical problems. The system uses a color-coded alert process to notify medical staff about the status of the airway tubes.

The project requires a total of 80,000 dollars in funding provided by Meta AI to operate. A green light indicates the tube is correctly in place, while orange means the system is uncertain. A red light triggers an alarm to warn staff that the tube has come out. The ultimate goal of the Eyes-On project is to keep babies healthy until they can breathe independently.

Michael Dunham, the Head of Pediatric Otolaryngology at the LSU School of Health, is responsible for the project. He stated that artificial intelligence should not be relied upon to perform these medical tasks entirely. Dunham believes humans must evaluate the input data and make the final decisions based on the AI output. He argued that keeping humans integrated ensures the foundation of healthcare remains people taking care of other people.

stories.Headline: Online literature platforms crack down on AI generated content to protect human creators
stories.Summary:
A viral statement calling for a one day pause on AI updates earned 43,000 likes on November 20, 2026. This movement reflects a deep divide between the short drama industry and the online literature circle. While short dramas embrace the technology, literature platforms are actively fighting against AI generated content. Multiple purges of AI texts have occurred throughout the current year. These actions aim to protect original creators from being replaced by automated systems.

Tomato targeted low quality AI content in February and May of this year. Qidian banned AI written texts in July and processed hundreds of novels in August. On October 30, Qidian and QQ Reading announced further crackdowns on AI abuse in contracted works. These platforms will now cancel welfare benefits for authors who use AI. These rules apply to works with over ten thousand paid subscribers on the Qidian platform.

Platform editors and administrators are responsible for these governance rounds to stop AI abuse. They state that AI generated works are often not good to read. Officials argue that substantial cash rewards are flowing to the wrong recipients. They believe AI books seize benefits that should belong to original human creators. Platforms want to ensure that paid readers are not paying for machine generated words.

Readers complain that works on the leaderboards are still written by AI. Nigerian writer Jerry Adedayo Farad lost a 2 million US dollar deal for his novel. Publishers now avoid novels suspected of being AI generated to protect their investments. Some penalized authors claim they only used AI for grammar and polishing. These creators feel wronged because they wrote the original manuscripts manually.

High output was once a core competition threshold for online literature authors. Top creators like Tangjiasanshao and Mai Bao Xiao Lang Jun updated 8,000 words daily. Qidian previously required 4,000 words for VIP attendance bonuses, while Jinjiang required 3,000. One Qidian author averaged 20,000 words daily using the Doubao large language model. This high volume removed the competitive edge previously held by manual writers.

Qidian uses an AI detection tool called Motong to identify machine written texts. A Nature study showed humans only identify AI poems with 46.6 percent accuracy. Research in Science Advances suggests AI makes stories similar, reducing collective creativity. Another study found AI polishing decreases writing complexity by 21 to 50 percent. The articles leave open whether AI detection tools are truly reliable for platforms.

stories.Headline: Dira wins $10,000 education prize at African Agentic AI Design Challenge in Nairobi
stories.Summary:
The Kenyan education technology startup Dira won the US$10,000 Education track prize at the African Agentic AI Design Challenge on November 20, 2026. This announcement occurred during a closed-door side event held alongside the Model Context Protocol Dev Summit Nairobi, which took place from November 19 to 20 at the Hyatt Regency Nairobi Westlands. Founded by Michelle Gati, Jacinta Wanjiru, and Irene Mukii, the startup developed an AI assistant that helps teachers identify students needing extra support. The tool converts spoken observations from educators into structured records known as Evidence Cards to reduce manual record-keeping.

The competition also awarded US$8,000 to first runner-up Marga AI and US$6,000 to second runner-up TALO, which was created by university students aged 21 and 22. All three winning teams received computing credits to help cover their initial hosting and model-inference costs. This event highlighted the Model Context Protocol as a standard for linking AI agents to external tools and institutional workflows. Such technical gatherings in Nairobi aim to integrate African engineers into global conversations typically dominated by Asia, Europe, and North America.

The Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy launched the Kenya National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 to 2030 on March 27, 2025, with a reported KSh 152 billion budget. However, legislative progress has stalled, as a Senate committee in October 2026 recommended against the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026, sponsored by Senator Karen Nyamu. That proposed bill would have created an AI Commissioner with the power to levy fines of KSh 5 million or impose two years of imprisonment. Organizers have not yet disclosed the judging rubric or how the voice-driven data is encrypted and stored.

The success of Dira will depend on whether the prize money and credits can lead to sustained pilots within school budgets. While the national strategy is in place, the lack of a dedicated regulator leaves startups to navigate general data-protection obligations on their own. Future adoption of these agentic tools requires reliable institutional procurement and comprehensive teacher training. It remains unclear if these early experiments will move from hackathon validation into everyday Kenyan classrooms.

stories.Headline: Anthropic faces a compute shortage after its IPO as it races for GPUs to train Claude models
stories.Summary:
Anthropic recently completed a high profile initial public offering that attracted significant retail investor demand. The company now faces a critical shortage of computing power needed to train its Claude AI models. This infrastructure crisis emerged as the company transitioned from its private status to the public market. The compute crunch threatens the company's ability to serve millions of users and develop new models. This operational risk follows a period of intense market enthusiasm for the AI maker.

The IPO priced shares at 83 dollars, but they popped 17 percent to reach 97.17 dollars. This surge helped the company reach a valuation of nearly 2 trillion dollars. Anthropic secured a 26 billion dollar private placement with Google, Nvidia, and AMD before its debut. The company expects a compute bill of 895 billion dollars over the next several years. It currently utilizes Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and its own managed infrastructure.

Industry analysts state that compute access is the biggest operational risk hanging over the business. They suggest the company may need to design its own AI accelerators to reduce Nvidia dependence. These experts note that custom silicon would require massive capital and years of development. Some analysts believe this is the only path to guaranteed long term compute access. They argue that the current bottleneck is getting worse as every AI lab races for GPUs.

Institutional investors remain cautious because Anthropic depends on resources it does not fully control. Claude users could face service interruptions or slowdowns if the company cannot provision enough inference compute. This dependency could cause Anthropic to fall behind rivals like OpenAI and Google in AI supremacy. OpenAI benefits from a 10 billion dollar Microsoft Azure partnership, while Google owns its own data centers. These competitors have more dedicated compute pipelines than Anthropic's complex multi cloud strategy.

Training large language models requires thousands of high end GPUs running for weeks or months. Nvidia is sold out of H100 and H200 chips months in advance, and AMD struggles to scale. The AI industry is currently a zero sum game for limited silicon, power, and data center capacity. Anthropic's multi cloud approach provides redundancy but adds complexity and potentially higher costs. The company's success depends on outbidding or out partnering rivals for this scarce hardware.

Anthropic will use its IPO capital to lock in long term compute commitments and fund development. The company must now prove it can solve these hard infrastructure challenges to justify its valuation. It remains unclear if the company will successfully transition to developing its own custom AI chips. The articles do not state when the company will secure enough GPUs for next generation models. Future investor scrutiny will intensify every quarter that a guaranteed compute path remains missing.

stories.Headline: US and Singapore authorities investigate Megaspeed International over AI chip trade
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Commerce and Singapore Police Force investigated Megaspeed International for its AI chip trade. This company, formerly 7 Road International, grew rapidly into a high-profile player in the NVIDIA supply chain. Investigations peaked in June 2025 with raids on the company's business site in Singapore. Investigators questioned the then CEO, Huang Le, regarding the destination of advanced chips. The probe spanned the United States, Singapore, and Malaysia.

Megaspeed shifted to cloud computing in 2023 and joined the NVIDIA Cloud Partner ecosystem. From May 2024 to February 2026, related businesses imported NVIDIA products worth 4.13 billion U.S. dollars. In November 2025, it imported 17,454 GB300 units worth approximately 787 million U.S. dollars. Total NVIDIA hardware imports reached 4.6 billion U.S. dollars and 136,000 GPUs by November 2025. Assets grew from 32.9 million U.S. dollars in 2023 to nearly 3 billion U.S. dollars in 2024.

The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security checked if chips reached restricted end users. Singapore Police investigated false declarations and whether equipment was shipped to undeclared locations. Huang Le provided inaccurate information to downplay her role and received a stern warning. She had her passport confiscated and was later barred from re-entering Singapore. The Singapore Police sought limited support from the FBI and server supplier Supermicro.

Clients used remote access to obtain computing power without owning chips or building computer rooms. Some users flew 80TB of training data on hard drives to Malaysia to rent servers. The Malaysian government now requires a strategic trade license for U.S. high-performance AI chips. This regulation, announced July 14, 2025, focuses on whether chips flow to other destinations. The business model affected brokers who converted hardware into rentable cloud computing power.

Megaspeed began as a gaming firm focused on overseas game distribution and operation. It utilized Malaysia's abundant land and power resources, especially in the state of Johor. The company posted a post-tax loss of 20 million U.S. dollars in 2024. High upfront costs included GPU procurement, data center leasing, and electricity prepayments. This growth occurred during a global GPU shortage and rapid Southeast Asian data center expansion.

The investigation into Megaspeed and six other related individuals is still ongoing. A gap of 50,000 chips exists between NVIDIA's government reports and external trade records. NVIDIA claimed this discrepancy resulted from equipment in other warehouses not previously counted. It remains unclear if the company violated specific export control requirements. The articles leave the final legal status of the company open.

stories.Headline: AI power systems integrate lighting and industrial electronics to meet rising data center energy demands
stories.Summary:
Modern AI power supply systems emerged from a mixed evolution of lighting, automotive, and industrial electronics capabilities. This technological convergence happened as AI chip power consumption and cabinet power density rose to megawatt levels. The process integrates gallium nitride, silicon carbide, and silicon based power technologies into computing infrastructure. These older industrial capabilities became important again to meet the massive power demands of AI data centers. This evolution allows for more GPUs to be deployed in the same computer room space.

The system requires rectification, backup power, and multi-level DC conversion to deliver power to GPUs. Google released a plus or minus 400V DC solution for 1MW cabinets in 2025. NVIDIA promoted an 800V high-voltage DC architecture in 2026 with Google, Microsoft, and the Open Compute Project. Texas Instruments estimates that 48V architectures for 1MW cabinets would require nearly 200 kg of copper. Higher voltages like 800V reduce current from 20833 amperes to about 1250 amperes to lower resistance loss.

Texas Instruments launched high-density power devices integrating 650V gallium nitride power transistors in 2025. Infineon released a high-voltage intermediate bus conversion reference design based on 650V gallium nitride in 2026. Innoscience cooperates with NVIDIA to promote 800V DC AI data center power supplies. These companies aim to reduce copper loss and space burdens caused by large currents. They use different materials to divide work based on voltages, power densities, and switching frequencies.

AI data center operators and GPU manufacturers are affected by these power supply architecture changes. Gallium nitride is used for high-frequency and high-power density conversion links in these systems. Silicon carbide provides advantages in high power and voltage resistance for the infrastructure. Silicon remains necessary for low-cost control, protection, and power management functions. These materials ensure that input power is effectively delivered to the chips without excessive heat.

Gallium nitride technology grew from the semiconductor lighting industry and the development of blue LEDs. Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano, and Shuji Nakamura won the 2014 Nobel Prize for their early achievements. Japan invested 550 million yen between 1987 and 1990 to commercialize blue LEDs through Toyoda Gosei. China launched the National Semiconductor Lighting Project in June 2003 to expand this industrial scale. China's semiconductor lighting industry grew from 90 billion yuan in 2003 to 4.245 trillion yuan by 2015.

Jingcan Semiconductor enabled the production of 12-inch gallium nitride wafers in China as early as 2021. Shanghai New Micro Semiconductor is building a gallium nitride power foundry platform for various voltages. Shenzhen Pinghu Laboratory provides a public pilot platform for 8-inch silicon carbide and gallium nitride chips. The articles leave open how these global technology competitions will evolve between China, the US, and Japan. Future developments will determine how these materials further integrate into the global AI power chain.

stories.Headline: Shanghai AI Laboratory releases Sage S2.1 Flash science multimodal agent
stories.Summary:
The Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory released Sage S2.1 Flash on November 16, 2026. This science multimodal agent combines tool use, coding, and search with instrument and molecular inputs. The lab published a benchmark table comparing it to Claude Opus, GPT-5.6 Sol, Qwen, and GLM. Weights for the model are available on Hugging Face under the InternLM organization. It is a full-stack science agent SKU designed for automating notebook-style machine learning engineering.

The 320B MoE model requires FP8 builds or full precision shards for hosting. It unifies ten scientific modalities, including crystal structures, molecular graphs, and protein or nucleic acid sequences. It also ingests light curves, ECG, EEG, spectra, mass spectrometry, and X-ray diffraction. The model uses a shared agent harness for tool-use and search after modality encoders. Demos show the agent using CAD, QGIS, Blender, and 3D Slicer for scientific workflows.

The Shanghai AI Laboratory claims the model is a single-model story rather than a chain. They report a 90.3 score on MLE-bench Lite and 72.2 on OfficeQA Pro. The lab states the model achieved 37.1 on SpreadsheetBench 2 and 25.0 on Harvey LAB. They report a 60.6 on SWE-bench Pro and 87.9 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The lab frames the agent as a tool for multi-step workflows with visual feedback.

Third-party commentators noted that weights appeared on Hugging Face before the official marketing site launched. ML engineers are affected by the model's positioning for automating machine learning engineering tasks. Finance and operations teams may use the SpreadsheetBench 2 and Workspace-Bench productivity capabilities. Users in regulated industries must align usage with institutional IRB and export rules. Some reports mention promotional API pricing relative to GLM-5.3-Flash through early December 2026.

The lab's release follows an open-weight push similar to DeepSeek usage limits and Alibaba Qwen4 Max. Science agents intersect with biosafety and export debates, including DHS DeepSeek removal orders. Western labs have released different science agents, such as Periodic Labs Neon and Nvidia Nemotron. Terminal-Bench-Science previously showed that leading Western agents had sub-30% resolution on real research tasks. The model's design mimics how graduate students work across various tools in one afternoon.

Users should now confirm licenses, VRAM needs, and data residency rules for their jurisdictions. Teams are encouraged to run private benchmarks on their own instrument suites for verification. The articles leave open whether the vendor-reported benchmarks will be matched by independent harness logs. It remains unclear if the promotional API pricing will be maintained after December. The actual reliability of the agent depends on governed chat patterns and MCP hygiene.

Ant Digital Technologies and JB Financial Group signed a memorandum of understanding on November 18, 2026. This partnership occurred during the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 to explore AI powered innovation. The collaboration focuses on applying AI agents to banking operations for risk management and efficiency. These developments highlight a shift toward autonomous systems that can plan tasks and execute actions.

The MOU involves Ant Digital Technologies, a subsidiary of Ant Group, and Korea's JB Financial Group. JB Financial Group includes Jeonbuk Bank, Kwangju Bank, JB Woori Capital, JB Asset Management, and JB Investment. Their overseas network includes PPCBank in Cambodia, JB Capital Myanmar, JB Securities Vietnam, and PT Bukopin Finance. Microsoft provides a stack including Entra ID, Agent 365, Purview, Defender, Work IQ, Fabric IQ, and Foundry IQ. The Foundry Agent Service acts as the runtime for deploying and managing agents in production.

Dmitry Tikhomirov stated that agentic AI is a good fit for industries full of rules and documents. He argued that AI agents excel where humans currently act as costly middleware between different systems. Leo Li of Ant Digital Technologies said he looks forward to developing responsible and practical AI capabilities. Ki Hong Kim of JB Financial Group said the technology will strengthen competitiveness in credit assessment. He also noted that the collaboration will improve financial access for their various foreign customers.

Banking clients are affected through improved onboarding, KYC refresh, alert handling, and financial crime investigations. Insurance users benefit from better underwriting intake, claims triage, policy servicing, and fraud referral processes. Capital markets see changes in post-trade exceptions, reconciliations, and surveillance triage to reduce manual coordination. McKinsey research from October 2026 notes a banking industry shift from AI copilots toward agentic AI systems. These systems are designed to collaborate across business workflows to create lasting value for the industry.

Ant Digital Technologies has operated independently since April 2024 and established Hong Kong headquarters in 2025. The company has partnered with over 300 partners to serve more than 30,000 enterprise customers worldwide. They have established collaborations in Asia with Ryt Bank, Touch 'n Go, Kenanga Investment Bank Berhad, and Bank CenterCredit. Omdia recognized Ant DT as a Market Leader in the 2026 Market Radar for agentic AI solutions. The 2026 Future of Fintech in APAC report describes a transforming landscape for digital lending and payments.

Firms are encouraged to redesign workflows from the ground up around digital labor rather than adding AI. Leaders must calibrate autonomy by setting specific mandates, clear permissions, and visible boundaries for every AI agent. It remains to be seen how these firms will measure business outcomes like leakage and false positives.

stories.Headline: Cornell's Eun-Ah Kim leads machine-learning work in a $12 million Energy Department quantum AI project
stories.Summary:
A $12 million award from the U.S. Department of Energy will fund a collaborative project linking artificial intelligence and quantum computing, according to an announcement reported on November 20, 2026. The effort is called Application-Aware Error Correction Codesign for Scientific Quantum Computing, and it is one of twelve Phase II awards under the Genesis Mission. Eun-Ah Kim, the Hans A. Bethe Professor at Cornell, will lead machine-learning work focused on a reinforcement-learning compiler that translates quantum algorithms into physical movements on a reconfigurable neutral-atom quantum computer. Harvard Professor Mikhail Lukin, co-director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative, leads the project overall, with Kim serving as a co-investigator.

Kim's group will concentrate on two key stages, beginning with compilation, and they will build a reinforcement-learning compiler to convert algorithms into specific atom movements and gate operations. The project unites expertise from MIT and Harvard alongside industry partners QuEra Computing, NVIDIA and Anthropic, demonstrating a broad collaborative effort. Researchers from Los Alamos, Lawrence Berkeley and Sandia national laboratories also contribute to the initiative, which is administered by the Department of Energy's Advanced Scientific Computing Research division. The collaboration extends beyond algorithm translation, aiming to improve the entire pipeline from scientific question to hardware execution.

According to the Department of Energy's announcement of the Genesis Mission awards, the goal is to integrate the world's best supercomputers, experimental facilities and AI systems to advance American research and innovation. The project's funding signifies a commitment to linking AI and quantum computing for scientific advancement, the report said. The award places Harvard and Cornell arts and sciences researchers within a twelve-award Phase II cohort under the Genesis Mission. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the funded work described.

stories.Headline: UK AI minister rejects calls for Britain to build its own sovereign frontier model
stories.Summary:
Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI minister, rejected calls for Britain to build its own sovereign frontier model during an event in Silicon Valley, arguing that access to American technology matters more than developing a homegrown rival. Speaking on a panel alongside representatives from OpenAI and Google DeepMind, he said he did not think the UK needed to build a frontier model from scratch to be a serious AI player. He added that if the country wanted a sovereign capability, it should focus on safety and regulation rather than competing at the frontier. His remarks drew immediate criticism from startup founders, one of whom said she was so angry she could barely speak.

The minister's position conflicts with the UK's stated ambition to build sovereign AI capability, which the articles describe as a goal the government has previously set out. Narayan argued that the UK should rely on partnerships with foreign labs rather than fund its own frontier model, and he pointed to the UK's AI Safety Institute as the country's real sovereign asset. Critics said the approach leaves British startups dependent on American companies and undermines the UK Sovereign AI Fund, a vehicle the articles mention without giving its size or budget. The articles give no date for when any policy decision will be made.

Eleanor Ward, a partner at venture firm Entrepreneurs First, said the minister's comments were a slap in the face for founders building in the UK and asked who would want to build a frontier model here under those conditions. She said the UK was outsourcing its AI future to US labs and that the government should be backing British companies instead. Another founder, whose name the articles give only as the head of a UK AI startup, said the UK risked becoming a client state of American AI. Narayan did not respond directly to the criticism in the articles.

The backlash comes as the UK government has been trying to position itself as a leader in AI safety and regulation while falling behind the US and China on frontier model development. The articles say the UK Sovereign AI Fund was set up to support domestic AI companies, though they give no figures for its funding or the number of firms it has backed. Several founders said they would reconsider building in the UK if the government's stance did not change. The articles do not say whether the government plans to review its position.

Hoplite, an Irish-US startup that lets developers run teams of AI coding assistants in the cloud, has raised $5.5m in a funding round backed by Stripe founders Patrick and John Collison, Paul Graham and other investors, Sifted reported on 20 November 2026. The round was led by venture firm Khosla Ventures, with participation from Susa Ventures and BoxGroup, according to the article. Hoplite was founded by Killian Loughman and Salvatore Cagliostro, and the company says its platform is already used by more than 100 teams. The startup describes its product as the easiest way for developers to run AI coding agents, which are programmes that can write and test software largely autonomously.

The funding is intended to support Hoplite's work on letting developers run swarms of AI coding agents in the cloud, the article says. Loughman said the company wants to make it simple for developers to run many agents at once without managing infrastructure themselves. The article states that Hoplite's platform is used by teams at companies including OpenAI and Anthropic, though it does not give further details on those customers. It also says the company plans to use the money to grow its team and expand its product.

Loughman said in the article that the goal is to let developers focus on building rather than on managing agents, and he described the current tools as requiring too much setup. He said Hoplite handles the infrastructure so that developers can run many agents in parallel. Cagliostro said the company is seeing strong demand from teams that want to use AI agents for coding tasks. The article does not include further direct comments from the investors.

The article notes that Hoplite is based in Ireland and the US, and that the AI coding agent space has attracted growing investor interest. It says the company will use the funding to hire and to expand its platform. The article does not say what specific product changes are planned or when they will arrive. More to follow.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA releases 14 Nemotron-Labs-Sigma diffusion language model checkpoints at 3B and 8B scales
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA released a collection of 14 open checkpoints called Nemotron-Labs-Sigma on November 20, 2026. This new family of continuous diffusion language models denoises text within a smooth 16-D embedding space. The release includes models at 3B and 8B parameter scales to provide various options for users. This approach differs from most diffusion models that work on discrete tokens.

The system requires one NVIDIA GPU from the Ampere, Lovelace, Hopper, or Blackwell series to run in bfloat16. It offers a context window of 4,096 tokens, though the Sigma-8B-instruct version supports 8,192 tokens. The 14 checkpoints include instruct versions, self-speculative variants, and few-step distilled models at NFE 2, 4, 8, and 16. Performance varies, with the Sigma-8B-instruct model reaching 91.96 on GSM8K but only 17.00 on AIME25.

The NVIDIA research team is responsible for the project and describes Sigma as the first large-scale family of its kind. They stated that working in a smooth latent space makes trajectory steering and few-step distillation practical for text. The team noted that the 8B speculative model runs 3.46 times faster than autoregressive decoding on one GB200. They also highlighted that the 8-step distilled 8B model maintains a high average score of 70.34.

The model uses a Ministral-style decoder-only Transformer with rotary embeddings and grouped-query attention. Training involved an autoregressive warm start of 1T tokens followed by 0.3T tokens of diffusion training. Generation occurs in blocks of 64 tokens, which are committed to a KV cache. The researchers recommend using a temperature of 0.3 and guidance of 3 at 32 DDIM steps for inference.

stories.Headline: Pasadena councilmember Justin Jones renews call for local AI policy and cybersecurity review
stories.Summary:
Pasadena City Councilmember Justin Jones renewed his call for the city to develop a local artificial intelligence policy and to review its cybersecurity protections, telling Pasadena Now on Thursday that residents should be able to find out how the city uses AI and provide input. His renewed push followed a week of communication outages at email systems, the Federal Aviation Authority, banks and intelligence agencies, and a Microsoft outage that left the city and other organizations unable to send or receive email. No cyberattack has been reported so far, though several legislators have expressed doubts about that claim, and the City Council discussed the need for talks on local technology on Tuesday. Jones first called for a local AI policy at a City Council meeting last month, and Councilmember Steve Madison has expressed support for the policy. Jones said he wants the city to review its cybersecurity protections and its plans for keeping services running through a major technology failure, noting that the city depends on computer systems for emergency communications, public safety, water, electricity, traffic signals and finances.

He said the council needs to understand the city's vulnerabilities and the cost to fix them, and that he will bring the matter to the Municipal Services Committee, which he chairs and which oversees public works, transportation and Pasadena Water and Power. Rick Cole, who also sits on the committee, echoed the call, saying technology is reshaping every aspect of life including the public sector and that Pasadena can lead, follow or get crushed. No date has been announced for a Municipal Services Committee discussion on cybersecurity. The article cites recent attacks on local organizations, including a June 2026 ShinyHunters extortion campaign against Pasadena-based Inter-Con Security that exposed employee and contact records, and a broader cyberattack one month earlier that disrupted access to the Canvas education platform for Pasadena City College and Pasadena Unified School District. In June 2024, a ransomware attack forced network shutdowns across all 36 Los Angeles County Superior Court locations, including the Pasadena Courthouse, and after a 2024 ransomware attack in Columbus, Ohio, its City Council approved $23 million in July 2025 for a new security network.

Jones said a discussion could review which services are most important to protect, whether backups are adequate and how long recovery from a longer outage would take, and that upgrades and a new network could cost millions if the city were hit. Councilmembers are also concerned about data retention, and on Tuesday the city voted to end its contract with Flock Cameras, whose license plate readers store data on an Amazon server out of local control. Councilmember Tyron Hampton called for keeping information obtained by technology in Pasadena, recommending servers owned and operated by city employees, and noted that 300 other agencies and every sworn Pasadena police officer could access the information. Councilmember Jason Lyon called the discussion on mass surveillance and data retention one of the most important of our time, and the Council unanimously agreed that the limited public safety benefits of the technology do not outweigh the privacy risks.

stories.Headline: AI training platforms pay $7 to $150 an hour but gate most work behind degrees
stories.Summary:
AI training jobs pay people to write prompts, rate chatbot answers and check code, and in November 2026 published rates run from $7 an hour on one Outlier listing in the Philippines to $150+ an hour for DataAnnotation coding work. The work is remote, flexible and real, but it is also unstable, mostly gated behind a degree, and full of unpaid minutes that no landing page mentions. Every platform in the guide promises "no AI experience required", a line the guide calls true and misleading. The guide sets out the pay each platform publishes itself, checked on 10 November 2026, along with the requirements behind that pay, the unpaid time and the scams that copy the format. Outlier, DataAnnotation, Mercor, Handshake AI, Alignerr, Mindrift and Prolific are named as real companies that pay, and most publish a fixed weekly or twice-monthly payout schedule.

Outlier lists general work at up to $18 an hour and Handshake AI lists evaluation work at up to $17, while DataAnnotation's FAQ now lists $25 to $50 though reviews from mid-2026 put its base nearer $20. Outlier requires at least an associate degree and DataAnnotation a bachelor's or equivalent experience, while Prolific is the main door with no credential check. DataAnnotation's Starter Assessment takes about an hour and you get one attempt, and Handshake AI does not pay for onboarding unless the Project Terms say so. Outlier pays weekly on Tuesdays through PayPal, Airtm or ACH bank transfer, DataAnnotation pays through PayPal within a few days of a request, and Mercor pays every Wednesday through Stripe or Wise. Outlier is run by Scale AI and claims more than 900,000 experts, and its onboarding takes 30 to 90 minutes and needs a valid ID, a phone from your country, a resume and a LinkedIn profile.

DataAnnotation's trust page says plainly that it will never ask you for money or any other form of payment, and that it pays you, not the other way around. The FTC's alert on task scams describes an unexpected message on WhatsApp, Telegram, text or social media offering quick money for online "tasks" such as "optimization" or "product boosting". You watch fake earnings pile up in an app, then you are told to deposit your own money, usually in crypto, to unlock the next tasks or withdraw what you earned. Three checks catch nearly all of it: you found the platform yourself rather than being messaged, you applied on the platform's own website, and you never paid anything for a starter kit, a training course or a verification fee. Real platforms do ask for ID verification and tax forms, but only inside their logged-in dashboard.

An Oxford Economics report estimated that data annotation supported nearly 200,000 flexible earning opportunities in the US in 2024 and contributed $5.7 billion to US GDP. Outlier claims 900,000+ experts and $600M+ paid out, and Handshake AI claims $500M+ in payouts to 188,000+ fellows, though those are company figures, not audited ones. Outlier names three core tasks on its own homepage: write a challenging prompt, create grading rubrics, and rate and rank answers. DataAnnotation describes its general projects as evaluating chatbot responses, comparing AI outputs and testing image generation, and it stresses that the work needs critical thinking and fact-checking, not clicking.

Independent review sites such as Breaking Even describe empty task queues, removal from projects without explanation, and unpaid assessments that never turn into paid work. Mercor recruits domain experts such as scientists, doctors and lawyers and matches them to AI labs on contracts, and in October 2025 it told TechCrunch it had 30,000+ experts earning over $85 an hour on average and paid out more than $1.5 million a day. Its first Stripe payout has a 7-day hold, which is Stripe's rule, not Mercor's. Handshake AI runs the Handshake AI Fellowship, open to generalists as well as experts, and its AI Evaluation Specialist role tops out at $17 an hour while specialist roles in energy, finance, game development and software engineering go up to $80 to $150.

The Fellowship is US-only, and Handshake says you must be based in the US and have valid work authorization. Alignerr, powered by Labelbox, claims 100,000+ experts and pays only for tasks that pass quality review on its pay-per-accepted-task projects. Mindrift is built by Toloka and shows the price of each task before you start it, and it states openly that it is not a job, with no employment contract and no fixed hours. Prolific is a research platform, not an AI training platform first, but some of its studies ask participants to evaluate AI models, and researchers must pay at least £6 or $8 an hour while Prolific recommends £9 or $12.

Asked whether you need a degree, Outlier's FAQ answers that you need at least an associate degree, and DataAnnotation's baseline is a bachelor's degree or equivalent real-world experience. Handshake AI's sign-up page says "no AI experience required" directly above listings tagged Bachelor's, Master's and PhD. DataAnnotation says someone with a bachelor's degree and no work history could qualify for its general projects, and that real-world experience counts as much as formal education. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Hugging Face researchers create harness adapters to boost AI model performance and efficiency
stories.Summary:
Hugging Face researchers introduced harness adapters on November 20, 2026, to improve model performance and cost. They used reinforcement learning to adapt a favorite model to a specific agent harness. This process creates a custom adapter for a target harness and task distribution. The team focused on real world software engineering tasks to test their method. They aimed to share a reusable recipe for other users to reproduce these results.

The team used Qwen3.8-27B and trained LoRA adapters for Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7, and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. They used TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, OpenEnv, and harbor on the Hub in Jobs for training. The process involved Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE benchmarks. They used SWE-smith for Python and Go, SWE-Gym from TaskTrove, and Tasksmith for tasks. These tools helped them filter 1,127 candidates down to a final set of 278 tasks.

The researchers stated that models target general performance rather than specific harnesses and tasks. They explained that combining a model and harness often leaves performance and efficiency on the table. By using reinforcement learning, they claimed they could squeeze everything out of a model. They noted that RL on a custom task distribution yields more accurate and efficient models. The team provided a collection of adapters, GGUFs, RL tasks, and a safeagents plugin.

The base Qwen3.8-27B model scored 39 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1 using the pi harness. With a custom adapter, the pass@1 score rose to 55 percent for the same harness. Average token usage dropped from 2.9K to 1.5K tokens per task because the model reasoned less. The model performed better the first time and called fewer tools during its operations. Each harness adapter beat the base model on both performance and efficiency for its harness.

The team built a data pipeline using the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv for agentic coding. They used Tasksmith to generate 24 tasks from 30 merged pull requests in 10 Python repositories. They filtered tasks to remove duplicates, those with restrictive licenses, and 253 tasks from target benchmarks. They used openenv validate to ensure reference solutions earned maximum rewards and canaries scored low. Qwen3.8-27B attempted 442 scored tasks to identify 171 tasks it solved only some of the time.

The researchers merged the three LoRAs into one super adapter for pi, Hermes Agent, and OpenCode. They used docker images with pre-installed harnesses to train the model inside the chosen environments. The trainer learned from exact tokens recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. They repaired and complexified 522 rejected tasks with Tasksmith to repeat the validation process. The authors left open the question of what the model really learned to do.

stories.Headline: Thinking Machines Lab releases Inkling 2 Mini multimodal model for local AI setups
stories.Summary:
Thinking Machines Lab released the Inkling 2 Mini model on November 20, 2026, to provide cutting-edge performance for local AI setups. This new multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model uses a looped transformer architecture to increase its capacity without adding more physical parameters. It accepts both text and image inputs and supports a context size of one million tokens for its users. The model features 26 billion total physical parameters, but only 3 billion parameters are active for each token processed. A DSpark drafter is included with the release to provide additional speed-up at a small cost to memory.

The model uses 24 decoder layers, where the 12 middle layers from 6 to 17 run three times in a loop. This design makes the model act as if it has 48 logical layers, including layers 0 to 5 and 18 to 23. It has a hidden size of 2,304 and selects eight experts from 128 available experts per layer at each visit. Weights are shipped in mixed-precision format using NVFP4 and MXFP8, with support for transformers, MLX, Llama App, and SGLang. The Llama App provides GGUF 4-bit and 8-bit quants for the flagship model and the TML-d24-varloop-research variant.

Thinking Machines Lab stated that this model is a refreshingly new great local model for users to employ. They noted that their vibe tests show the model is at least comparable with the Qwen 3.8 27B model. The developers mentioned that more validation is needed, but they are super excited about the release of this tool. They provided a research artifact that allows a variable number of passes through the loop to increase inference speed. They admitted that they have not evaluated this specific variable loop variant in depth yet.

The model leads in 32 out of 48 benchmarks in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, affecting various knowledge work categories. It outperforms Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL in coding, reasoning, safety, and vision interpretation. In coding, it leads in FrontierCode v2.0 and ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, though it trails on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. The model can call tools, such as getting the current temperature in Paris, France, using a provided tool function. Users can set reasoning effort levels from none at 0.0 to max at 0.99 via the chat template.

The architecture is similar to Inkling 2 Small, but Mini uses 128 experts per layer instead of 384 experts. It differs from Nanbeige by starting every pass through the looped core from the output of the first six layers. Information moves between these passes through cross-pass messages, which are mixed into inputs using four rank-64 gates. Each six-layer block contains one full-attention layer and five sliding-window layers, with the local window holding 1,024 tokens. Attention uses eight KV heads, 24 query heads, a learned sink, learned relative position logits, and an output gate.

Users can now deploy the model on datacenter hardware using SGLang, provided they run it on SM103 hardware. The model is available for use via the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class for those using the transformers library in their setup. People using macOS or Windows can manage the model through the Llama App, which provides an OpenAI-compatible API. The articles do not state the specific scores for the 32 benchmarks where the model leads other AI models. It remains open whether the variable loop research variant will be fully evaluated for quality and performance.

stories.Headline: Hebbia's tests show GPT-6 Astra leads on source citation and presentation quality for financial research
stories.Summary:
Hebbia tested a prerelease build of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra in August and September 2026, using the same financial research cases and grading criteria for each model, with domain experts writing or auditing the criteria against source documents. The tests covered two parts of a banker’s work: finding the sources a question requires and building a presentation that follows the banker’s brief. In the tests, GPT-6 Astra scored 13.6 percentage points above the best alternative tested on citing the required types of sources, and 99.5% of the excerpts it cited were relevant to the question. It also met 97.9% of the applicable presentation requirements, putting it 14.4 percentage points ahead of the best alternative tested on that measure, and it ranked first on both following the brief and presentation quality. Hebbia’s Matrix tool links answers to the documents behind them, and users can open a citation to see the underlying document and highlighted passage, while slide footnotes lead back to the source material.

In a hypothetical example described in the article, a banker helping a client assess a strategic acquisition of an industrial-software company with roughly 2,000 files to review could load the data room into Matrix and examine customer concentration, contract terms and churn in cited cells. Matrix could then bring in peer filings and industry news to help develop the deal thesis and turn that research into a diligence summary and valuation deck in the firm’s template. In that workflow, GPT-6 Astra selects documents or Matrix cells to support an answer and then turns the analysis into native PowerPoint slides that follow the user’s structure and guidelines. Kavita Anand, a member of technical staff for product at Hebbia, said the company had been strong partners with OpenAI over Hebbia’s lifetime and that the leaps GPT-6 Astra has made in quality outputs and accuracy have been truly surprising. She said traceability is really important to users because they base millions of dollars of decisions on what the AI comes back with, and citations help with traceability as well as giving users confidence that the AI found the right answer.

She said that when looking at a data room with thousands of documents even a single percentage-point gain can yield a lot of marginal benefit, and that she wants a deck made in her firm’s branding that looks like a human-made slide. She said past models shone on one dimension or the other, while GPT-6 Astra is the first model Hebbia has seen that is number one on both craft and instruction following. Anand described what a better first draft could make possible, saying GPT-6 Astra can create precise outputs and artifacts that adhere to user guidelines and that the overnighters professionals have to pull get reduced to a few minutes of reviewing its output. She also sees a future role for agents that monitor information in the background and surface signals for finance professionals to assess, and she said getting an important signal a few hours before competitors could let users start thinking about it and process more opportunities a human is not manually hunting. Hebbia wants to build on these results to help finance professionals assess deals with research they can trace back to its sources, and it wants bankers to spend less time reformatting decks and checking sources and more time assessing a deal.

stories.Headline: Stand for Children releases guidelines for school districts to govern student devices and educational technology
stories.Summary:
A national nonprofit organization called Stand for Children released a new research-backed framework on November 20, 2026. This document, titled Instructional Technology and School-Issued Devices: District Policy Guidelines, helps school districts manage the risks of student devices. The guidelines provide a way for school systems to regulate educational technology without using sweeping bans. These standards were developed with input from national experts to curb digital risks on school hardware.

They aim to preserve essential tools that support academic development and early literacy for students. The framework requires school districts to anchor their technology policies in student safety, data privacy, and student outcomes. Administrators must evaluate if individual tools meet a defined instructional need and protect the privacy of students. The guidelines call for minimizing or eliminating non-instructional screen time based on American Academy of Pediatrics research.

Districts are encouraged to establish a strict review cycle to prune unused or ineffective software platforms. Consolidating approved applications helps K-12 IT teams shrink their cybersecurity attack surface by reducing third-party vendors. The nonprofit organization is responsible for these guidelines and suggests that structured governance addresses direct operational challenges. They argue that unrestricted software access increases data exposure risks and creates significant compliance problems for districts.

The organization warns that blanket bans may push students and staff toward unvetted applications and unmonitored personal devices. Reducing passive digital exposure on district-managed devices limits classroom distractions and narrows windows for cyberbullying. This approach allows schools to balance educational access with the need for student safety. More to follow.
