stories.Headline: Ipswich Middle School enforces a new policy banning AI deepfakes and digital impersonation to protect student dignity
stories.Summary:
The School Committee unanimously approved a new handbook resolution on Thursday night for Ipswich Middle School. This policy prohibits the use of synthetic media and generative artificial intelligence to violate the identity or dignity of others. The new rules take effect immediately following a similar resolution passed for the high school last June. This action follows several AI related issues the school has already encountered recently.

The policy forbids cyberbullying and bullying that uses technology to create deepfakes, including audio recordings, videos, or images. Prohibited actions include AI voice cloning, face swapping, and the digital manipulation of a person's likeness for defamatory or mocking purposes. Students may not engage in digital impersonation or the unauthorized use of a person's image and name. These rules apply online, off campus, and during school sponsored activities or on school grounds.

Assistant Principal Sean Fitzgerald stated that the school must investigate and mitigate issues that impact a student's life at school. He explained that the specific AI policy was necessary because the district has already seen related problems. He emphasized that the administration has a duty to ensure all students feel safe when coming to school. Other issues from the past year were handled under the existing anti bullying policy.

Students who violate these rules may face expulsion, suspension, or the loss of school issued technology. The school also reserves the right to report the creation of harmful synthetic media to the Ipswich Police Department. This policy aims to prevent the distribution of content that falsely represents staff members or students. The administration will monitor both on campus and off campus behavior to maintain student safety.

stories.Headline: OpenAI strengthens GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol safeguards, cutting reasoning extraction attack success from 54.0% to 0.2%
stories.Summary:
OpenAI published a post on November 20, 2026 titled "Combatting adversarial distillation," describing how it detects and disrupts adversarial distillation and how it strengthened protections for its models' protected reasoning. Adversarial distillation is when an actor uses a frontier model's outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities. OpenAI said it combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated extraction attempts. OpenAI said it strengthened defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, the average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT-6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT-6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

OpenAI said its updated safeguards align more closely with those it uses for biology and cybersecurity. OpenAI said it places particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting protected reasoning, the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. OpenAI said these traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model. OpenAI described a September disclosure of attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. OpenAI said it strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user's encrypted reasoning.

OpenAI said that with GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol it ties a model's protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. OpenAI said that as new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning, and that if an earlier message is rewritten, its API drops the reasoning that followed it. OpenAI said it also prevents older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol's protected reasoning. OpenAI said that when its systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract its models' reasoning, it investigates the accounts responsible. OpenAI said that when it identifies violations, it enforces against the network of accounts, consistent with its policies and terms of service.

OpenAI said that through investigations of each campaign it generates insights that allow it to upgrade its defenses to better detect similar activity. OpenAI said it shares indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services. OpenAI said its consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering its models. OpenAI said it works closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments. OpenAI said sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models.

OpenAI said distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another, for example another model's answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. OpenAI said that beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks, because a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them. OpenAI said the concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology, where a model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them. OpenAI said that in an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, it used the content normally visible to users, final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions, as its baseline for distillation. OpenAI said it started each training run from the same pretrained student model and created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks.

OpenAI said each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. OpenAI said it evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments. OpenAI said that after supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. OpenAI said that after reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets. OpenAI said its cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under its usage policies.

OpenAI said that across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. OpenAI said it will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes. OpenAI said it defends against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of its safeguard stack, with model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls at the request level and patterns in request-level and account-level signals at the campaign level. OpenAI said attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing its safeguards.

OpenAI said its adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. OpenAI said adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners. OpenAI said it uses input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments, applying to both streaming and non-streaming responses. OpenAI said tool-call coverage is important because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool's arguments without including it in its final answer, and output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.

OpenAI said that in static evaluations it replays a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning, and in adaptive evaluations automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds. OpenAI said black-box testing gives testers the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. OpenAI said that in its adaptive black-box evaluation it tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. OpenAI said that on GPT-6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type, and both rates were substantially lower than on GPT-6 Astra with its original safeguards.

OpenAI said it is now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT-6 Astra as well. OpenAI said it has seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on its platform this year. OpenAI said it shared initial findings from those campaigns. More to follow.

stories.Headline: ICO seeks evidence on agentic AI to shape its statutory code of practice
stories.Summary:
The Information Commissioner's Office published a call for evidence on agentic AI on 8 October 2026, seeking feedback from organisations before 20 November. The call sets out the ICO's challenges and expectations across six themes: data security, transparency, accountability, automated decision-making, fairness and purpose limitation, and lawfulness of processing. The ICO also published a report on 8 October 2026 titled Building trust and transparency into generative AI development: our work to create regulatory certainty. That report followed a supervision programme set up in 2025 under the ICO's AI and Biometrics Strategy, which originally targeted 11 priority foundation model developers. The ICO held its annual Data Protection Practitioners' Conference online on 13 October 2026, with an afternoon programme of twelve practical seminars.

The call for evidence will feed into the ICO's statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making, which is set to become a key pillar of UK AI regulation in the absence of standalone UK AI legislation. The ICO's report sets out next steps including developing that statutory code, releasing guidance on emerging technologies such as agentic AI, continued scrutiny of foundation model developers, and engagement with government on special category data use. The report states that broad interests such as training models are unlikely to be a valid and specific interest for processing. It states that effective mechanisms for exercising rights are likely to require a combination of dataset and model-focused measures and output-focused safeguards across the AI development lifecycle. It also states that reliance on Article 11 of the UK GDPR should not be applied broadly.

DRCF Chief Executive Kate Jones said in a keynote speech on 23 September 2026 that one agentic example, an AI agent booking a consumer's holiday, engaged the remits of all four DRCF members. She said technology converges whereas regulation historically specialised, and that AI does not arrive in neat regulatory boxes. She said AI autonomy does not remove organisational responsibility and urged organisations to end internal silos just as regulators have done via the DRCF. The ICO notes that agentic systems can involve multiple organisations, models, agents and tools that may change with the workflow, making it hard to identify who determines the purposes and means of processing. The ICO states that organisations must assess whether Articles 22A to 22D of the UK GDPR apply across the complete workflow, not to agents or decision points in isolation.

The DRCF brings together the ICO, the CMA, Ofcom and the FCA. The ICO's report provides examples of how foundation model developers have implemented data protection improvements, including completing computability assessments, publishing sources used in training, including details about safeguards in legitimate interests assessments, and adopting de-duplication, filtering, testing across different languages and classifiers and hash matching to reduce risks with special category data. The ICO's conference sessions covered the DUAA complaints requirement, AI and automated decision-making, international transfers using Article 49 derogations, and cyber resilience. The ICO recently decided to join the National Cyber Resilience Centre Group's National Ambassador programme. On data subject access requests, the ICO said the use of AI to create DSARs does not change if and how organisations comply with and fulfil them, and that organisations should consider the intention of the request and ask for clarification if needed.

The ICO's report follows a supervision programme set up in 2025 under the ICO's AI and Biometrics Strategy, which selected 11 priority foundation model developers by reference to compliance risk, UK market share and reliance on higher-risk training datasets. The report addresses transparency, lawful basis, data subject rights, whether AI models contain personal data, and special category data. On whether AI models contain personal data, the ICO states that the extent to which a model memorises training data requires a case by case assessment considering factors such as the size of the model and training dataset and the amount of duplication in training data. The ICO considers that the manifestly made public and scientific research processing conditions are potentially applicable to special category data processed for foundation model training. The ICO's conference included a session on the new obligation for controllers to handle data protection complaints under the DUAA.

The ICO's call for evidence closed on 20 November and will feed into the statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making. The ICO's report sets out continued scrutiny of foundation model developers through ongoing engagement and continued reliance on legitimate interests. The ICO states that organisations piloting or deploying AI agents should review the report alongside the call for evidence. The articles state that comparable guidance is lacking at EU level, with no European Data Protection Board opinion or guidance, leaving developers and deployers to rely on piecemeal guidance from individual regulators such as the Spanish data protection authority's guide on agentic AI. The articles state that organisations cannot wait for complete regulatory clarity, and that AI developers and deployers are making compliance decisions now.

stories.Headline: Siemens launches Eigen Engineering Agent in India
stories.Summary:
Siemens launched its Eigen Engineering Agent in India on November 20, 2026, at the Transform - Siemens India Innovation Day in New Delhi, according to TechGig. The industrial AI agent is designed to automate repetitive engineering tasks, and the company said it can autonomously perform tasks such as PLC coding and Human-Machine-Interface visualisation while adhering to industrial safety standards. Before the India launch, Eigen was piloted by 16 Siemens clients in the country. Siemens reported that the agent can execute tasks two to five times faster than manual methods, and humans remain responsible for the final deployment of tasks even with Eigen's autonomous capabilities.

Pilot results indicated that the agent reduced repetitive engineering work by over 50 per cent and boosted productivity by 20 to 30 per cent in specific cases. Small and medium enterprises can access the agent through Siemens' existing TIA Portal, which the company said gives them a route to the technology without a separate platform. The launch ties the agent to India's manufacturing sector, with the company positioning it for both large operations and smaller firms. The article gives no pricing, availability timeline or further rollout details beyond the India launch and the TIA Portal access route.

Siemens AG CTO Dr Dirk Didascalou said Eigen can help accelerate growth in India by giving engineers more time for innovation, and he added that bringing AI into the engineering workflow helps manage complexity and strengthens India's industrial transformation. Siemens India CEO Sunil Mathur highlighted Eigen's potential to drive India's manufacturing leap, especially for small and medium enterprises. The company states that automating repetitive work frees engineers for more complex work and accelerates development. Humans remain responsible for the final deployment of tasks, according to the article.

The launch was held during Transform - Siemens India Innovation Day in New Delhi, and the pilot involved 16 Siemens clients in the country before the India release. The article reports the productivity gains of 20 to 30 per cent in specific cases and the reduction of over 50 per cent in repetitive engineering work as pilot results rather than guaranteed outcomes. SMEs can reach the agent through the existing TIA Portal, which the article presents as the access path for smaller firms. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the launch and the pilot results.

stories.Headline: Cognizant opens 165,000 sq ft AI learning centre in Chennai to build global AI workforce
stories.Summary:
Cognizant inaugurated Phase-1 of its Immersive Learning Center at its Siruseri campus in Chennai on Thursday, according to a company release reported by TechGig on November 20, 2026. The Nasdaq-listed technology company said the facility is meant to develop AI skills at scale and to support its commitment to an AI-ready global workforce. Cognizant stated that the centre will undergo further expansion in subsequent phases beyond this first one. The company described the centre as integrating modern workplace design with digital learning infrastructure and flexible environments for instructor-led learning, collaboration and ideation.

The facility spans 165,000 square feet and features 58 classrooms equipped with 1,822 learning seats, along with 208 multipurpose seats, collaborative spaces and meeting rooms. A work café, a library and flexible town hall spaces are also part of the new centre, the company said. Cognizant is advancing its frontier workforce model, which focuses on building the human capabilities required to translate AI investments into enterprise outcomes. Earlier this year the company committed to scaling its Frontier-certified workforce to 5,000 Frontier Certified Engineers and 10,000 Frontier Business Operators.

Rajesh Varrier, President of Global Operations and Chairman and Managing Director of Cognizant India, commented on the investment in the release. He said that as an AI Builder the company's focus is on harnessing AI to transform businesses and on developing the skills its associates need to lead that transformation. Varrier added that the facility reflects continued investment in creating spaces for learning and collaboration. He said associates will build innovative, AI-enabled solutions for clients within these spaces.

Cognizant maintains an operational presence across India, with locations including Bengaluru, Bhubaneswar, Chennai, Coimbatore, Delhi-NCR, GIFT City, Hyderabad, Indore, Kochi, Kolkata, Mangaluru, Mumbai, Pune and Visakhapatnam. The articles do not say what the later phases of the centre will involve or when they are expected to be completed. They also do not give a timeline for reaching the targets of 5,000 Frontier Certified Engineers and 10,000 Frontier Business Operators. No further details on the next steps were provided in the reports.

stories.Headline: EY, Microsoft launch agentic cyber defence centre for AI security
stories.Summary:
EY and Microsoft jointly launched an Agentic Cyber Defence Centre, according to a TechGig report published on November 20, 2026. The centre integrates Microsoft technologies with policy controls and tamper-evident records for the actions taken by AI agents. It extends the existing alliance between the two companies into agent-led security operations, with the stated aim of connecting fragmented cyber defences. EY says the platform helps organisations retain human responsibility for automated decisions while agents take on more security work.

The platform applies policy-based controls to agent actions and keeps tamper-evident records that let organisations track changes and coordinate responses. The announcement describes an integrated transformation and operations model that spans identity, data, applications, cloud and operational technology. EY plans to apply agentic blueprints across these domains, using reusable patterns to connect security capabilities rather than relying on separate deployments. The stated aim is sustained and repeatable improvement in cyber defence.

EY is implementing Microsoft security for agentic cyber defence across its global organisation as what it calls Client Zero. This internal deployment is meant to validate operating models, codify controls and develop reusable patterns, with the aim of reducing implementation risk for clients. Richard Watson, EY Global Consulting Cybersecurity Leader, said the future of cybersecurity requires an entirely new operating model. Naseem Tuffaha, Corporate Vice President, Security at Microsoft, said securing the AI-powered enterprise requires a new model for cyber defence that keeps pace as AI changes how organisations operate and are attacked.

stories.Headline: Salesforce begins new layoffs while setting AI spending budgets for staff
stories.Summary:
Salesforce has begun another round of job cuts, according to internal messages reviewed by Business Insider, and the scale of the current reductions is not yet known. Business Insider reported the new cuts by citing messages shared on an internal Slack channel, where staff discussed layoffs taking place this week and some employees noted recent reductions. One employee also reported that their manager had been let go, and a senior manager in IT compliance and content strategy confirmed their own reduction in force on LinkedIn. That manager also stated that other team members were impacted on Monday morning, while the company has not disclosed the total number of roles affected in this latest round.

The new cuts follow earlier workforce reductions at Salesforce this year, including a regulatory filing that showed the company cut 86 jobs in California on August 7. Those affected roles were in sales, general administration, technology, and product teams, and Salesforce also reduced headcount in Washington state and in markets outside the United States. Internal documents reviewed by Business Insider detail the standard severance package for US employees, under which eligible staff can receive up to 30 weeks of base pay depending on their level, tenure, and age. The company also set AI budgets for employees this week, after an internal memo indicated that some staff had spent thousands of dollars monthly on AI tokens last quarter.

CEO Marc Benioff is responsible for the company and has rejected investor concerns about AI's impact on traditional software business models. He stated at the company's most recent earnings report that the software-as-a-service industry is not facing a collapse. The job cuts occur in a year marked by investor concern over AI's impact on traditional software business models, and Salesforce shares fell 9 per cent on Tuesday. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the reported cuts and the new AI budgets.

stories.Headline: Federal Circuit ruling shows AI patent applicants how concrete claim language shapes eligibility, Phelan says
stories.Summary:
The Federal Circuit recently decided Ceiva Opco, LLC v. Amazon.com, Inc., a patent case about digital picture frames that the court used to show how concrete claim language can change the outcome of a patent-eligibility analysis. The court reversed an ineligibility ruling for one digital picture frame claim while it affirmed that same ruling for representative claims of three related patents. The claim that survived specified the interactions among a physically separable user interface, a server, and a digital frame, and the court found that this combination addressed technological limitations of earlier devices. By contrast, the related claims broadly described desired functions without sufficiently specifying how those results were actually achieved.

Although Ceiva did not involve artificial intelligence, the decision offers a practical lesson for AI patent applicants, according to Marshall, Gerstein & Borun LLP partner Ryan Phelan, who analyzed the ruling in a contribution to IPO Daily News. Phelan wrote that applicants should identify the technical improvement, connect it to shortcomings in existing technology, and claim the features and relationships that produce that improvement. He made the point that concrete claim language can make a meaningful difference in the patent-eligibility analysis. Phelan is a regular contributor to the newsletter's AI Insights column, where he analyzes court decisions, regulatory developments, and other issues affecting patents and emerging technologies, and he also authors the firm's PatentNext blog on artificial intelligence and other next-generation technologies.

The article was published by Legal 500 on 20 November 2026 and carries the headline about the claim-drafting lesson for AI patents. It presents the Ceiva decision as an illustration for applicants rather than as a change in the law, and it does not say what happens next in the case or whether any further review is expected. The piece states that its content is intended as a general guide to the subject matter and that specialist advice should be sought about specific circumstances. Members can read Phelan's latest AI Insights article on the IPO website, according to the article.

stories.Headline: Teachers at WHS debate how to regulate student AI use as departments split on its value
stories.Summary:
For the past four years, educators have scrambled to change curriculums around the emergence of AI in a way that reduces the ability to potentially cheat with AI tools. As the use of AI in schools becomes more prominent and commonly used, debates surrounding the topic have increased. Reports analyzing various advantages and harms to AI in school prompt further conversations on what the role of AI should look like. In a survey by Pew Research Center about 32% of K-12 educators say there is an equal mix of benefit and harm using AI tools in an education background. At WHS, departments share different needs for AI, and in certain subjects teachers argue AI creates a lack of critical thinking, especially in an academic setting.

History Department Head David Schmirer said AI is literally taking away your power to be able to think for yourself. Schmirer said the ability to make critical decisions and choices as you get older is going to become a lot more difficult. Math teacher Emily Grant said AI can be useful in math when students use it to understand how to do problems and not to just get the answers. Grant said if students put in a problem and ask for AI to make a similar problem and show the steps, that can be a really helpful way to learn the material. English Department Head Peter Galalis doesn’t believe there will ever be a use for AI in English classes.

Galalis said writing is a human practice, and it always is going to be. Galalis also points out that writing at a professional level means there are certain legal barriers to producing something written by AI, because AI isn’t protected under copyright. Galalis said it’s going to continue to be really important that human writers produce and own their own words, because what you produce with a chatbot is not the same as something that you’ve written. Galalis argues that the physical act of writing something human can’t be replaced by generative AI. Galalis said writing is something we don’t do just to produce more words for other people to read, and if you outsource that to a chatbot, you rob yourself of those opportunities.

Math Department Head Kanchan Kant believes policies should adapt to focus on teaching what will be helpful for students seeking a math degree in the world of AI. Since AI will have an impact on careers in math, Kant believes a specific part of math jobs will no longer be focused on writing proofs, but instead critiquing what already exists. Kant said if critiquing AI’s work is a part of what our students will end up doing, we should be preparing them for that. Schmirer said AI’s capability and availability has increased so rapidly that it’s really difficult for any teacher at the school to keep up with it. In the history department, Schmirer comments that teachers are allowed to choose their own pathway regarding AI usage.

While some teachers attempt to sway students away from AI by giving students zeroes on assignments completed with AI, Schmirer’s method is to inform students on just how harmful AI can be and encourage them to use their own thinking. Schmirer said ultimately all we can do is appeal to students to make good choices, just like we do in other areas of life. The in-class essay, rather than a take home essay, is becoming increasingly popular as a way to remove AI from the equation. Some teachers assign print-out readings rather than the typical online readings that teachers worry will be copy and pasted into an AI tool. Research shows that reading off a paper, annotating, and taking notes by hand is more helpful in successfully absorbing information than reading a screen.

One anonymous student was given a zero on a homework assignment after it was flagged by an AI detector, and later met with their teacher over the issue to defend their academic integrity, where the student was able to receive full credit. The anonymous student said they were very confused and thinking maybe there was a glitch or something like that. The anonymous student said it should be a bit more holistic with teachers meeting with students before assigning a grade for AI use. Up until last year, take-home essays were common, if not expected, in WHS humanities classes. Junior Archie Baker said they started here in 2024, so in freshman year and sophomore year it was almost entirely take-home essays, which they appreciate a lot more.

English teacher Phillip George said in his first year teaching here in 2023, he thinks he had something like 16 instances of catching students cheating using online resources, and that shocked him. George said that forced him after that first year to start revising his approach. George used the analogy of marathon runners and sprinters, and said now he’s making them sprint, and they are sprinting for at least an hour. George said the in-class essay is great for authentically assessing student thought and writing, but it is very narrow in scope. George said it eliminates the opportunity for revision, improvement, and the drafting process, which is usually so essential to writing, and it limits the kind of time under tension that students experience.

Junior Archie Baker said during an in-class essay they feel much more rushed, and they can’t refine their thoughts, so they just write it and then that’s it. Baker said they’re trying to develop ideas but can’t get as in-depth or as nuanced as they’d like to. George said what is lost is a sense of intellectual endurance, and the reward for the virtue of prolonged thought and hard work. Schmirer said he’d rather get less than good work from a student that’s their own work and that they put time and effort into than something that is just simply not their own at that point. Schmirer describes it as a fluid situation where teachers react in the interest of educating students and preparing them for their futures as new advancements in AI continue to present themselves.

stories.Headline: Council of Europe trains 20 local authority teams to govern AI responsibly
stories.Summary:
The Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe organised the first-ever Academy on responsible AI governance at local level, held in Paris from 17 to 19 November 2026. Twenty teams from local and regional authorities, selected in an open call, took part in the academy. The teams came from 18 municipalities and two counties, spanning the continent from Diyarbakır in Türkiye to Fingal in Ireland. The academy was organised by the Centre of expertise for multilevel governance (CEMG) at the Congress, in partnership with the Council of Europe's Steering Committee for new and emerging digital technologies (CDNET). It put into practice the Congress's call to strengthen local and regional authorities' capacity to use and manage AI.

Participants were provided with practical tools for responsible AI governance, based on the Council of Europe's HUDERIA methodology for assessing the impact of AI systems. Over three days, participants applied the methodology to a fictional AI-supported public consultation, identifying and analysing risks, mapping stakeholders and developing mitigation measures. The programme was designed to strengthen authorities' capacity to assess the impact of AI in public services on everyone they serve, from a human-rights, democracy and rule-of-law perspective. The participating authorities were Amaroussion (Greece), Bălți (Republic of Moldova), Bergen (Norway), Bitola (North Macedonia), City of Arezzo (Italy), City of Vigo (Spain), Diyarbakır (Türkiye), Fingal County (Ireland), Harghita County (Romania), Kutaisi (Georgia), London Borough of Camden (United Kingdom), Lviv (Ukraine), Nõo (Estonia), Resen (North Macedonia), Rivne (Ukraine), Shkodër (Albania), Szentendre (Hungary), Turnišče (Slovenia), Valongo (Portugal), and Ventspils Education Board (Latvia). The academy was also an official part of the "Road to Geneva" programme, leading up to the 2027 Geneva AI summit.

Opening the discussions, Congress co-rapporteur on AI Annika Vaikla (Estonia, ILDG), Deputy Mayor of Viimsi, urged authorities to use AI to give public servants more time for people, while keeping people in control. She called for AI literacy among political leaders, staff and citizens. She also called for smaller municipalities to have access to shared expertise. Deputy Mayor Vaikla is co-rapporteur for the 2026 Congress report on strengthening the capacities of local and regional authorities in the use of artificial intelligence. The articles give no further remarks from her.

The articles state that local and regional authorities are on the frontline of the AI revolution in Europe's town halls. Faced with shrinking budgets, they see real potential in efficiency gains promised by AI. They also face hard questions such as planning applications for data centres and democratic accountability for decisions informed by AI. The articles say they lack capacity in understanding and governing AI technologies, particularly smaller municipalities.

The academy served as a Congress contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe and was held in support of the implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence. The articles give no further background beyond the academy's organisation and aims. They state that artificial intelligence is already in Europe's town halls. They describe the academy as the first-ever of its kind at local level.

They state that the twenty teams were selected in an open call. They state that the programme was designed to strengthen authorities' capacity to assess the impact of AI in public services. They give no further details on the Congress report or the Framework Convention. The articles state that the academy was an official part of the "Road to Geneva" programme, leading up to the 2027 Geneva AI summit.

They state that it was held in support of the implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence. They state that it served as a Congress contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe. They give no further details on what follows the academy. They leave open what the participating authorities will do next and what the 2026 Congress report will contain.

stories.Headline: Senators question whether Meta's $6.6 billion in AI data center tax credits qualify as research
stories.Summary:
A New York Times article has renewed attention on the tax credits that Meta claimed for its artificial intelligence data centers, according to a report published by Accounting Today on November 20, 2026. In a letter dated October 14, 2026, Senate Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden of Oregon and six other senators said Meta claimed about $6.6 billion in federal research and development tax credits between 2023 and 2025. The senators questioned whether Meta described its AI data centers as experimental pilot models in those claims and asked the company for a breakdown of the credits tied to the data centers. The inquiry highlights two separate questions, which are whether the development activities count as qualified research and whether the claimed expenditures count as qualified research expenditures for the credit. Treasury Regulation 1.174-2(a)(4) defines a pilot model as any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty about the product during its development or improvement.

The rules say production costs paid or incurred after the uncertainty is eliminated are not eligible, and a pilot model must involve genuine uncertainty in the design that the model is needed to resolve. Meeting that definition does not by itself satisfy Section 41 of the tax code, which sets additional requirements for the credit and for eligible expenses. Only wages, supplies, computer leasing and contractor costs tied to qualifying research activities can be claimed as qualified research expenses. Section 41(b)(2)(C) excludes land, improvements to land and property subject to depreciation from the definition of qualified supplies, so a taxpayer cannot turn depreciable equipment into qualified supplies by calling it experimental or by not claiming depreciation on it.

For Meta's data centers, the treatment of purchased servers, chips and other equipment is a central issue, because using equipment for qualified research does not by itself make its purchase price a qualified supply expense. Meta asserts that uncertainty existed in the data centers and that it could only be resolved by building a physical data center and testing it. To support that claim, Meta would need to show the technical uncertainty that existed before the data center was built and how building it resolved that uncertainty. The article says taxpayers claiming pilot model costs should build a record that connects the technical work to the claimed expenditures, including initial design questions, alternative designs, simulation results, test plans, test findings and engineering designs.

Cost records for employee activities, materials and contractor charges should be traceable to the relevant development work and should complement the technical evidence. The article, written by David Seibel, a senior manager in the research and development tax credit practice at Indianapolis-based McGuire Sponsel, says the credit is one of the most fact-intensive and subjective areas of tax law. It says the questions raised by the Meta claim extend well beyond AI infrastructure, because manufacturers, equipment developers and other businesses face similar challenges in showing why a model was built, how its development involved experimentation and which costs the credit permits. The articles do not say what happens next in the Senate inquiry or whether Meta has responded to the senators' request.

stories.Headline: Governor Kathy Hochul pauses a proposed AI data center project in Niagara Falls
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul ordered a freeze on certain state environmental permits for new data centers on July 14. This action paused the proposed Niagara Digital Campus project in Niagara Falls. A private developer wants to spend 1.5 billion dollars on this facility. The project aims to build a hub for artificial intelligence. This freeze happened while America competes with China in an AI race.

The pause affects data centers using at least 50 megawatts of power and can last one year. The Niagara Digital Campus would include nine buildings using 140 megawatts near the Robert Moses plant. The project requires a state air permit for backup diesel generators. The Responsible Data Center Development Act would lower the permit pause threshold to 20 megawatts. Governor Hochul must act on this legislative bill by December 31.

Governor Hochul said the pause allows the state to study effects on water, environment, and electric bills. She stated that developers should pay for required infrastructure rather than households. Niagara Falls Redevelopment, owned by the Milstein family, says it will pay for grid upgrades. The state council of building trades urged the governor not to adopt the freeze. NFR first proposed this data center project in 2021.

Opponents of the project express concerns regarding noise, water usage, and local electric bills. A consultant projects 675 annual construction jobs for nine years and 550 permanent positions. The project could generate 414.9 million dollars in taxes. Residents across the country are fighting data centers over water and power costs. Data Center Watch reports 75 projects worth 130 billion dollars were blocked in early 2026.

China added 543 gigawatts of generating capacity in 2025, mostly through wind and solar power. Chinese data centers pay about 3 cents per kilowatt-hour, which is one third of the American price. Morgan Stanley projects a 44-gigawatt power shortfall for American data centers by 2028. Stanford University found American and Chinese chatbots were nearly equal by March 2026. Liu Liehong called electricity a competitive advantage for China in March.

The project awaits a decision on its merits regarding generators, infrastructure, and environmental effects. The developer's builder, Urbacon, uses cooling systems that require little or no water. The project could move to states like Texas, Ohio, or Virginia if New York declines. Lawmakers in 16 states have considered bans, and Pennsylvania proposed a three-year moratorium. The articles leave open whether the state will ultimately approve the permits.

stories.Headline: US export rules restrict a wider range of chips including those for consumer electronics
stories.Summary:
The United States government introduced tighter export controls on Thursday, November 20, 2026, to restrict the flow of semiconductor technology. Industry insiders report that these new rules are causing a much wider disruption across the global supply chain than was first anticipated. The restrictions are not limited to advanced artificial intelligence chips but also impact system on chips used in common consumer electronics. Consequently, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. has already suspended some of its shipments to various clients.

These updated regulations affect a diverse range of developers, including those who are not based in China and do not create AI hardware. The rules target mobile and everyday consumer applications, which forces companies to change how they source and distribute their semiconductor components. Because the world's largest contract chipmaker is involved, the changes impact major customers like Nvidia who rely on leading-edge processors. Every developer using these specific types of integrated circuits must now navigate these stricter American trade requirements.

Multiple industry executives told Nikkei Asia that the scope of these controls is unexpectedly broad and damaging to the supply chain. They expressed concern that the rules extend far beyond the intended targets of high-end AI technology to hit general electronics. These leaders believe the current environment creates significant uncertainty for developers who were previously unaffected by trade wars. They warned that the sudden suspension of shipments could lead to larger shortages of essential components for mobile devices.

stories.Headline: AI linked stocks drop as investors worry over Anthropic revenue growth and new chip export rules
stories.Summary:
Several artificial intelligence linked stocks experienced significant price drops during an afternoon trading session on November 20, 2026. DigitalOcean saw the steepest decline of 13.2 percent, while Oracle and C3.ai both fell by approximately 8 percent. Snowflake shares decreased by 5.3 percent, and SentinelOne shares dropped by 4.7 percent. These losses followed a more than 10 percent slide for Anthropic after its initial public offering.

The market reaction followed an 81.3 billion dollar initial public offering for Anthropic and quarterly earnings results from Nvidia under interim CEO Colette Kress. Investors grew concerned that Anthropic would not meet the fast revenue growth required to justify its 83 dollar offer price. Additionally, the Commerce Department Bureau of Industry and Security now requires licenses for advanced chips sent to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. These rules aim to stop Chinese firms from leasing Nvidia compute resources in those foreign countries.

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook warned against delaying interest rate hikes before an expected increase in December. Governor Michael S. Barr stated that on-balance-sheet debt for the seven largest AI firms could exceed 800 billion dollars by the end of the year. He further noted that nominal guarantees and off-balance-sheet leases for these companies might top 3 trillion dollars. President Donald Trump also added to the volatility by threatening penalties on data centers built outside the United States.

The current downturn follows a period of extreme volatility for companies like DigitalOcean, which reached a 52-week high of 181.29 dollars in June 2026. Market analysts suggest that selling pressure on major artificial intelligence leaders often spreads to other software and semiconductor companies. Future capital flows and unit economics for the sector will likely be tested by upcoming financial results. Investors are now monitoring whether these price drops represent buying opportunities for high-quality stocks.

stories.Headline: AI spending concerns and high rates push Dow and Nasdaq sharply lower
stories.Summary:
The Dow Jones 30 and Nasdaq 100 dropped significantly last week as uncertainty in the Middle East, concerns about AI spending and high interest rates continued to pressure US stocks, according to FXEmpire analyst Muhammad Umair. The Dow Jones closed at 48,350.30, down 1.52%, and the S&P 500 closed at 6,954.55, down 3.09%, both on Nov 20 at 21:59 UTC. The US Tech 100 closed at 25,237.55, down 4.68%, on Nov 20 at 21:59 UTC. Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) lost 13.8% and closed at 125.53, down 14.01%, on Nov 20 at 20:59 UTC. Caterpillar Inc. (CAT) dropped 5% and closed at 510.45, down 5.01%, on Nov 20 at 20:59 UTC.

The Nasdaq 100 dropped 9.38% last week to close at 25,237.50 and broke key support at 26,200, which suggests a decline towards 23,500. A break below 23,500 may trigger a deeper decline to the 200-week SMA near 21,000, and the index must recover above 28,000 to initiate the next rally. The Dow Jones broke below key support at 50,000 last week and closed with a loss of 7.24%, which suggests a drop towards 45,000 if it remains below 50,000. A break below 45,000 may trigger a deeper correction towards 38,500, a break below 48,000 may continue momentum towards 45,000, and a break above 50,000 may open the way towards 55,000. The Fed minutes released on 18 November kept the risk of higher interest rates in the near future, and officials discussed the risk of AI spending and rapid growth of related debt.

President Donald Trump said the US is very close to agreement with Mexico after meeting Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum in Asia, and Sheinbaum said talks about vehicles, steel and aluminum have made progress. She mentioned that agreement can be made during the next meeting at the G20 summit in December. The White House mentioned that The Boeing Company (BA) and GE Aerospace have finalized a $12 billion sale to Philippine Airlines for up to 20 Boeing 787 aircraft with GE engines. Boeing (BA) traded at $157.09, down 1.09%, on Nov 21 at 09:44 UTC. Umair wrote that confirmed relief in tariffs may provide clear benefits to industrial sectors of the Dow.

The final University of Michigan survey released on Friday showed consumer sentiment increased to 51.5 in November from 48.0 in October. One-year inflation expectations dropped to 3.7% from 4.7% while long-term expectations eased to 3.3% from 3.5%. Initial jobless claims increased by 1000 to 203,000 and continued claims increased by 70,000 to 1.763 million for the first week of November. The 10-year US Treasury yield dropped to 4.91% on Friday after a strong spike to 5.17% following US consumer inflation data, and the 10-year yield lies at 0.96% above the three-month bill rate.

WTI crude oil closed at 84.9520, up 0.94%, and gold (XAU) closed at 3,538.19, down 1.92%, both on Nov 20 at 21:59 UTC. The weekly Nasdaq 100 chart shows a cup and handle formation from November 2021 to November 2023, and the RSI is approaching oversold levels as the index drops towards 23,500. The daily chart shows a broadening wedge pattern from June 2026, and the index broke the 200-day SMA at 28,000 and dropped 4.63% on Friday. The Dow Jones long-term support at 38,500 is defined by an ascending broadening wedge pattern from January 2024, and 45,000 represents the neckline of an inverted head and shoulders pattern formed from December 2024 to August 2025.

Iran may make the US blockade of Iranian ports as difficult as possible with the hope that the US will withdraw, and shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz are shrinking. The recent selloff in WTI oil, gold and US stocks may be the symptom of shrinking liquidity. Umair wrote that the Nasdaq 100 and Dow Jones remain under extreme pressure in the short term and that a lasting recovery needs strong confidence in corporate profits and returns from AI investment. He wrote that concerns about profitability from AI spending outweigh the benefits of cheaper long-term funding.

The articles leave open whether the US-Mexico agreement will be announced and whether the Fed will raise rates in December. The articles do not state whether the 23,500 support for the Nasdaq 100 or the 45,000 support for the Dow Jones will hold. The articles do not give the outcome of the next meeting at the G20 summit in December. The articles do not state when the US blockade of Iranian ports began or how far shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz have shrunk.

stories.Headline: EU consortium 2DFIRE develops graphene and barium titanate modulators for AI data center optics
stories.Summary:
A new European Union project called 2DFIRE has officially started with seven partners from five European countries, and the Universitat Politècnica de València in Spain coordinates the consortium. The other partners are Lumiphase from Switzerland, KU Leuven from Belgium, Graphenea from Spain, Annealsys from France, Riga Technical University from Latvia and PNO Innovation from Spain. The project has a total budget of €4.92 million, which is about US$5.4 million, and it will run for 36 months. The work is funded by the European Union under the Graphene Flagship. The project aims to develop faster, smaller and more energy-efficient photonic devices for artificial intelligence and high-performance computing.

Its approach is a hybrid platform that combines barium titanate, a ferroelectric material, with two-dimensional materials such as graphene and MoS₂. The core target is electro-optic modulators for optical interconnects in data centers, and the consortium points to electricity use in AI data centers, which it expects to more than double by 2030. According to the project page, the devices are barium titanate coupled-modulated ring modulators, and the target is data transmission at 400 Gbps per wavelength. Besides graphene and MoS₂, the work covers hydrogen-doped indium oxide as a transparent conducting oxide. The aims include thermal phase shifting with low optical losses and new electrode designs that cut driving voltage and energy use.

The partners will work on reliable methods to deposit and transfer the two-dimensional materials and integrate them with barium titanate devices. The project also aims to show that the modulators are compatible with existing semiconductor manufacturing processes and value chains, including 200 mm wafer technology. The consortium says this compatibility should support industrial adoption and strengthen Europe's semiconductor and photonics supply chains. The articles do not name individual people or give direct statements beyond the consortium's published positions on the project page. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the 36-month work plan and the stated aims.

stories.Headline: OpenAI requires prior approval for platforms that give third parties direct access to its models
stories.Summary:
OpenAI began requiring operators of platforms that give third parties direct access to its models to obtain the company's prior review and approval, under a rewritten version of its Usage Policies. The new text carries an effective date of November 20, 2026, and replaces the version that had applied since October 29, 2025. OpenAI announced the changes in a changelog entry dated October 21, 2026, which gave customers 30 days before the rules took hold. The rewrite also adds a section barring the use of OpenAI models and outputs to prepare training material for rival AI systems. The policy body grew from about 830 words in the October 2025 version to about 1,400 words in the new one, according to a PPC Land count of the two texts.

The policy states that operators of a model-access intermediary platform or other service enabling third parties to directly access OpenAI models must obtain prior review and approval. It states that this requirement does not apply solely because an application integrates OpenAI models to power its features or functionality. The rewrite rewrites the child safety rules and widens the human review rule from automated decisions to automated actions, with a definition covering actions, decisions, transactions, submissions, and other steps. Three headed sections are new: Training and developing models, OpenAI-approved use, and Providing access to our models. The training section states its restrictions do not prohibit uses expressly permitted by an applicable Agreement with OpenAI, including any Permitted Exception under the Services Agreement.

The changelog entry states that OpenAI updated its Usage Policies to clarify restrictions on using OpenAI models and outputs to train other models. It states that OpenAI also clarified protections for children and teens and requirements for high-stakes uses, and that the update incorporates existing national security principles and sets out approval requirements for national security and law enforcement uses, as well as for model-access intermediaries. A help center notice titled "We're updating our Usage Policies" lists the same four themes and describes the training language as a clarification of restrictions that already existed rather than a new prohibition. It describes the intermediary rule as an added approval requirement and states that existing agreements and other applicable terms, including any express permissions granted in them, continue to apply. Under the heading "OpenAI-approved use," the policy states that OpenAI may grant specific partners case-by-case exceptions to certain restrictions, naming the factors reviewed as the partner, proposed use, applicable safeguards, and the partner's compliance commitments.

Elena Gurevich, an AI and intellectual property attorney who advises companies on AI governance, wrote in a LinkedIn post on November 20 that OpenAI's updated usage policies kicked in that day. She summarized the intermediary rule as meaning that a business providing customers direct access to OpenAI's models needs OpenAI's approval first, while using the models to power an application's features does not trigger the requirement. She gave OpenRouter, which she described as a platform that streamlines access to multiple AI models from different providers, as an example of the kind of service in scope, and OpenAI's policy names no company. The changelog records that on October 25, 2022, developers no longer needed to wait for approval after submitting as long as they complied with the policies.

It records that on November 9, 2022, OpenAI no longer required developers to register their applications, using a combination of automated and manual methods to monitor for policy violations instead. In August, data drawn from OpenRouter showed AI agents using nearly five times as many tokens per task as human users, with agent usage up about 14 times since February 2026 and more than 85% of agent token spend going to cached prompts. When Anthropic's rewritten Usage Policy took effect on November 12, 2026, it added a prohibition on reselling, proxying or otherwise providing access to Claude through unauthorized means, naming services that route requests through consumer subscriptions or misrepresent which product or client is in use. The training section opens with a rationale stating that capable models must have safeguards proportionate to the risks they pose before they are deployed, and that training another model on OpenAI outputs can transfer capabilities without carrying those safeguards over.

The operative prohibition states that users must not use OpenAI models or their outputs to generate, prepare, select, or supply training material or signals for models intended as alternatives to or substitutes for OpenAI models or services. The policy lists what that covers, including creating or preparing training data, training tasks, rubrics, or reinforcement-learning environments, and providing feedback used in training, including labels, scores, rankings, preferences, rewards, or corrections. Neither the policy page nor the help notice describes how to apply, how long a review takes, whether services already running on November 20 have a transition window, or whether any intermediary has already been approved. The policy gives no application route, form or review time for the access rule.

OpenAI's documents do not state a rationale for the intermediary section. The introductory text remains unchanged word for word, including the statement that OpenAI reserves all rights to withhold access where it reasonably believes it necessary to protect its service or users or anyone else. The privacy section still bars uses such as facial recognition databases built without data subject consent and reads exactly as before. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers find elderly health monitoring AI lacks human centered privacy features
stories.Summary:
An international research team published a comprehensive review in Discover Artificial Intelligence on November 21, 2026. The investigators examined how remote health monitoring systems for elderly patients protect patient confidentiality. They found that privacy mechanisms rarely incorporate human-centered artificial intelligence principles. Most systems do not involve elderly end users directly in the design. The review revealed a lack of user-facing controls in existing engineering studies.

The team analyzed forty-five primary studies published between 2020 and 2025 from IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and Web of Science. Search cycles occurred in May 2025 and May 2026, retrieving 202 initial records. India led research with eight studies, followed by China with six and Japan with five. The United States and Taiwan contributed three each, while Australia and Canada provided two each. Fourteen other nations and two multi-country partnerships also provided single studies.

The researchers stated that most studies rely on technical data transformations rather than human-centered design. They noted that nominal transparency is not meaningful if elderly users cannot comprehend the feedback. The authors argued that technical explainability must become actionable, low-burden indicators for vulnerable populations. They found that ethical awareness is often reduced to mathematical data perturbation. The team emphasized that these systems often lack direct evidence of stakeholder participation.

Older adults are affected by cognitive, accessibility, and digital-literacy barriers when navigating complex privacy settings. Patients are vulnerable to risks from unprocessed audio, video feeds, thermopile arrays, and wearable telemetry. Third-party cloud infrastructure may be untrusted or susceptible to unauthorized access. Some systems use non-invasive equipment like LiDAR and millimeter-wave radar to detect falls. However, distributed architectures introduce localized security vulnerabilities and risks of physical tampering.

Remote monitoring helps older adults maintain medical oversight and reduces the need for frequent in-person examinations. These systems gather sensitive physiological, behavioral, and environmental information outside conventional clinics. Most reviewed models focus on prediction tasks, specifically fall detection and activities of daily living. Research accelerated in 2024, with 60 percent of literature coming from international conferences. Only two of the forty-five studies explored generative artificial intelligence models.

The researchers will continue to examine how algorithmic safeguards align with human-centered dimensions. They leave open the psychological impact of persistent ambient surveillance on patient dignity. The review did not evaluate human-centered features directly with any elderly participants. Future work may need to include non-English language literature to find more studies. It remains unclear how to effectively integrate personal autonomy into these technical frameworks.

The Discounted Cash Flow approach looks at the cash Capgemini can return to shareholders over time and discounts it back to today. stories.Headline: Human auditors fully identify only 17 percent of planted sabotage mechanisms in a Redwood Research study
stories.Summary:
Human auditors fully identified only 17 percent of the sabotage mechanisms planted in a Redwood Research study, the outlet reported on November 21, 2026. The experiment covered 22 research logs, 10 benign and 12 sabotaged, containing 33 distinct mechanisms. Twenty-five auditors completed 104 reviews, each with a 90-minute time limit. Their ability to distinguish sabotaged work from honest work was barely above chance, and the difference was not statistically significant. They missed 74 percent of mechanisms entirely.

Keshav Shenoy and seven coauthors submitted the paper to arXiv on November 16 and revised it November 18. Their November 20 Redwood Research post details the methods and caveats. Seventeen of the 33 mechanisms were classified as major, meaning each could independently change the project's main conclusion. The authors describe potential sabotage ranging from subtle bugs and poor methods to omitted results and unsupported conclusions. Auditors assigned a probability that sabotage had occurred and offered five guesses about its mechanism, without penalties for wrong guesses.

The researchers see potential in AI systems that can audit research repeatedly at scale. But detecting suspicious work is not the same as knowing what to fix, and false accusations could penalize legitimate research. The authors say using audit findings to train away sabotage creates another problem, because false accusations could degrade capabilities or make training less efficient. They describe stronger models as likely outperforming humans rather than establishing a clear winner. The authors say targeted sabotage may be harder than their setup implies.

Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra both scored above the human auditors, but those advantages also weren't statistically significant. Awarding half credit for partially identifying a mechanism, humans scored 21.9 percent, compared with 37.1 percent for Claude Fable 5.1 and 32.6 percent for GPT-6 Astra. Weaker models scored near or below the human auditors. Astra and Fable also scored higher than humans at distinguishing sabotaged logs, with AUROCs of 0.74 and 0.73. Combining every human and AI audit still left 13 of the 33 mechanisms never fully identified.

Human auditors' 0.59 AUROC for separating sabotaged from benign work was not statistically better than chance. No decision threshold caught most sabotaged runs without also flagging many benign ones. In one log, four of five auditors found one major mechanism, but nobody found the other two. Restricting analysis to attacks rated harder to catch reduced mechanism identification, reaching zero for the two hardest-rated attacks. Overall ability to distinguish sabotaged from benign research did not fall, however.

The saboteur knew the honest experimental results before designing attacks. Asked to predict those results, Redwood researchers fully predicted only about 40 percent of outcomes. All logs came from one researcher, and the statistical uncertainty was wide. Projects were small, and the largest took two weeks of serial work. Auditors had less AI safety experience than the authors would want in real-world reviews.

Articles.Title: Human auditors miss most planted sabotage in AI safety research study

stories.Headline: Bytedance releases an open model to show that AI training pipelines can be simplified
stories.Summary:
A team from the parent company of TikTok, Bytedance, and several universities in the United States released a new paper on November 21, 2026. These researchers argue that the complex training pipelines currently used for AI agents are largely unnecessary for achieving high performance. They aim to prove that only three specific training steps are required to create a competitive open model. This effort challenges the current industry trend of stacking numerous nested training phases one after another.

The proposed approach simplifies how models learn to research the web, run code, and solve multi-step tasks. By reducing the number of phases, the team believes it will be easier to identify which specific steps actually improve the model. This change addresses the growing problem where reproducing AI work has become prohibitively expensive for many developers. The researchers suggest that the current method of layering training stages makes it nearly impossible to track effectiveness.

The Bytedance team is responsible for these findings and believes that the industry has overcomplicated the development of AI agents. They state that the current reliance on deeply nested pipelines creates unnecessary barriers to innovation and transparency. By providing a competitive open model, they intend to demonstrate that a streamlined process can yield similar results. This move encourages other developers to move away from expensive and opaque training methodologies.

stories.Headline: Gene Munster attributes AI stock sell-off to investor fear rather than fundamentals
stories.Summary:
Gene Munster of Deepwater Asset Management reported on Friday, November 21, 2026, that a recent sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks is driven by investor fear. Several companies focused on this technology have seen their values drop between 30% and 50% over the last six weeks. The Nasdaq index has declined by roughly 16% since the beginning of October, though this is not an unprecedented event. This downturn is fueled by anxiety regarding future earnings, financing conditions, and the sustainability of data center construction.

The current market situation requires more buyers than sellers to end the decline and stabilize prices. Investors are specifically worried about potential estimate cuts over multiple quarters and the impact of export restrictions related to China. Other critical factors include political resistance to new data centers and the ongoing role of Nvidia in supporting the ecosystem. Munster noted that the market previously experienced a 24% sell-off during the DeepSeek shock and tariff uncertainty in early 2025.

Munster stated that the sell-off is about psychology rather than deteriorating fundamentals, though he admitted that getting the fundamentals right does not always mean getting the stock price right. He suggested that late January could be a turning point when companies report their December-quarter results. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives also argued that the downturn is disconnected from reality and that the AI opportunity is less than 15% complete. Ives believes that chip demand remains robust and that this period represents a generational opportunity to buy winning companies.

stories.Headline: Gemini 3.0 Pro matches expert algorithms on cancer symptom guidance but falls short on depression
stories.Summary:
A multicenter research team from the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Northeastern University, Elimu Informatics, Brigham and Women's Hospital, and the Medical University of South Carolina tested Google DeepMind's Gemini 3.0 Pro on two clinical informatics functions. The team evaluated the model's ability to interpret narrative and semi-structured updates in published clinical guidelines and incorporate them into existing symptom management algorithms. The team also assessed the model's ability to translate complex decision trees into patient-specific clinical recommendations for simulated patient vignettes. The study was published in Frontiers in Medicine and covered cancer-related fatigue, pain, and depression. The artificial intelligence system demonstrated high concordance with expert consensus standards and rule-based decision support logic.

The study evaluated decision support algorithms from the Sapphire Cancer Symptom Management system, known as CDS-Sx, which classify clinical knowledge across four operational layers. The original fatigue algorithm comprised 29 decision nodes and 19 unique clinical pathways. The depression algorithm spanned 42 decision nodes and 39 pathways. The pain algorithm encompassed 1,425 decision nodes and 3,194 separate pathways. The authors supplied Gemini 3.0 Pro with explicit Level 2 semi-structured decision trees alongside formal guideline documents.

Two-member expert review panels used an agile rapid qualitative analysis methodology combined with evidence mapping. The panels scored each proposed algorithmic update across four predefined rubric domains. Detection was scored on a zero-to-two scale, completeness on a zero-to-three scale, accuracy on a zero-to-three scale, and safety risk on a zero-to-two scale. Pre-specified acceptable study-level performance required a mean detection score of at least 1.5, mean completeness of at least 2.0, and mean accuracy of at least 2.0. At least 80 percent of items had to meet acceptable individual thresholds and at least 95 percent had to introduce no meaningful clinical risk.

For cancer-related fatigue, the model exceeded all pre-specified acceptability thresholds across 19 evaluated items. It recorded a mean detection score of 1.9, a mean completeness score of 2.8, a mean accuracy score of 2.8, and a safety score of 2.0, with 100 percent of items deemed free of clinical risk. The system elevated evidence-based non-pharmacologic interventions such as exercise, cognitive behavioral therapy, and mindfulness to first-line status while discouraging routine psychostimulant use. The model incorporated critical opioid safety measures, identified contraindications for meperidine, and highlighted pharmacokinetic drug-drug interactions between dexamethasone and opioids metabolized by CYP3A4. It confirmed transdermal buprenorphine as a valuable therapy in patients presenting with renal impairment.

For depression, mean detection reached 1.0, completeness averaged 1.6, and accuracy averaged 1.5, with only 57 percent of items meeting acceptable accuracy criteria. This decline was driven by the omission of non-pharmacologic integrative modalities from Society for Integrative Oncology companion guidelines, including music therapy, reflexology, relaxation techniques, Tai Chi, and Qi Gong. The model generated explicit agent-level suggestions, such as favoring specific selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or avoiding paroxetine in patients taking tamoxifen due to CYP2D6 inhibition. Clinician judges noted that the suggestions were safe, clinically appropriate, and concordant with practice.

The model maintained an uncompromised safety profile. The first vignette described a 62-year-old man with stage IV small cell lung cancer, bone metastases, stage 3b chronic kidney disease, and severe persistent fatigue. The second vignette detailed a 55-year-old woman with metastatic colon cancer receiving FOLFIRI chemotherapy who presented with severe depression, moderate abdominal pain, and chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy. The third vignette involved a 55-year-old man with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer invading the brachial plexus who experienced severe mixed somatic and neuropathic pain despite escalating sustained-release and immediate-release morphine regimens.

Across all three vignettes, the model registered overall F1-scores between 0.86 and 0.96 and a precision score of 1.00 in all three cases. For the fatigue vignette, the system achieved a recall between 0.86 and 0.92, reproducing 12 of 14 reference recommendations and omitting only late-line integrative therapies and short-course dexamethasone intended primarily for end-of-life care. In the depression vignette, the model achieved a recall of 0.85 by reproducing 11 of 13 recommendations, correctly suggesting mental health referral, duloxetine initiation to address co-occurring neuropathy, physical therapy, and bowel prophylaxis, while omitting oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and naloxone co-prescription. In the pain vignette, the model produced an F1-score of 0.86 and a recall of 0.75, generating 9 of 12 reference recommendations.

The system correctly guided opioid titration, recommended topical lidocaine patches for focal neuropathic burning, initiated gabapentin titration, incorporated cold and heat therapy, recommended bone-modifying agents, and added naloxone co-prescription and bowel prophylaxis. The three missing elements were scheduled acetaminophen, upward duloxetine titration, and future consideration of a tricyclic antidepressant if initial therapies failed. Qualitative analysis confirmed that discordance stemmed entirely from omission rather than commission. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Meta rejects plans to build AI that posts for deceased users
stories.Summary:
Meta announced on November 21, 2026, that it has no plans to build an AI that posts for dead users. The company was granted a patent for an SNS avatar that could simulate social media activity. This technology would use a language model trained on a user's past interactions to act on their behalf. Meta clarified that receiving a patent does not mean the company will implement the technology. The patent, identified as US12513102B2, describes a system for users who are absent or deceased.

Facebook and Instagram currently allow families to convert profiles into memorialised accounts that lock logins. TikTok and X allow families with death certificates to request full account removal. Facebook offers tools to hide memories by date range, while Instagram lets users filter names. A Meta spokesperson stated the company has no plans to move forward with the posthumous AI example. Mark Zuckerberg said interacting with memories could be helpful for those who are grieving.

The patent filing argued that a user's absence is more permanent and severe if they are deceased. These statements frame the technology as a potential fix for the loss of a user. Minedco and Re;memory already sell conversational versions of remembrance using stored posts, photographs, and recordings. Minedco uses a patent-pending engine called Coop to power its Epitaph line of Conversational Memorials. Re;memory provides lifelike avatars based on voice and photos to help users find solace.

These startups target mourners who want more than the static pages offered by larger platforms. The articles explain that memorialised accounts preserve a snapshot and treat a person's voice as finished. This approach avoids the risks of voice cloning or putting words in a dead person's mouth. In contrast, generative AI tools simulate patterns from data but cannot know new thoughts. Meta's other AI experiments, like the Muse agent, have previously suffered from technical flaws.

The sources leave open whether users actually find closure through digital avatars or conversational memorials. There are no confirmed launch dates, consumer prices, or user counts for the Epitaph product line. It remains unconfirmed if any posthumous AI account system is currently available to the general public. The articles do not detail the processing times for account removal requests on TikTok or X.
