stories.Headline: Majisemi holds webinar on moving industrial AI past proof-of-concept stage
stories.Summary:
Majisemi Inc. announced on November 22, 2026 that it will hold a webinar titled "Siemens Expert Talk FY27 Part 3: Industrial AI, why does it stop at PoC? Enhanced Edition," according to a press release distributed through PR Times. The company, based in Chiyoda Ward, Tokyo, with capital of 10 million yen and established in January 2018, presents the session as part of a Siemens expert talk series for fiscal 2027. The announcement says many companies achieve certain results in proofs of concept for generative AI and AI agents but still struggle to expand them into actual on-site work, leaving their use limited. It also notes that with attacks exploiting PHP vulnerabilities and corporate information leaks being reported, concerns remain about security when AI is built into business operations.

The release says industrial AI stalls at the proof-of-concept stage not only because of AI performance but also because industrial data is fragmented, with information from ERP, PLM and MES managed separately by department. Because the relationships between data and their business meaning are not organized, the release says, it is difficult for AI to correctly grasp on-site conditions and connect that to decisions and execution of work. For production operation, it adds, it is also essential to design roles and authority that clarify the scope left to AI agents and the scope confirmed and approved by people. The webinar will explain secure integration and governance for linking data split across ERP, PLM and MES together with business context so AI can be used in actual work.

The session will cover Siemens Intelligence Center X, or ICX, and how it connects enterprise data with AI and business applications, and it will address role and authority design for AI agents using Mendix, along with application visualization, testing and continuous verification and maintenance. It will also introduce the Mendix product roadmap toward 2027 and the outlook for AI, presenting perspectives for clarifying the responsibility of AI and people while continuously using individual proof-of-concept results across an entire company. The release lists intended attendees including people in manufacturing, information systems and DX promotion departments at large companies, people who have run AI proofs of concept but cannot move to on-site or company-wide deployment, people who want to connect data dispersed across ERP, PLM and MES, and people who want to strengthen security and governance such as AI agent permission management and application vulnerability measures. Majisemi says it will continue to hold webinars useful to participants, and it points readers to its past seminar materials and other seminars currently accepting applicants.

stories.Headline: AI bug hunting prompts rushed patches that overwhelm systems and cause outages
stories.Summary:
A series of recent technology outages affecting JPMorgan Chase transactions, Microsoft Outlook and a classified National Security Agency network may stem from a rapid effort to patch security vulnerabilities, according to officials who briefed members of Congress. Wall Street executives and the NSA told lawmakers that the disruptions were caused by attempts to fix flaws identified by artificial intelligence models, The Washington Sun reported. The outages do not appear to be cyberattacks, and officials said the sheer volume of fixes temporarily overwhelmed the systems they were designed to protect. A congressional official noted that AI models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, which increases the urgency for immediate patching.

Microsoft fixed a record 1,400 security flaws in a single monthly update recently, a significant jump from about 170 a year earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported. That increase is linked to AI bug-hunting models such as Anthropic's Mythos and similar models from OpenAI. The NSA's classified internal network, NSANet, went offline because of a software patch for major PHP vulnerabilities discovered last month, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton confirmed. PHP powers approximately 70 per cent of the world's websites, and Clayton stated that the incident was not a cyberattack or a coordinated nation-state action.

Not all the outages fit that explanation, since Microsoft's Outlook disruption, which affected over 450 million Microsoft 365 users, was traced to a latent bug on its networking gateway servers. The Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop resulted from a data flood hitting its network, possibly linked to a new router, and the FAA blamed legacy equipment. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin indicated that pushing new technology onto older systems seems to overwhelm them, suggesting more such incidents are likely. Companies and government agencies are using powerful AI models to find weak spots before hackers exploit them, and that pressure has led to faster rollout of fixes, according to The Washington Sun.

stories.Headline: Google gives AI Ultra subscribers Genie 4 with real-time world editing
stories.Summary:
Google made Genie 4 available to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers on November 20, 2026, introducing a new Project Genie experience for those users. Project Genie is an experimental research prototype that lets users generate and explore interactive worlds, and the update provides first-time access to Genie 4 along with upgrades to Genie 3. Genie 4, which Google describes as its most realistic world model, enables users to prompt mid-session to alter worlds they have created. This allows for real-time editing of environments while users are navigating them, and users can change weather conditions, add characters, or redirect actions within their worlds.

Genie 4 also integrates real-time native audio that adapts as scenes unfold, including ambient soundscapes and character dialogue. The Project Genie agent assists users in building their visions, and a community gallery is available for discovering, exploring, and remixing worlds. Project Genie combines advanced world models with Gemini models, allowing users to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from their browser. The update enhances the Project Genie experience by enabling users to generate and explore interactive worlds with real-time editing and audio.

Google is the company responsible for the rollout, and it made Genie 4 available to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers as the article reports. Google describes Genie 4 as its most realistic world model, and the article says the model enables users to prompt mid-session to alter worlds they have created. The article does not include any further statements from Google or from named individuals about the release. The rollout gives subscribers first-time access to Genie 4 and upgrades to Genie 3, according to the article.

The context is that Project Genie is an experimental research prototype that combines advanced world models with Gemini models for browser-based world shaping. The article does not say what happens next beyond the availability of Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers and the features described. The community gallery remains available for discovering, exploring, and remixing worlds, and the Project Genie agent assists users in building their visions. stories.Headline: Calif researchers use GPT-6 Cyber to find a critical Java memory bug
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the cybersecurity startup Calif used OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber to uncover a critical memory corruption bug in Java, a programming language widely used across banking, aviation and other critical sectors, according to TechGig. The vulnerability affects the memory safety of Java's base64 decoder, which is a common method for representing binary data as text. Calif stated that malformed input, specifically 64 "A" characters followed by one equal sign, can overwrite neighbouring memory. That corruption can reveal sensitive memory or lead to remote code execution, which grants unauthorised access to the underlying system. The discovery was published on November 20, 2026.

Oracle, Java's current steward, has issued patches for the flaw and urged customers to apply them without delay. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, known as CERT-In, has issued a high-severity advisory and urged Indian organisations across public sector, private banking, fintech and consumer internet verticals to apply the Oracle patch. Java powers 90 per cent of Fortune 500 companies and is used in critical sectors globally. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency also urged users to identify all Java installations and monitor for security patches.

Calif's researcher Quang Luong used AI to find and weaponise the Java vulnerability, and the startup coined the term "centaur hacker" for human-AI collaboration in security research. The company said the approach combines AI and human expertise to discover the flaw. This discovery follows Calif's AI-assisted research that exposed critical flaws in PHP a month prior. The articles do not say what further steps, beyond patching and monitoring, are planned.

Articles.Title: AI finds critical Java vulnerability, CERT-In issues advisory

stories.headline_source: AI finds critical Java vulnerability, CERT-In issues advisory

stories.Headline: Trina Storage unveils Elementa Hybrid Genset for AI data centers at RE+ 2026
stories.Summary:
Trina Storage introduced a new hybrid power product on Nov. 18, 2026 at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, combining gas-fired generation with the company's battery storage platforms under a single hybrid plant controller. The Elementa Hybrid Genset is aimed at data center developers that need on-site power while grid interconnection is delayed, limited, or unavailable. The launch follows a preview of the solution at Data Center World Power in September. Trina Storage unveiled Elementa Hybrid Genset at RE+ 2026, according to a PR Newswire release dated Nov. 19, 2026 in Las Vegas. The solution combines gas-fired generation from qualified partners with Trina Storage's Elementa DC battery systems and Electra AC platform, coordinated by a hybrid plant controller.

The system consists of three main components, with gas generation providing sustained power using reciprocating engines rated up to 2.5 MW in modular configurations. Trina Storage acts as the system integrator, while qualified engine partners supply the generation equipment. The Elementa and Electra BESS solution provides rapid power response and grid-forming capabilities, with reference configurations based on 5 MW/10 MWh building blocks. A hybrid plant controller coordinates all power sources in real time, and its scalable control architecture is designed to support applications ranging from 5 MW to 1 GW. The solution supports four reference scenarios: grid-connected with backup generation, grid-constrained, bridge-to-grid, and off-grid, and solar PV can also be integrated where appropriate.

Load Transient Sensing uses the power plant controller to predict changes in power demand and coordinate a rapid BESS response, allowing the system to accommodate swift load fluctuations before slower-responding power sources can adjust. Hybrid Power Coordination dynamically coordinates power output between the BESS and gas generators, so when a sudden load increase occurs the BESS responds immediately while the gas generators gradually ramp up. Fault Isolation and Resilient Power Supply addresses failures, and when a fault occurs the control system identifies and isolates the affected equipment while the BESS and remaining available gas generators respond to support critical loads. Two system architectures are available, with Load Sensing prioritizing cost efficiency and system performance while Double Conversion provides full electrical isolation and enhanced power quality. The choice between the two depends on the IT load profile and grid conditions at a given site.

Eric Cao, Vice President of Trina North American PV and BESS Business, said AI data centers have demanding power requirements, particularly when grid capacity is constrained or workloads fluctuate rapidly. Cao said Elementa Hybrid Genset brings gas generation, battery storage, and hybrid controls together in one system architecture, designed to coordinate these resources according to project needs. Trina Storage describes itself as a global leader in energy storage solutions and enters the growing field of hybrid power solutions for data centers where grid access cannot keep pace with demand. The company framed the product as a response to a pairing of limitations, since AI workloads can cause rapid and substantial fluctuations in power demand that gas generators alone may struggle to follow. Battery storage responds quickly to those fluctuations but is not designed to supply energy through extended outages on its own, according to Trina Storage.

Trina Storage says it continues to develop and validate the product through simulation, hardware-in-the-loop testing, and an integrated validation platform incorporating real power generation, conversion, and storage equipment. Further testing of grid-forming functionality and hybrid control strategies is ongoing, alongside relevant certification activities. Final system configurations and performance specifications will be assessed based on individual project requirements. The company describes the product as designed to accommodate different power requirements and grid conditions, from grid-connected sites seeking additional power flexibility to projects operating with limited or no grid access. System architecture and equipment selection can be tailored to each project's load profile, site conditions, and operational requirements.

Trina Storage is currently engaging with data center developers and project partners to explore potential applications and develop project-specific configurations. The articles state that these capabilities help coordinate different power sources within one system, with the specific operating strategy depending on the project configuration and requirements. The articles leave open the final system configurations and performance specifications, which will be assessed based on individual project requirements. The articles also leave open the outcomes of the ongoing grid-forming functionality testing, hybrid control strategy testing, and relevant certification activities. The articles do not state when the Elementa Hybrid Genset will be commercially available or which specific projects will use it.

stories.Headline: Torus raises 500 million dollars and launches Foundry modular AI inference system
stories.Summary:
Torus, a Salt Lake City-based manufacturer of distributed power and compute infrastructure, announced on November 11, 2026 that it has raised 500 million dollars in growth capital led by Magnetar, and the financing coincided with the debut of its newest product, Foundry, a modular AI infrastructure system built for inference workloads. Each Foundry unit provides 1 to 20 megawatts of inference capacity per site and moves from signed contract to running AI workloads in 12 to 16 weeks, a timeline Torus contrasts with the years required to build a conventional hyperscale campus. Foundry units are prefabricated at GigaOne, Torus's manufacturing facility in Salt Lake City, where the smallest unit measures roughly the size of a small cargo van and the modular systems require no building construction at all. On-site timelines are correspondingly compressed, with site preparation taking about a week while installation and commissioning take one to two days, and the product is designed, engineered, and manufactured in Utah by Torus's team of nearly 400 employees, with key components built in-house. Every Foundry deployment ships paired with Torus Reserve, the company's energy storage and management product, which delivers grid-enhancing technologies that Torus groups into three capabilities: inertial-based firm power, grid flexibility with load curtailment, and ramp-rate support.

These functions are executed through what Torus calls load-shaping recipes, predefined controls that govern how power is dispatched and that shape loads to manage demand, support grid stability, and ramp power in milliseconds. The integrated inertial flywheel and battery storage and management serve a dual purpose, covering demand peaks so that more compute can fit on an existing interconnection and supplying backup power during grid outages. Torus describes Foundry as a vertically integrated offering spanning fiber to site, chiller to coolant distribution unit, and grid to rack, comprising three products: Torus Reserve for load shaping and redundancy, Torus Foundry for inference compute, and Torus Protect for integrated networking and security, with every deployment turnkey and ongoing operations and maintenance handled by Torus itself rather than left to the customer. Founder and CEO Nate Walkingshaw said that inference does not have to wait, that the company has spent years learning how to make the grid more affordable, flexible, resilient, and intelligent, and that Foundry applies that to compute capacity in weeks with power that is already available. He added that most providers are bringing power to the chips while Foundry brings the chips to power, and he said the industry has largely tried to solve AI's power problem by building net-new infrastructure, an approach he described as costly and slow to bring compute online.

Torus instead treats the situation as a capacity problem before it is a generation problem, contending that many sites already have unused grid capacity that its systems can make usable, and because Foundry installs behind the meter, drawing on available headroom at individual transformers, the company says the units add steady, high-load-factor demand without triggering the infrastructure upgrades that often produce rate increases and without compromising grid reliability. Torus frames Foundry as a response to a structural change in AI demand, as workloads shift from training models to serving inference for enterprises and compute is being pulled toward on-premises and edge sites closer to where users are, with inference running continuously, responding in real time, and lending itself to distributed deployment according to the company. McKinsey data referenced in the launch forecasts annual growth of 35 percent in data center demand for AI inference through 2030, outpacing the 22 percent projected for training, and Torus notes that its customers want security, protection of intellectual property, and control over where their workloads execute, which the company says a distributed architecture can satisfy more readily than centralized capacity. Foundry debuts with first customers Hydra Host and another AI cloud provider and is offered in three commercial models: the Strategic model is a powered shell supplying power and enclosure without GPUs, the Partner model is a turnkey bare metal unit that bundles power, enclosure, and GPUs, and the Direct model delivers sovereign inference capacity straight to enterprise customers with single-tenant hardware allocated exclusively to one company's workloads. Taken together, the launch and the 500 million dollar Magnetar-led round position Torus to scale a distributed model of AI capacity delivery, one that leans on existing grid interconnections, factory-built modular hardware, and compressed deployment timelines rather than new construction.

Articles.Title: Torus Launches $500 Million AI Compute Line in Utah

stories.Headline: Developers say AI coding tools remove the struggle and risk eroding core engineering skills
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence coding tools have become part of the daily work of every software engineer Gemma Rodgers knows, and in a 2026 Stack Overflow survey 83% of software developer respondents said they use at least one AI tool, CNBC reported on November 20, 2026. Rodgers, a software developer based in the United Kingdom who began her computer science degree in 2002, told CNBC that the sense of joy and fun she used to get from working through a challenge has been removed somewhat, and that using AI can now feel like a breadcrumb of joy rather than a full meal of joy. She said AI tools have lowered the barrier to entry significantly and let many people thrive who would not have thrived five or even three years ago, but she also warned that the core skills engineers traditionally learned on the job are being lost as engineers churn work out. James Broadhead, chief technology officer of the AI decision-making company Taktile, told CNBC that engineers who might once have spent three weeks building a prototype can now generate 10 in an afternoon, and that the hardest part is having the judgment to decide which of those are any good.

Broadhead said AI agents produce so much code that engineers no longer read all of it, and that the old sense of comfort and awareness of how a whole code base was structured has given way to constant change. Joshua Wöhle, chief executive of the London-based AI training company Mindstone, told CNBC he sees a growing divide between workers who know how to use AI effectively and those who do not, and he said the industry's old talk of 10X engineers is widening into 100X engineers. Wöhle said companies will increasingly have to decide whether to help employees catch up with AI or prioritize those who get the most out of it, and he described as very real the grief of people who once excelled at writing code finding that the thing they love is no longer what the company should be paying for. Chris Sees, a software engineer of more than 20 years and chief executive of the London-based virtual office company Hoxton Mix, told CNBC he views AI as a capable junior engineer that still needs supervision, and he said the important thing is knowing what to delegate and when human judgment is needed.

Sees said he gets a lot of satisfaction from proving and spotting where AI has gone wrong, but he worries about the next generation of engineers if AI takes over the routine coding and debugging through which they traditionally learned, tasks he called where you learn lessons and build scar tissue. He said companies need to make sure AI becomes part of the learning process rather than a shortcut. Rodgers, who is self-employed, said she can use AI to automate the tedious parts of a project while keeping the more interesting problem-solving for herself, and she believes friction and discomfort are vital parts of the human experience. She said people need to feel accomplished in something and that part of accomplishment requires challenge, and that without working that through you never get the full force of the good feeling on the other side.

Articles.Title: AI is changing software engineering — and some developers miss the struggle

stories.headline_source: AI is changing software engineering — and some developers miss the struggle

stories.Headline: Pontifical Gregorian University forum participants develop solutions for Catholic AI accountability in Rome
stories.Summary:
The Builders AI Forum, an interdisciplinary conference hosted by the Pontifical Gregorian University, held a two-day program of workshops in Rome on Nov. 5-6, 2026, aimed at identifying problems facing Catholic AI development. The forum was formed two years ago and holds annual gatherings in Rome. This year's theme was "Uniting to Shape AI Before It Shapes Us." The gathering brought together church leaders, technology developers, venture capitalists and policymakers from around the world. It took place in the same weekend that Pope Leo XIV spoke to Argentines about the "challenges posed by artificial intelligence and unregulated automation."

The conference examined the lack of human accountability within AI models, potential system biases against particular languages and cultures, and the dangers of treating machines as human persons. Participants then worked together to develop possible solutions for their communities and dioceses. The conference focused on the need for positive action in addition to technology regulations. It emphasized that forming thriving Catholic communities, building responsible and properly sourced AI tools, and calling governments and tech developers to protect human labor are essential tasks for the church today. The forum's theme framed the two-day program of workshops held at the Pontifical Gregorian University.

Matthew Harvey Sanders, founder of the forum and CEO of Longbeard, the company behind AI tools such as Magisterium AI and Vulgate, framed responsible human development of AI as a duty for the church in his opening address. He quoted Leo and called Catholic developers to fill the gaps of agency, instances where AI lacks human oversight and accountability, that are often created by AI developers. Sanders said a machine that can be blamed is a convenient place for everyone above it to leave the blame. He said that before any parish, school or hospital lets an agent act for a person, someone must be able to stop it, and someone must answer for it. Sanders presented a vision for "digitizing the church's patrimony and universalizing access to it" that he has worked to implement through Longbeard's AI products.

Cardinal Michael Czerny, who heads a Vatican commission on artificial intelligence, used an image from Magnifica Humanitas contrasting two biblical construction sites, Babel and Jerusalem, as examples of different ways that technology can be developed. He said both are collective efforts, yet the manner of constructing and the outcome are very different in the two sites. Czerny said the difference between Babel and Jerusalem lies in the desire that guides the act of building. He said the contrast between the two cities presents today's primary question: out of what desire shall we build, deploy and employ artificial intelligence? Sanders told the National Catholic Reporter that he sees AI as an "unfortunate means" to evangelize the world, emphasizing that building authentic Christian community is the ultimate goal.

Sanders said he does not think Catholic AI should need to exist, and that if everyone were well formed and living in good, vibrant Catholic communities, pressing fundamental existential questions would get answered by osmosis. He said the only reason they decided they needed to develop Catholic AI was that they could see a wave of interest in the Catholic faith and were not prepared for the scale. He said their thinking was AI could be a really good instrument in the short term to help ensure people get answers to fundamental questions, but then they need to get this person into community. In his closing speech, Sanders encouraged participants not to stand idle in the face of AI's challenges, but to take action in building communities and technologies that uphold and promote human dignity. Sanders said that a year ago, Pope Leo prayed that this forum's work would bear fruit, and that fruit is something you can see and hold, and it feeds someone.

Leo's encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, called AI "a valuable tool ... [that] calls for a measured and vigilant approach." Leo warned tech developers to "embed values in their projects with due seriousness: with transparency, responsibility toward affected communities and careful attention to ensuring that what is being cultivated is a genuine good." Leo's Nov. 6-17 Latin America trip included a stop in Argentina, where he spoke to representatives of the country's work community about the dignity of labor and the dangers of encroaching technology.

On Nov. 8, the pope addressed workers, business and trade union leaders, and teachers and students at the Catholic University of Argentina in Buenos Aires. Leo reminded the crowd of "the dignity of the human person ... [who] is the author, the center and the goal of all economic and social life." Leo warned that "the challenges posed by artificial intelligence and unregulated automation can put countless jobs at risk and become a real threat to proper integral human development."

The pope's address came as Argentina's Congress considers legislation submitted by the Javier Milei administration that would grant legal recognition to companies operated solely by AI. Milei's proposed legislation comes after an announcement last October that a massive AI data center project, Stargate Argentina, will be constructed in Patagonia. The articles leave open what the forum's participants will do with the solutions they developed for their communities and dioceses. They also leave open the outcome of Argentina's Congress consideration of the Milei administration's legislation on companies operated solely by AI.

Articles.Title: Rome forum explores how AI can serve Catholicism, guided by Pope Leo's warnings

stories.Headline: John Deere acquires Orchard AI to add plant-level crop intelligence for growers
stories.Summary:
John Deere announced on November 19, 2026, that it has acquired Orchard Robotics, which operates as Orchard AI, a San Francisco-based agriculture technology company founded in 2022 that develops crop intelligence solutions for high-value crop growers. The deal strengthens Deere's ability to help growers make more informed decisions throughout the growing season by combining Orchard AI's detailed, plant-level crop insights with Deere's own expertise in precision agriculture, equipment, and farm technology. Orchard AI uses vehicle-mounted, AI-powered cameras to capture data for every individual tree, vine, or plant across a farm, all season long. With every pass through the field, the system analyzes hundreds of images per tree, giving growers a detailed view of crop conditions alongside accurate yield estimates, precise fruit counts, fruit size and color data, canopy measurements, and more. Its FruitScope software platform enables growers to visualize and use this data to make more informed farm management decisions, improving their efficiency of labor, time, and inputs across their operations.

For high-value crop growers, months of work and investment can depend on making the right decisions within narrow windows, since a missed spray application or mistimed harvest can affect fruit quality, yield, and an entire season's profitability. Weather, labor constraints, and changing crop conditions add pressure, leaving growers little time to determine what each block needs and get the work done. Combining Orchard AI's detailed view of crop conditions with Deere technology and equipment can help growers understand exactly what their trees need and act at the right time throughout the growing season. These capabilities can better inform critical decisions, from pruning and thinning trees, applying crop treatments where they are needed, and identifying which blocks are ready for harvest. The integrated AI software translates precision data into actionable recommendations, so growers can identify areas with higher bloom counts and receive a prescription on where to spray, delivered directly to a mobile device for in-field application or into an in-cab G5 display.

Tim Marquis, Director of Farm Systems Innovation at John Deere, said everything the company does starts with helping its customers succeed, and that the acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field. He said bringing these capabilities together gives Deere an opportunity to help growers make more informed decisions across their operations and get more value from the technology they already rely on. Charlie Wu, CEO of Orchard AI, said the company was started to give growers the crop intelligence they need to farm more profitably and sustainably than ever before, and that joining John Deere lets it accelerate that mission. Justin Rose, President of the Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division, Small Ag & Turf at John Deere, said a big part of what makes Orchard AI successful is its speed of innovation and the close relationships it has built directly with customers. He said Deere wants to preserve those strengths while bringing its scale and capabilities to help Orchard AI reach more growers and solve real challenges in agriculture.

Tyler Klick of Redwood Empire Vineyard Management, an early user of Orchard AI's technology, said what impresses him most about Charlie and the Orchard AI team is their ability to listen to what growers need and put it into action. He said he has been very impressed with the insights the scans are providing from a precision farming standpoint. Orchard AI describes itself as "The AI Farming Company," and says industry leaders across specialty crops trust it for precise crop data that helps them make better decisions. The announcement did not disclose the purchase price or other financial terms of the deal.

stories.Headline: FCA launches AI Spotlight Observatory to share financial sector use cases
stories.Summary:
The Financial Conduct Authority published a press release on 19 November 2026 announcing the launch of its pioneering AI Spotlight Observatory, an online resource that brings together real-world examples of artificial intelligence use across the financial services sector. The regulator describes the Observatory as a first of its kind tool developed by a regulator, which can make AI adoption easier to explore and understand. It is intended to help firms, innovators, researchers and policymakers identify emerging trends, learn from developments across the market and support responsible innovation. The platform features a broad range of use cases, from solutions designed to combat financial crime and enhance compliance processes to emerging technologies such as agentic payments and neurosymbolic AI. The Observatory builds on the FCA's previous initiatives, including the AI Lab, which supports innovating firms as they develop new AI models and solutions.

It also follows the Supercharged Sandbox, an enhancement to the FCA's existing Digital Sandbox that gives firms access to high-performance computing, databases and AI tools so they can innovate and experiment with AI safely. The regulator recently published examples of AI good practice and areas of improvement to support the safe and responsible adoption of AI in financial services. The new platform is open and available to anyone interested in understanding emerging trends and opportunities in this field, learning from real-world implementation and supporting responsible innovation. The FCA openly invites a wide range of firms, especially those developing particularly innovative AI solutions, to register to access more detailed insights and to submit their own AI use cases. The regulator says the platform will evolve with new use cases submitted over time.

The press release does not name individual FCA officials or give any further statements beyond the description of the platform and its aims. Responsibility for the Observatory rests with the FCA, which developed the tool as part of its wider work on AI in financial services. The launch comes amid the FCA's broader efforts to support responsible AI adoption across the sector, following its AI Lab, Supercharged Sandbox and published good practice examples. The articles do not say what further steps the regulator plans beyond inviting firms to register and submit use cases. The Observatory is available now to anyone interested in emerging trends and opportunities in this field.

Articles.Title: FCA launches world-first platform giving firms new insight into AI innovation

stories.Headline: Chinese tech giants double AI spending as lab revenue fails to cover costs
stories.Summary:
Major Chinese technology firms are expected to double their capital spending to 139 billion dollars in 2026, according to research from Rhodium Group. These companies are struggling to fund the soaring costs of training powerful artificial intelligence models while facing a difficult financial landscape. This massive investment occurs as the United States and China compete for supremacy in the field of artificial intelligence. Many Chinese startups are finding it harder to secure funding compared to American rivals like Anthropic.

The financial gap is significant because revenue from artificial intelligence labs covers less than 8 percent of the projected spending. Rhodium Group forecasts that these expenditures could continue to rise and potentially top 193 billion dollars by 2027. Meanwhile, the STAR 50 index has plunged 43 percent since the end of July, reflecting a deep sell-off in Chinese tech stocks. Tech giants such as Alibaba, Baidu, and Tencent are currently grappling with negative cash flows while backing leading AI firms.

Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, stated that the financial numbers suggest these companies are running on a treadmill that is speeding up. He believes the economic pressure is becoming increasingly difficult for these organizations to manage. This financial strain may prove to be a more critical obstacle than the American export controls on advanced semiconductors. While some labs rented data centers in Southeast Asia to access Nvidia chips, the Trump administration is now moving to close that loophole.

stories.Headline: Nemetschek Group showcases AI-powered Archicad Max, Allplan Max and Bluebeam Max at Big 5 Global 2026
stories.Summary:
Nemetschek Group announced on 19 November 2026 that it will return to Big 5 Global 2026 as a Bronze Sponsor to showcase AI, connected data and open digital workflows for the Middle East's architecture, engineering, construction and operations sector. The 47th edition of the event runs from 23 to 26 November 2026 at the Dubai World Trade Centre. At the centre of the company's participation will be its new family of premium AI-powered offerings, Archicad Max for architecture, Allplan Max for engineering and Bluebeam Max for construction. These are powered by the Nemetschek Intelligence Platform, the Group's common AI and data foundation, and embed practical AI capabilities into established workflows to reduce repetitive work, ease access to project information and improve quality while users keep control over key decisions.

Visitors to Hall 4, Booth 4A173 can explore the connected ecosystem across Planning & Design, Build & Construct and Operate & Manage, with solutions from ALLPLAN, Graphisoft, Solibri, Vectorworks, dTwin, Bluebeam, GoCanvas and Spacewell. The showcase follows Nemetschek being named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Construction Management Software 2026 Vendor Assessment, which highlighted its suite supporting the construction lifecycle, cross-team collaboration through Bluebeam and GoCanvas, and a 24% R&D reinvestment rate. The company, founded by Professor Georg Nemetschek in 1963, employs over 4,500 experts globally, is ISO 27001-certified, has more than 7.5 million users worldwide, and has been listed in the MDAX and TecDAX since 1999. It reported revenue of EUR 1.19 billion and EBITDA of EUR 371.1 million in 2025.

Eng. Muayad Simbawa, Managing Director for the Middle East at Nemetschek Group, said the region is delivering some of the world's most ambitious built-environment projects, which makes Big 5 Global an important platform to show what practical digital transformation looks like. He said visitors will be able to walk through the building lifecycle and see how AI, connected data and interoperable workflows help teams work with greater clarity, consistency and confidence. He added that the focus is on empowering the region's professionals with technology that supports their expertise and turns digital innovation into tangible project value.

Beyond the stand, Marc Nezet, Chief Strategy Officer and Chief Division Officer Operate & Manage, will join the Global Leaders' Summit on 23 November in a session titled "Decisions that will shape the decade ahead." Simbawa will join the FutureTech Summit on 26 November for an executive panel titled "Proof, not pilots: Why transformation stalls and where the value is missed." Bjørn Kristian Stangeland, Director of Interoperability and Standards, will discuss "Turning Open Standards into Industry Practice" on 24 November as part of the buildingSMART & Geospatial Talks sessions. The articles do not say what happens after the event.

stories.Headline: Amazon nears a $7.5 billion deal to buy AI startup Decart
stories.Summary:
Amazon is nearing a deal to buy the artificial intelligence startup Decart for $7.5 billion, according to sources cited by the Financial Times. The talks between the two companies are at an advanced stage, and a deal could come together as soon as next week. The report was published by the Financial Times on November 21, 2026. The sources spoke to the newspaper about the negotiations, which have not been publicly confirmed by either company.

The reported price of $7.5 billion is the only figure the articles give for the transaction. The articles do not say what Decart does, how large it is, or how Amazon would use the company. They also give no details on the terms, the structure of the deal, or any conditions attached to it. No closing date beyond the possibility of next week is mentioned.

The articles do not name the sources beyond describing them as sources, and they do not include any statement from Amazon or from Decart. No executive from either company is quoted, and no spokesperson for either side is quoted either. Because the talks are described as advanced but not complete, the deal could still fall through. The articles do not say what would happen to the negotiations if no agreement is reached.

The articles give no background on earlier talks between the two companies or on any previous offers. They do not say what happens next beyond the possibility that a deal could come together as soon as next week. stories.Headline: GPT-6.1 Sol reads and writes executable binaries directly from hex dumps
stories.Summary:
GPT-6.1 Sol demonstrated the ability to read and write executables byte by byte from hex dumps. This capability was tested on November 21, 2026, by researchers using the Codex CLI 0.166.0. The model programmed directly in binary without using any compilers or disassemblers. It analyzed five binaries and wrote three new programs from scratch. The model also successfully identified the behavior of an unknown malware sample.

The process requires an xxd hex dump, which uses about 2.4 tokens per byte. Tests included a FreeBSD tool called ministat, a wordcount program, an AES tool, and a bank ledger. The malware sample was a 4,608-byte PE32+ file that contacted server 165.154.205.34 on port 443. All tests ran under qemu-x86_64 on Apple Silicon. The model edited segment headers at 0x44 and 0x60 to add new features.

The researchers defined this as Machine Code Programming, where models reason directly about executable bytes. They stated that LLMs may eventually write in machine code instead of using high level languages. The authors noted that the model found a real bug in the ministat tool. They explained that the model treats patching like a human by finding padding for new code. They claimed this could challenge the foundations of reverse engineering and malware analysis.

Malware analysts are affected because they usually spend hours turning samples into assembly or C code. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash also reached the same conclusion about the malware, showing this is not limited to closed models. The model identified 13 APIs by comparing rotate-right-13 hashes and found a kill switch at %TEMP%\log_de.log. It also discovered a response XOR key of 0x99. These results suggest general-purpose models can perform triage without specialized tools.

The articles explain that humans typically use compilers and linkers because x86-64 instructions vary in length. This research follows work by Takehi et al. regarding Weight-Space Programming for neural network weights. The researchers used a local relay to remove all tools and audited every event stream. They allowed only one reply per program with no feedback or second tries. The largest test binary was 67 KB, which used about 163,000 tokens.

Future work may involve a harness based on Recursive Language Models to handle larger files. The current one-shot approach is limited by context size, as a 10 MB program needs 24 million tokens. It remains unknown how the quality of the output holds up as files approach the 67 KB limit. The articles leave open whether the model can handle much larger programs. They do not specify if the model can modify or write actual malware.

stories.Headline: Researchers develop PIPETTE system to stop AI agents from retraining on repetitive prompt injections
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the University of Waterloo, Zhejiang University, and KTH Royal Institute of Technology discovered that AI agents retrained on larger sets of prompt injections often became easier to hijack. During tests conducted on models ranging from 4 billion to 27 billion parameters, the team found that automated red-teaming tools frequently repeated the same attack techniques. In one specific contest using the Qwen3-4B model across 560 tasks, the PISmith tool produced 7,132 working attacks compared to 4,282 from RL-Hammer. Despite having more successful injections, the version of the model trained on PISmith's data was hijacked 47.5 percent of the time during a stress test, while the RL-Hammer version was hijacked only 27.5 percent of the time.

This vulnerability requires a shift in how developers harden agents, as simply increasing the number of successful attacks used for retraining does not guarantee better security. The researchers developed a system called PIPETTE that sorts attacks by technique and rewards tools for finding new methods rather than repeating old ones. When tested on the AgentDojo public test bed, agents trained with PIPETTE allowed off-the-shelf injections to succeed less than half a percent of the time on average. Furthermore, the hardened Qwen3-4B model finished 64.95 percent of clean tasks, which was a slight improvement over the 61.86 percent completion rate of the original model.

The researchers explained that the gap in defense occurs because attack tools often get stuck using a single trick, such as claiming a user's task is already finished. They noted that existing variety checks often only measure differences in wording, which leads to retraining on thousands of rewordings of a few basic attacks. The team argued that the most useful metrics for security are the number of distinct techniques covered and how the agent performs against attackers allowed hundreds of attempts. They also observed that PIPETTE outperformed detection tools like PromptGuard, which blocked necessary data and caused the agent to finish the user's real task only 16.19 percent of the time.

stories.Headline: UK accelerating elite law firms gain ground by adopting AI early, Chambers finds
stories.Summary:
The first US and UK editions of the Chambers Advantage Index, a debut analysis by the legal ranking firm Chambers of a decade of its rankings data, were published on November 20, 2026, and only four law firms reached the top tier in both countries: Latham & Watkins, Kirkland & Ellis, Goodwin, and White & Case. Each firm was scored on how strong its market position is today and how fast that position is improving, which split the market into four groups: Accelerating Elite, Stable Elite, Accelerating Challengers, and Stable Challengers. The gap between the movers and the rest is stark, with US accelerators growing premium practices at a 78% higher rate and UK accelerators growing premium practices at a 54% higher rate, where premium practices are those that attract the highest value work and the firms with the highest revenue or profit margins. Latham and Kirkland made the greatest strides of all, each with significant increases in ranking volume and promotion into higher bands, while Gibson Dunn, one of the UK’s fastest-growing challengers, is close to joining the Elite there. For US firms in London, much of the growth comes through lateral hiring, as talent has moved toward US firms where UK lawyers see more opportunity and bigger rewards, and Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison is one example, adding partners across M&A, finance, and tax as part of expanding its private equity offerings.

That route carries big risk, because high-profile partners are expensive and firms have mixed success in earning a return on them or even keeping them over the long term, and mergers offer another route to a marked jump in market presence that many top performers have taken. Client feedback shows priorities differ, since a broad international footprint matters less to many US-based clients but is critical to many UK-based clients, and the UK’s leading firms are growing in the US too but have yet to match that breadth there. Not every success rests on a big bet, as Davis Polk shows practice depth with Band 1 rankings in New York for corporate M&A, banking and finance, and tax in Chambers USA 2026, and Macfarlanes has accelerated with a tightly focused domestic strategy built on premium practices and repeat work from private capital clients. In the UK, the Accelerating Elite are winning on AI, as many were early adopters of legal technology who set up alternative service delivery hubs akin to the Management Services Organization model in the US, bringing together data, technology, and paralegal expertise to drive efficiency and build data assets. That experience is now paying off, since they already have the know-how, the multidisciplinary teams, and the culture to adopt new technology at pace, and their junior lawyers report more confidence in using AI.

In the US the picture flips, with the Accelerating Challengers’ associates reporting the most successful AI adoption, while the US Accelerating Elite came to AI later but are now investing heavily. Chambers’ research with in-house legal teams shows AI is now the fastest-growing trend affecting clients’ legal needs and how they handle legal work, and fewer than 5% of clients were negative about firms using AI in the latest research. Clients still buy expertise, judgment, and great service first, but they increasingly expect firms to use technology to give them more for less, and the firms already set up to deliver that are the ones gaining ground. For everyone else, the question is how long they can afford to wait.

stories.Headline: A distributor finds agentic AI costs 20 times more than traditional architecture for the same ROI
stories.Summary:
A large regional distributor set out to build a new sales transaction management system to automate order intake, discount approvals, exception handling, customer communications and inventory checks, as David Linthicum reported in InfoWorld on November 20, 2026. After vendor presentations, the company decided to go agentic, using AI agents to manage decision flows, invoke tools, check policies and interact with enterprise systems. One vendor pitched its offering as a common LLM brain that could make decisions as if the company had hired 10,000 experts who were not on the payroll. Building the system required far more integration work than expected, with each agent needing clean data, governed APIs, business rules, security controls, observability and human override mechanisms. The project ran fine in production, but six months later the company found the system cost roughly 20 times more than a traditional architecture and delivered about the same ROI.

Linthicum wrote that he hears versions of this story once or twice a week from clients, colleagues and friends. He said agentic AI is powerful but is being pushed into places where simpler technology would deliver the same business value for far less money. He described the pattern as familiar, with names, diagrams and conference sessions changing while every enterprise architecture discussion starts with the trend instead of the business problem. He cited cloud-native, microservices, service-oriented architecture, distributed objects and CORBA as earlier approaches that promised flexible, reusable, distributed systems. He said each pattern had value and solved real problems but caused expensive failures when adopted as a default answer rather than a fit-for-purpose architecture.

Linthicum said SOA gave enterprises a language for service reuse and integration and pushed teams away from tightly coupled monoliths and point-to-point chaos. He said SOA became expensive and complex quickly, with enterprise service buses turning into central chokepoints and governance becoming heavyweight. He said teams spent more time debating service contracts, standards, registries and middleware than delivering business features, and SOA became an architecture tax in many companies. He said microservices worked well for organizations with strong devops practices, mature automation, disciplined domain boundaries and high-scale needs. He said many companies shattered ordinary applications into dozens or hundreds of services and traded code complexity for network complexity, creating distributed failure modes, data consistency problems, monitoring challenges and testing headaches.

Linthicum said containers and Kubernetes brought portable workloads, declarative deployment, elastic scaling, automated recovery and a modern operating model. He said many enterprises moved systems into containers and Kubernetes without a clear reason, adding clusters, service meshes, observability stacks, platform engineering teams, security layers and specialized skills. He said the architecture nearly doubled the cost of running systems that did not need that level of abstraction in many cases. He said agentic systems require model access, prompt management, tool orchestration, evaluation frameworks, security controls, audit trails, human-in-the-loop design, data governance and new operational skills. He said they introduce nondeterministic behavior into processes that may require deterministic outcomes and can make simple automation much more expensive than it needs to be.

Linthicum said enterprises should start with value, not architecture, and that the value must be measurable rather than vague promises of automation. He said agentic AI works best where a problem requires interpretation, adaptation and semi-autonomous action, and is less compelling when a process is stable, rules-based, highly regulated or easily expressed through traditional logic. He said a traditional workflow engine, rules platform, API integration or conventional application delivering the same result at one-tenth the cost matters. He said enterprises need to separate impressive demos from practical use cases, because a system that looks intelligent in a conference demo may be expensive, fragile and hard to govern in production. He said skepticism is healthy and every architecture has positives and negatives.

Linthicum said the job of enterprise architects is not to follow the trend but to understand it, test it against business value and apply it only where it fits. He said otherwise we are destined to make the same mistakes over and over again. He wrote that agentic AI will have automation benefits along with governance, security and operations challenges. He said SOA gave us value and complexity, microservices gave us agility and operational burden, and cloud-native delivered scalability and cost expansion. He is an internationally recognized industry expert who has authored 13 books on computing, the latest being An Insider's Guide to Cloud Computing, and his views are his own.

stories.Headline: Apple settles Siri lawsuit for $250 million as claimants seek at least $61 per iPhone
stories.Summary:
In May, Apple agreed to pay $250 million to settle a U.S. class action lawsuit over Siri AI's delayed launch, MacRumors reported on Saturday, November 21, 2026. The report said one month remained to submit a claim through the settlement website. In a court document earlier that week, lawyers said claimants will likely receive at least $61 per eligible iPhone, based on early participation data so far. The article was published at 9:08 am PST and written by Joe Rossignol. The lawsuit alleged false advertising after Apple delayed the personalized version of Siri in March 2025.

Apple will pay a minimum of $25 per eligible iPhone to eligible customers, who can submit a claim via the settlement website until December 21 of this year. The exact payment may be higher or lower than $25 depending on the total number of valid claims submitted and other factors, with the maximum amount set at $95. To be eligible, a person must reside in the U.S. and have purchased one of the listed iPhone models in the U.S. for purposes other than resale between June 10, 2024 and March 29, 2025. Eligible customers should have already been notified by email, which contains a claim ID and a PIN code, though the settlement website also offers an option to submit a claim without this information. The claims form asks for personal information and the eligible iPhone's serial number, and if the serial number is unavailable, it asks for the Apple Account email address and the eligible iPhone's phone number.

Apple denies all of the allegations made in the lawsuit and agreed to the settlement to avoid the costs and risks of a trial. In a statement, Apple touted a range of other Apple Intelligence features it had already released. Nevertheless, Apple agreed to settle the lawsuit "to stay focused" on "delivering the most innovative products and services to our users." The lawyers representing the class members expect payouts of at least $61 per eligible iPhone, unless there is a significant uptick in claims submitted. According to the terms of the settlement, each person who files an eligible claim will receive a per-device payment of $25, but this amount could increase up to $95 if the total number of claims submitted is lower than anticipated.

On November 16, the lawyers representing the class members estimated that claimants will receive at least $61 per eligible iPhone. A final approval hearing is scheduled for February 24, 2027, so payments to customers are not expected to begin until some point next year. The settlement website answers some common questions about opting out of the settlement and other important topics, and the article advised reading it carefully. The article said Apple finally announced Siri AI at WWDC 2026 in June, and Siri AI is available on iPhone 15 Pro models and newer running iOS 27, which was released in September. Siri AI is still considered a beta feature even though iOS 27 is no longer in beta.

In June 2024, Apple previewed new Siri capabilities powered by Apple Intelligence, including understanding of a user's personal context, on-screen awareness, and deeper per-app controls. For example, Apple showed an iPhone user asking Siri about their mother's flight and lunch reservation plans based on info from the Mail and Messages apps. Apple advertised those Siri features in product presentations, on its website, in a TV commercial starring actor Bella Ramsey, and elsewhere. In March 2025, Apple delayed the launch of the personalized version of Siri, leading to the company being hit with a class action lawsuit alleging false advertising. The article noted that in May, Apple agreed to pay $250 million to settle the lawsuit.

The claims deadline is December 21, and the final approval hearing is scheduled for February 24, 2027. Payments to customers are not expected to begin until some point next year. stories.Headline: Paul Schrader uses AI to write scripts and create synthetic actors for his films
stories.Summary:
In New York on November 21, 2026, filmmaker Paul Schrader discussed his use of artificial intelligence. The eighty year old director is using the technology to create scripts, special effects, and synthetic actors. He believes that the takeover of cinema by this technology is inevitable for the entire world. Schrader describes the process of unleashing this power as opening the cage of a monster without a leash. He is embracing these tools as he enters the final act of his long professional career.

The filmmaker is collaborating with the San Francisco studio Fable on a horror thriller called The Doors of Perception. This movie uses AI generated psychedelic hallucinations to tell a story about two brothers hunting their mother's killer. Schrader is also using AI characters for a script titled Three Guns at Dawn about three Black criminal brothers. He is considering an AI version of a western movie which he has titled Nine Men from Now. These projects allow him to make films without expensive star actors or the involvement of major studios.

Schrader told the Guardian that he does not see a place for humans in the larger scheme of things. He stated that any story where man defeats the threat of AI is simply a bogus story. The director said that AI actors are beneficial because they are always available, free, and on time. He believes the film world is driven by money and that unions cannot stop the technology. He remarked that current resistance from the industry is the last cry of a dying species.

Other directors like Steven Spielberg and Christopher Nolan express deep scepticism about the use of artificial intelligence. The performers union Sag-Aftra requires producers to show that AI performers bring significant additional value over live actors. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences banned AI actors and screenplays from winning Oscars this year. Leading Black actors declined roles in Three Guns at Dawn because there were no good Black people in the script. These groups and individuals are trying to fend off existential threats and wholesale copyright infringement.

Schrader has a history of exploring human alienation, such as with Travis Bickle in the 1976 film Taxi Driver. He previously collaborated with Robert De Niro, Martin Scorsese, Sigourney Weaver, and Richard Gere on various acclaimed projects. In March, he experimented with the drug ayahuasca during a two week retreat in Costa Rica after his wife died. He took the drug eight times but was disappointed that he did not experience any visual hallucinations. He has also used technology to match himself with strangers for dining dates in his personal life.

Schrader will now test if audiences feel let down by films made with artificial intelligence. He previously felt spooked when AI wrote a script in his own concise tone and stage directions. He wondered if the technology is his tool or if he has become a tool for the AI. The articles leave open whether the public will accept synthetic actors in place of human performers. It remains unclear if the industry can successfully erect fences against the progress of the technology.

Businesses are also affected, especially when executives travel or temporary workers join operations.

Brown noted that some recent technology incidents involved infrastructure problems while others remain under investigation. He explained that scams are more likely to be built from publicly available data. The holiday season creates vulnerabilities as employees take time off from their jobs. AI allows for the impersonation of familiar voices to trick victims into believing relatives are distressed. These tools help criminals create messages that are increasingly difficult for people to recognize.

Kari designed and manages the CI/CD and deployment pipeline that builds, tests, security-validates, and deploys software changes for that project, where patient safety depends directly on dependable performance. Her architecture combines GitLab, Jenkins, Terraform, Ansible, Docker, and Kubernetes, while Checkmarx, Semgrep, Snyk, and Coverity add scanning layers so security and code-quality risks are caught before release. Shortlisted applicants are scored with the Rasch model, a statistical framework that converts subjective grading into a linear measurement scale. Kari's Google Scholar profile lists 52 citations, an h-index of 4, and an i10-index of 2, and her most cited paper on machine-learning-based zero-trust intrusion detection for cloud computing has earned 26 citations. A second paper on how artificial intelligence affects the software development lifecycle has gathered 13 citations, and its findings mirror the automation and validation tasks she performs on the Impella project. Her wider portfolio covers automated defect prediction, AI-assisted database query optimization, deep-learning phishing detection, network-security fault prediction, and a comparative study of the MD5, SHA-256, and SHA-512 hashing algorithms.

She treats each failure, deployment blocker, and security finding as a direct threat to patient-facing stability and takes ownership of the root-cause investigation whenever one appears. Alex Sterling, a spokesperson for Global Recognition Awards, said Kari represents the kind of candidate the Innovation, Research category exists for, someone whose academic work and daily engineering responsibilities reinforce each other rather than sitting apart. stories.Headline: Cryptographer Matthew Green warns AI advances threaten public-key cryptography and urges improved cryptographic agility
stories.Summary:
Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green warned in a series of posts on X last month that existing public-key cryptography systems were at risk because machines have begun outperforming humans in their ability to address some mathematical problems. Green wrote that he saw a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in existing public-key encryption algorithms. He said he was worried about standardized public-key encryption and some signatures, and specifically the fact that most of it is based on a small number of hard problems. Green warned that a disruptive loss of confidence in internet security systems would arise if a major cryptanalytic surprise arrives faster than standards and deployments can adapt. The comments sparked discussions on LinkedIn and elsewhere about how public-key crypto could fail, and Green is yet to respond to CSO's request for comment on the debate he sparked.

Green's warning concerned the cryptographic foundations beneath public key infrastructure, the system of certificates, keys, and certificate authorities that secures Transport Layer Security, code signing, and many other information security functions. He said the industry needs to focus on improved cryptographic agility. Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, a cryptographer and professor at Finland's Tampere University, told CSO that he takes Green's warning seriously but urges caution and said there is no need to rip and replace established industry cryptographic standards. Saarinen said cryptography has good standards, best practices, and active modernization paths, the PQC transition, and that just following those is the most sensible approach from an information security perspective. He said what has happened in 2026 is that mathematics had its Lee Sedol moment and analytical problems previously thought to be in the human domain are now being solved by computers.

Saarinen said the fear in cryptography is that AI will find a shortcut for some hard computational problems and make them easy, though AI is very good at optimizing computation and is not expected to turn all hard computational problems into trivial ones. He explained that a cryptographically relevant break can be exponential but might halve the number of bits, and that such an analytic break has happened to some relatively new schemes, such as HAWK by AI in 2026, and to numerous older proposals by humans. He said AI also played a significant role in finding a significant shortcut to the parameters of the McEliece cryptosystem, one of the earliest public-key schemes, designed in 1978. Saarinen added that the German cyber agency had been recommending a variant called Classic McEliece for quantum security since 2020, but withdrew its recommendation at the end of September.

He clarified that in both cases the schemes could still be considered secure if security parameters were adjusted, but that would have doubled public and secret keys, signatures, and ciphertexts. Saarinen said RSA and Elliptic-Curve cryptosystems are already broken from a computational-complexity viewpoint because polynomial-time quantum algorithms for them have been known since 1994, and building quantum computers is just an engineering problem. He said the main post-quantum alternatives, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA, have received more than a decade of intense analysis. Saarinen suggested a mathematical shortcut is more likely to exist in public-key cryptography given that it by definition requires mathematical structure for the trapdoor, and that symmetric-key cryptography, hashes and keyed ciphers, has simply more design freedom in this sense.

Professor Alan Woodward, a computer scientist at the University of Surrey, said LLMs are yet to make a huge dent on cryptography and that what is actually happening is that the LLMs are acting as a great tool for mathematicians, cryptographers, and computer scientists to speed up their research. Woodward said the leap of intuition needed to find the fatal flaw still seems to need humans, and that LLMs are very effective at finding flaws in implementations rather than the underlying mathematics. Woodward compared the threat posed by AI in breaking encryption schemes to the danger to legacy encryption schemes posed by quantum computers, and said both problems highlight the need for improved agility in the cryptographic schemes in use. He said people have already been migrating in preparation for Q-Day, the hypothetical future time when quantum computers are powerful enough to break public-key encryption, so in some ways that should already be addressing the risks posed, if they are real, by LLMs.

Woodward said the most effective route so far seems to be a hybrid route where we have a mix of cryptographic schemes that, whilst one or two might fall away, leaves us with others we can rely upon. He said any found to be flawed for whatever reason can be deprecated rapidly and the intact schemes used instead. Cryptography uses numerical problems, traditional ones like factoring the products of large prime numbers and discrete logarithm, and newer ones like learning with errors, and analyzing those algorithms and their complexity is part of theoretical computer science. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Metal artist Christina Thompson creates The Touch sculpture with AI to explore human and machine connection
stories.Summary:
Christina Thompson, a metal artist and welder of vacuum furnace equipment during the day, created a sculpture called “The Touch” that reflects the rapid development of artificial intelligence and the many possibilities, concerns, and unanswered questions people have about what is going on. She said she wanted to take that conversation and represent it in a physical sculpture, according to an article published by The Fabricator on November 21, 2026. Thompson first picked up a welding torch about 13 years ago when some welders in the fab shop of the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, where she worked as an emergency services officer, encouraged her to give it a try. She was hooked from that moment, purchased a small welding machine shortly afterwards, began making metal flowers, and eventually decided to pursue a welding career by taking formal classes and earning her certifications.

For “The Touch,” Thompson wanted the creative process to reflect her motivation as well, so she wanted to collaborate with AI, which meant striking up conversations with ChatGPT. She decided to use Michelangelo’s “The Creation of Adam,” where God and Adam reach out to almost touch fingers, as an inspiration, with the difference being that man is the creator in this scenario. Thompson said she laid a lot of metal while TIG welding the human and robotic hands and then removed a good bit by grinding the pieces into the shapes she wanted, noting that with TIG welding she really can control what she is doing and is basically sculpting with a pencil. Because the sculpture is called “The Touch,” she thought it should be an artistic piece that encouraged the viewer to reach out and touch it, which is where her husband, Darren Thompson, helped by developing an electric base that houses a speaker and wiring.

When viewers push an illuminated button at the base of the sculpture, they hear a three-minute narration about the sculpture, voiced by Christina, which says that the viewer becomes part of the work and completes the circuit between human intention and machine response. The narration says that without touch there is silence and with touch there is creation, and that the piece is not just a sculpture but a question, a warning, and a celebration. Thompson has spent the last year working on “The Touch,” and even with that work and some of her other works displayed at an art gallery, she said she is in no hurry to jump into another large sculpture. She is spending her time working on smaller pieces, like ocean scenes and palm trees, according to the article.

stories.Headline: Swedish MASAI trial finds AI supported breast screening meets noninferiority criterion for interval cancers
stories.Summary:
The Swedish MASAI trial reported in 2026 on interval cancers, which are cancers found after a negative screening and before the next scheduled round, and among about 106,000 randomised participants there were 82 interval cancers in the AI supported group and 93 with standard double reading, rates of 1.55 and 1.76 per 1,000 women. The trial met its criterion for noninferiority, and the numerically lower rate should not be presented as proof of superiority, while sensitivity was 80.5% with AI support and 73.8% under standard screening and specificity was 98.5% in both groups. An earlier report from the same MASAI population found detection rates of 6.4 per 1,000 women with AI supported screening and 5.0 with standard double reading, a relative increase of 29%, and these are successive analyses of one trial rather than independent replications. The intervention combined risk based allocation to single or double reading with detection support for radiologists, and it reduced screen reading workload by about 44%, a figure about reading examinations rather than all labour across a breast screening service.

The German PRAIM study, published in Nature Medicine in 2025, evaluated 461,818 women at 12 screening sites with 119 radiologists, and AI supported examinations had a cancer detection rate of 6.7 per 1,000 women against 5.7 without AI support, a relative difference of 17.6%, while recall rates were 37.4 and 38.3 per 1,000. This was a prospective observational study in which radiologists could choose whether to use the AI supported viewer, so the comparison was not randomised, and statistical adjustment cannot guarantee that every relevant difference has been removed. ScreenTrustCAD examined another arrangement in Stockholm, where in a prospective study of 55,581 women examinations were assessed by two radiologists and an AI system, and one radiologist plus AI detected 261 cancers against 250 with two radiologists, meeting the study's noninferiority criterion. That paired design compared combinations evaluating the same screening material, and its primary assessment concerned cancers identified within three months, so it answers a different question from later interval cancer follow up.

The article says the findings strengthen the case for the tested workflow but do not establish a reduction in breast cancer mortality, and longer term outcomes, including the consequences of detecting additional disease, remain relevant when programmes decide how much confidence to place in earlier diagnosis. For regional screening authorities the combined evidence supports a more specific procurement conversation about which clinical task was tested, in which workflow, and with what downstream consequences, since a detection headline alone cannot answer those questions. Hospitals considering a change need an explicit route for disagreement, where an AI flag may require arbitration, further imaging or a decision that no action is needed, and the staffing and expertise for that route belong in the deployment plan. For implementation, the next step is to compare the tested arrangement with the proposed local pathway, with arbitration, assessment capacity and monitoring specified alongside the software.

stories.Headline: MIT and Cornell researchers create an AI text detector that identifies rewritten machine content
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Cornell University created a new method for detecting AI-generated text on November 20, 2026. This system can identify machine-produced content even after it has been rewritten by tools designed to make the writing appear human. The technology uses test-time adaptation to learn from new material during the analysis process instead of relying only on original training data. It analyzes groups of passages to find shared patterns through a phenomenon called inference-time homogeneity.

The new approach detected 93.3% of AI-generated texts rewritten by humanizer tools, while the benchmark tool called Pangram only found 27%. When tested on language models outside its original training data, the system achieved detection rates between 87% and 94%. It also maintained an accuracy of 86% to 90% when identifying human-written texts, whereas one conventional detector dropped from 85.9% to 73.4% over ten years. These results demonstrate a significant improvement over existing tools that have not been updated.

The researchers stated that this technology could help employers, publishers, news organizations, and universities determine the true origins of written material. They also suggested that the system has cybersecurity applications for identifying AI-generated phishing emails or attempts to manipulate search engine results. While the results are promising, the developers noted that the method is not error-free and still requires human verification. The findings are scheduled to be presented later this year at the international artificial intelligence conference known as NeurIPS.
