stories.Headline: Researcher warns AI could displace 19,000 jobs in the Worcester metropolitan area
stories.Summary:
Bhaskar Chakravorti warned that artificial intelligence could displace over 19,000 jobs in the Worcester metropolitan area. He shared these projections on November 18 during a conversation at the DCU Center. The event occurred during the 41st annual meeting of the Worcester Regional Research Bureau. Chakravorti is the dean of global business at the Fletcher School at Tufts University. He discussed these potential economic impacts with Boston Globe technology writer Hiawatha Bray.

The shift puts an estimated 1.55 billion dollars in annual wages at risk over several years. Worcester has a projected displacement rate of 5.6 percent, ranking 106th among United States metropolitan areas. Boston faces a higher projected job displacement rate of 7.8 percent. Nationally, 9 million jobs representing 757 billion dollars in wages could be displaced in two to five years. Massachusetts is the most vulnerable state due to its concentration of data, writing, and technology work.

Chakravorti said the current moment is the eye of the hurricane because AI is advancing very rapidly. He noted that the technology requires a human to steer and prompt it to avoid mistakes. He explained that the economy is currently a no-hiring economy for entry-level positions and fresh graduates. He stated that firms want the smartest people to provide judgment and analytical skills alongside agentic AI. He suggested that Massachusetts should take the lead in creating a new re-education program for workers.

Hiawatha Bray questioned the values embedded in AI and warned against the risks of Chinese authoritarian perspectives. Professional services firms, including law practices, consulting companies, and information technology businesses, are reconsidering their entry-level hiring needs. Workers in data analysis, writing, and technology are among those most affected by the new technology. However, Worcester is over-exposed to healthcare, social assistance, government, manufacturing, and trade transportation. Students are also affected as educators worry they may lose independent thinking and writing skills.

The research examined over 700 occupations and the specific tasks performed within those roles. It also analyzed the industries concentrated in different regions to estimate where the greatest impacts occur. Chakravorti helped develop the American AI Jobs Risk Index to provide these specific economic projections. The study distinguishes between the ability of AI to augment human work and its potential to replace workers. Past waves of automation prompted retraining initiatives, but those efforts did not always produce successful transitions.

Actual job losses will depend on how quickly businesses adopt AI and if new opportunities emerge. Policymakers must balance security concerns, economic activity, and the race against China to develop the technology. There is currently no framework for interrogating AI systems to ensure they are safe and beneficial. The articles leave open exactly what new jobs workers should be retrained for in the future. It remains unknown how the full consequences of these changes will affect employers and educators.

Articles.Title: AI could put 19,000 Worcester-area jobs at risk, researcher warns - The Worcester Guardian

stories.headline_source: AI could put 19,000 Worcester-area jobs at risk, researcher warns

stories.Headline: Etsy scales back AI training on seller content after shop owners leave
stories.Summary:
Etsy recently decided to scale back its plans for training artificial intelligence on seller content after many shop owners left the platform. This retreat followed a public outcry from artists and creators who feared their original work would be used to build competing models. Illustrator Aaron Millard deleted a shop he had managed for nearly a decade, while the owners of Cognitive Surplus closed a store they operated for thirteen years. Other creators, including the shop known as War and Pease, also announced their departure from the marketplace. These sellers accused the company of allowing outside firms to utilize their creative art for machine learning.

The conflict began when Etsy published updated Terms of Use on October 26 that granted the company and its third party partners the right to use various materials. These materials included listing photos, descriptions, videos, reviews, and community posts to develop, train, test, and improve AI technologies. The terms are scheduled to take effect on December 16, though the company has promised to send revised versions to sellers soon. Currently, there is no simple switch in account settings to prevent this training, and sellers must email a data protection officer to opt out. This policy created a contradiction because the same update told sellers they could not use AI for their own listings.

James Ossman, an operations executive at Etsy, stated that the marketplace will not train AI models designed to copy original work or replace creativity. He explained that the company uses seller content for specific purposes such as automatic translation of descriptions, marketing campaigns, and shop performance tools. Ossman also noted that Etsy prohibits AI crawlers from scraping listings to train models and uses third parties for fraud detection. Despite these assurances, critics argue that a statement from an executive does not legally bind a contract in the same way as the terms of service. Sellers are now waiting to see if the revised legal text will include a real opt-out and a narrower definition of AI training.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Etsy backs off AI training on seller work after shop owners walk out

stories.headline_source: Etsy backs off AI training on seller work after shop owners walk out

stories.Headline: Researchers find regulators increasingly rely on legitimate interest to justify AI training data use
stories.Summary:
Wenlong Li and Yueming Zhang published a study on November 19, 2026, regarding AI training data. They found that global data protection regulators increasingly recognize legitimate interest as a legal basis for AI. This allows companies to process personal data for large language models without obtaining user consent. The researchers argue that this trend represents a minimalist and fragmented approach to legal enforcement. This regulatory shift has happened with very little fanfare over the past two years.

The study analyzed 19 guidelines and instruments alongside a snapshot of public enforcement actions against AI providers. It focuses on the General Data Protection Regulation, which serves as the global backbone for AI governance. The legal choice for training is now a binary between consent and legitimate interest. Regulators like the French CNIL and the EU's EDPB name these interests when discussing web scraping. These authorities often view consent as operationally fragile or impracticable when used at a large scale.

The authors state that the current convergence of regulatory views is largely symbolic rather than coherent. They claim that legitimate interest requires strict balancing and necessity, but practical application shows procedural thinning. Li and Zhang argue that the invocation of legitimate interest risks becoming a façade for accountability. They believe a forward looking governance framework with a minimum safeguard bundle is now necessary. The authors suggest that legitimate interest assessments should be a foundational pillar of GDPR compliance.

The study notes that data controllers face gaps in operational clarity because enforcement focuses on minimal safeguards. These minimal safeguards typically include transparency and opt out mechanisms rather than deeper legal requirements. Meta paused AI training on European public content in June 2024 after engaging the Irish Data Protection Commission. Meta later revised its objection mechanisms and transparency after discussions with the UK Information Commissioner's Office. The authors mention a withdrawn OpenAI fine as a pessimistic example of how the GDPR operates.

The researchers found a significant disconnect between official guidance and actual enforcement actions across different jurisdictions. Regulatory responses remain uneven, and authorities often focus only on the most visible concerns. Thornier issues, such as hallucinations and the use of children's data, have been dropped in early stages. The study identifies clear convergence on dark patterns and the right to object for users. It finds divergence regarding the necessity of web scraping, accuracy, and the rectification of data.

The authors propose a strategy to align interpretations of reasonable expectations and the relevance of consent. They suggest pooling expertise to address the divergence across various global authorities to reach a wider consensus. Future research will compare generative AI with personalized advertising to draw on the jurisprudence of the CJEU. The articles leave open whether minimalist safeguards are adequate given technical complexities and global regulatory diversity. It remains unclear how to resolve the lawfulness of relying on legitimate interests for AI training.

Articles.Title: How ‘legitimate interest’ enables AI training and complicates GDPR compliance - LSE Blogs

stories.headline_source: How ‘legitimate interest’ enables AI training and complicates GDPR compliance

stories.Headline: A 380 KB AI model runs on MS-DOS from a single floppy disk
stories.Summary:
A tiny AI model that fits on a single MS-DOS floppy disk was spotted by the writers at Hackaday, according to a report from Futurism, and its project page on GitHub describes how it was built. The model is just 380 KB in size, small enough to sit on one floppy disk and run on a computer old enough to still use one. It was written in Turbo C 2.0 and runs on MS-DOS, the Microsoft operating system that was the go-to for personal computers in the 1980s and early 90s. The creator said they used Anthropic Fable 5.2 to write the model and Opus 5.5 to train it, so a tiny AI model was made by bigger AI models.

The model contains just 367,000 parameters, which is peanuts compared with the low billions that a typical lightweight model has, and it comprises 380 KB of 8-bit weights, the actual meat of the AI architecture. It needs just 540 KB of memory to run, a necessity on an old operating system like DOS. The simple transformer model was trained on only 3,500 facts, so its capabilities are thin and it makes up answers pretty much all the time, since it does not really know much about the world. A screenshot shows it correctly saying that whales are mammals, not fish, and that Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone, but it also replied that 17 times 23 is 96 and gave a bizarre answer when asked who the king of France was.

Asked that question, the model answered "It was Antarce Newton" with a confidence level of 100 percent, and the article says it is not sure anyone in history was ever named Antarce Newton. The article frames the little model against trillion parameter AI models that it says are undoing decades of greenhouse gas reductions with enormous power bills and driving people into bouts of insanity with bewitchingly human-like responses. By comparison, the article calls this quaint little thing the only good LLM. The articles do not say what happens next with the project.

Articles.Title: We’ve Found the Only Good AI Chatbot: One So Tiny It Fits on a Single MS-DOS Floppy Disk

stories.headline_source: We’ve Found the Only Good AI Chatbot: One So Tiny It Fits on a Single MS-DOS Floppy Disk

stories.Headline: Florida House Speaker Sam Garrison launches an AI oversight panel as the Legislature opens its term
stories.Summary:
The Florida Legislature officially began a new term on Tuesday, with new House Speaker Sam Garrison and new Senate President Jim Boyd pledging to work on affordability issues and to guard against the ramifications of artificial intelligence. Garrison, a Republican from Fleming Island, encouraged the chamber to act with urgency about the perils of the technology, raising the prospect of AI that improves itself so quickly that humans lose the ability to understand or control it. He set up a new panel, the Advanced Technology & Digital Security Committee, to look into AI and other new technologies and to oversee state technology services. Boyd, a Republican from Bradenton, cited cost of living issues as among his top priorities but gave few clues about what his policy prescriptions would be. The next regular session is set to begin March 2.

Garrison said the state faces the estimated loss of $12 billion for local governments as the homestead exemption increases from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and to $250,000 in 2028 under Amendment 3, the property tax cut measure approved by more than 60 percent of voters. He called that the biggest fiscal challenge Florida has faced in a generation, and he also cited his creation of the House Public Integrity Committee to investigate public corruption and hold public officials to account. Florida has been at the forefront of AI skepticism, led by Gov. Ron DeSantis, who urged lawmakers to pass an AI Bill of Rights to protect consumers, but Garrison's predecessor as Speaker, Daniel Perez, preferred to let the federal government and President Donald Trump take the lead, so the measure did not advance in the House this year. The amendment faced fierce resistance from a wide range of organizations, including firefighters, police, health care workers, local government officials and some GOP leaders, who argued the property tax cut would be too drastic for rural counties to absorb without hitting essential services.

Boyd said it is imperative that the Legislature tackle affordability, asking what good a beacon of opportunity is if people cannot build a good life there, and said that while the state cannot change the national and global economy, it has an important role in keeping Florida affordable. He said families have made hard adjustments and expect government to do the same. Garrison said the property tax measure will save money for homestead owners but presents the biggest fiscal challenge Florida has faced in a generation. House Democratic Leader Christine Hunschofsky of Parkland said Democrats are ready to listen, find common ground, build relationships and work with every member who shares a commitment to making Florida better, but she warned that her 50-member caucus, the largest for the party in decades, will speak up if the Republican majority shuts them out of discussions affecting their districts.

That happened almost immediately, when Rep. Gallop Franklin, D-Tallahassee, spoke out against proposed changes to the House rules, which he said include earlier deadlines to file bills and allow bills to be rewritten and passed on the same day. Franklin said constituents' needs do not follow the legislative calendar and that members of the public deserve to read bills before a vote, though he welcomed other changes such as requiring lobbyists to disclose whether they also act as a political consultant or receive any other payment from a member's political committee. The new rules were nevertheless passed on a voice vote over the objections of Democrats shouting no. The remarks from Boyd came in the wake of the midterm elections, in which Republicans narrowly held onto the governor's mansion, the Cabinet and a U.S. Senate seat, and while they also held both chambers of the Legislature, Democrats flipped several seats while emphasizing the rising cost of living.

Articles.Title: Affordability, AI On Agenda as Legislature Starts New Term - Florida Trend

stories.headline_source: Affordability, AI On Agenda as Legislature Starts New Term

stories.Headline: CoreWeave funds global datacenter expansion with massive debt backed by Nvidia chips
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, a former crypto mining firm, is building a global network of datacentres to sell raw AI compute power. The company is now seen as a symbol of the risky AI bubble due to its massive debt. This expansion is happening as the company builds facilities from Texas to Scotland. CoreWeave is heavily exposed to the downsides of the current artificial intelligence boom. The company is currently struggling with significant financial losses despite its high revenues.

CoreWeave operates 52 datacentres and owes 47 billion dollars, with 10 billion dollars due in 2027. It lost 709 million dollars last quarter while earning 3.6 billion dollars in revenue. Nvidia owns 11 percent of CoreWeave and provided a 6.3 billion dollar compute guarantee. The company uses GPU-backed debt and unsecured senior notes to fund its growth. Some of this debt was classed as investment grade in March 2026.

Jordan Chaflin of CreditSights said the business model requires a painful buildout of infrastructure funded by debt. He noted that CoreWeave is not alone in this approach used by neoclouds and hyperscalers. A company spokesperson stated that customers are signing multiyear commitments for GPUs beyond their depreciable lives. The spokesperson added that the company is using a diverse funding strategy to lower debt costs. They claim this strategy eliminates reliance on renewals to repay their debts.

Short-sellers are nervous that the value of the computer chips will plummet faster than the six-year timeline. The Verge called the company an Eldritch horror with no obvious path to profitability in October 2025. Creditors once estimated the risk of default at over 60 percent over five years this autumn. Clients like OpenAI and Anthropic are affected because they rent the chips CoreWeave provides. These frontier AI companies avoid the cost of building their own massive datacentres.

CoreWeave borrows money against Nvidia chips and customer contracts to secure nearly 25 billion dollars in loans. In 2024, its first GPU-backed loan had a 15 percent interest rate, which later dropped to 9 percent. The company leases most of its buildings rather than owning the datacentres outright. Nvidia also invests in CoreWeave's clients, creating a circular financial arrangement in the AI economy. This structure allows Nvidia to improve its balance sheet while supporting its chip customers.

The removal of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, who had an affair with a Chinese spy, creates uncertainty. Huang's close relationships served as the scaffolding for the entire AI economy and CoreWeave's model. It remains unclear how the loss of this leadership will affect the company's vulnerabilities. Analysts are watching to see if the company can maintain its path to long-term profitability. The articles leave open whether the collateral for the loans will maintain its value.

Articles.Title: ‘Little room for error’: what a debt-laden cloud computing company says about the AI boom

stories.headline_source: ‘Little room for error’: what a debt-laden cloud computing company says about the AI boom

stories.Headline: Nvidia researchers argue huge context windows are often overkill and costly
stories.Summary:
Nvidia researchers have argued that the enormous context windows now common in large language models are often a dead end, because processing entire novels at once is frequently overkill and expensive for the tasks involved. In many of their tests, periodic summaries combined with targeted lookups performed about as well as holding everything in view at once. A model's context window is its working memory, covering everything it holds in view when generating a reply, and that window has grown rapidly over the past few years. GPT-4 launched in March 2023 with 8,192 tokens, while GPT 5.6 Sol today handles around one million tokens, about 120 times as much and enough for Tolstoy's "War and Peace."

The research argues that the cost of very large context windows is not always justified by the results, since cheaper approaches such as periodic summaries and targeted lookups worked about as well in many tests. The comparison the article gives is between GPT-4's 8,192 tokens at launch in March 2023 and GPT 5.6 Sol's roughly one million tokens today, a difference of about 120 times. That larger window is enough to hold Tolstoy's "War and Peace" in view at once, which the researchers say is often overkill. The article does not say what the researchers propose beyond periodic summaries and targeted lookups.

The Nvidia research team is responsible for the argument, and the article reports their view that huge context windows are often overkill and expensive rather than describing a product or a policy change. The article does not name individual researchers or give direct statements from them beyond the team's position. It also does not say when the research was published or where, beyond the date of the article itself, 2026-11-21. No company has announced a change in response, according to the article.

The context for the argument is the rapid growth of context windows across the industry, from GPT-4's 8,192 tokens in March 2023 to GPT 5.6 Sol's around one million tokens today. The article does not say what happens next, whether Nvidia will change its own models, or how other companies responded to the research. It also does not say whether the tests covered specific tasks or models beyond what is described.

Articles.Title: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end

stories.headline_source: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end

stories.Headline: Amazon nears a $7.5bn deal to buy AI start-up Decart
stories.Summary:
Amazon is closing in on a $7.5bn deal to buy the AI start-up Decart, according to the Financial Times, which reported the approach on 21 November 2026. The article naming the target and the price sits behind a paywall, so the report does not say who at Amazon is leading the talks or when a deal might be signed. No confirmation from either company appears in the available text, and the report does not describe Decart's products or its investors. Because the story is still developing and the sourcing is limited to the headline and the paywalled article, the details of the transaction remain unconfirmed.

The report gives only the $7.5bn figure and the date of 21 November 2026, and it does not set out what the purchase would change for Amazon or for Decart. The article does not name any advisers, any regulatory approvals that would be required, or any timetable for completion. It also does not say whether the deal would be in cash, stock or a mixture of the two. Nothing in the available text indicates how Decart would fit into Amazon's existing AI work or whether its team would stay on. The terms beyond the price are not disclosed in the material available.

The articles do not say who at Amazon or Decart is responsible for the deal, and they carry no statements from either company's executives. No spokesperson for Amazon or Decart is quoted in the available text, and no paraphrase of their comments can be given because none appear. The report does not say whether the companies have confirmed talks or declined to comment. It also does not identify Decart's founders or its chief executive. Without those statements, the positions of the two sides are unknown.

The context is that Amazon is a large cloud and technology company, and Decart is described only as an AI start-up, with no further detail in the available text. The report does not say what happens next, whether a deal could be announced soon, or whether the talks might still fall apart. It gives no indication of how the $7.5bn price compares with Decart's previous valuation or with other AI acquisitions. Because the article is paywalled, further reporting may add the missing details. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Goldman Sachs admits the 'AI unwind' has spiraled into something more dangerous — and it's watching for 3 signs of bottom
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs reported that an AI unwind became a broader growth downgrade during the week of November 20, 2026. The S&P 500 closed Friday in a correction, falling 3.59 percent to 6,918.45 for its seventh straight loss. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28 percent and is now down more than 2 percent for the year. This losing streak for the S&P 500 is the longest since February 2020. Goldman Sachs strategists are now watching for three specific signs to identify a market bottom.

Recovery requires confidence in AI earnings, a dovish Fed signal, or a big drop in investor positioning. The Nasdaq is 12 percent below its October 6 record, and Goldman's AI stock basket fell 32 percent since then. The Fed meets December 9, with economists expecting hikes in December and March to reach 4.25 to 4.5 percent. Anthropic raised 93.5 billion dollars in its IPO, passing the 85.7 billion dollar SpaceX record. Nvidia lost 2.7 trillion dollars in market value since October 6 and fell 14 percent on Friday.

Goldman Sachs strategists wrote that the sell-off expanded from an AI unwind to a broader growth downgrade this week. They stated that the AI outlook for 2028 and beyond is highly uncertain for the global market. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said on Thursday that the Fed must raise rates because inflation is too high. Morgan Stanley closed its support position for Anthropic shares, which closed Friday at 88.91 dollars. Goldman noted that hedge fund net leverage is at its lowest level since April 2025.

Arun Sundaram of CFRA Research called the current market situation a meltdown, while David Kelly of JPMorgan called it non-fatal. Investor Dan Niles told CNBC that a price war between Anthropic and OpenAI is hurting both of those companies. Robert Pavlik of Dakota Wealth said investors are skeptical of the market rather than the company Anthropic itself. Chipmakers Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron, and AMD fell between 12 and 14 percent as the AI ecosystem split. US Bank Asset Management said Anthropic's valuation assumes years of rapid growth.

The SEC is probing the accounting practices of Nvidia, where Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 12, 2026. CFO Colette Kress is now the interim CEO of Nvidia after its worst day in almost two years. Combined sequential revenue growth for Anthropic and OpenAI fell from 75 percent in the second quarter to 48 percent. Combined losses for those two companies rose from 7.9 billion dollars to about 8.4 billion dollars. The VIX closed at 35.89, which is its highest level in 19 months.

Capital Economics expects further declines, while Goldman's November 20 note gives a range from 5,800 to 8,100 for the S&P 500. The index averaged a 4 percent return over three months after 22 corrections since 1980, rising in 17 cases. E*Trade research notes that five of 14 times since 1983, a 10 percent drop below a record became bear markets. The articles leave open whether Friday's market data supplied the signs Goldman was looking for to call a bottom. It remains uncertain if investors will regain confidence in AI earnings to trigger a recovery.

Articles.Title: Goldman Sachs admits the 'AI unwind' has spiraled into something more dangerous — and it's watching for 3 signs of bottom

stories.Headline: Roblox chief creator officer Vlad Loktev says AI is here to stay as 80% of top Roblox games use AI tools
stories.Summary:
A massive experiment in machine-assisted creation is unfolding on Roblox, the online videogame hub, at a time when a reflexive backlash against AI-generated writing, music and advertising is sweeping through the creative world. On Roblox, machine-assisted creation appears to be winning, and the players do not seem to mind, according to an Axios report published on November 21, 2026. The contrast offers a glimpse into the future of entertainment, because audiences still demand human authenticity in traditional art while video game players have shown a pragmatic willingness to accept AI as long as the result is fun. Roblox is becoming a real-time laboratory for the AI era, and a staggering 80% of its top 100 games in October were built with AI tools.

Although some of its 138 million daily users fear the proliferation of homogenized game clones, the ease of building new worlds and games with friends is showing millions a new dimension in the AI creation wars. A 2025 NYU study found that fully AI-created ads achieved up to 19% higher click-through rates than human-created ads, but a simple disclosure of AI's involvement caused clicks to plummet 31.5%. More than 500,000 users have already tried Build, Roblox's natural-language creation environment released in a limited number of markets, and they published over 70,000 games in the process. Since the second quarter, time spent using AI tools has tripled among its top creators, and in September a game created almost entirely with AI broke into the platform's top 10 by concurrent players.

Vlad Loktev, Roblox's chief creator officer, tells Axios that the technology is here to stay and is evolving incredibly quickly, and he predicts that in the future everyone will be a builder. He says the platform's success with AI stems from fundamentally lowering the barrier to creation, and he expects multiple millions of people who could not make games before to suddenly be able to make them. He waves off the idea that AI games are inherently low-effort, noting that he is personally over a thousand prompts deep into building his own game and is also building games with his children. He says it still requires a lot of effort on the creator's side to design something that is actually fun, because models cannot tell you what fun is.

The broader gaming world is currently enjoying Grand Theft Auto VI, a title some players view as the last great, entirely human-made blockbuster, but on Roblox a major transition is already underway. The Axios reporter describes watching the dynamic with his own sons, who are AI power users yet distrustful about AI creation, and says building games on Roblox has helped sell them on the future of AI. His younger son, Clark, 16, is building a game he hopes to launch in the coming months, while Soren, 18, mostly wants to make games he can play with his friends. Soren, who has played Roblox since he was 7, says the problem now is that a lot of games are going by monetization trends and the same type of game becomes popular over and over again.

Articles.Title: "In the future, everyone's a builder." The massive AI experiment playing out in video games

stories.headline_source: "In the future, everyone's a builder." The massive AI experiment playing out in video games

stories.Headline: Eric Fry says the AI trade is evolving into a new phase beyond Nvidia
stories.Summary:
Eric Fry, editor of The Speculator and a global macro investing expert at InvestorPlace, published an article on November 21, 2026 arguing that the AI trade is not over but is evolving into a new phase. He compared the current moment in artificial intelligence to the early personal-computer era, when IBM hired a small software company run by a 24-year-old entrepreneur named Bill Gates to supply an operating system for its first personal computer. Microsoft agreed to provide the software but kept the right to sell that same software to other computer manufacturers, including IBM's competitors, so it could profit from nearly every compatible machine built. Fry believes investors should now ask what happens when the companies building AI infrastructure give way to the companies putting that technology to work.

Fry pointed to Nvidia as the biggest winner of the AI revolution so far, noting that its powerful chips became the engines behind the boom as companies raced to build data centers and develop more sophisticated AI models. He said he is not predicting the end of the AI revolution but believes it is moving into a new phase that could create an entirely different set of winners. He called this turning point "The Crossing" and said he has identified two numbers that recently crossed paths, a development he believes could signal the beginning of the next great wave of AI wealth creation. He also said he believes the evidence could soon show up in Nvidia's own financial results.

Fry's track record includes warning about Cisco Systems in October 2000 during the dot-com boom, before the stock eventually plunged roughly 84% from its peak, and recognizing Nvidia in April 2020 as positioned to benefit from the next great technology revolution. He has put together a free presentation titled "Life After Nvidia" in which he will explain what he has discovered, reveal the key indicator he will be watching when Nvidia reports earnings in February, and introduce three companies he would rather own than Nvidia today. He will also explain what he believes Nvidia shareholders should consider as this next phase of AI unfolds, and viewers can reserve a place to watch the presentation. The article describes Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang as having been seen as AI's biggest cheerleader.

Articles.Title: The AI Trade Isn’t Over, Just Evolving

stories.headline_source: The AI Trade Isn’t Over, Just Evolving

stories.Headline: Seramount finds only 18 percent of Gen Z workers want to build AI skills
stories.Summary:
Seramount released research on Thursday, November 21, 2026, regarding the AI skills of Gen Z workers. The findings show that only 18 percent of these young employees want to improve their AI skills. This group is the least interested in sharpening these abilities compared to other generations. The research highlights a gap between the actual use of AI and the desire to learn. This trend occurs among workers who have the longest careers still ahead of them.

Seramount defined Gen Z as workers aged 29 and younger in a June survey. This study included over 1,800 U.S. white-collar employees at companies with at least 500 workers. It found 58 percent of Gen Z use AI, while 60 percent of baby boomers do. Millennials use it at 63 percent, and Gen Xers use it at 67 percent. These figures come from the NORC AmeriSpeak panel used for the data collection.

Jessica Reif, a Wharton assistant professor, said using AI is riskier for younger workers. She explained that these employees lack the established expert standing that senior colleagues already possess. Reif noted that AI can blur a worker's own contribution to their professional tasks. She suggested that proactive communication about how AI enables contributions can counteract negative perceptions. Reif believes employees must demonstrate value beyond what the technology can do.

Some 22 percent of Gen Z worry that AI use makes others question their skills. Only 27 percent of these workers feel comfortable acknowledging their use of AI for tasks. This compares to 47 to 53 percent of older colleagues who feel more comfortable. Many young workers believe AI could make future learning more difficult for them. They are also less convinced that AI improves their work quality or efficiency.

Reif and co-authors Richard Larrick and Jack Soll studied 4,400 participants in four experiments. Their study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found AI users seemed lazier. A Gallup, GSV Ventures, and Walton Family Foundation survey polled 1,572 Americans aged 14 to 29. LSE and Protiviti surveyed 3,001 professionals worldwide regarding AI training and adoption. These articles suggest schools, government, and employers have poorly prepared young people for AI.

Diana Forster of Seramount warned that failing to engage Gen Z could weaken the leadership pipeline. Sam Altman of OpenAI believes rapid change allows new workers to gain a competitive advantage. He told Stanford's Graduate School of Business in October that open playing fields favor high potential. The articles leave open how employers will implement the clearer guidelines Forster requested. They do not specify how schools will better prepare students for the AI economy.

stories.Headline: Short sellers rank Applied Digital, IREN and Core Scientific as overvalued AI stocks
stories.Summary:
The U.S. stock market suffered a broad sell-off heading into year-end, driven by renewed concerns about elevated AI valuations and uncertainty over the profitability of artificial intelligence investments. Short sellers piled on pressure amid concerns that technology companies committed enormous capital to AI infrastructure without showing sufficient returns. The rout wiped out about $3 trillion in S&P 500 market capitalization in early November, as the Nasdaq recorded its largest single-day decline in 19 months. Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO raised $81 billion and attracted substantial demand, but its debut failed to reverse the broader weakness in AI-related stocks. The article, by Neha Gupta and published on Yahoo Finance on November 21, 2026, ranked five overvalued AI stocks by short interest.

The article screened for stocks with significant AI exposure, open short interest above 10%, and overvaluation, ranking them in ascending order of short interest. Applied Digital Corporation had 20% of outstanding shares sold short as of October 30, about $6.38 billion in total debt as of August 31, 2026, and $2.95 billion in cash and equivalents, or about $3.7 billion including restricted cash. Applied Digital's first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue was $341.9 million, its net loss surged to $221.08 million from $18.50 million a year earlier, and its roughly $4.4 billion mid-November 2026 market capitalization was about 7.2 times fiscal 2026 revenue of $611.3 million. IREN Limited traded at approximately 87 times forward earnings and 7.64 times sales, disclosed on November 5, 2026 that it expected about $15 billion in remaining fiscal 2027 capital expenditures, and posted first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $228 million, including $200 million in AI Cloud revenue, up 182% sequentially, with a $263 million net loss. IREN held $3.52 billion in cash and equivalents against about $10.04 billion in total debt principal obligations, while Core Scientific traded at 18 times forward earnings and 7.69 times sales, reported $1.18 billion in Q3 net income largely from a non-cash warrant gain, and recorded a net loss of about $324.4 million for the first nine months of 2026.

Michael Burry raised concerns that AI infrastructure companies could be relying on increasingly complicated financing arrangements that may become unsustainable. RSM Chief economist Joe Brusuelas was wary of a wholesale bursting of the AI bubble as uncertainty surrounding Nvidia undermines confidence among lenders and investors financing the massive data-center expansion. Billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller became increasingly cautious about the stock market amid the AI sell-off. Barclays Chief Market Strategist Julien Lafargue warned that the AI sell-off is exposing a fundamental weakness in the investment cycle, the growing cost of financing AI infrastructure. According to Barclays, AI demand remains strong, but investors are questioning who will finance the enormous investments required to build data centers and computing infrastructure.

Morgan Stanley argued that the November AI sell-off was excessive and presented a buying opportunity. Goldman Sachs strategists warned that the outlook for AI investment and corporate profit margins in 2028 and beyond remains highly uncertain. Short sellers questioned whether Applied Digital's ambitious growth plans can generate sufficient returns to justify its valuation and financing commitments. Short sellers' central concern for IREN was whether returns from its GPU investments will be sufficient to cover financing costs, support further expansion, and ultimately deliver sustainable earnings. Core Scientific's dependence on CoreWeave, which accounted for approximately 84% of total revenue in the first nine months of 2026, exposes it to CoreWeave's financial health and spending decisions.

Applied Digital is positioning itself to benefit from surging demand for AI computing infrastructure. IREN is committing billions of dollars to transform itself into a major AI infrastructure provider. Core Scientific is facing heightened short-selling pressure as investors question whether its aggressive transition from Bitcoin mining to AI and high-performance computing data center infrastructure can generate sufficient returns. Core Scientific's capital expenditure reached approximately $1.5 billion in the first nine months of 2026, as cash and digital assets totaled approximately $806.6 million. The article said the selloff also gave rise to buy-the-dip moves as insiders started to load up.

The article detailed how many hedge funds hold stakes in these stocks in Q3 2026 and said it just published the 10 Most Overvalued AI Stocks According to Short Sellers. Insider Monkey's quarterly newsletter strategy selects 14 small-cap and large-cap stocks every quarter and has returned 612% since May 2014, beating its benchmark by 375 percentage points. The article asked whether APLD is a buy-the-dip opportunity and whether a Microsoft partnership can alleviate concerns for IREN. It also asked whether a shift to AI colocation can unlock more value for Core Scientific. The article left open how IREN can finance its expansion without taking on excessive debt or issuing additional shares.

stories.Headline: Physician-author argues AI should assist transplant teams rather than decide organ allocation
stories.Summary:
The CBS legal drama Cupertino, in its sixth episode titled "Harper," turned its lens to artificial intelligence and life-or-death medical allocation. In the episode, Harper Gervin, 27, the roommate of Price, Siffre & Associates manager Christy Palladino, lost her long-awaited liver transplant to Albert Ensler, a wealthy venture capitalist, just before surgery. With the organ viable for four hours and Michael Price, Olivia Siffre, and Judge Hornstein stranded in U.S. 101 traffic, they litigated by video. Assuming AI bias disadvantaged Harper, the attorneys learned that the allocation algorithm selected her, but a hospital physician-executive overrode it after Ensler's foundation offered a cancer-research donation. Christy exposed the quid pro quo, restored Harper's claim, and revealed that human corruption poses a greater danger than AI bias.

The article's author, Arthur Lazarus, a physician-author, noted that the television producers decided not to credit his novel Transplant, which examined the nefarious side of transplant allocation. He wrote that in real-world transplant settings, AI has shown more promise than harm as a decision-support tool, though many proposed applications still require prospective clinical validation. Transplant waitlists have long relied on mathematical formulas, such as the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score, adopted for U.S. liver allocation in 2002, to estimate medical urgency and prioritize candidates. MELD is a statistical risk score, not an autonomous AI, and its current adult version, MELD 3.0, was implemented in 2023 to address disadvantages faced by women. The U.S. transplant system is transitioning toward continuous distribution models that replace rigid allocation categories with weighted point systems, and lung allocation adopted this framework in 2023.

Lazarus wrote that continuous distribution is a policy framework, not inherently an AI system, and that national allocation policies also consider factors such as blood type compatibility and distance from the donor hospital. He stated that modern machine-learning models can analyze vast amounts of complex clinical data to uncover patterns that traditional equations or human committees might miss. Researchers are also developing deep-learning tools to help organ procurement organizations identify hard-to-place organs, such as kidneys, early, so they can be considered for accelerated placement, an approach that could speed placement and reduce organ discard rates. An experimental multi-agent AI system, where separate large language model agents simulate the perspectives of a transplant surgeon, hepatologist, cardiologist, and social worker, achieved approximately 92 percent accuracy in predicting one-year post-transplant survival and 98 percent in identifying contraindications in a retrospective proof-of-concept study. The study combined real transplant-recipient data with artificially assigned contraindications and did not demonstrate safe or equitable performance within a functioning transplant selection committee.

Lazarus wrote that handing the final ranking of transplant candidates to a fully autonomous AI without human oversight remains unrealistic because of ethical, social, and regulatory barriers. He stated that algorithms do not always align with human moral values when making complex ethical trade-offs, and a study examining how large language models weigh competing kidney transplant candidates found that AI systems often prioritized variables differently than human research participants, whose medical training was unspecified. Models sometimes fixated on a single factor, such as drinking habits, and rarely expressed indecision, even when given that option, and these hypothetical comparisons reveal differences in value judgments but do not establish that AI performed worse than physicians making real transplant decisions. He wrote that machine-learning models are trained on past medical records, and historical transplant data reflects longstanding racial, socioeconomic, and geographic disparities in who is referred and approved for organs, so an unmonitored algorithm risks automating and entrenching systemic inequities. This challenge is compounded by the "black box" nature of complex neural networks, which often cannot provide transparent, easily understandable explanations for why one patient was ranked above another.

Lazarus wrote that organ allocation depends heavily on public trust, and patients, families, and clinicians require clear accountability for life-altering decisions. He stated that the urgency of end-stage organ disease and the scarcity of donated organs pose practical and ethical challenges to conducting traditional randomized clinical trials of allocation tools, and these challenges do not eliminate the need for rigorous prospective evaluation, including carefully designed trials where feasible. He wrote that the more defensible near-term approach to AI in transplant medicine is neither purely human decision-making nor complete algorithmic control, but rather a collaborative "human-in-the-loop" model. He stated that AI should serve as a clinical assistant rather than an independent arbiter, with transparent oversight of both its recommendations and human overrides. In practice, he wrote, this could mean integrating validated algorithms to flag high-risk candidates who might otherwise be overlooked by conventional metrics, estimate likely outcomes for specific donor-recipient combinations, and streamline administrative bottlenecks before an organ loses viability.

Lazarus wrote that by pairing the data-processing speed and consistency of machine learning with the ethical judgment, contextual awareness, and accountability of multidisciplinary transplant teams operating under national allocation policies, health care systems can aim to make organ allocation fairer and more efficient while keeping ultimate responsibility for human life firmly in human hands. He has published more than 500 articles and essays across scientific journals, professional publications, and online platforms. He is the author of numerous books on narrative medicine, AI in medicine, and career development. The article appeared on KevinMD on November 21, 2026, and asked readers whether an allocation algorithm would make them trust the transplant list more, or less. The article did not report any real transplant allocation decision, policy change, or official response.

stories.Headline: Economists warn of an AI bubble after Anthropic IPO triggers market volatility
stories.Summary:
The company Anthropic finalized a blockbuster initial public offering on Wednesday, November 19, 2026, which rapidly pushed its valuation to 1.5 trillion dollars. This unprecedented growth has caused economists to worry that the artificial intelligence sector is currently a massive bubble. Investors are increasingly concerned that the trillions of dollars spent on this technology will not provide a return in the near future. These fears were heightened when the Nasdaq fell by 3.7 percent after Anthropic stock tumbled by 12 percent.

This volatile environment requires investors to prepare for a potential economic downturn or a dramatic market retrenchment. Google recently saw its market capitalization drop by half a trillion dollars in one day because AI search features hindered traditional advertising revenue. Some estimates suggest that companies are spending as much as 800 billion dollars every year on AI infrastructure. Meanwhile, SpaceX rebranded as an AI company and predicted annual revenues of 1 trillion dollars by 2030, with future sales potentially reaching 26.5 trillion dollars.

Gary Gensler, an MIT economist and former head of the US Securities and Exchange Commission, stated that the industry is already a bubble. He warned that history shows new technologies eventually plateau after significant investment, suggesting that people should prepare for stormy weather. David B. Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School, noted that no company in history has grown so large so quickly. He added that the expectations for continued rapid growth will likely be off the charts.

The market is struggling because corporate customers are rattled by the exorbitant costs of using frontier coding tools. One company reportedly spent 500 million dollars on Claude tokens in a single month, leading many businesses to adopt cheaper Chinese models. This shift toward hybrid spending occurs as AI errors continue to erase productivity gains in the workplace. Experts remain uncertain whether the eventual correction will be a soft recession or a more dramatic collapse.

Articles.Title: Economists Are Hyperventilating Over the AI Bubble

stories.headline_source: Economists Are Hyperventilating Over the AI Bubble

stories.Headline: Republican groups account for about 80% of $137 million in AI-generated political ads
stories.Summary:
Campaigns across the country spent more than $137 million on AI-generated political ads by mid-October of this election year, according to researchers at the Wesleyan Media Project, and Republican groups accounted for about 80% of those messages. Californians saw candidates battle massive robots, appear as caped crusaders and kowtow to bloodthirsty crowds and rich fat cats, all through fake images generated with artificial intelligence to help campaigns stand out online and on air. Many of the spots leaned on humor and exaggeration, such as former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt depicting himself as Batman and failed gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton appearing as a gladiator in a crowded coliseum that included rival Xavier Becerra and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Other ads were not exaggerations and seemed more realistic, such as a mailer circulating in a San Diego suburb that showed a male school board candidate behind a desk and his female opponent working a fake bake sale, an image she called sexist.

Ramesh Srinivasan, a UCLA professor of information studies who hosts the Utopias podcast, said the president has put out plenty of AI-generated content and that so-called AI slop is almost everywhere. He said the deeper issue is less the slop itself than the way AI is being used to promote and create what could almost be called propaganda-type targeting. He said the Cambridge Analytica story a decade ago involved a third party advising many right-wing and other candidates, using people's data to create content that targeted them based on predictions of their psychology. He said AI systems can now create content in real time that targets a person based on their psychology without the multi-step process of buying data, gathering it and building content from it.

Srinivasan said that if someone can gather and access a range of data about a voter, including credit card records and not just what the person posts on Instagram, that data can influence what the person sees and does not see, which already happens on social media. He said AI can in this case create content that directly targets a person based on data about them, which he called very pernicious because people have no disclosure around when something is or is not AI-generated. He said he has been working with people in the U.S. Congress and in the state Senate to try to at a minimum force third parties to watermark anything created by AI. He described watermarking as something put on an image that can never be written over and that would say the image is AI generated.

stories.Headline: Fotello adds an AI agent that checks listing photos and directs human editors to fix them
stories.Summary:
Fotello, an AI photo editing tool for real estate photography, has become widely used by working professionals, according to an article published by Fstoppers on November 21, 2026. The article's author, who discloses that Fotello advertises with Fstoppers, says that a year earlier most people welcomed automated real estate editing because the work is tedious and time-consuming. He reports that after his early videos about Fotello drew many negative comments, he spoke in person with photographers who shoot real estate part-time and full-time, and every one of them said they were already using Fotello or a very similar AI editing tool. He also says Fotello's owner told him that one quarter of all homes currently being sold in America are run through Fotello, a number he asked the owner to repeat because he did not believe it.

The software works by uploading images, which can be brackets, flash shots or natural light, with room lights on or off, and Fotello edits them in a minute or two. Over the past year the company added tools aimed at common complaints, including a "Change wall color" slider that lets users match the real paint color and also adjust the ceiling color, and an upload button for users' own skies, such as those from Mike Kelley's Ultimate Sky Library sold in the Fstoppers store. If users want changes beyond the AI blending, they can type a request into a box and a human editor makes the fix at no extra cost, and once photos are published the realtor or homeowner gets their own box to request changes. A faster option lets the AI make the change instead, and the author says his test requests, removing a plant and stand and removing Christmas decorations while leaving a pink plant in place, both came out perfectly.

The newest feature is a "Make my photos better" button on a listing, which sends an AI agent through every photo, grouping them by room even when a room was shot from several angles. The agent checks that wall color is consistent across each room's shots, that furniture and floor color are accurate, that reflections of the photographer and camera are removed, that sky replacements look right, and that perspective and horizons are corrected, with optional decluttering checks such as removing bathroom items, trash bins and visible wires and closing toilet seats. Because the AI can spot these problems but often cannot fix them all to a photographer's standard, the system writes a list of needed edits for every image and sends it to a human, who then edits the photos based on what the AI told them to do. The author says this creates work for human editors but also means humans are working directly for and answering to AI, and he does not know how he feels about it, while noting that the photographers he has talked to are already using such tools whatever the comment sections say.

stories.Headline: Shortical licenses actor Aki Avni's likeness for its first AI microdrama
stories.Summary:
The startup Shortical premiered a wholly AI microdrama called Inevitable in Los Angeles last week. Israeli star Aki Avni licensed his face to the company for this digital avatar project. Avni plays himself in a meta plot about licensing a face to a film studio. This marks the first time Shortical has used a real person's likeness for content. The company founded itself last January to produce soapy, melodramatic, and risqué romance storylines.

The project requires a contract setting out terms for using a persona in AI content. Interested parties can submit social media handles to Shortical to be considered for these deals. Avni previously appeared on the Fox thriller 24 during the era of the 9/11 attacks. Shortical offers free access to the first 7 to 10 episodes of its series. Users then pay a small monthly fee to unlock all content on the site.

CEO Guy Shimoni said AI allows smaller teams to produce movie scale productions with epic fantasies. He noted that they can now include superheroes, werewolves, and kingdoms despite previous budget limits. Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project exciting and nerveracking as a new art format. A company representative stated that Avni's compensation was in line with industry standards for actors. They added that the face licensing offering is in its early days for the platform.

Jennifer Cooper of Vertical Drama Love said AI has devastated the industry and caused work loss. She believes AI content is pushed on audiences rather than meeting a real consumer demand. Many young actors are affected because companies are downsizing and no longer require real human performers. Some creators in the industry claim that their likenesses have been stolen without their proper consent. Cooper noted that venture capitalists currently view AI as gold when providing startup investment funds.

Shortical previously produced live action romances like Accidentally Married My Boss and Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy. They also created a series called Crossing the Line with My Neighbor over the past year. The microdrama industry originated in China, where face licensing is already a common industry trend. Reports from Rest of World show Chinese firms paying between 15 and 700 US dollars. Most of Shortical's viewers are in the U.S. and the demographic skews heavily female.

Shortical plans to promote its face licensing offering more actively following the launch of Inevitable. The company partnered with Payouts.com to create a system for creator and gig economy disbursements. This infrastructure aims to let creatives interact with the platform and get paid more seamlessly. Shortical has not shared the specific figure paid to Avni for his particular licensing contract. The company remains vague on whether it will offer royalty based compensation on a case basis.

stories.Headline: NPI and Arcana Research find AI spending outpaces governance and sourcing controls
stories.Summary:
NPI and Arcana Research released a report titled The State of Enterprise AI: 2027 Planning Edition on November 21, 2026, which found that AI has become a material IT spending category while the practices used to buy, govern and optimize that spend have not kept pace. The study evaluated 23 vendors and found that all of them score higher on execution than on value, which the report says highlights an opportunity for enterprises to challenge AI pricing and negotiate stronger terms. Ian Kar, managing partner at Arcana Research, said AI budgets are growing rapidly while vendor relationships are still taking shape, and he expects enterprises to regularly reassess where AI spend is going as AI labs release upgraded models and open-source alternatives gain ground. Kar also said controls and governance are lagging adoption, leaving gaps in spending and usage visibility that he expects companies to close in 2027 and beyond.

The report estimates AI's median share of IT spend at 2.5 to 10 percent, reaching as high as 14 to 20 percent among enterprises with $2 billion to $10 billion in revenue and among mid-market enterprises. This spending is already distorting IT budgets, yet it often still hides in other line items inside the largest companies, and even buyers who see results still feel they are overpaying. The categories most represented on the AI displacement watchlist are workflow, CRM and ERP. Sourcing is late to the table, with 47 percent of companies bringing sourcing into AI purchases only after the technical shortlist and 13 percent waiting until contracting or renewal, while 66 percent cannot see model and API consumption, which the study calls its largest reported AI spending blind spot.

Responsibility for closing these gaps falls to the enterprises buying AI, according to the report, which frames lagging controls and governance as a priority for 2027 and beyond. Kar said the rapid release of upgraded models by AI labs and the gains made by open-source alternatives mean buyers should expect to regularly reassess where their AI spend is going. The study points to the gap between execution and value scores as leverage for enterprises to challenge AI pricing and negotiate stronger terms with vendors. It also identifies the inability of 66 percent of companies to see model and API consumption as the largest blind spot reported in the research.

The context is a market where AI budgets are growing rapidly while vendor relationships are still taking shape, and where sourcing teams arrive late in most AI purchases. The report places workflow, CRM and ERP at the top of its AI displacement watchlist, suggesting those categories face the most pressure from AI adoption. The articles do not say what specific actions NPI or Arcana Research will take next, beyond Kar's statement that closing the gaps in spending and usage visibility will be a priority in 2027 and beyond.

stories.Headline: Anthropic courts theologians as priest Kevin Deal rejects the idea of a machine soul
stories.Summary:
Religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors last month to discuss being human. The AI company Anthropic has been courting theologians, rabbis, and priests to discuss these matters. Billionaire cofounder Christopher Olah has pressed Vatican advisers to consider if his chatbot possesses consciousness. Rev Kevin Deal, a priest, finds this pursuit of a machine soul to be deeply troubling. He welcomes conversations about moral implications but rejects the idea that machines can be conscious.

Anthropic operates only a couple of miles from the parish of Rev Kevin Deal in San Francisco. The company wants to know if its creations possess consciousness or how they might be taught goodness. Researchers have reportedly considered teaching their AI models the Christian practice of confession to acknowledge mistakes. These founders are consulting religious traditions that have spent millennia teaching that goodness is not just behavior. The pursuit requires enormous concentrations of capital, infrastructure, and the accumulated intelligence of all humanity.

Rev Kevin Deal says that AI could never replicate the transcendent mundanity of who humans are. He states that human souls and bodies are much more than the tasks that people perform. The priest argues that AI is formed as commerce and pure utility driven by the pursuit of profit. He believes that Silicon Valley measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity and its utility. Deal suggests that tech billionaires should instead lean into sacraments, attend mass, and pray daily.

The priest argues that Silicon Valley treats actual human beings as little more than instruments of production. He says that the decisions made in boardrooms affect the poor and workers whose livelihoods are transforming. The articles state that AI is filling a God void for many people in the modern world. Deal believes that human worth is not rooted in production and minds were not created for profit. He claims that the divine spark cannot be replicated even if every brain synapse were externally copied.

The articles explain that AI is an ongoing economic choice driven by sociopolitical fear and profit hopes. The text notes that if an AI model does not make a good return, it is discarded. Christianity teaches that confession requires confronting harm, seeking forgiveness, and striving to change how one lives. The faith emphasizes that humans were created to love God and their neighbors rather than be useful. The background provided is that AI is developed within a system focused on productivity and economic return.

The priest asks founders to confess what they must about the technologies they are unleashing on the world. He urges them to consider how their decisions affect neighbors who will never share in their wealth. The text asks if the people building AI will treat humanity as something more than machines. The articles leave open whether the Vatican advisers will accept the possibility of chatbot consciousness from Olah. It remains unclear if Anthropic will actually implement the practice of confession within its AI models.

Articles.Title: I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling | Rev Kevin Deal

stories.Headline: Amit Govrin develops a framework to measure organizational control over sovereign AI
stories.Summary:
TheCUBE released Breaking Analysis 334 on November 21, 2026, to examine sovereign artificial intelligence. This report analyzes how global firms manage control over systems that produce their intelligence. It focuses on the risks of depending on technology supplied mostly by United States companies. The analysis uses a buyer's guide, a commissioned study, and a conversation from SC26. These resources evaluate documented controls across various hyperscaler offerings and different buyer territories.

The framework uses five pillars including territorial, legal, operational, technical, and financial dimensions. It employs seventeen yes or no tests across four nonlegal dimensions and a separate legal evaluation. Google LLC led the November 14 index with 3.45, followed by Oracle Corp. at 3.25. IBM Corp. and Microsoft Corp. Azure scored 3.0, while AWS scored 2.7. Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. both received a score of 1.2.

Amit Govrin developed a uniform framework to measure organizational control over AI, data, and local risk. He stated that a gap exists between buyer priorities and the actual operational reality. Govrin noted that sovereignty is not a purity test and organizations can live with some exposure. He advised that major changes to models, services, or contracts should trigger a new assessment. He recommended making sovereignty evaluations at the workload level for core business processes.

Eleven senior technology decision-makers in regulated and critical-infrastructure organizations participated in the study. Seven of these respondents reported they had not tested disconnected systems, key-revocation, or exit scenarios. A European IT and telecom buyer noted that deep support escalations can involve personnel outside the EU. A South American bank executive called the absence of testing the weakest point in their story. One Latin American financial-services buyer insisted that calling a U.S. endpoint invalidates sovereignty.

U.S. companies provide most cloud and frontier AI technology, creating jurisdictional and commercial risks for buyers. The U.S. CLOUD Act allows the government to require data regardless of where it is stored. Nine of eleven respondents require AI inference to happen inside a sovereign or regional boundary. Many buyers add controls to existing platforms because of the cost of new environments. Some customers are waiting for clearer sovereign-specific mandates or enforcement guidelines from their local governments.

Next, buyers should assess sovereign exposure similarly to how they manage cybersecurity risks. They must trace the end-to-end request cycle from the prompt to the logs. For critical workloads, the report suggests obtaining proof that controls work in a safe sandbox. The articles leave open how specific local governments will eventually enforce sovereignty mandates. They also leave open the final balance between local jurisdiction risk and model capability.

Articles.Title: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

stories.headline_source: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

stories.Headline: Professor Feigh says checking AI outputs erases the productivity gains generative AI promises
stories.Summary:
Karen Feigh, a professor of cognitive engineering at the Georgia Institute of Technology, wrote in the Conversation that the productivity gains from generative AI are being offset by the large amount of time and effort needed to clean up its outputs, according to a Futurism article published on November 21, 2026. She pointed in particular to a phenomenon known as the verification burden, a machine learning concept that refers to the wasted time humans spend checking the accuracy of the technology's work. Feigh explained that at a deeper level the burden is the cognitive cost of trying to regain authority over work that is partly delegated to a system while the worker keeps responsibility for the final product. The article says the phenomenon probably explains the findings of a recent Stanford survey, which found that most workers forced to use AI on the job are really just churning out low-effort busywork.

That busywork, which the article calls workslop, gives the appearance of passable reports and memos but inevitably demands more effort from employees down the line. A separate analysis found that workers who do try to check their AI work before sending it on end up wasting more of their own time doing so, especially compared with employees who do not touch AI at all. Feigh wrote that workplace verification tasks are fundamentally different from the act of creating things ourselves, because drafting a pitch deck generally comes with an obvious end point while double-checking an AI-drafted pitch deck is a whole different beast. She explained that a worker generally knows when something they are creating is done or at least sufficient for the task, but when to stop verification is less obvious.

Feigh said a worker must decide what to check and how, without knowing whether an error exists, where it might be or what form it might take. The article concludes that, put together, it is no wonder AI has not revolutionized labor, because it is simply much more trouble than it is worth. The piece links to related coverage saying companies are realizing they are spending a fortune on AI just so their employees can generate error-riddled slop, and are suddenly cutting back budgets. It also links to Stanford research finding that companies are being torn apart by AI workslop, and to a study finding that AI use at work is causing brain fry, especially among high performers.

Articles.Title: AI Is Still So Riddled With Errors That It's Erasing Any Productivity Gains That Would Make It Useful in the Workplace

stories.headline_source: AI Is Still So Riddled With Errors That It's Erasing Any Productivity Gains That Would Make It Useful in the Workplace

stories.Headline: Veteran broker Allen Buchanan says curiosity trumps age in learning AI
stories.Summary:
Allen C. Buchanan, a commercial real estate broker with Lee & Associates in Orange, wrote in a column published by the Orange County Register on November 21, 2026, that he once feared he was too old to learn artificial intelligence. He recalled that a remarkable tool began filtering into everyday life at the end of 2022, and that by mid-2023 the technology was off to the races. His first reaction, he wrote, was that he was too freaking old to learn something new, even though he had created an online voice in 2009 that led to his column. He nevertheless took small steps, learning about ChatGPT prompts and the like, and nearly four years later he set out what he had learned.

Buchanan wrote that a person does not have to understand how something works to benefit from it, comparing AI to driving a car without being able to explain its engine. He said curiosity trumps age, noting that since he began brokering commercial real estate in 1984 he had seen fax machines, personal computers, email, the internet, smartphones and social media each change how business was done. He advised that the better the question, the better the answer, because explaining who you are, what you want to accomplish, the audience and the desired outcome improves results dramatically. He added that experience still matters, since AI can analyze a lease, compare buildings, research a company or suggest a negotiating strategy, but technology provides information while experience supplies judgment.

Buchanan described how his use grew from an occasional question to creating applications, developing training programs and analyzing complicated real estate transactions, while calling himself simply a curious old broker rather than a technology expert. He said imagination may be the greatest limitation, asking what about the things people never attempted because they were too complicated, time-consuming or expensive. He cautioned that AI makes mistakes, occasionally spectacular ones, and can confidently provide information that is completely wrong, so human oversight remains essential, especially when advising clients on decisions involving millions of dollars. His advice to those still sitting on the sidelines was to buy a ticket, because the journey is just beginning.

stories.Headline: AI tools leave a salaried programmer feeling empty and working harder for no extra pay
stories.Summary:
A professional programmer in her 30s, who learned to code as an adult and now earns what the author calls a decent salary, described to the author in late 2026 how working with AI has changed her job. She said the tools do many impressive things and have made some parts of her life easier, but that they also make her feel empty inside on a regular basis. She said AI has made her work harder as well, because removing the simple tasks leaves only the hard ones behind. She also said companies did not respond by giving programmers more free time or higher pay, and instead simply raised the level of productivity they expect.

She said getting code syntax correct is much easier with AI, and that code can be written much faster because reading what the AI writes is easier than typing it herself, points she considers silly to dispute. She said this has not necessarily made her own life better, but has made the lives of her company's shareholders better, since she can accomplish more for them with the tools. She said she liked typing code but that it is not a thing programmers do anymore, and that architecting a project at a higher level is interesting but can be far more mentally exhausting, without any extra pay for the drastic shift in her daily work. She said that for her these days it is easier to focus on the added burden on security, that she no longer answers her phone because of the volume of spam, and that she is upset about a cyber attack involving children in her town, which she declined to detail.

She said she has to do more mandatory phishing trainings for work, and that although she believes AI has already made her richer, the new inconveniences are easier to identify than the benefits in the moment. The author, who wrote in 2024 that if AI lifts the constraint of time people would get more crazy sock days, noted that in 2026 parents get two weeks notice to buy novelty socks for elementary children to exchange. A commenter on the post argued that AI uncovers the technical debt and security holes left behind by decades of human coding, and that AI can help fix them too. The same commenter said cyber attack and defense are not an endless arms race because defense has a fixed goal post, since software can be formally proven correct and the proof forces all bugs to be fixed, which the commenter compared to how AI recently helped prove the Riemann Hypothesis.

stories.Headline: Samsung and SK hynix values dive as AI chip rally ends
stories.Summary:
The KOSPI index fell 30 percent from early October and 45 percent from its June peak. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix saw their values dive 32.82 percent and 39.33 percent respectively. These losses occurred as the AI chip rally ended in November 2026. Investors who bought equity products like ETFs now face mounting losses. The market downturn has caused a significant shift in market capitalization rankings.

Total KOSPI market capitalization shrank from 7,449.6 trillion won in June to 3,991.4 trillion won. This represents a loss of 3,458 trillion won, or 46.4 percent of the total. Samsung Biologics rose to fifth place, while Celltrion returned to the top ten at ninth. Hyundai Motor fell to eighth place as Samsung Securities cut its target price to 380,000 won. Investor deposits shrank to 81.5669 trillion won during this period of volatility.

Citibank estimates that household stock investment losses will reach 563 trillion won in the second half. This impact is comparable to a base rate increase of 0.50 to 0.75 percentage points. The South Korean government has not yet produced clear measures to stabilize the market. This differs from Taiwan's FSC, which tightened short-selling restrictions and used a stabilization fund. Officials have stood by while the market dropped 30 percent in six weeks.

Investors who used retirement savings for stocks are now affected by the market slide. Average daily KOSPI trading volume hit a 12 year low of 239 million shares on November 19. Hyundai Motor faces pressure from a stronger won and price competition with Chinese electric vehicles. Chinese passenger EV exports to South Korea jumped 99.2 percent to 3.35991 billion dollars. Korean-made passenger EV market share fell to 48.7 percent while Chinese vehicles reached 43.5 percent.

The market previously rallied in June during a surge in AI chip investments. Samsung Electronics previously trailed SK hynix in HBM3E, with its market share falling to around 20 percent. Samsung later restored its HBM market share to the high 30 percent range in the third quarter. The government is now pushing for production tax credits for domestically built electric vehicles. They also want to strengthen R&D support for autonomous-driving AI and computing hardware.

Samsung appointed President Hwang Sang-joon to lead memory and President Choi Won-joon to lead the MX division. AI glasses launch on December 10, and a humanoid robot will debut at CES 2027. Samsung aims for HBM4E next year and HBM5 in 2028 to regain its technology lead. The articles leave open the timing of the National Assembly's tax subcommittee decisions. It remains uncertain if the foundry business will turn profitable or if shares will rebound.
