stories.Headline: AI stocks plummet as interest rate hikes and regulatory fears trigger market collapse
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence stock market experienced a severe collapse during the week ending November 21, 2026, causing widespread alarm across the financial system. Investors initially hoped the stock market debut of the AI giant Anthropic would boost the markets, but the entire sector plummeted on Friday. The tech-heavy Nasdaq suffered its worst weekly performance since March 2020 by dropping 10 percent, while the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average both entered a correction. Even Anthropic saw its shares slump more than 8 percent on Friday after an initial gain of 17 percent.

This downturn follows a September decision by the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates for the first time in over three years, making it more expensive for AI firms to borrow billions for data centers. Political shifts also contributed, as Democrats won both chambers of Congress and key governorships, including Gina Hinojosa in Texas, while promising tougher regulations on the sector. Additionally, Nvidia faced leadership turmoil this month when CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid suspicions that he had an affair with a woman spying for China. These combined factors have led to fears that a massive financial bubble is bursting, potentially mirroring the dot-com crash of 2000.

Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, stated that the market is unlikely to recover quickly and AI could remain out of favor through next year. He argued that the current trade is powered by stable companies like Meta and Apple, meaning it is not based on unrealistic expectations. However, Smith noted that the interconnected nature of the industry, where Nvidia lends money to firms like Anthropic and CoreWeave, could trigger a chain reaction if companies fail. Because AI investments helped the economy grow at an annual rate of 3.4 percent last quarter, a total unraveling could impact pensions and retirement funds.

Articles.Title: The AI boom had a really bad week — and it's raising loud alarms

stories.Headline: South Korea surpasses one trillion dollars in annual exports driven by AI chip demand
stories.Summary:
South Korea surpassed one trillion dollars in annual exports for the first time this year on Thursday, driven largely by a boom in artificial intelligence chips. This milestone makes the nation the fourth country ever to reach this threshold, following the United States and Germany in 2006 and China in 2007. The achievement occurred despite significant global trade headwinds, including higher tariffs from the administration of President Donald Trump and ongoing conflicts in the Middle East. This growth follows a previous record of 709.3 billion dollars last year, which narrowed the gap with Japan's 738.3 billion dollars. The surge was led by semiconductor exports, which rose 193.1 percent to 396.8 billion dollars between January and October, representing 42.7 percent of total exports.

This demand for memory chips used in data centers benefited major companies like Samsung Electronics Co. and SK hynix Inc. The cumulative trade surplus for the first ten months reached 294.9 billion dollars, more than triple the 2017 record of 95.2 billion dollars. Consequently, the economy is expected to grow by more than 3 percent in 2026, the first such expansion since 2021. Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan credited the workers and businesses for this success and promised continued government support for exporters. He stated that the government would help companies overcome various challenges in financing, logistics, and trade to maintain this growth. Meanwhile, Professor Lee Jae-min of Seoul National University School of Law called the event historic but warned about potential trade restrictions.

He noted that managing these risks is essential to ensure the sustainability of growth driven by semiconductors and artificial intelligence. While shipbuilding, defense, and biohealth industries grew, automakers and electronics manufacturers faced pressure from Chinese rivals and American tariffs. Experts warn that a heavy reliance on semiconductors makes the economy vulnerable to price drops or a slowdown in global AI investment. To mitigate these external shocks, the country must develop new markets and diversify its export industries beyond traditional heavy manufacturing. South Korean companies are currently reviewing their supply chains and overseas production plans to adapt to these uncertainties.

stories.Headline: Commerce Department approves sales of over 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies
stories.Summary:
The Commerce Department approved sales of over 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies as of May 2026. The Bureau of Industry and Security handled these approvals for Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices. Documents released on Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee revealed these specific sales figures. This news emerged following the resignation of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang. The release occurred amid increasing scrutiny regarding the export of chips to China.

The Bureau of Industry and Security licensed H200 sales to ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent. Approvals included sales to firms the Department of Defense designated as Chinese Military Companies. Between December and May, companies requested 3.4 million AI chip sales to China. License requests also included firms like Baidu and Tesla Shanghai. Some approvals went to Maginfra and New Matrix, which are suspected smuggling fronts.

Representative Gregory Meeks said the administration's handling of export controls put national security at risk. He stated the Bureau of Industry and Security failed to enforce rules and requires oversight. A Bureau of Industry and Security spokesperson said licensing decisions resulted from multiple agency consultations. Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo stated that approvals were subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. AMD stated it maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance with all export laws.

Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said the number of approved chips is not that many. He noted that the government approved about one out of every four requested sales. Analyst Patrick Moorhead said Beijing did not approve large scale imports, which limited sales. Hunterbrook Media alleged AMD has a China problem involving firmware for blacklisted IEIT Systems. Lawmakers are concerned that Jensen Huang's relationship with a spy jeopardized American AI dominance.

Export controls on AI chips began under the Biden administration in 2022. In December, Trump said Nvidia could ship H200s if the U.S. got 25 percent. Nvidia reported 2.4 billion dollars in quarterly revenue from H200 sales in China. Former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed. Investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China before Alice Huang left in 2025.

Jensen Huang will have a closed door interview with three committees on December 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels December 2. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also agreed to testify before the Senate banking committee. The Commerce Department issued a rule Monday to stop Chinese companies leasing computing power. The articles leave open whether the new rule will successfully close the leasing loophole.
